Do this first: put fresh batteries in your smoke alarm tonight, put one gallon of water per person on a shelf, and read the rule of threes below until you can say it from memory. Those three things cover the failures that kill people in apartments in the first hour, the first day and the first week. Everything else in this course builds on them. This chapter is the map: it teaches you how to think when you are frightened, which dangers actually kill New Yorkers, and how to write a one-page household plan. The later chapters go deep on each subject.

1. How this course works and how to read the labels

Every chapter has the same shape: a lesson written in the order you would act, a quiz of scenarios, and flashcards. The lessons use coloured boxes. Learn what they mean now, because the two green and grey ones decide how much you should trust a sentence.

BoxWhat it means for you
DEFINITIONA word or acronym explained once so the rest of the lesson reads fast.
REMEMBER THISThe one line to memorise if you memorise nothing else.
DEADLY MISTAKEThe error that actually kills people in that situation. Read these first when you are short on time.
IN NEW YORK CITYThe local rule, phone number or agency that changes the answer here.
DO THIS NOWThree to eight cheap actions for this week, cheapest first.
VERIFIEDEvery number in the lesson was checked against the named source on the date shown. Open the link on your phone if you doubt it.
NOT VERIFIEDSomething that probably matters but could not be confirmed. It always says who to ask. Do not bet your life on it until you have.

The chapters after this one, in the order most people should read them: Water (storing, finding, making it safe), Food, Shelter (staying warm and cool in place), New York City (official help, evacuation zones, shelters), Medical, Sanitation, Power, Light and Communication, Fire, Gas and Bad Air, Personal Safety and Misinformation, Growing Food, Carpentry and Repairs, Navigation and Evacuating on Foot, Documents, Money and Insurance, Children, Elders, Pets and Your Own Mind, and finally Checklists and Drills, which turns all of it into a twelve-month build-up. If you can only read three chapters this month, read this one, Water, and Fire.

2. The rule of threes: what to fix first

📘 DEFINITION

The rule of threes is a memory aid used in survival training. It says a person can survive roughly 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in harsh conditions, 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food. Each line assumes the one above it is already handled.

📊 FIGURE — The rule of threes as an order of work in an apartment
Read top to bottom: air (3 minutes) is fixed first, then shelter, water and finally food. The middle column is what each line means in a New York apartment; the right column names the chapter.

It is not a medical fact. People have lived far longer than each number and some have died sooner. Its job is to stop you wasting the first hour on the wrong problem.

For a woman in a New York apartment the rule turns into this order of work:

PriorityRule of threesWhat it means in your apartmentChapter
13 minutes: airSmoke, carbon monoxide, a gas leak, a chemical release outside. A working smoke alarm and a battery carbon monoxide detector are the first money you spend.Fire, Gas and Bad Air
23 hours: shelterYour apartment with no heat in January, or no air conditioning in a July heat wave. Body temperature, not the building, is the shelter that matters.Shelter
33 days: waterTaps in high-rises can stop when the electric pumps stop. Stored water is the cheapest life insurance you will ever buy.Water
43 weeks: foodImportant, but last. A pantry full of rice does nothing if you cannot breathe or drink.Food

Notice what is missing: weapons, bunkers, months of canned food. In a city, the killers are ordinary: smoke, heat, cold, water in a basement, and a phone that dies. Prepare for those.

3. S.T.O.P.: the four steps that replace panic

📘 DEFINITION

S.T.O.P. stands for Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. It comes from search-and-rescue and hunter-safety training for people who realise they are lost. It works for any sudden emergency because the first mistake is almost always moving before thinking.

  1. Stop. Stand still. Take three slow breaths. Do not run toward the exit, the window or the elevator yet. The body wants to move; the job is to buy ten seconds.
  2. Think. What just happened? What is the actual danger: smoke, water, cold, a person? What is the one thing that would kill me in the next three minutes?
  3. Observe. Look, listen, smell. Is the alarm in my apartment or the hallway? Is the door warm? Is water coming under it? Do I have a phone, a light, shoes? Who else is here?
  4. Plan. Pick the next single action, do it, then S.T.O.P. again. Small loops, not one big decision.

Example: the lights go out at 9 p.m. in August and the whole street is dark. Stop: stay seated. Think: this is probably a grid failure, not a fire; the dangers are heat, no water pressure upstairs, an elevator, and a phone at 30 percent. Observe: the hallway is dark; neighbours are opening doors; the radio in the kit works. Plan: switch the phone to low-power mode, fill the bathtub and every bottle while the pressure lasts, put on shoes, put the flashlight in your pocket, then text the out-of-area contact. Not in that order because it is elegant, but because water pressure is the thing that goes away first.

4. Why panic kills and routine saves

People rarely die because they did not know what to do. They die because under stress they did the familiar thing: took the elevator, went back for the laptop, drove into the water, opened the door to see where the smoke was coming from. Routine is the cure. What you have physically practised is what your hands will do at 3 a.m.

  • The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) says you may have as little as one or two minutes to get out once a smoke alarm sounds, and tells households to practise the escape twice a year, once at night.
  • The National Weather Service (NWS) says 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult down and 12 inches can carry away most cars. Its rule is four words: Turn Around, Don't Drown.
  • In a disaster, phone lines are jammed but a text message needs far less capacity and may be delivered when a call cannot; texts also queue and send when the network frees up. Long-distance texts often get through when local calls do not.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Doing the normal thing in an abnormal moment. The elevator during a fire or a flickering blackout. Going back into the apartment for a bag. Wading through the flooded street because it is the way you always walk. Opening the apartment door without feeling it first.

Every one of these is a decision made in under a second by habit. The only fix is a different habit, built by doing the drill in Section 3 with your body, not your eyes.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Air, then warmth, then water, then food. Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Call if you can, text if you can't.

5. What to buy first on a small budget

The Ready.gov basic kit is the list below. You do not need to buy it in one weekend. Buy in this order, one line per paycheck, and you will be safer than most of the city within a month. Prices change, so none are printed here; every item on the first four lines can be found at a hardware store or supermarket.

  1. Batteries for the smoke alarm you already have, plus a battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) detector if you do not have one. This is the 3-minute line.
  2. Water: at least 1 gallon per person per day. Start with 3 gallons; the goal in the Water chapter is a two-week supply, 14 gallons per person, built a jug at a time.
  3. A flashlight and a headlamp with spare batteries, kept by the bed. Not candles.
  4. A whistle on your keys. It carries farther than your voice and costs almost nothing.
  5. Non-perishable food for several days that needs no cooking, plus a manual can opener.
  6. A phone power bank, charged every Sunday.
  7. A battery or hand-crank radio that receives NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) weather broadcasts, for when the phone network fails.
  8. First-aid kit, dust masks, plastic sheeting and duct tape, moist towelettes, garbage bags, a wrench or pliers for the utilities, a paper map of the city.
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Two numbers, one text. 911 is for a life-threatening emergency: fire, someone not breathing, a gas smell, a crime in progress. 311 is everything else the city does: no heat, a downed tree, where the cooling centres are. From outside the city 311 is 212-639-9675 (not toll free); by text it is 311-692; TTY 212-504-4115.

Text-to-911 has worked in New York City since June 2020. The rule is \"call if you can, text if you can't\": a text is for when speaking would put you in danger or you cannot hear.

Notify NYC is the city's official alert service. Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 to enrol; text your ZIP code to 692-692 for alerts about your own neighbourhood; or use the app. It is free and it is the first thing to set up tonight.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and then your ZIP code to 692-692. Save 311 and 212-639-9675 in your phone.
  • Press the test button on your smoke alarm. If it does not sound, replace the battery today; if there is no alarm, tell the landlord in writing and call 311.
  • Put a flashlight and your shoes by the bed. Tie a whistle to your keys.
  • Buy three gallons of water and put them in a closet. Write the date on them.
  • Say the rule of threes and S.T.O.P. out loud twice, then teach them to one other person.
  • Read the Fire chapter next, then Water.

Do this first: find out today whether you live in a hurricane evacuation zone and whether any part of your apartment is below street level. Those two facts decide which of the hazards below can kill you at home and which you will only watch on the news. New York City does not have earthquakes or wildfires to speak of. It has water, heat, cold, darkness, fire and bad air, and each one kills in a particular, predictable way. This lesson is the list of those ways and the first move for each. Later chapters hold the detail.

1. The map in one table

📊 FIGURE — What kills New Yorkers in each hazard and the first move for each
One row per hazard. The middle column is the way that hazard actually kills people in this city; the right column (highlighted) is the single first move the lesson gives for it.
HazardWhat actually kills people hereYour first move
Hurricane and storm surgeDrowning in coastal zones that did not evacuate; falling treesKnow your zone; leave when your zone is ordered out, before the wind
Flash flood (inland rain)Drowning in basement apartments; walking or driving into waterMove up a floor before water arrives; never enter moving water
Extreme heatHeat worsening heart and lung disease in apartments; heat strokeCool room or cooling centre; check on neighbours; 911 for confusion
BlackoutCarbon monoxide from generators; candle fires; falls in the dark; heat or cold with no pumps or fansFlashlight, fill water, unplug, stay out of elevators
Winter storm and coldHypothermia in unheated rooms; carbon monoxide from improvised heating; falls on iceLayers and a warm core; call 311 for no heat; Code Blue for anyone outside
PandemicInfection, plus the collapse of routine care and suppliesTwo weeks of essentials at home; medications; masks
Chemical, radiological, nuclearBreathing the release; being outside when fallout arrivesGet inside, seal the room, stay tuned
Fire and gasSmoke, not flame; explosion after a leakFeel the door; close doors; leave and call from outside

2. Hurricanes and storm surge

📘 DEFINITION

Storm surge is sea water pushed onto land by a storm's wind and low pressure, on top of the normal tide. It arrives fast, it is the deadliest part of a hurricane, and it is why the city evacuates by zone rather than by wind speed.

The Atlantic hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November; the National Hurricane Center puts the statistical peak at 10 September, with most activity from mid-August to mid-October. Hurricane Sandy, October 2012, killed 147 people in all and 48 in New York State, most by storm surge and some by falling trees. At the Battery in Lower Manhattan a storm surge of about 9 feet landed on a high tide and produced a record water level.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The city has six hurricane evacuation zones. Zone 1 is the highest risk and is evacuated first; Zone 6 is the lowest. Living outside all six zones means surge is not your problem, though rain and wind still are.

Find your zone before the season, not during it: maps.nyc.gov/hurricane, nyc.gov/knowyourzone or call 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115). Evacuation centres open only when an order is issued, they accept pets, and the finder shows which ones are open. Any address you write down must be confirmed via 311 or the official finder at the time, because centres change with each emergency.

3. Flash floods and basement apartments

Rain can kill in this city far from any coast. On 1 and 2 September 2021 the remains of Hurricane Ida dropped rain at 3.5 inches per hour, about double the 1.75 inches per hour the sewers were designed for. 14 people died in New York City; 10 of them drowned in basement apartments, most of them unregulated. Water entered faster than doors could be opened against it.

  • If you live in a basement or ground floor that has flooded before, know your exits and be ready to move to a higher floor before the water arrives, not when it is at the door. That is NYC Emergency Management's wording.
  • Sign up for the Notify NYC basement alert group, which sends targeted warnings for life-threatening rain.
  • 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock you off your feet; 12 inches moves most cars. Over half of flood drownings are people who drove into water.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting in a basement to see if it gets worse. Water pressure against a door grows with every inch; a door that opens inward can become impossible to open in under a minute, and the electricity in the room may still be live.

The rule is simple and unpopular: a flash flood warning for your area means you sleep upstairs or at a friend's tonight. Belongings can be replaced.

4. Extreme heat, the quiet killer

Heat kills more New Yorkers than any other weather. The NYC Health Department estimates about 500 heat-related deaths a year; for 2014 to 2023 the annual average of heat-exacerbated deaths from May to September was 489. Most are not dramatic collapses in the street. They are people with heart or lung disease whose bodies could not cope in a hot apartment. Deaths have risen mainly because there are more \"non-extreme\" hot days of 82°F and above, not just the 95°F extremes.

NWS alert for the New York areaTrigger
Heat AdvisoryHeat index 95–99°F for at least two days in a row, or 100–104°F for any period
Extreme Heat Warning (called Excessive Heat Warning before March 2025)Heat index at least 105°F for at least two consecutive hours

Warning signs: heat exhaustion is heavy sweating, weakness, nausea and cool clammy skin; move to a cool place, loosen clothing, sip water. Heat stroke is confusion, hot skin, a temperature of 103°F or above, and sometimes no sweating at all: call 911 and cool the person at once; do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious. Cooling centres open during heat emergencies: finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or 311.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

NYC Health's heat reports have said that most heat-stress deaths happen in homes without working air conditioning, and that the risk is highest for older adults living alone. The exact wording and figures were not re-read today: confirm before you rely on this at the NYC Health heat mortality report (a816-dohbesp.nyc.gov, Heat Mortality Report) or by calling 311 and asking about the Home Energy Assistance Program cooling benefit.

5. Blackouts

On 14 August 2003, a few minutes after 4 p.m., a cascading grid failure cut power to an area of about 50 million people from New York to Ontario. In New York City the subway stopped with up to 400,000 people in the cars, all 11,600 traffic signals went dark, and full power did not return to the city until 16 August. High-rise buildings lost water because their pumps are electric. Most people walked home.

  • Use flashlights, not candles. Turn off or unplug large appliances and electronics so the surge when power returns does not damage them.
  • Elevators: if you are stuck, press the alarm or help button and wait. Never pry the doors or climb out; the car can restart without warning when power returns. If the lights are flickering, take the stairs.
  • Food: keep the doors shut; a fridge stays safe about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full freezer about 24 hours. Throw out perishables that have been above 40°F for more than 2 hours.
  • Generators run outdoors only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent. In an apartment that almost always means: no generator at all.
  • Report it. Con Edison assumes nothing: call 1-800-752-6633 (1-800-75-CONED), report online at coned.com, or text REG to 688-243 once to get outage updates on your phone.

6. Winter storms and cold

Cold kills indoors as well as out. Your rights: during Heat Season, 1 October to 31 May, building owners must keep apartments at 68°F when it is below 55°F outside, and hot water at a constant minimum of 120°F all year. Tell the super or owner at once, and call 311 if it is not fixed quickly. Code Blue is in effect when the temperature including wind chill is at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m.: shelters and drop-in centres take walk-ins, and if you see someone outside who looks homeless and in need, call 311 for an outreach team. Hypothermia looks like shivering, confusion, slurred speech and drowsiness; move the person to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm the chest, neck, head and groin first, and call 911.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Public health agencies warn never to heat a room with a gas oven, a stove burner or a charcoal grill because of carbon monoxide, and never to run a car in an attached garage. The exact source text was not re-read today: confirm before you rely on this in the Fire, Gas and Bad Air chapter, on the CDC carbon monoxide page, or by calling 311. What is verified: a battery carbon monoxide detector in the apartment.

7. Pandemics, and chemical, radiological or nuclear events

A pandemic is the one hazard that lasts months rather than days, and the plan for it is boring: two weeks of the things you cannot go out for, especially prescription medication, and the ability to stay home while sick. The two-week water goal in the Water chapter (14 gallons per person) is sized for exactly this. The Fire chapter covers N95 masks and making one clean room.

For a chemical release Ready.gov says: go inside, close and lock windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning, go to an interior room, and seal gaps with plastic sheeting and duct tape, which is why they are in the kit. For a nuclear event: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. A brick or concrete building, a basement, or the middle floors of a large building are best; you may have 10 minutes or more before fallout arrives, and you stay in for at least 24 hours unless told otherwise. In a city of high-rises, this is a hazard where staying put is usually the right answer.

8. Fire and gas

NFPA says you may have as little as one or two minutes from the alarm to get out. Smoke kills, not flame. The fire safety notice on your apartment door says whether your building is fireproof (usually stay in your apartment with the door shut if the fire is elsewhere) or non-fireproof (usually leave at once). If you smell gas: leave, do not touch light switches or phones inside, and call from outside. Call 911, then the gas company printed on your bill: Con Edison 1-800-752-6633, or National Grid 718-643-4050 for Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island. The Fire, Gas and Bad Air chapter holds the full drill.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Water kills in basements and in Zone 1. Heat kills in hot apartments. Blackouts kill through carbon monoxide, candles and elevators. Fire kills with smoke. None of these needs a bunker; all of them need a plan you have practised.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week:

  • Look up your evacuation zone at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane and write the number on the plan in Section 3.
  • If any room is below street level, choose tonight where you would sleep on a flash-flood warning, and join the Notify NYC basement alert group.
  • Find your nearest cooling centre at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters and write the address with the words \"confirm via 311 at the time\".
  • Save Con Edison 1-800-752-6633 and your gas company's number in your phone; text REG to 688-243.
  • Put a battery carbon monoxide detector on the shopping list if you do not have one.
  • Check the thermometer in January: below 68°F inside on a cold day is a 311 call, not something to endure.

Do this first: tonight, on one sheet of paper, write five things: the name and number of one person outside the New York area, two meeting places, the way out of your apartment in the dark, and who you will check on. That sheet is your household emergency plan. It takes twenty minutes and it is the single item in this course most likely to be missing when it is needed, because most people only ever keep it in their head or in a phone that has died. Both Ready.gov and NYC Emergency Management give the same three steps: make a plan, gather supplies, stay informed. This lesson is step one.

1. The out-of-area contact

When something happens in the city, local cell towers jam. Everyone calls everyone, nobody connects, and families lose hours. The fix is one person, far away, that every member of your household texts. Long-distance texts and calls often get through when local ones do not, and a text needs far less network capacity than a call and will queue and send itself when the network frees up. Texting also keeps lines open for emergency workers.

  • Pick someone outside the New York area, ideally in another state, who is usually reachable and calm. Ask them. Tell them their job: collect \"I'm OK, I'm at ___\" messages and relay them.
  • Everyone in your household, and the two or three people who would worry about you, gets the same name and number, on paper.
  • Agree the first text in advance so it is fast: your name, \"OK\" or \"HURT\", where you are, where you are going. Fifteen words.
  • Write the number down. If your phone dies, your contact list dies with it.

2. Meeting points, near and far

Ready.gov says to pick places in your neighbourhood and outside it, in case you cannot get home, and to consider a third outside the city. For a New Yorker, each one has a local twist.

Meeting placeUsed whenNew York rule
Right outside the buildingFire, gas leak, building evacuationA fixed spot across the street, not the front door, so firefighters have the door. Say which corner.
Outside the neighbourhoodYou cannot get home: flood, police cordon, no power in the areaA library, community centre or place of worship you can walk to. Check it is not in a lower-numbered hurricane zone than your home.
Outside the cityEvacuation, long blackout, a hazard that empties the boroughA relative or friend reachable without the subway if needed. Write the address and how you would get there on foot or by bus.

Assume the subway is not running. In 2003 it stopped mid-tunnel and stayed down for hours; in a hurricane the MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority) shuts it before the storm arrives. The Navigation chapter covers walking routes; for now, write meeting places you could reach on foot.

3. The two-minute drill

NFPA gives you one or two minutes from the alarm and asks for two practices a year, one at night. Do it like this, once with the lights on and once in the dark:

📊 FIGURE — The two-minute drill from bed to door, and what a hot door changes
Follow the arrows from the bed to the door. Feeling the door decides the branch: cool means stairs (never the elevator); hot or smoky means stay, seal, go to the window and call 911.
  1. Lie on the bed. Start a timer. Get up, put your feet in the shoes by the bed, take the flashlight and keys, and get to your apartment door.
  2. Feel the door and the knob with the back of your hand. Say \"cool\" or \"hot\" out loud.
  3. If cool: open it a crack, look and smell, go to the stairs, counting doors as you pass them. Close every door behind you. Never the elevator.
  4. If hot, or the hallway is full of smoke: shut the door, stuff a towel at the bottom, go to the window, and call 911 with your apartment number. Know the second way out: a fire escape, a second stair, a window onto a roof.
  5. Stop the timer at the street or at the window. Under two minutes is the goal.

Count the doors between your apartment and the stairwell tonight and write the number on the plan. In smoke you will not see the exit sign; you will feel doors.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

A plan that lives only in your phone. After the 2003 blackout most people walked home because nothing else worked; phones at 5 percent battery and jammed networks are the normal condition of a disaster, not the exception.

If the out-of-area number, the meeting places and the medication list exist only on a screen, they do not exist. Paper, in three places, is the rule.

4. Stay kit and go bag: two different jobs

📘 DEFINITION

A stay kit (Ready.gov calls it the basic emergency supply kit) is what keeps you alive at home for several days when the water, power or shops stop: water at one gallon per person per day, food that needs no cooking, light, radio, first aid, sanitation. It is heavy and it lives in a closet.

A go bag is what you carry out of the door in a hurry: a sturdy backpack, one per person, with water, ID, medications, chargers, copies of documents and anything a child or pet needs. NYC Emergency Management says everyone in the household should have one.

Stay kit (home)Go bag (leaving)
Water1 gallon per person per day, several days minimum, 14 gallons per person the goalWhat you can carry: two bottles
FoodSeveral days of non-perishable food and a manual can openerA day of bars or ready food
Light and newsFlashlight, batteries, battery or hand-crank radio with NOAA weather bandHeadlamp, power bank, the radio if small
HealthFirst-aid kit, dust masks, moist towelettes, garbage bagsMedications with the prescription labels, glasses, a copy of the medical list
ToolsWrench or pliers for utilities, plastic sheeting, duct tape, whistle, paper mapKeys, cash, ID, insurance and lease copies in a zip bag, phone charger
New York extrasA filled bathtub the moment pressure looks at risk; a battery CO detectorComfortable walking shoes if you live high up and the elevators are out; the paper plan

The go bag lives where you would grab it in the dark: by the apartment door or under the bed. The full lists are in the Checklists and Drills chapter; the point today is that the two kits answer two different questions, \"can I stay?\" and \"can I leave?\", and you need both.

5. Who checks on whom

NYC Emergency Management's cold and heat warnings say the same thing every year: check on family, friends and neighbours who may need help, especially older adults and people with disabilities. Most heat deaths and many cold deaths are people alone in an apartment. Make it specific:

  • Write two names: one neighbour in the building you will knock on in a heat wave, blackout or storm, and one person who will knock on you. Swap phone numbers and, if you trust them, a spare key.
  • Anyone who depends on electricity for medical equipment, a walker or an elevator goes at the top of the list.
  • Someone outside in the cold who looks homeless and in need: call 311 and an outreach team is sent. Someone confused and hot to the touch in a heat wave: 911.

6. Write it down and keep it in three places

Ready.gov has a fill-in form at ready.gov/plan. New York City has its own workbook, Ready New York: My Emergency Plan, in 13 languages and audio, at nyc.gov/readyny, or call 311 (TTY 212-504-4115) and ask for a paper copy. Use either, or a sheet of paper, but include all of this:

  1. Out-of-area contact: name, mobile, a second number, email.
  2. Meeting places: outside the building, outside the neighbourhood, outside the city, with how to get to each on foot.
  3. Your evacuation zone number, and the sentence \"check the finder or 311 for open centres\".
  4. Doors to the stairwell, second way out, where the go bag is.
  5. Medications, allergies, doctor, insurance policy numbers, landlord and super's numbers, Con Edison 1-800-752-6633, your gas company, 311, Notify NYC.
  6. Who you check on, who checks on you.

Then make three copies: one on the fridge or inside a kitchen cabinet door, one in the go bag, one folded in your wallet. Send a photo to the out-of-area contact so a fourth copy is outside the city. Review it twice a year on the same nights you run the fire drill.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Sign up for Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, then your ZIP code to 692-692, or the app). It is how the city tells you an evacuation order, a Code Blue or a flash-flood warning exists. If you live in a basement, also join its basement alert group.

Ask the landlord which building the fire safety notice on your door describes, whether the building has a backup generator for water pumps and elevators, and where the stairwell doors are. If there is no notice on your door, the owner is required to post one; request it in writing and call 311 if nothing happens.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

Tonight and this week:

  • Text one person outside New York and ask them to be your contact. Write their number on paper.
  • Walk to the stairwell and count the doors. Write the number down. Put shoes and a flashlight by the bed.
  • Choose the three meeting places and write them with the corner or address.
  • Fill in ready.gov/plan or the Ready New York workbook; print or copy it three times.
  • Put ID copies, medications and a charger in one backpack by the door.
  • Knock on one neighbour and agree to check on each other in the next storm or heat wave.
  • Put two dates in your calendar, six months apart, labelled \"fire drill and plan review\".

Buy water this week, before you need it: two cases of bottled water or four one-gallon jugs is a start, and fourteen gallons is the goal for one person. Water is the one supply you cannot improvise on the day the taps stop. In a blackout the electric pumps that lift water to the upper floors of New York apartment buildings stop within seconds, a water-main break can shut a whole block off with no warning, and a boil-water notice can arrive when the stove has no gas. Stores sell out of bottled water in hours. The person who stored water in advance drinks; the person who did not stands in a line. This lesson tells you how much to store, what to store it in, where it fits in a small apartment, and how to keep it drinkable.

\n\n

1. How much: the numbers

\n

Ready.gov (the federal preparedness site run by FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency) and the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) agree on the rule. Store at least one gallon of water per person per day. About half of that is for drinking and half for cooking, washing hands and brushing teeth. A three-day supply is the bare minimum; a two-week supply is the goal, because water-main repairs and long blackouts run longer than three days.

📊 FIGURE — Gallons to store for 3 days and 14 days, by household size
Each household has two bars: the grey bar is the three-day minimum, the highlighted bar the fourteen-day goal, with the weight of the goal supply beside it. Everything scales from one gallon per person per day.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
Household3 days (minimum)14 days (goal)Weight of the 14-day supply
1 adult3 gallons14 gallonsabout 117 lb (water weighs 8.34 lb per gallon)
1 adult + 1 cat or small dog4 gallons21 gallonsabout 175 lb
2 adults6 gallons28 gallonsabout 234 lb
2 adults + 1 child9 gallons42 gallonsabout 350 lb
\n

Ready.gov adds that a normally active person drinks about three-quarters of a gallon of fluid a day, that needs can double in very hot weather, and that children, nursing mothers and sick people need more. Plan for the hot week: New York summers put apartments above 90 °F when the air conditioning has no power, and a person with fever or diarrhoea loses water fast. If you take a medicine that must be swallowed with water, or if you have a condition such as kidney disease or diabetes, count on the high end.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Potable water means water that is safe to drink. Non-potable water can still flush a toilet, wash floors or cool the body, but must not go in your mouth. Keeping the two separate in your head, and in labelled containers, is the whole art of water in an emergency.

\n\n

2. What to buy: the cheapest safe options

\n

Store-bought bottled water is the simplest choice for an apartment: it is sealed, it is already safe, and it needs no cleaning. Ready.gov says to keep it in its original container and to observe the expiration date printed on the case. Prices in the city vary, so compare the cost per gallon on the shelf label. Options in rough order of cost per gallon:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
ContainerHoldsGood forWatch out for
Case of 24 half-litre (16.9 fl oz) bottlesabout 3.2 gallonsGrab-and-go, sharing, stacking under a bed; five cases is a 14-day supply for one personThin plastic; do not stack more than a few cases high; keep away from heat and sun
Store-bought 1-gallon jugs1 gallonCooking, washing; cheap per gallonThe thin jugs sometimes split or leak after a year; check the case for damp every month
Food-grade 5-gallon or 7-gallon jerry can5–7 gallonsBulk storage you fill yourself from the tapWeighs 40–60 lb full; keep it on the floor, not on a shelf
Bathtub liner bag (a large food-grade bag that fits the tub)up to the size of the tubFilling fast when a storm or blackout is announcedOnly works while the taps still run; buy it before the emergency, not during
\n

If you fill your own containers, Ready.gov gives exact steps. Use food-grade water storage containers (look for that phrase on the label). Before filling, wash the container with dishwashing soap, rinse, then sanitize it with a solution of one teaspoon of unscented liquid household chlorine bleach in one quart of water, swirl it so the solution touches every surface, wait, then rinse thoroughly with clean water. Fill from the tap, cap tightly, and write the date on the container.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Ready.gov and FEMA guidance that I have seen in the past says not to reuse milk or fruit-juice jugs for water because milk protein and fruit sugar cannot be washed out and feed bacteria. I could not confirm that page today. Confirm before you rely on this at ready.gov/water; until then, buy purpose-made containers or sealed bottled water.

Some guides say a thin store jug lasts about a year before it weakens. That is the guide writer’s experience, not a tested figure; confirm by checking your own jugs for damp every month.

\n\n

3. Where it fits in a small apartment

\n

Fourteen gallons sounds like a lot. In cases and jugs it is about the size of two carry-on suitcases. Think in flat, low, dark places: water is heavy and does not belong on a high shelf that can fall, and heat and sunlight age plastic. Ready.gov says to store water in a cool, dark place.

\n
    \n
  • Under the bed. A standard bed hides three to four cases of bottles. Slide them in on a piece of cardboard so you can pull them out.
    • \n
  • Closet floor. Two 5-gallon cans on the floor under the hanging clothes. Nothing above them that can fall.
    • \n
  • Behind the sofa or under a desk. A row of gallon jugs against the wall is invisible once the sofa is pushed back.
    • \n
  • Kitchen cabinet under the sink? No. That is where cleaning chemicals live, and a leak from the drain pipe lands on your water. Keep water away from bleach, gasoline, paint, pesticides and anything that smells: the plastic can absorb odours and fumes.
    • \n
  • Not the fire escape, not the hallway. Storing anything on a fire escape or in a public hallway is a fire-code problem and your neighbours’ escape route. It will also freeze in winter and split.
    • \n
  • Not the radiator side of the room. Steam radiators cook the plastic every winter.
    • \n
\n

Label every container with the date you bought or filled it, and a big “DRINK” or “WASH ONLY” in marker. At 3 a.m. in a blackout you should not have to remember which jug is which.

\n\n

4. Rotation: keep it fresh

\n

Ready.gov’s rule: water you bottled yourself should be replaced every six months; store-bought bottled water is fine until the printed date. The easy way to rotate is to drink from the oldest case in normal life and replace it on the next shopping trip, so the supply is never older than a few months. Put a reminder in your phone for the first day of April and the first day of October: pour the old self-filled containers into plants or the bathtub, wash and sanitize them, refill and re-date them. Two rules of thumb:

\n
    \n
  • Sealed bottled water that has passed its printed date is not poisonous; the date is a quality mark. In an emergency, drink it. Ready.gov simply says observe the date, so replace it in normal times.
    • \n
  • Water you filled yourself that smells or looks cloudy is not for drinking until you treat it (lesson 3), but it still flushes a toilet.
    • \n
\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

One gallon per person per day. Three days is the floor, fourteen days is the goal. Self-filled containers every six months; bottled water until its printed date. Cool, dark, low, and away from chemicals.

\n\n

5. The people and animals who need more

\n\n\n\n\n\n
WhoWhy they need moreWhat to do
Someone with fever, vomiting or diarrhoeaReady.gov lists sick people as needing more; they lose fluid fastAdd at least half a gallon a day per sick person; keep oral rehydration packets with the water
Nursing mothers and childrenNamed by Ready.gov as needing more than the base gallonPlan 1.5 gallons a day for a nursing mother; count a child as a full person
Anyone in a hot apartmentReady.gov: needs can double in very hot temperaturesIn a summer blackout, budget two gallons a day and drink before you feel thirsty
Older neighbours, people with disabilitiesMay not be able to carry water up the stairs when the elevator stopsStore an extra case for the neighbour you would check on; it is the cheapest life you will ever save
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Several preparedness guides say to plan one quart to one gallon per day per pet, depending on size. I could not find that figure on a federal page today. Confirm before you rely on this with your vet or the pet-food label; until then, add a gallon a day for a dog and a quart for a cat and you will have a margin.

\n\n

6. Why this matters in a New York apartment

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

In the blackout of 14 August 2003, high-rise apartments across the city lost water because the electric pumps that fill the rooftop tanks stopped. A public-health study of that blackout (published by the National Institutes of Health) records that residents of taller buildings were without water. For a long time the city required buildings taller than six stories to keep a rooftop tank; that tank is filled by an electric pump, and gravity feeds the apartments from the tank. When power fails, the tank empties floor by floor and is not refilled.

Sign up for Notify NYC so the city’s water-main and boil-water alerts reach your phone: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts, or use the app or a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov.

If you live in NYCHA (New York City Housing Authority) housing or any building with a super, find out today who controls the building’s water pump and rooftop tank and whether the building has a generator for it. In a small walk-up, ask whether the building has a single shared hot-water tank in the basement and where its shut-off is. You will use this in lesson 2.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting until the emergency to buy water. When a hurricane watch or a heat emergency is announced, bottled water disappears from Manhattan and Brooklyn shelves the same afternoon, and delivery apps stop taking orders. In a blackout, stores are shut, the elevator is off and you cannot carry 117 lb of water up ten flights. The supply has to be in the apartment before the day it is needed.

Storing water next to chemicals or in the sun. Plastic breathes. Water that has sat beside gasoline, pesticide or drain cleaner can pick up fumes that no boiling removes. A case left on a sunny windowsill for a summer is the case you should not drink.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Buy two cases of bottled water or four gallon jugs on the next grocery trip and slide them under the bed. That is your three-day floor.
  • Put two phone reminders, 1 April and 1 October, titled “rotate water”.
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and your ZIP code to 692-692.
  • Ask the super: does the building rely on a rooftop tank and pump, is there a generator, where is the shared hot-water tank?
  • Add one case a week until you reach fourteen gallons; then one extra case for the neighbour you would check on.
  • Buy one bathtub liner bag and keep it in the bathroom cabinet.
  • Write “DRINK” and the date on every container with a marker.
\n
✅ VERIFIED

Ready.gov (FEMA), “Water”: one gallon per person per day; two-week goal; three-quarters of a gallon of fluid for a normally active person; needs can double in very hot temperatures; children, nursing mothers and sick people need more; food-grade containers; clean with dish soap then sanitize with one teaspoon of unscented bleach per quart of water; replace self-bottled water every six months; observe expiration date on commercial bottled water; cool, dark place. https://www.ready.gov/water, checked 26 Sep 2026.

CDC, “How to Create and Store an Emergency Water Supply”: one gallon per person per day, two-week supply. https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/how-to-create-and-store-an-emergency-water-supply.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.

National Institutes of Health / PMC, “Health Impact in New York City During the Northeastern Blackout of 2003”: high-rise residents lost water when electric pumps stopped. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3072860/, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Wikipedia, “Rooftop water tower” (background only): New York City long required buildings taller than six stories to have a rooftop tank filled by pump. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rooftop_water_tower, checked 26 Sep 2026.

NYC Emergency Management, Notify NYC: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692; https://a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov (from FACTS.md, verified 26 Sep 2026). Weight of water, 8.34 lb per gallon, and the case arithmetic (24 × 16.9 fl oz = 3.17 gallons) are plain calculation, not a safety threshold.
