The moment the power fails or a water-main break is announced, fill the bathtub, every pot and every clean container before the taps go dry. Do it first, before you look for a flashlight or check the news. On an upper floor of a New York building the water in the pipes above you is all you will get once the electric pump stops, and it runs out in minutes, not hours. After that you are living on what you stored (lesson 1) and on the hidden water already inside the building. This lesson lists that hidden water in the order to use it, the water you must never drink no matter how thirsty you are, and the New York rules that cover hydrants, main breaks and boil-water notices.

\n\n

1. The first ten minutes: why the taps die and what to fill

\n

New York water reaches street level under pressure from the city’s reservoirs, without pumps. Above roughly the sixth floor that pressure is not enough, so buildings use an electric pump that lifts water to a rooftop tank, and gravity feeds the apartments from the tank. When power fails, the pump stops. The tank keeps feeding the taps until it is empty; the higher the floor, the sooner the tap runs dry. In the blackout of 14 August 2003 this is exactly what happened across the city’s high-rises. So the order of work is:

📊 FIGURE — Why high-rise taps stop in a blackout and what to fill first
Left: the electric pump lifts water to the roof tank; when power fails the tank drains and the top floors run dry first. Right: the four fill steps in the order the lesson gives them.
\n
    \n
  1. Plug the bathtub and open the cold tap. If you own a bathtub liner bag, unroll it into the tub first and fill it: that water stays clean enough to drink. Water in a bare tub is for flushing, washing and, if treated, drinking.
    2. \n
  2. Fill every pot, pitcher, bottle and clean bucket with cold water and cover them.
    3. \n
  3. Fill the kitchen sink and the bathroom basin last; they leak slowly and this water is for washing.
    4. \n
  4. Then go back to the rest of the blackout plan: flashlight, stove off, one lamp on.
    5. \n
\n

In a walk-up of six floors or fewer the street pressure may keep the taps running through a blackout. Fill anyway: a main break, a burst pipe in the building or a boil-water notice can follow the same day.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Water-main break: a city pipe under the street cracks, water floods the street, and nearby buildings lose pressure or get brown, gritty water while the NYC DEP (Department of Environmental Protection) repairs it. Boil-water notice: an official order, from the DEP or the Health Department, that tap water in an area may hold germs and must be boiled before drinking until the notice is lifted. Both arrive through Notify NYC, 311, the DEP website and the news.

\n\n

2. Hidden water already in the building

\n

The EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) lists the safe alternative sources: bottled water first; then ice cubes melted in a clean container; then the hot-water tank; then water drained from the pipes. Use them in this order:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SourceHow to get itTreat before drinking?Apartment reality
Bottled water you storedOpen a bottleNoThis is why lesson 1 exists
Ice in the freezerMelt in a clean potNo, if the ice was made from tap water before the emergencyKeep the freezer full of ice trays or bagged ice: it is water, and it keeps food cold longer
Water in the pipesOpen the highest tap in the apartment to let air in, then drain from the lowest tap (usually the bathtub or a kitchen tap on the lowest floor) into a clean containerYes if a boil-water notice or main break is the cause; otherwise it is the same water you drank yesterdayA single-floor apartment holds only a few quarts in its pipes; the building’s risers hold more but are not yours to open
Hot-water tankTurn off the electricity or gas to the heater, close the cold inlet, open a hot tap somewhere to let air in, then open the drain valve at the bottom of the tank into a clean container; pour through a clean cloth to catch sedimentTreat it (lesson 3) unless you are sure the supply was clean when it filledMost New York apartments have no tank of their own: the building has one shared tank or boiler in the basement controlled by the super. Ask now who can drain it and how it will be shared
Toilet tank (the cistern behind the seat, never the bowl)Lift the lid and dip a clean cupYes, alwaysBest use is flushing; see the note below before drinking
RainSet a clean bowl, bucket or opened tub liner where rain falls straight in from the sky, not off a roof, awning or air-conditionerYes, always: CDC says rainwater is not necessarily safe and should be filtered and disinfectedFire escapes and window ledges catch soot and pigeon droppings; a wide clean bowl on a balcony in the open works, a gutter does not
\n
🦺 SAFETY

Draining a water heater: switch off its electricity at the breaker, or turn its gas valve to OFF, before you open the drain. An electric element that heats an empty tank burns out; a gas burner under an empty tank is a fire. Do not turn the heater back on until the tank is full again. The water may be hotter than 120 °F; let it cool or drain it slowly into a metal pot.

Do not open the building’s risers, valves or roof-tank fittings yourself. That is the super’s job and, in NYCHA buildings, the housing authority’s. Opening the wrong valve can flood the apartments below you.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The EPA page lists toilet flush tanks among the sources not to use. Several extension-service guides say tank water (never bowl water) can be disinfected and drunk if no blue cleaning tablet or hanging cleaner has ever been used in that tank. I could not confirm the second statement on a federal page today. Confirm before you rely on this by reading the EPA page yourself; treat toilet-tank water as flushing water, and drink it only as the last option after boiling or bleach, and never if any cleaner has been in the tank.

\n\n

3. Water you must never drink

\n

Thirst makes people stupid. Every one of the sources below has been drunk by someone in an emergency, and each one can kill.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SourceWhy notCan lesson 3 fix it?
Flood water in a street, basement or subway entranceCDC: flood water may contain sewage and chemicals; it also carries fuel, oil, rat urine and whatever was in the shops it flowed through. Do not drink it and do not bathe in itNo. Boiling and bleach kill germs but do nothing for chemicals, fuel or heavy metals (EPA)
The East River, the Hudson, the harbourThe East River is a salt-water tidal strait, not a river; salt water dehydrates you. Both waterways receive combined sewer overflows (CSOs), which is raw sewage released when it rains hardOnly distillation removes salt (EPA). Boiling salt water makes it saltier
Swimming pools and spasEPA lists them as sources not to use: pool chemicals and body wasteNo
Radiators, boilers, waterbedsEPA lists them as sources not to use: rust, anti-corrosion chemicals, algaecideNo
Water with a chemical smell, an oily sheen or a rainbow filmCDC: water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals is not made safe by boiling or disinfection; use bottled waterNo
Anything in a container that once held chemicalsThe residue leaches into the waterNo
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Drinking flood water or river water because it “looks clean” or because you boiled it. During Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021, water rose in basements and streets across Queens and Brooklyn at 3.5 inches of rain an hour. That water was sewage and fuel mixed with rain. Boiling kills germs; it concentrates chemicals. In an apartment emergency, the choice is never “flood water or nothing”: it is the stored water, the ice, the pipes, the building tank, the rain, and then the city’s distribution points (ask 311).

Drinking salt water. The East River looks like a river and is the sea. Salt water pulls water out of your body; the kidneys need more fresh water to clear the salt than the salt water gave you. Without a still (lesson 3) it is not a source at all.

\n\n

4. Hydrants: illegal, and what to do instead

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Opening a fire hydrant without a spray cap is illegal in New York City. The DEP says it can bring a fine of up to $1,000, up to 30 days in jail, or both. It is also dangerous: an open hydrant pours out more than 1,000 gallons a minute, drops the water pressure on the block so that fire crews cannot fight a fire, and can knock a child into traffic. A hydrant fitted with a spray cap releases 20 to 25 gallons a minute.

The legal route: an adult aged 18 or over can ask at the local firehouse for a free spray cap and have the hydrant opened for cooling in a heat wave. That is for cooling off, not for drinking: hydrant water is street-main water that has sat in the hydrant barrel and is not treated as drinking water by anyone.

In a water outage the city sets up distribution points for bottled water and water tankers. Call 311 or check Notify NYC and the DEP’s water service disruptions page for their locations; they change with each emergency, so confirm via 311 or the official finder at the time. Report a broken main, a running hydrant or brown water to 311.

\n\n

5. Water-main breaks and boil-water notices

\n

The DEP repairs main breaks; you will see water in the street, low pressure, and often rusty water for hours afterwards. What to do:

\n
    \n
  1. Report it to 311 (call, app or online) if it is not already on the news.
    2. \n
  2. Fill containers if you still have pressure, then stop using the taps for drinking until the DEP says the water is safe. Brown water is rust and sediment, not necessarily germs, but low pressure in the mains can pull dirty groundwater into the pipes, which is why notices follow breaks.
    3. \n
  3. Run the cold tap for a few minutes when service returns until it runs clear before using it.
    4. \n
\n

When a boil-water notice is issued, the New York State Department of Health rules are:

\n
    \n
  • Bring tap water to a full rolling boil for one minute, let it cool, then use it. Or use bottled water.
    • \n
  • Use boiled or bottled water for drinking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing food, preparing food and baby formula, and for washing hands before handling food.
    • \n
  • Throw away ice made during the notice and any drinks or formula made with untreated tap water.
    • \n
  • Showering and washing clothes are allowed for healthy adults; keep water out of your mouth and out of open cuts. Bathe babies with boiled-and-cooled or bottled water.
    • \n
  • A notice usually lasts 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer. It is lifted by the same channel that issued it. Do not assume it is over because the water looks fine.
    • \n
\n

If the stove is electric and the power is out, or the gas is shut off, boiling is not available; lesson 3 covers bleach and filters for exactly that case.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Taps die from the top floor down. Fill the tub first. Hidden water in order: bottles, ice, pipes, building tank, rain, toilet tank. Never flood water, river water, pool or radiator water. Hydrants are illegal without a cap and are not drinking water. Boil-water notice: rolling boil one minute, throw away ice made during it.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Find the bathtub plug now; if it is missing, buy a flat universal drain stopper.
  • Fill two ice-cube trays or a bag of ice and keep the freezer full: it is stored water that also keeps food cold.
  • Put a marker line on a clean bucket at 1 gallon so you can measure water for treatment.
  • Ask the super where the building’s hot-water tank is, who drains it, and whether the pump has a generator.
  • Walk past your nearest firehouse and note its address; that is where spray caps come from and where you ask in a heat wave.
  • Save the 311 number, the 311 app and the DEP water service disruptions page on your phone.
  • Read the CDC flood-water page once, so the sight of clear-looking flood water never tempts you.
\n
✅ VERIFIED

EPA, “Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water”: alternative sources are bottled water, melted ice cubes, the hot-water tank and drained pipes; do not use water from toilet flush tanks or bowls, radiators, waterbeds, swimming pools or spas; boiling and disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals; distillation removes them. https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water, checked 26 Sep 2026.

CDC, “Safety Guidelines: Floodwater”: flood water may contain sewage and chemicals; do not drink or bathe in it. https://www.cdc.gov/floods/safety/floodwater-after-a-disaster-or-emergency-safety.html, checked 26 Sep 2026. CDC, “How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency”: water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals is not made safe by boiling or disinfection; use bottled water. https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.

CDC, “Collecting Rainwater and Your Health”: rainwater is not necessarily safe to drink; filter and disinfect it; dust, smoke and soot dissolve in it. https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/about/collecting-rainwater-and-your-health-an-overview.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.

NYC DEP press release, “DEP Issues Safety Alert on Opening Fire Hydrants” and 2026 heatwave release: illegal without a spray cap; fine up to $1,000 and/or up to 30 days; more than 1,000 gallons a minute open versus 20–25 with a cap; free caps from local firehouses for adults 18 and over; report to 311. https://www.nyc.gov/html/dep/html/press_releases/11-45pr.shtml and nyc.gov/site/dep/news/26-018, checked 26 Sep 2026 (search snippet; nyc.gov cannot be opened from this machine).

NYC 311, “Water Main Break”: report to 311 so the DEP can respond. https://portal.311.nyc.gov/article/?kanumber=KA-01233; NYC DEP, “Water Service Disruptions”, nyc.gov/site/dep/water/water-service-disruptions.page, checked 26 Sep 2026.

New York State Department of Health, “Boil Water Notices: FAQ for Residents and Homeowners”: rolling boil one minute then cool; boiled or bottled water for drinking, teeth, food and hand washing before food; discard ice made during the event; typically 24–48 hours. https://www.health.ny.gov/environmental/water/drinking/boilwater/faq_residents_and_homeowners.htm, checked 26 Sep 2026.

NIH/PMC, “Health Impact in New York City During the Northeastern Blackout of 2003”: high-rise residents lost water when electric pumps stopped. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3072860/, checked 26 Sep 2026. Wikipedia, “East River”: a salt-water tidal strait; Hudson River Estuary Program fact sheet: East River water quality affected by combined sewer overflows. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_River, hudsonriver.org fact sheet, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Hurricane Ida figures (1–2 September 2021, 3.5 inches of rain per hour, basement drownings) from FACTS.md, verified 26 Sep 2026 from NYC Emergency Management. Water-heater shut-off steps: A. O. Smith and Lennox manufacturer guides, hotwater.com, checked 26 Sep 2026.

"}, "SURVIVE/water/s3": {"body": "

If you doubt the water, boil it for one minute; if you cannot boil, add 8 drops of plain unscented bleach per gallon and wait 30 minutes. Those two lines cover almost every germ that makes people sick after a main break, a flood or a boil-water notice, and they cost nothing. Everything else in this lesson is about the cases those two lines do not cover: cloudy water, water with no fuel to boil it, filters that promise more than they deliver, and the poisons that no boiling, bleach, filter or sunlight can take out. Learn the order: clear it, then kill the germs, and never treat water that smells of chemicals at all.

\n\n

1. First: is this water even treatable?

\n

Before you spend fuel or bleach, look and smell. The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) is blunt: water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals will not be made safe by boiling or disinfection; use bottled water instead. The EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) says the same: boiling and disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals.

📊 FIGURE — Deciding whether water can be treated, and how
Work down the left column; a yes sends you right to the verdict. Only water that reaches the bottom box (clear, or cloudy and pre-filtered) gets boiled or bleached; chemical, salty or flood water is never treated.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
What you see or smellWhat it meansDo
Clear, no smell (tap water under a boil notice, pipe water, ice, rain caught in the open)Germs are the only likely problemBoil, or bleach at the clear-water dose
Cloudy, coloured, or with bits floating (tub water after days, rain, tank water)Particles shield germs from bleach and sunlightLet it settle, pour the clear top through a clean cloth or coffee filter, then boil or use the cloudy-water bleach dose
Rainbow sheen, petrol or solvent smell, soapy foam, bitter or metallic tasteFuel, oil, solvents, cleaners, metalsDo not drink, do not treat. Only distillation helps, and not with every chemical
Salty (harbour, East River, storm surge)SaltOnly distillation removes salt
Flood water from streets or basementsSewage plus chemicals plus fuelNever
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Disinfection kills or removes germs: bacteria (such as E. coli and cholera), viruses (such as norovirus and hepatitis A) and protozoa (parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium). Purification is a looser word that people use to mean removing everything, including chemicals. Boiling, bleach, most filters and sunlight disinfect. None of them purifies. Only distillation comes close, and even it misses some chemicals that boil at the same temperature as water.

\n\n

2. Boiling: the gold standard

\n

CDC: bring the water to a rolling boil for one minute. New York is at sea level, so the three-minute rule for high altitude does not apply. Let it cool on its own; it will taste flat, and pouring it between two clean containers a few times puts the air back. Boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites. It uses fuel and time: a gas stove works in a blackout if the building’s gas is on, but a lighter is needed if the electronic igniter is dead; an electric stove is useless without power. A small camping stove used only by an open window or on a balcony, never in a closed room, can boil a pot; carbon monoxide from any flame in a sealed apartment is a killer. If boiling is impossible, go to bleach.

\n\n

3. Bleach: the blackout method

\n

Use only regular, unscented household liquid chlorine bleach whose label says 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite (in the United States almost all plain bleach is in that range). Never use scented, colour-safe, splashless or “with added cleaners” bleach; those additives are not meant to be swallowed. The CDC doses:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
WaterBleach (5–9%)Then
1 gallon, clear8 drops (a little less than 1/8 teaspoon)Stir, wait 30 minutes. EPA: it should have a slight chlorine smell; if it does not, repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes
1 gallon, cloudy (after settling and pouring through cloth)16 drops (about 1/4 teaspoon)Stir, wait 30 minutes
1 quart, clear2 dropsStir, wait 30 minutes
1 quart, cloudy4 dropsStir, wait 30 minutes
\n

You need a way to count drops: a clean medicine dropper or a pipette from the pharmacy, kept with the bleach. A spoon is a poor dropper; if you must use one, 1/8 teaspoon is the gallon dose for clear water. Mark the gallon line on your treatment bucket in advance (lesson 2). Bleach kills bacteria and viruses well and is weaker against Cryptosporidium, which is why boiling is better when you can.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Several cleaning and hardware guides say that bleach loses roughly 20% of its strength each year after opening and should be replaced yearly, and that bleach with no chlorine smell is spent. I could not confirm the percentage on a CDC or EPA page today. Confirm before you rely on this by reading your bottle’s label and the manufacturer’s shelf-life note; until then, buy a fresh small bottle of plain bleach every year, write the purchase date on it, and keep it cool and dark.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Guessing the bleach dose. Too little leaves the germs alive; too much burns the throat and, in a child, poisons. The dose is 8 drops per gallon of clear water, not a capful, not “a splash”. If a child or adult swallows strong bleach, call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).

Using scented or “splashless” bleach, or pool chlorine, because it is what is in the cupboard. The additives and the concentration are wrong for drinking water. Only plain unscented 5–9% household bleach.

Treating chemical-tainted water. Boiling concentrates the chemicals; bleach adds one more. If it smells of fuel, solvent or cleaner, it is not water for you.

\n\n

4. Filters: what they catch and what they miss

\n

A filter removes things by size. The CDC guide to water filters says: to remove Cryptosporidium and Giardia, use a filter with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller. “Absolute” means every pore is that size or smaller; a “nominal” 1-micron filter can let 20% to 30% of 1-micron particles through. Most portable filters remove parasites but not viruses or bacteria; the CDC says to add a chemical disinfectant (bleach, chlorine dioxide tablets or iodine) after filtering to kill what got through.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Filter typeRemovesMissesUse it for
Pitcher filter (activated carbon)Chlorine taste, some lead, some chemicalsBacteria, viruses, parasites; it is not a disinfection deviceTaste of stored water; improving already-safe water
Hiking “squeeze” or straw filter, absolute 0.1–1 micronParasites; most bacteria if rated for themViruses (too small), chemicals, saltClearing and partly disinfecting rain or tank water, then bleach or boil
Coffee filter, clean cloth, paper towelGrit, insects, visible particlesEvery germ and chemicalPre-filtering cloudy water before boiling or bleach
Purifier rated for viruses (labelled to a virus standard) or a reverse-osmosis unitParasites, bacteria, viruses; reverse osmosis also salts and many chemicalsReverse osmosis needs pressure or a pump and power; check the label for what it claimsRead the label; if it does not say viruses, add bleach
\n

The rule that keeps you safe: filter first to make it clear, then disinfect. A cheap squeeze filter plus a small bottle of bleach and a dropper is a complete apartment kit for germ-contaminated water.

\n\n

5. Sunlight: solar disinfection (SODIS) when there is no fuel and no bleach

\n

The CDC Yellow Book (its guide for travellers) describes solar disinfection: fill clear plastic beverage bottles with clear water, lay them on their side in direct sunlight for at least 6 hours, shaking them now and then; in cloudy weather, 2 consecutive days. Ultraviolet light and heat kill bacteria, viruses and parasites. Rules that make it work: the water must be clear (filter it through cloth first), the bottle must be clear and clean with the label peeled off, no bigger than two litres, and the bottle must sit where the sun hits it directly for the whole time, such as a south-facing windowsill with the window open (glass blocks part of the ultraviolet), a balcony or a roof if you are allowed there. It does nothing for chemicals or salt. It is the method of last resort in a long blackout with no bleach, but it works and it is free.

\n\n

6. Distillation: the only method for salt and most chemicals

\n

EPA: distillation is the only process that removes biological contaminants and also protects against a broad spectrum of other contaminants, because the steam leaves behind bacteria, viruses, heavy metals, salts and most chemicals. A kitchen still: fill a large pot halfway, tie a cup inside it so the cup hangs above the water (or float a heavy cup), put the lid on upside down so its handle points down into the cup, and boil gently. Steam condenses on the lid and drips into the cup. Ice on top of the lid speeds it up. It is slow (a cup or two an hour), it burns fuel, and it still misses chemicals that evaporate at the same temperature as water, such as some fuels and solvents. Use it for salt water or hard-water tank water, never for water that smells of petrol.

\n\n

7. Which method when

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SituationMethod
Boil-water notice, gas stove worksRolling boil 1 minute
Boil-water notice, no stove8 drops bleach per gallon, 30 minutes
Bathtub water after a few days, slightly cloudySettle, cloth, 16 drops per gallon, 30 minutes; or boil
Rain caught in the openCloth, then boil or bleach; a squeeze filter first if you have one
Long blackout, bleach gone, gas off, sunnyCloth, then SODIS 6 hours (2 days if cloudy)
Salt water is the only waterDistillation only
Fuel or chemical smell, sheen, flood waterNone. Find another source; 311 for distribution points
\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Boil 1 minute. Bleach: 8 drops per gallon clear, 16 cloudy, 30 minutes, plain unscented 5–9% only. Filters catch parasites, miss viruses; filter then disinfect. Sun: clear bottle, 6 hours, 2 days if cloudy. Distillation alone removes salt and most chemicals. Fuel smell means never.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

New York City tap water is not the problem on a normal day; the problem is what gets into the pipes during a main break, and the days when you cannot boil. Many apartments in the city have electric stoves and induction cooktops, and gas can be shut off building-wide after a leak or a fire. That makes the bleach-and-dropper kit, not the stove, the reliable New York method. Keep it with the stored water.

Never run a camping stove, a charcoal grill or a gas burner indoors to boil water. Carbon monoxide from a flame in a closed apartment kills quietly; the CDC and FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) both say flame appliances stay outside or at an open window with a battery carbon monoxide alarm running.

Boil-water notices in the city are issued by the DEP and the Health Department and come through Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692), 311 and the news. Questions about a notice: call 311. A sick person who is confused, cannot keep fluids down or has bloody diarrhoea: call 911.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Buy a small bottle of plain unscented 5–9% bleach and a medicine dropper; write the date on the bottle and tape the dose card below to it.
  • Write a dose card: “8 drops per gallon clear, 16 cloudy, wait 30 min; 2 drops per quart” and keep it with the bleach and in your phone notes.
  • Buy a box of paper coffee filters or set aside a clean cotton cloth for pre-filtering.
  • Check whether your stove is gas or electric and whether it needs power to light; put a lighter in the water kit.
  • Peel the labels off two clear 1-litre plastic bottles and keep them for solar disinfection.
  • Buy a squeeze or straw filter rated absolute 1 micron or finer when the budget allows; read the label for what it claims.
  • Practise once: treat one gallon of tap water with 8 drops, wait 30 minutes, smell it, drink it. You will not be doing this for the first time in the dark.
\n
✅ VERIFIED

CDC, “How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency” and the print sheet “Make Water Safe During an Emergency”: rolling boil 1 minute; 8 drops (a little less than 1/8 teaspoon) of 5–9% unscented household bleach per gallon of clear water, 16 drops if cloudy, wait 30 minutes; water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals is not made safe by boiling or disinfection, use bottled water. https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/index.html and https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/media/pdfs/make-water-safe-during-emergency-p.pdf, checked 26 Sep 2026.

EPA, “Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water”: boiling or disinfection will not destroy heavy metals, salts and most other chemicals; distillation removes biological contaminants and protects against a broad spectrum of other contaminants because the steam leaves behind bacteria, viruses, heavy metals, salts and most chemicals; use only regular unscented chlorine bleach suitable for disinfection as stated on the label; treated water should have a slight chlorine odor, otherwise repeat the dosage and let stand another 15 minutes. https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/emergency-disinfection-drinking-water, checked 26 Sep 2026.

CDC, “A Guide to Water Filters” (Cryptosporidium) and “About Choosing Home Water Filters”: absolute pore size 1 micron or smaller removes Cryptosporidium and Giardia; nominal 1-micron filters can pass 20–30% of 1-micron particles; most filters remove parasites but not viruses or bacteria, so add a chemical disinfectant after filtering. https://www.cdc.gov/drinking-water/prevention/about-choosing-home-water-filters.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.

CDC Yellow Book, “Water Disinfection for Travelers”: solar disinfection in transparent bottles laid on their side, minimum 6 hours of sunlight with intermittent shaking, 2 consecutive days if cloudy. https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/preparing-international-travelers/water-disinfection-for-travelers.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Help line, national); Notify NYC text 692-692 and generator/flame carbon monoxide guidance from FACTS.md, verified 26 Sep 2026 from CDC and NYC Emergency Management. Quart doses (2 and 4 drops) are the gallon dose divided by four, printed on the CDC print sheet.

"}, "SURVIVE/food/s1": {"body": "

Tonight, open your cupboards and count how many days you could eat with no power, no stove and no store. Count only food that is ready to eat straight from the package. Then write the number on a sticky note on the fridge. Do this first because the number is almost always smaller than people think, and because everything else in this chapter (what to buy, in what order, for whom) starts from that honest count. The city says to be ready to survive at home on your own for at least three days and recommends keeping three to seven days of supplies. This course takes you further: two weeks, then three months, one shopping trip at a time.

\n\n

1. How much food is \"enough\": calories, not cans

\n

A pantry is measured in calories, not in the number of cans. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans put an adult woman's needs at roughly 1,600 to 2,400 calories a day (about 2,000 to 2,400 for women aged 19 to 25; 1,600 to 2,000 after 60). Use 2,000 a day as your planning number: it covers a stressful day of carrying water up the stairs.

📊 FIGURE — The four pantry goals measured in calories, not cans
Each bar is a storage goal in calories at 2,000 per day, drawn to scale: the three-month layer is thirty times the city minimum. Below: how to count what a container really holds.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
GoalDaysCalories to store (1 adult at 2,000/day)Who says so
City minimum36,000NYC Emergency Management: \"at least three days\"
City recommendationup to 714,000NYC Emergency Management: \"3 to 7 days\"
This course, stage 11428,000Matches the two-week water goal in the Water chapter
This course, stage 290180,000Long outages, job loss, illness, supply-chain failure
\n

How to count what you have: read the Nutrition Facts label, multiply \"calories per serving\" by \"servings per container\", and add the containers up. Example of the arithmetic: a jar whose label reads 190 calories per serving and 14 servings holds about 2,660 calories, more than a full day. A can of green beans whose label reads 20 calories per serving and 3.5 servings holds about 70 calories: it is water, fibre and salt, and it will not keep you on your feet. Volume is not food. Nut butters, oils, canned fish in oil, canned beans, dried fruit, crackers and granola are dense; canned vegetables and broth are not.

\n\n

2. What to buy: food that needs no cooking, no fridge and no extra water

\n

Ready.gov's list for a power outage lasting several days is deliberately boring: canned foods, dry mixes and other staples that need no refrigeration, cooking, water or special preparation. Buy from this list, and buy the versions you already eat, so the food gets used and replaced instead of expiring.

\n
    \n
  • Ready-to-eat canned meats, fish, beans, fruit and vegetables (pull-tab lids help, but still own the opener).
    • \n
  • Peanut butter or other nut butter: the densest cheap calories on the shelf.
    • \n
  • Protein or fruit bars; dry cereal or granola; dried fruit; crackers.
    • \n
  • Canned juices and shelf-stable (non-perishable pasteurized) milk: cartons that live on the shelf until opened.
    • \n
  • Comfort food you actually like: it matters on day five.
    • \n
  • Food for infants, the elderly and anyone with an allergy or a medical diet (section 5).
    • \n
\n

Rice, pasta, oats and dry beans are cheap per calorie but they need water and fuel. In an apartment where the stove may be off and every gallon of water is carried up the stairs, they are stage-2 food. The first two weeks should be eatable cold from the package.

\n\n

3. The budget order of purchases

\n

You do not need a single big shopping trip. Add one or two items to every normal trip, in this order, cheapest and most decisive first.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
StepBuyWhy this comes now
1A manual can opener (and a spoon that lives in the kit)Ready.gov lists it in the basic kit. A shelf of cans with no opener is a shelf of metal. Test it on one can the day you buy it.
2Water (see the Water chapter) before more foodEvery day of food needs its gallon of water; dry food needs more.
3Peanut butter, crackers, canned beans, canned fishDense calories that need nothing else. Three days covered for a few dollars.
4Canned fruit, canned soup and stew, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk, juiceVariety, vitamins, something warm if the gas is on, something sweet if a neighbour's blood sugar drops.
5Bars, granola, instant oats, powdered drink mix, salt, cooking oil, multivitaminFills the gaps; oil and salt make stage-2 rice and beans eatable.
6Stage 2: rice, dry beans, pasta, flour, sugar, plus a way to cook safely (next section)Only once two no-cook weeks are on the shelf.
7A small cooler, a fridge/freezer thermometer, a battery carbon monoxide alarmTurns the next section from theory into practice.
\n\n

4. Rotation: first in, first out

\n

Write the month and year of purchase on the top of every can and box with a marker. Put new cans at the back, take from the front. Eat from the shelf normally and replace what you eat. This is the whole system; it costs nothing and it means the food is never older than what you would eat anyway.

\n\n\n\n
FoodKeeps at best quality (USDA)Examples
High-acid canned foods12 to 18 monthsCanned juices, fruit, pickles, sauerkraut, tomatoes, tomato soup
Low-acid canned foods2 to 5 yearsCanned meat, poultry, fish, stew, soups, beans, green vegetables, carrots, corn, peas, potatoes
\n

USDA rules for the shelf itself: store cans in a cool, dry place; heat above 100°F sharply raises the risk of spoilage (not the radiator cupboard, not the top of the fridge); discard heavily rusted cans; and treat a can that is bulging, leaking, badly dented at the seam or that spurts when opened as poison, not dinner. Do not taste it to check.

\n\n

5. Food for people who are not you

\n
    \n
  • Babies. Ready-to-feed infant formula is the safest choice in an emergency: it is sterile and needs no water. Powdered formula is not sterile and needs safe water plus clean bottles; if tap water is unsafe use bottled water, or boil water for one minute and let it cool. The CDC says ready-to-feed is especially important for a baby under two months, born prematurely or with a weak immune system. If you have no baby, one small pack of ready-to-feed formula is still a good thing to own in a building with families.
    • \n
  • Older neighbours. Soft, easy-to-open food (pull-tab cans, cartons, cups with foil lids), and help opening it. Ask now whether they have a week of medication, because many medicines must be taken with food.
    • \n
  • Allergies. Keep the allergy-safe food in its own labelled bag so no one grabs the wrong jar in the dark. Peanut butter is the classic pantry item that can kill an allergic child: know who in your building must never be handed it.
    • \n
  • A neighbour with diabetes. Low blood sugar is a medical emergency you can treat with your pantry. The CDC's rule: a blood sugar below 70 mg/dL is low. Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes, check again, and repeat until it is back in range; then give a balanced snack with protein. Fifteen grams is about 4 ounces (half a cup) of juice or regular (not diet) soda, 1 tablespoon of sugar, honey or syrup, or 3 to 4 glucose tablets. Below 55 mg/dL is severe: that needs injectable glucagon if they have it, and a 911 call. Never put food or drink in the mouth of someone who is confused or cannot swallow. Keep juice boxes and hard candy in the kit for exactly this.
    • \n
\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Non-perishable (shelf-stable) food is food that stays safe at room temperature in its unopened package: cans, jars, sealed pouches, dry goods, and shelf-stable cartons of milk and juice. Once opened it becomes perishable and follows the fridge rules in the next section.

First in, first out (FIFO) is the rotation rule: the oldest package is always the next one eaten, so nothing sits until it is unsafe.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Buying food you cannot open, cannot cook or cannot digest. The three ways a full pantry fails: a wall of cans and no manual opener; twenty pounds of rice and beans with no safe way to boil water; and food nobody in the household will eat when they are frightened and nauseous. The fix costs almost nothing: one manual can opener tested on day one, two weeks of food that is eaten cold from the package, and only the brands you already eat.

The second way to die with a full pantry is to ration water to stretch it. Water first, always. Two weeks of dry food is worthless without the gallon a day that goes with it.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

New York City Emergency Management tells every household to be able to shelter in place for at least three days and recommends three to seven days of supplies; the checklist names non-perishable, ready-to-eat canned foods and a manual can opener. Two weeks is this course’s target, because the city’s figure assumes help arrives on schedule.

Apartment storage: shallow bins under the bed, the top shelf of a closet, the space under the kitchen sink if it is dry. Keep the food away from the radiator and the oven; heat shortens canned shelf life. Never store food in the basement of a flood-zone building (see the Ida figures in the NYC chapter).

In a blackout, bodega card readers, delivery apps and supermarket doors all fail at once. Keep small cash with the food, and assume the store is not an option for the first three days.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Store what you eat, eat what you store. Count calories, not cans. Opener first, water second, peanut butter third. Mark the month on the lid and take from the front.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Count your no-cook days tonight and write the number on the fridge.
  • Buy one manual can opener and open a can with it.
  • Add two jars of peanut butter, a box of crackers and six cans of beans or fish to your next shop.
  • Write the purchase month on every can you own with a marker.
  • Move any food stored near the radiator or above the stove.
  • Ask one neighbour who is elderly, diabetic or has a baby what they would need; add one item for them (juice boxes, ready-to-feed formula, pull-tab cans).
  • Set a monthly phone reminder: eat the oldest item, buy one to replace it.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • Ready.gov, \"Food\": store at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food; power outages may last several days, so stock canned foods, dry mixes and staples that need no refrigeration, cooking, water or special preparation; suggested items include peanut butter, protein or fruit bars, dry cereal or granola, dried fruit, canned juices, non-perishable pasteurized milk; manual can opener and utensils. https://www.ready.gov/food and the kit list https://www.ready.gov/kit
  • NYC Emergency Management, \"Be Ready New York\": shelter in place on your own for at least three days; keep 3 to 7 days of supplies; non-perishable ready-to-eat canned foods and a manual can opener. https://www.nyc.gov/site/em/ready/be-ready-new-york.page
  • Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020–2025, calorie needs by age and sex (adult women about 1,600 to 2,400 calories a day; ages 19–25 about 2,000 to 2,400; 61 and over about 1,600 to 2,000), as summarised by Medical News Today, \"How many calories should a person eat per day?\" https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/245588
  • USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, \"Shelf-Stable Food Safety\": high-acid canned foods 12 to 18 months, low-acid 2 to 5 years; cool dry storage; heat above 100°F raises spoilage risk; discard heavily rusted cans. https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/shelf-stable-food
  • CDC, \"Facts About Infant Feeding During Emergencies\" and \"Feeding Your Child Safely During a Disaster\": ready-to-feed formula is safest (sterile, no water needed); powdered formula is not sterile; bottled water or water boiled for 1 minute and cooled; extra care under 2 months, premature or immunocompromised. https://www.cdc.gov/infant-feeding-emergencies-toolkit/php/facts.html
  • CDC, \"Treatment of Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia)\": below 70 mg/dL is low; 15 grams of carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes, recheck; 4 oz juice or regular soda, 1 tablespoon sugar/honey/syrup, 3–4 glucose tablets; below 55 mg/dL is severe, glucagon. https://www.cdc.gov/diabetes/treatment/treatment-low-blood-sugar-hypoglycemia.html
  • Water figures (1 gallon per person per day; boil 1 minute) come from the Water chapter, Ready.gov \"Water\" and CDC \"Making Water Safe in an Emergency\".

The moment the power fails, do two things: keep the fridge and freezer doors shut, and write the time on a piece of tape on the fridge door. Then do not bring any fuel-burning device indoors, whatever the weather. The clock matters because the FDA's safety windows are counted from the moment the power stopped, not from when you noticed. The fuel rule matters because carbon monoxide from a grill, camp stove or generator in an apartment kills quietly, and it is the most common way people die in the days after a blackout, not hunger.

\n\n

1. The clock on the fridge and freezer

\n\n\n\n\n
ApplianceStays safe, door kept shut (FDA)What to do
RefrigeratorAbout 4 hoursEat from here first. Move milk, meat and leftovers to a cooler with ice at hour 3 if the outage looks long.
Full freezerAbout 48 hoursDo not open it to look. Freeze water bottles now, in normal times, to keep it full.
Half-full freezerAbout 24 hoursGroup the food together in one block; gaps warm faster.
\n

Use food in this order: refrigerator first, then freezer, then the pantry. Two thresholds decide everything:

📊 FIGURE — The safe-time clock for fridge and freezer after a power failure
The bars are the FDA windows counted from the moment the power stopped, with the doors kept shut. Below them is the 2-hour rule that decides what gets thrown out.
\n
    \n
  • 40°F. The fridge must be at or below 40°F and the freezer at or below 0°F in normal times. A cheap appliance thermometer in each is the only way to know the truth when the power comes back.
    • \n
  • The 2-hour rule. Perishable food (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers, milk) that has been above 40°F for 2 hours or more is discarded; 1 hour if the temperature is above 90°F, which is a real risk in a top-floor apartment in a summer blackout. Never taste food to check it.
    • \n
\n

Refreezing. When power returns, food that still has ice crystals or reads 40°F or below on the thermometer can be refrozen safely; quality may drop, but it is safe. If the freezer thermometer reads above 40°F and you do not know for how long, the meat, fish and leftovers go out. The FDA's own words: when in doubt, throw it out.

\n\n

2. Ice, dry ice and the cooler

\n
    \n
  • Ordinary ice. Bags of ice or frozen water bottles in a cooler keep fridge food cold past hour 4. Pack it full; a half-empty cooler warms fast.
    • \n
  • Dry ice. USDA: 50 pounds of dry ice should hold an 18-cubic-foot freezer for 2 days. Never touch it with bare hands and do not put it in direct contact with food. In a blackout it sells out within hours, so know where it is sold before you need it.
    • \n
  • A friend's freezer. USDA also suggests moving food to a freezer that still has power, for example a relative in another borough on a different part of the grid.
    • \n
\n\n

3. Cooking: what is safe in an apartment and what is not

\n

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless gas produced by anything that burns fuel. The CDC rule has no exceptions: never use a generator, charcoal grill, camp stove or other gasoline- or charcoal-burning device inside your home, basement or garage, or outdoors less than 20 feet from a window, door or vent. Opening a window does not make it safe. Never burn charcoal indoors. Never use a portable gas camp stove indoors. Do not use the oven or a gas range to heat the room.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Heat sourceIn an NYC apartmentWhy
Charcoal grill, hibachiNever indoors. Outdoors: legal only on a terrace or in a backyard, 10 feet from the building, with an extinguisher or hose at hand; not on a balcony, roof or fire escapeCO indoors; FDNY fire code outdoors
Propane grillNever indoors. Illegal even to store a standard propane grill on the balcony, roof, roof deck, rear yard or courtyard of an apartment buildingCO plus the fire code; only one- and two-family homes may keep one
Camp stove (gasoline, propane, butane)Never indoors. Outdoors only, 20 feet from any window, door or ventCDC carbon monoxide rule
GeneratorNever indoors, never in a basement or garage; outdoors 20 feet from openings, exhaust pointed awayCDC and CPSC (see the Power chapter)
Your gas stove, if gas service is still onUsable for cooking only, never for heating the room; see the NOT VERIFIED callout about lighting it without powerIt is designed to vent into a kitchen; a grill is not
Cold food from the pantryAlways safe. This is why section 1 insisted on two weeks of no-cook foodNo flame, no fumes, no fuel
\n

Symptoms of CO poisoning, from the CDC: headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion. Several people in the same apartment feeling sick at once, or a pet collapsing, is CO until proven otherwise: get everyone outside into fresh air and call 911. It is often mistaken for flu or food poisoning, which is exactly why it kills.

\n\n

4. The carbon monoxide alarm you already have a right to

\n

NYC Local Law 7 of 2004 requires the owner of your building to provide and install at least one approved, working CO alarm within 15 feet of the primary entrance to each room used for sleeping. Test it this week. If there is none, or it chirps, or it is more than a few years old, tell the landlord in writing and call 311; in the meantime buy a battery-powered CO alarm of your own, because a plug-in alarm without battery backup is dead in a blackout, which is the one time you need it.

\n\n

5. Washing, cleaning and the dishes

\n

Use bottled or treated water (Water chapter) to rinse cans before opening, to wash hands before eating and to clean utensils. Never wash food or dishes in floodwater. If water is short, eat straight from the can with one spoon per person and wipe rather than wash; a moist towelette from the Ready.gov kit does the job.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Perishable food is food that spoils at room temperature: meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked leftovers, cut fruit, and anything opened from a shelf-stable package. It lives at or below 40°F and follows the 2-hour rule when it does not.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is the colourless, odourless gas produced by burning charcoal, gasoline, propane, natural gas or wood. It is why the cooking rule is \"outdoors, 20 feet from openings\" and why a battery CO alarm belongs next to the pantry.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Bringing the grill inside because it is raining, cold, or the fire escape is \"outside\". A charcoal grill or camp stove in a kitchen, a hallway, a bathroom with the window open or a basement fills the apartment with carbon monoxide. The CDC rule is indoors never, outdoors 20 feet from windows, doors and vents. In NYC a fire escape is neither legal nor 20 feet from anything: it is a window with a railing.

The quieter mistake is opening the freezer \"just to check\". Every opening costs cold you cannot get back; a full freezer’s 48 hours assume the door stays shut.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Fire code (FDNY). Charcoal grilling is legal only on a terrace or in a backyard, 10 feet from the building, with a fire extinguisher or hose within reach. Grilling on a balcony, roof or fire escape is illegal, and so is storing a grill on a fire escape. A standard propane grill may not even be stored on the balcony, roof, rear yard or courtyard of an apartment building; only a propane container smaller than 16.4 ounces may be used briefly on a roof.

Local Law 7 of 2004. Your landlord must install a CO alarm within 15 feet of the primary entrance of each sleeping room. Missing or dead: report to 311 and buy a battery unit meanwhile.

High-rise and summer. Top-floor apartments in a July blackout pass 90°F quickly, which cuts the perishable window from 2 hours to 1. Move the fridge contents to a cooler early, and see the Heat chapter for yourself.

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Lighting a gas stove when the electric ignition has no power. Many gas ranges can be lit with a match or lighter held to the burner while the knob is turned, but not all models, and a gas oven should not be lit by hand unless the manual says so. Confirm before you rely on this: check your stove’s manual or the manufacturer’s site, and if you smell gas at any time leave the apartment and call 911 or Con Edison from outside.

Condiments and hard cheeses after an outage. The FDA and FoodSafety.gov publish a chart saying which fridge items (some condiments, hard cheeses, whole fruit) may be kept after 4 hours above 40°F and which must go. The details were not re-read for this lesson; confirm before you rely on this at foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/food-safety-during-power-outage.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Stick a strip of tape and a marker on the fridge so you can write the time the power fails.
  • Fill empty bottles with water and freeze them; a full freezer lasts 48 hours, a half-empty one 24.
  • Press the test button on the CO alarm; if there is none within 15 feet of the bedroom door, write to the landlord and call 311.
  • Buy an appliance thermometer for the fridge and one for the freezer.
  • Buy a small cooler or insulated bag.
  • Find out where dry ice and bagged ice are sold near you and save the addresses in your phone.
  • Read your stove manual for the \"no power\" lighting instructions and write them on a card taped inside the cupboard.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • FDA, \"Food and Water Safety During Power Outages and Floods\": fridge safe about 4 hours unopened; full freezer about 48 hours, half full 24; fridge at or below 40°F and freezer at or below 0°F; discard perishables held above 40°F for 2 hours or more (1 hour above 90°F); appliance thermometers; when in doubt throw it out. https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/food-and-water-safety-during-power-outages-and-floods
  • USDA FSIS, \"Keeping Food Safe During an Emergency\": refreeze if the food still contains ice crystals or is 40°F or below; 50 pounds of dry ice holds an 18-cubic-foot freezer for 2 days; do not touch dry ice with bare hands or place it on food; move food to a friend’s freezer. https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/keeping-food-safe-during
  • Ready.gov, \"Food\": keep doors closed; use refrigerator food first, then freezer, then non-perishables. https://www.ready.gov/food
  • CDC, \"Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics\" and \"What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage\": never use a generator, charcoal grill, camp stove or other gasoline- or charcoal-burning device inside the home, basement or garage, or outside less than 20 feet from a window, door or vent; never burn charcoal indoors; never use a portable gas camp stove indoors; symptoms headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, confusion. https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html and https://www.cdc.gov/natural-disasters/response/what-to-do-protect-yourself-during-a-power-outage.html
  • NYC Local Law 7 of 2004 (carbon monoxide alarms): owner must provide and install at least one approved, operational CO alarm within 15 feet of the primary entrance to each sleeping room. https://www.nyc.gov/html/dob/downloads/bldgs_code/locallaw07of04.pdf
  • NYC Department of Buildings / FDNY barbecue rules (Fire Code 307.5): charcoal grills on terraces or backyards only, 10 feet from the building, extinguisher or hose at hand; no grills on balconies, roofs or fire escapes; standard propane grills may not be stored at apartment buildings; propane containers under 16.4 oz only briefly on roofs. https://www.nyc.gov/assets/buildings/pdf/tool_kit_barbecues.pdf, summarised by StreetEasy https://streeteasy.com/blog/grilling-laws-nyc/

Do not plan to feed yourself from the parks, the rivers or a windowsill. Plan to feed yourself from a shelf, and put rice, beans, oil and salt on it this month. Foraging, fishing and sprouting come last on purpose: in New York City they are illegal in the parks, contaminated in soil and water, poisonous when you guess wrong, and return almost no calories. A ten-pound bag of rice costs less than a foraging book and cannot kill you. This section explains why the alternatives are a last resort, what the law says, and how to use the few that are useful.

\n\n

1. Why foraging in New York City is a last resort

\n\n\n\n\n\n
ProblemWhat it means for you
It is against Parks rulesNYC Parks rule § 1-04 (Prohibited Uses): no person shall deface, sever, mutilate, kill or remove from the ground any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation under Parks jurisdiction without permission of the Commissioner. That covers every park and street tree bed. Picking is a summons, not a survival strategy.
The soil is contaminatedThe New York State Department of Health tested more than 500 soil samples from 54 NYC community gardens: in 70% of the gardens at least one sample exceeded health-based guidance values for lead and other metals. A roadside, rail cut or vacant lot is worse, and greens carry soil and dust.
Lookalikes killThe plants people eat by mistake (section 2) cause vomiting, liver failure and death. NYC Health’s advice: never eat wild mushrooms, berries or plants from the outdoors.
Almost no caloriesWild greens are leaves. A day of gathering dandelion returns less energy than one can of beans.
\n\n

2. The lookalikes: learn these to avoid them, not to eat them

📊 FIGURE — The deadly lookalikes and the features that give them away
Top: poison hemlock beside the wild carrot it is mistaken for, feature by feature (stem, smell, height). Bottom: the two other killers the lesson names. Learn these to avoid them, not to eat them.
\n\n\n\n\n
Deadly plantMistaken forHow to tell (Penn State, Cornell, Poison Control)What it does
Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum)Wild carrot / Queen Anne’s lace, parsley, parsnipHemlock: smooth, hairless stem with purple blotches, no carrot smell when crushed, 4 to 10 feet tall. Wild carrot: hairy green stem, carrot smell, often one tiny purple-black floret in the centre of the white flower, 1 to 4 feet.Paralysis and death; grows along rail lines, riverbanks and lots
Pokeweed (Phytolacca americana)Grapes, elderberries, \"wild spinach\"Clusters of dark purple berries on bright red stems, not a woody vine; big smooth leaves; common in lots and park edges.All parts are poisonous; as few as 10 berries can be toxic to an adult; roots are worst
Death cap (Amanita phalloides) and its white relativesPaddy-straw mushrooms, edible white mushroomsYou cannot tell reliably. The death cap causes about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings and has poisoned people in New York State; symptoms are delayed, then the liver fails.Rule: no wild mushroom, ever, in an emergency
\n

If anyone eats any part of a wild plant or mushroom, call the NYC Poison Control Center, 212-POISONS (212-764-7667), or the national Poison Help line 1-800-222-1222, free, 24 hours; if they are unconscious, having trouble breathing or seizing, call 911. Keep a piece of the plant for identification.

\n\n

3. The only plants to consider, and the rules that go with them

\n

Two common lawn weeds are widely described as having no poisonous lookalike that shares all their features. They are the only ones this course names, and they are vitamins, not calories.

\n
    \n
  • Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale): a flat rosette of deeply toothed leaves, and each bright yellow flower on its own single, hollow, leafless stalk that oozes milky sap. If the stalk branches or has leaves on it, it is not a dandelion.
    • \n
  • Broadleaf plantain (Plantago major): oval leaves in a low rosette with thick stems meeting at the base; when a stem is snapped, string-like veins pull out like celery threads.
    • \n
\n

Rules that are not optional: only from ground you control or have permission for (a private yard, your own container of bought soil); never from a park, tree bed, roadside, dog run or sprayed lawn; wash in safe water; cook them; and if you are not 100% sure of every feature, leave it.

\n\n

4. Fishing: legal in places, and what the state says about eating the catch

\n

Fishing is the one wild food here that returns real protein. Two sets of rules apply.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
RuleDetail
Licence: fresh water (park lakes, ponds)Everyone 16 and older needs a state freshwater licence; 2026 resident annual $25 (ages 16 to 69), $5 at 70 and over; sold online (DECALS), by phone or by licence agents.
Licence: salt water (the harbour, East River, Hudson, ocean beaches)Enrol in the free annual Recreational Marine Fishing Registry, also required in the Hudson and its tributaries when fishing for migratory sea fish.
Who is a \"sensitive population\"The state Health Department: people who may become pregnant (under age 50) and children under 15 follow the stricter advice. That includes Natasha.
EelsNo eels may be possessed for food from the East River, Harlem River or tidal Hudson.
Fish to avoid or eat less ofAmerican eel, bluefish, carp, striped bass, weakfish, white and channel catfish, white perch: highest in PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls), dioxin and old pesticides, which stay in the body for decades.
Hudson RiverFor decades the sensitive population was told to eat no fish or crabs from the Hudson (Corinth to the Battery). An April 2026 update allows them up to one 8-ounce meal a month of striped bass and some other species from the lower Hudson. Check the current table first.
Canals and creeksThe NYC region advisories also apply to tributaries such as the Gowanus Canal and Newtown Creek and to any connected water without a dam or barrier.
\n

Practical meaning: a rod is a reasonable long-term item and the marine registry is free, so enrol now. But the harbour is not a grocery: check each species against the current state table at health.ny.gov/fish and cook every fish thoroughly.

\n\n

5. Sprouting: a vitamin source, not a food supply

\n

A jar, a screen lid and seeds labelled for sprouting give fresh greens in days with no soil or sun. The limits:

\n
    \n
  • Sprouts are a high-risk food. Between 2000 and 2020 at least 53 sprout-associated outbreaks were recorded in the United States: 1,498 illnesses, 179 hospitalisations and 5 deaths, mostly Salmonella and E. coli. Warm, wet sprouting jars are ideal for bacteria too.
    • \n
  • The FDA says everyone should cook sprouts thoroughly, and that children, the elderly and people with weak immune systems should not eat raw or lightly cooked sprouts at all.
    • \n
  • Buy only seeds sold specifically for sprouting (untreated, no fungicide coating) from a reputable supplier; the seed is the usual source of contamination.
    • \n
  • Sprouts need rinsing with clean water twice a day; in a water emergency that is drinking water.
    • \n
\n\n

6. Rice, beans, oil and salt: the three-month layer

\n

Once the two no-cook weeks are on the shelf, dry staples are the cheapest way to add months, provided you have a safe way to boil water (section 2) and the water itself.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
StapleStorage life (Utah State University Extension)Notes
White riceUp to 10 years at a steady 70°F with oxygen absorbers; up to 30 years sealed oxygen-free in cool storageBuy white, not brown, for storage; keep it in a lidded bin away from the radiator.
Dry beans20 to 30 years in sealed containers with oxygen absorbers, kept coolThe older the bean, the longer it takes to soak and cook, and very old beans never soften. Rotate them.
Cooking oilRead the label; buy small bottles and rotateThe densest calories per dollar in the kit; makes rice and beans a meal.
Salt, sugarEffectively indefinite if kept drySalt for taste and for preserving; sugar is also the diabetic neighbour’s emergency supply.
\n

Kidney beans need a real boil. Raw or undercooked red kidney beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a natural toxin; the FDA’s Bad Bug Book says as few as four or five improperly cooked beans can cause severe vomiting within hours, followed by diarrhoea. The toxin is destroyed by boiling at 212°F for at least 10 minutes. A slow cooker, which reaches only around 167°F, can make the beans more toxic, not less. Where fuel is scarce this favours canned beans (already cooked); if you store dry beans, soak, then boil hard for ten minutes before simmering.

\n\n

7. Rationing without starving

\n
    \n
  • Do the arithmetic on day one. Total calories on the shelf divided by 2,000 per adult equals days. Decide honestly how many days until help, and divide the food across them.
    • \n
  • Never ration water to save food. A gallon a day per person comes first; the Water chapter explains why.
    • \n
  • Eat the perishables first (fridge, then freezer), then the pantry in FIFO order; the two-week no-cook layer is eaten before the rice and beans, which need fuel.
    • \n
  • Keep fat and protein in every ration (oil, nut butter, canned fish, beans); sugar alone leaves you shaking in an hour.
    • \n
  • Protect the medical food. The diabetic neighbour’s juice and glucose tablets are not a snack.
    • \n
  • Feed children and the sick full portions; cut the healthy adults’ portions first.
    • \n
\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Foraging is gathering wild plants, fungi or shellfish to eat. In New York City it collides with Parks rule § 1-04, with lead in the soil, and with lookalikes that kill.

A health advisory for fish is the state Health Department’s written limit (from \"eat up to four meals a month\" down to \"don’t eat\") for a species from a named water, set by the chemicals found in that fish. It is advice, not a fishing rule, but ignoring it means feeding yourself PCBs.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Eating a wild mushroom, or a \"wild carrot\", because it looked right. The death cap accounts for about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings and has killed in New York State; poison hemlock has killed people who thought it was carrot or parsley. Both are in the city. The symptoms of the death cap are delayed, so feeling fine six hours later means nothing. The rule for this course: no wild mushrooms ever, no plant in the carrot family ever, and nothing you cannot identify by every feature.

The second deadly mistake is treating foraging as a plan and skipping the ten-pound bag of rice. Greens are vitamins. Calories come from the shelf.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Parks. Removing or severing any plant in a NYC park without the Commissioner’s permission is prohibited (Parks rule § 1-04). Street tree beds are Parks property too. This includes \"just a few leaves\".

Poison. NYC Poison Control Center 212-POISONS (212-764-7667), or 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours, free. Unconscious, not breathing normally or seizing: 911.

Fish. The state advisory tables for New York City and marine waters are at health.ny.gov/fish; the 2026 update loosened some Hudson limits for the first time in 50 years, so read the current table, not a memory of the old one. No eels for food from the East, Harlem or tidal Hudson rivers.

Soil. The state garden study found raised beds of clean soil and fruiting crops (tomatoes, beans, squash) carried far less lead than in-ground beds and leafy crops. Grow in bought soil in a container and wash or peel everything (Garden chapter).

\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Where you may fish within the city. Some piers, park shorelines and beaches allow fishing and some prohibit it; the rules were not verified here. Confirm before you rely on this: call 311 or read the sign at the pier.

Rodent poison in parks. Rat bait stations are placed in many parks and tree beds, another reason not to eat plants there; the programme was not verified here. Confirm before you rely on this via 311.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Save 212-764-7667 and 1-800-222-1222 in your phone under \"Poison\".
  • Buy a 10-pound bag of white rice, 2 pounds of lentils or canned beans, a bottle of oil and a box of salt; put them in a lidded bin away from the radiator with the purchase month on the lid.
  • Enrol in the free Recreational Marine Fishing Registry on the DEC website if you ever intend to fish.
  • Open health.ny.gov/fish once and bookmark the New York City and marine waters table.
  • Find one dandelion and one plantain in a yard you have access to and check every feature against the list; do not eat them.
  • Write on your kit list: \"no wild mushrooms, no carrot-family plants, nothing from a park\".
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • NYC Parks, Rules and Regulations § 1-04 Prohibited Uses: no person shall deface, write upon, sever, mutilate, kill or remove from the ground any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation under Parks jurisdiction without permission of the Commissioner. nycgovparks.org/rules/section-1-04
  • NYC Health, \"Poison Prevention: Plants\" (never eat wild mushrooms, berries or plants; 212-POISONS, 212-764-7667); NYS DOH poison centres (1-800-222-1222). nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/poison-plants.page; health.ny.gov/professionals/poison_control/centers.htm
  • NYS Department of Health, \"New York City Community Garden Soil Study\" (figures quoted above). health.ny.gov/environmental/outdoors/garden/soilpaper.htm
  • Penn State Extension, \"Poison Hemlock Identification\" and Cornell Weed Identification, \"Wild Carrot\" (purple-blotched hairless stem, no carrot smell, 4–10 ft vs hairy stem, carrot smell, 1–4 ft). extension.psu.edu/poison-hemlock-identification; blogs.cornell.edu/weedid/wild-carrot
  • Poison Control (poison.org), \"Pokeberries: a grape look-alike\" and Oregon State University, \"Pokeweed\" (all parts poisonous, red stems, about 10 berries toxic to an adult, roots most toxic). poison.org/articles/pokeberries-and-grapes-look-alike; solvepestproblems.oregonstate.edu/weeds/pokeweed
  • Britannica, \"Death cap\" and AmericanMushrooms.com, \"The Death Cap Amanita phalloides\" (about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings; poisonings reported in New York; mistaken for paddy-straw mushrooms). britannica.com/science/death-cap; americanmushrooms.com/deathcap.htm
  • Dandelion and broadleaf plantain identification: DIY Garden, \"These common garden weeds are actually edible\" diygarden.co.uk (edible weeds); AgriPure, \"Plantain weed\" agripure.org/articles/plantain-weed
  • NYS Department of Health fish advisories for New York City & marine waters and for the Hudson River, and press release of 1 April 2026 (sensitive population definition; eel ban; avoid-or-eat-less list; lower Hudson one 8-oz meal a month; Gowanus Canal and Newtown Creek covered). health.ny.gov (NYC & marine waters advisories); health.ny.gov (Hudson River advisories); health.ny.gov press release, 1 April 2026
  • NYS Department of Environmental Conservation, \"Fishing Licenses\" (licence at 16 and older for freshwater; 2026 resident annual $25, $5 at 70+; free Recreational Marine Fishing Registry for marine waters and Hudson migratory fish). dec.ny.gov (Fishing Licenses)
  • FDA sprout guidance and Colorado State University Food Source Information, \"Sprouts\" (53 outbreaks 2000–2020, 1,498 illnesses, 179 hospitalisations, 5 deaths; cook sprouts thoroughly; high-risk groups avoid raw sprouts; seeds labelled for sprouting). fda.gov (sprouts guidance); chhs.colostate.edu/fsi/food-articles/produce/sprouts
  • Utah State University Extension, \"Storing White Rice\" (rice and bean storage lives quoted above). extension.usu.edu (Storing White Rice)
  • FDA, \"Bad Bug Book\", phytohaemagglutinin (kidney bean figures quoted above), summarised by Illinois Extension. fda.gov (Bad Bug Book PDF); extension.illinois.edu (kidney beans and slow cookers)
