First, decide in seconds whether the danger is outside the building or inside it. Danger outside (a chemical cloud, high wind, fallout) means get inside and stay inside. Danger inside or underneath you (fire, smoke, a gas smell, water coming into a basement) means get out or get up. Almost every death in an apartment emergency comes from choosing the wrong one: staying in a room that is filling, or leaving into air that is poisoned. This lesson gives you the rule for each hazard so you never have to work it out at 3 a.m.

📘 DEFINITION

Shelter in place means staying where you are, inside a building, and making that building as safe as possible: closing it up, going to the safest room, and waiting for the danger outside to pass or for officials to tell you it is over.

Evacuate means leaving the building (or the area) because staying has become more dangerous than moving. In New York City an evacuation order is given by the city for specific hurricane zones; for a fire, a gas smell or rising water you evacuate on your own judgement, immediately.

Stay or go: the rule for each hazard

Read the left column, act on the right column. The reason is in the last column so you trust it later.

📊 FIGURE — Stay or go, decided by whether the danger is outside or inside
Start at the top question. Danger outside (left) means get inside and stay; danger inside or under you (right) means get out or get up. Each card gives the move the lesson prescribes for that hazard.
What is happeningDo thisWhy
Fire or smoke in the buildingLeave by the stairs if the way is clear; never the elevator. If smoke blocks your exit, stay in your apartment, seal the door and call 911 with your floor and apartment number (the Fire chapter covers this)Smoke kills faster than flame; elevators can stop between floors
You smell gasLeave right away. Do not touch light switches or anything electrical on the way out. Call 911 and the gas utility from outsideA spark can ignite the gas
Chemical release or bad air outside (official alert, strange smell, visible cloud)Stay. Close and lock windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning, go to an interior room, seal itThe safest air is the air already in a closed room
Flash flood warning and you live in a basement or ground-floor unitGo up. Move to a higher floor before water arrives, not afterBasement doors jam under water pressure; ten of the fourteen New Yorkers killed by Ida drowned in basements
High wind (hurricane, tornado warning, severe storm)Stay. Interior room, lowest floor you can reach without going below ground in a flood, away from windowsWindows fail; flying glass is the injury
Hurricane evacuation order for your zoneGo, early, before transit stops. Take your go-bag (Section 4)The order is given because the surge will reach your zone
Nuclear explosion or fallout warningGet inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Brick or concrete, basement or the middle of a large buildingWalls and distance block radiation
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Staying below ground in a flood. During Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021, rain fell on New York City at 3.5 inches per hour, about double the 1.75 inches per hour the sewers were designed for. Fourteen people died in the city; ten of them drowned in basement apartments. Water came in faster than the doors could be opened.

If you live in a basement or ground-floor apartment, the moment a flash flood warning is issued for your area, go upstairs to a neighbour or into the building hallway on a higher floor. Do not wait to see water. Do not go back for belongings.

Sealing a room for a chemical release

This is the one shelter-in-place case where you actively seal yourself in. Ready.gov (the federal preparedness site) gives these steps; do them in this order.

  1. Get inside. If you are on the street, go into the nearest building, not home.
  2. Close and lock every window and door. Locking pulls the door tighter into its frame.
  3. Turn off fans, air conditioners and any heating that pulls in outside air.
  4. Go to an interior room, ideally one with few or no windows and a door: a bathroom, a walk-in closet, a hallway that can be closed off. Bring your phone, radio, water and a bucket.
  5. Seal the gaps around the door, windows and vents with plastic sheeting and duct tape. Pre-cut sheets are far faster than cutting under stress.
  6. Listen to Notify NYC, the radio or 911 instructions. Come out only when officials say the air is clear, then open windows to ventilate.
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

The plastic sheeting and duct tape in your kit are for a chemical event. They are not for a flood (water will not care) and not for wind (the window will fail anyway). Keep the roll and sheets in one bag with a marker so you can label the sheets by window now, at leisure.

Wind: the interior room

Wind does not usually kill people inside a masonry apartment building. Glass does. Your job is to put as many walls as possible between you and the outside, and to get away from anything that can shatter.

  • Choose the room now, not during the storm: a bathroom, hallway or closet with no exterior windows.
  • Stay away from windows and glass doors even if they look fine. Do not tape windows; tape does not stop them breaking.
  • Take a mattress, cushions or a thick blanket to cover your head and body.
  • Do not go outside during a lull. In a hurricane the calm eye passes and the wind returns from the other direction.
  • If you can move to a lower floor inside the building, do so, but never into a basement that could flood.

The basement rule

The safest floor depends on the hazard, and the two most likely New York hazards point in opposite directions. Wind says go low. Water says go high. When both are possible (a hurricane brings both), water wins: you can survive a broken window on the third floor; you cannot survive a flooded basement.

HazardSafest place in an apartment building
Flash flood, storm surgeAs high as you can get; never below street level
Tornado or straight-line windInterior room, low floor, but above any flood level
Chemical releaseInterior room, sealed; floor does not matter
FalloutBasement or the middle floors of a large brick or concrete building, away from outer walls and roof

Fallout: ten minutes to get inside

Ready.gov says that after a nuclear explosion you may have 10 minutes or more before fallout arrives. That is enough time to get inside a solid building, not enough to drive anywhere. The rule is three words: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.

  • Best shelter: a brick or concrete building, in the basement or the middle of a large building, away from windows, outer walls and the roof.
  • Stay inside for at least 24 hours unless officials tell you otherwise. The radiation from fallout drops fastest in the first hours.
  • If you were outside when the dust fell, take off your outer clothing before entering the room, bag it and wash your skin and hair with soap and water.
  • Keep listening: Notify NYC, a battery or hand-crank radio, and 911 only for a life-threatening emergency.
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Know your hurricane evacuation zone before the season. New York City has six zones; zone 1 is the highest risk and is evacuated first, zone 6 the lowest. Check yours at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115).

Evacuation centers are opened by the city only when an order is issued, and the finder at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane shows which are open. They are pet-friendly and accessible. Confirm via 311 or the finder at the time; centers change with each emergency.

Sign up for alerts now: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, and text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts, or use a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov. Flash flood warnings arrive this way before the water does.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

The following are widely repeated guidance I could not confirm from an official page today. Confirm before you rely on this by opening ready.gov/shelter and weather.gov/safety/flood on your phone, or by calling 311.

  • Ready.gov has said that about 10 square feet of floor space per person gives enough air in a sealed room for up to five hours. Treat the sealed room as a hours-long measure, not a days-long one.
  • The National Weather Service “Turn Around Don’t Drown” figures: about six inches of moving water can knock an adult down and about a foot can float a car. Do not walk or drive through water of unknown depth in any case.
  • A “watch” is usually said to mean conditions are possible; a “warning” means the hazard is happening or about to happen. Confirm the wording on weather.gov.
  • Guidance for high-rise residents in hurricanes has said that wind is stronger on upper floors and that residents above roughly the tenth floor should move to a lower floor inside the building. Confirm with NYC Emergency Management via 311.
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Write on a card taped inside a kitchen cabinet: your evacuation zone, the nearest higher floor you would go to in a flood, and your chosen interior room. Cost: nothing.
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and your ZIP code to 692-692. Cost: nothing.
  • Pick the interior room and clear a space in it big enough to sit or lie down.
  • Buy one roll of duct tape and a roll of plastic sheeting; cut a sheet for each window and vent in the interior room and label them. Under 20 dollars.
  • If you live in a basement or ground-floor unit, introduce yourself to an upstairs neighbour this week and agree that you can knock in a flood.
  • Put a flashlight and your phone charger in the interior room.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for the facts in this lesson, checked 26 Sep 2026:

  • Ready.gov (FEMA), “Shelter” and “Chemical Emergencies”: close and lock windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning, interior room, plastic sheeting and duct tape. https://www.ready.gov/shelter
  • Ready.gov (FEMA), “Nuclear Explosion”: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned; brick or concrete, basement or middle of a large building; 10 minutes or more before fallout; stay at least 24 hours. https://www.ready.gov/nuclear-explosion
  • NYC Emergency Management, “Know Your Zone”: six zones, zone 1 highest risk; maps.nyc.gov/hurricane; 311, video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115; centers opened when an order is issued, pet-friendly and accessible. https://www.nyc.gov/knowyourzone
  • NYC Emergency Management, Hurricane Ida after-action reporting: 14 deaths in NYC, 10 in basement apartments; 3.5 inches per hour versus 1.75 inches per hour sewer design. https://www.nyc.gov/site/em/index.page
  • Notify NYC: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692; ZIP code to 692-692. https://a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov

First, make one room warm and never bring a flame or an engine indoors to do it. When the heat goes out in a New York winter, people die two ways: slowly from hypothermia in a cold apartment, and quickly from carbon monoxide when they try to fix the cold with a gas oven, a grill or a generator. Both are preventable with one warm room, dry layers, and a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm. Do the alarm first; it is the cheapest thing in this chapter that can save your life while you sleep.

📘 DEFINITION

Hypothermia is a body temperature that has dropped low enough to affect the brain and heart. It happens indoors, in wet clothes, to people who are elderly, ill, drunk, or simply asleep in a cold room. Signs: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas with no colour and no smell made whenever fuel burns: gas, charcoal, wood, gasoline, propane. Indoors it builds up and replaces the oxygen your blood carries. A CO alarm is the only way to know it is there.

One warm room

Do not try to heat the whole apartment with your body. Pick the smallest room that has the fewest exterior walls and windows, and move into it with everyone in the household.

📊 FIGURE — The one warm room, and where a generator must stand
Left: everyone moves into the smallest room with the fewest outside walls, door closed, CO alarm at sleeping height. Right: anything that burns fuel stays outside, 20 feet from any opening.
  • Close the doors to every other room. Stuff towels or clothes along the bottom of the door to the warm room.
  • Close blinds and curtains at night; open them on a sunny south-facing window by day.
  • Hang a blanket over the window inside the curtain if the glass is cold to the touch.
  • Put a rug, cardboard or blankets on a bare floor; you lose heat downward.
  • Sleep together under shared blankets. Two people under one cover are warmer than two people under two.
  • Eat regularly and drink warm liquids. Your body makes heat from food. Alcohol makes you feel warm and cools you faster.

Layers and dry clothes

Wet clothes pull heat out of you many times faster than dry ones. Wet from sweat counts. The order of business is dry first, then layers, then a hat.

LayerWhat it doesCheap version
Base (against skin)Moves sweat awaySynthetic or wool tights and long-sleeve top; not cotton
MiddleTraps warm airFleece, sweater, second sweater
OuterBlocks wind and draftsRain jacket, even indoors by a drafty window
Head, hands, feetStops the heat leaking from the endsKnit hat, gloves, two pairs of socks, slippers or shoes on cold floors

Hypothermia: what to do

The American Red Cross guidance is simple. Watch each other for the signs, especially anyone who has become quiet.

  1. Signs: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness. Shivering that stops while the person is still cold is a worse sign, not a better one.
  2. Call 911.
  3. Move the person into the warm room. Remove wet clothing and replace with dry layers and blankets.
  4. Warm the core first: chest, neck, head and groin. Use blankets, skin-to-skin contact, and warm (not hot) compresses. Do not rub arms and legs and do not put the person in a hot bath.
  5. Give warm, sweet drinks only if the person is fully alert. Nothing by mouth if they are confused or drowsy; they can choke.

Never run a flame or an engine indoors

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Heating the apartment with the gas oven, a charcoal grill, a camp stove or a generator. Every winter storm, people in the Northeast die of carbon monoxide poisoning in their own kitchens and living rooms because the cold felt like the bigger danger. It was not.

The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) and the CPSC (Consumer Product Safety Commission) rule for generators: run it outdoors only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, with the exhaust pointed away from the building. Never in a garage, even with the door open. The same applies to any grill or fuel-burning stove. In an apartment that means: you do not own a generator, and you never light charcoal indoors.

If the CO alarm sounds, or several people in the home get a headache, dizziness or nausea at the same time, get everyone outside into fresh air and call 911. Do not go back in to look for the source.

Safe ways to add heat in an apartment during an outage are limited to what does not burn fuel indoors: extra layers, body heat, hot water bottles filled from a stove that is working normally, and an electric space heater when the power is on.

🦺 SAFETY

Electric space heater rules, from the fire safety chapter: keep it well away from bedding, curtains and furniture, plug it straight into the wall (never an extension cord or power strip), turn it off when you sleep or leave the room, and place it on a hard, level floor.

A battery-powered CO alarm belongs in the warm room, at sleeping height, with a spare battery taped to it. The CDC recommends one indoors whenever fuel-burning equipment is used anywhere near the home; in an apartment building you cannot control what a neighbour or the boiler room does, so keep one anyway.

The food in the fridge

A winter blackout usually takes the heat and the fridge together. The FDA (Food and Drug Administration) numbers, with the doors kept shut:

ApplianceFood stays safe for about
Refrigerator4 hours
Full freezer48 hours
Half-full freezer24 hours

Discard perishable food that has been above 40°F for more than 2 hours (1 hour if the room is above 90°F). When in doubt, throw it out. A cold windowsill is not a refrigerator; sunlight and animals get to it.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Code Blue. The city declares Code Blue when the temperature, including wind chill, is at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m. During Code Blue, Department of Homeless Services drop-in centers and shelters accept walk-ins, and more than 50 hospitals keep an open-door policy. If your apartment becomes unsafe to sleep in and you have nowhere else, you are allowed to walk into one of these. Call 311 to find the nearest.

Call 311 to report a building with no heat or hot water; the landlord has a legal duty to provide it during the heating season (the exact temperatures are in the callout below).

During the blackout of 14 August 2003, high-rise buildings in the city lost water pressure because the pumps stopped, subways stopped in tunnels and most people walked home. Plan for water, not just warmth: fill the bathtub and every pot the moment the power drops.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Confirm before you rely on this. These are figures I could not check against an official page today; ask 311, your building superintendent or the product label.

  • NYC heat season is widely stated as 1 October to 31 May, with landlords required to keep apartments at 68°F by day (6 a.m. to 10 p.m.) when it is below 55°F outside, and 62°F at night regardless of the outside temperature. Confirm with 311 or NYC Housing Preservation and Development before filing a complaint.
  • New York City law (usually cited as Local Law 7 of 2004) is said to require carbon monoxide detectors in residential units, with the landlord responsible for installing them. Confirm with 311; buy your own battery unit regardless.
  • The National Fire Protection Association “3 feet” rule: keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from a space heater. Confirm on the heater’s label.
  • To keep pipes from freezing, the Red Cross has advised letting the cold tap drip, opening the cabinet doors under sinks on exterior walls, and never thawing a frozen pipe with an open flame. Confirm on redcross.org; in a multi-unit building, tell the superintendent first.
  • Early carbon monoxide symptoms are usually listed as headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, described as flu-like without fever. Confirm on cdc.gov. Treat any alarm as real.
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Buy a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm and put it in your bedroom tonight. Test it. Tape a spare battery to the side.
  • Choose the warm room and put a rolled towel by its door. Cost: nothing.
  • Put a knit hat, wool socks and a fleece in a bag under the bed so you can find them in the dark.
  • Check what heats your building (gas boiler, electric, steam) and write the superintendent’s phone number on the fridge.
  • Buy a hot water bottle. Under 15 dollars and it warms a bed for hours.
  • Write “fill the bathtub” on the first line of your blackout list.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for the facts in this lesson, checked 26 Sep 2026:

  • American Red Cross, first aid guidance on hypothermia: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness; move to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm the core first (chest, neck, head, groin), warm drinks only if fully alert, call 911. https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/first-aid/performing-first-aid/hypothermia
  • CDC and CPSC, carbon monoxide and generator safety: outdoors only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust away; battery-powered CO detector indoors; never in a garage. https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html
  • FDA, “Food and Water Safety During Power Outages”: fridge 4 hours, full freezer 48 hours, half-full freezer 24 hours; discard above 40°F for more than 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F). https://www.fda.gov/food/buy-store-serve-safe-food/food-and-water-safety-during-power-outages-and-floods
  • NYC Emergency Management, Code Blue: at or below 32°F including wind chill, 4 p.m. to 8 a.m.; DHS drop-in centers and shelters accept walk-ins; more than 50 hospitals open-door. https://www.nyc.gov/site/em/ready/extreme-cold.page
  • Blackout of 14 August 2003: general history (high-rise water pressure lost, subways stopped, people walked home); figures deliberately not quoted.

First, learn the one line that decides whether you call 911: confusion. A hot, sweaty, weak, nauseous person has heat exhaustion and can be cooled at home. A hot person who is confused, whose skin is hot and dry, or whose temperature is 103°F or higher has heat stroke and is dying; you call 911 and cool them while you wait. Heat kills more New Yorkers than any other weather, and it does it quietly, in apartments without air conditioning, usually to someone who lives alone. Top-floor apartments under a flat black roof are the hottest rooms in the city.

📘 DEFINITION

Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool and clammy skin. The body is still cooling itself, but losing. Move to a cool place, loosen clothing, sip water.

Heat stroke: confusion, hot skin (sweating may have stopped), temperature 103°F or above. The body has stopped cooling itself. Call 911 and cool the person immediately. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious; they can choke.

The 911 line: exhaustion versus stroke

SignHeat exhaustionHeat stroke (call 911)
SweatingHeavyMay have stopped; skin hot
SkinCool, pale, clammyHot, red, dry or damp
MindTired, dizzy, nauseousConfused, slurred, agitated, passing out
TemperatureNormal or slightly up103°F or above
Your actionCool place, loosen clothes, sip water, restCall 911; cool the body now; nothing by mouth if confused

Cooling a person with heat stroke while the ambulance comes: move them to the coolest room, take off outer clothing, wet the skin with cool water and fan it, put cold wet cloths or ice packs on the neck, armpits and groin. If they can be put in a cool shower or bath and are conscious enough to be held safely, do it. Stay with them.

📊 FIGURE — Heat exhaustion vs heat stroke, sign by sign
Read across each row to compare the same sign in the two conditions. The right column is heat stroke: confusion, hot skin, 103°F or above. That column means 911 and cooling now, nothing by mouth.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Giving water to a confused person. It feels like the obvious help. A confused or unconscious person cannot protect their airway; the water goes into the lungs. Cool the outside of the body and let the paramedics handle fluids.

Assuming the fan is enough. A fan moves air; it does not lower the temperature of the air. On the hottest days, blowing hot air over a body that has stopped sweating cooks it faster. Use a fan only with wet skin or cool night air, and go somewhere with air conditioning.

Cooling yourself and the apartment

The cheapest cooling is water on skin and air moving across it. The second cheapest is leaving.

  • Take cool showers or baths. If the water runs warm from the pipes, let it run first.
  • Wet a towel or bandana, wring it out, and wear it around your neck. Rewet it when it dries.
  • Wet your wrists and forearms under the cold tap for a minute.
  • Sit with your feet in a basin of cool water.
  • Sleep on the lowest floor of the apartment; if you have a top-floor unit, the floor is cooler than the bed.
  • Drink water steadily through the day, before you are thirsty. Avoid alcohol and sugary drinks.
  • Wear light, loose, light-coloured clothing.
  • Do nothing strenuous in the middle of the day. Shift errands to early morning or after dark.

Night ventilation

A masonry apartment stores heat in its walls all day and releases it all night. You can use that timing.

  1. By day, keep windows closed and blinds or curtains shut on the sunny side. A sheet of cardboard or foil in a sun-facing window blocks much of the heat.
  2. After dark, when the outside air is cooler than the inside, open windows on opposite sides of the apartment to make a cross-breeze. Put a fan in one window blowing hot air out and let cool air in through the other.
  3. At dawn, close everything again before the sun hits the walls.
  4. Keep window guards in place and never lean out. If you have a child in the home, the window must not open more than the guard allows.

Who is most at risk, and checking on them

Most people who die in a New York heat wave are at home, alone, without a working air conditioner. The people to check on:

  • Older adults, especially those who live alone or on a top floor.
  • Anyone with heart disease, kidney disease, obesity, or a mental health condition.
  • Anyone taking medicines that affect sweating or heat (ask a pharmacist which ones).
  • People who drink heavily or use drugs.
  • Infants and small children.
  • Anyone whose air conditioner is broken or who is afraid of the electric bill and is not running it.

Checking on someone means knocking twice a day during a heat emergency, seeing them with your own eyes, and asking two questions: are you drinking water, and is the room cool. If the answer to the second is no, walk them to a cooling center or your own air-conditioned room. If they are confused, call 911.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Cooling centers. During a heat emergency the city opens air-conditioned public spaces (libraries, community centers, senior centers). Find one at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or call 311. Confirm via 311 or the finder at the time; centers change with each emergency. Bring water, a phone charger and something to do; stay through the hottest part of the day.

Sign up for heat alerts from Notify NYC: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692. Heat emergencies are declared with notice, so you can plan the day before.

Public libraries, malls, movie theatres and large supermarkets are air-conditioned on every hot day, not only when a center opens. Spending the afternoon there costs nothing.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Confirm before you rely on this. I could not check these against an official page today; ask 311, your doctor or a pharmacist.

  • The CDC has advised that fans do not prevent heat-related illness once indoor temperatures reach the 90s Fahrenheit. Confirm on cdc.gov; the safe reading is that a fan is not a substitute for air conditioning.
  • New York State’s HEAP (Home Energy Assistance Program) has run a Cooling Assistance benefit that provides an air conditioner to eligible low-income households with a medical need for cooling. Confirm eligibility and dates with 311 or NYC Human Resources Administration.
  • NYC Health reports have said that most heat-stress deaths happen at home to people without air conditioning, and that Black New Yorkers die of heat at a higher rate. Confirm the current report on nyc.gov/health.
  • The National Weather Service in New York has issued heat advisories based on the heat index (temperature plus humidity) reaching the mid-90s for two or more days or 100 or more on any day. Confirm the current thresholds on weather.gov.
  • Con Edison has asked customers to reduce electricity use during heat waves to avoid outages, and reports outages at 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633). Confirm the number on coned.com.
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Write the two lists on one card and stick it to the fridge: heat exhaustion signs (sweaty, weak, nauseous, clammy) and heat stroke signs (confused, hot, 103°F). Cost: nothing.
  • Find your nearest cooling center on the finder now, while it is not hot, and note the walk time.
  • Buy a cheap digital thermometer for the apartment and a body thermometer for the first-aid kit.
  • Buy a spray bottle and two bandanas for wet-cloth cooling. Under 10 dollars.
  • Identify one neighbour who is elderly or lives alone and agree to check on each other during heat emergencies.
  • Measure your sunniest window and cut cardboard to fit it; store it behind the sofa.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources for the facts in this lesson, checked 26 Sep 2026:

  • American Red Cross, first aid guidance on heat-related illness: heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool clammy skin; cool place, loosen clothing, sip water) and heat stroke (confusion, hot skin, temperature 103°F or above, may stop sweating; call 911 and cool immediately; no fluids if confused or unconscious). https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/first-aid/performing-first-aid/heat-related-illness
  • NYC Emergency Management, “Extreme Heat”: cooling centers opened during heat emergencies; finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters; 311. https://www.nyc.gov/site/em/ready/heat.page
  • Notify NYC: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692. https://a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov
  • NYC 911 and 311: 911 for a life-threatening emergency, 311 for city services; text-to-911 available in NYC since June 2020. https://www.nyc.gov/311

First, pack the bag that lets you walk out the door in two minutes and sleep somewhere else for three days. In New York the question is rarely “how will I survive in the wild”; it is “where will I sleep tonight, and did I bring my medication and my ID”. An evacuation order, a fire in the building, a gas leak, a flooded basement: each one means leaving fast, and each one is survivable if the bag is already by the door. Improvised shelter with a tarp is the last resort, and you will learn it here so that you never need it.

📘 DEFINITION

Go-bag: one backpack per person, packed now, kept by the door, holding what you need to leave in minutes and manage for about three days away from home: water, food, light, first aid, medicines, documents, cash, chargers.

Evacuation center: a public building (usually a school) opened by the city when an evacuation order is issued, where anyone can go for shelter, food and information. In New York City they are pet-friendly and accessible. They are not opened for every emergency; the finder and 311 tell you which are open.

What goes in the go-bag

Ready.gov’s basic kit is the backbone. Build the bag from cheap to expensive; a half-packed bag by the door beats a perfect list on your iPad.

ItemWhyNotes for an apartment
Water1 gallon per person per day is the storage rule; carry what you canTwo or three bottles in the bag; the rest of your two-week supply stays home
Non-perishable foodSeveral daysBars, nut butter packets, crackers; nothing that needs cooking
Battery or hand-crank radio, NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) weather radioInformation when the network is downHand-crank models also charge a phone slowly
Flashlight and extra batteriesStairwells go darkHeadlamp keeps hands free
First-aid kitCuts, blisters, burnsAdd a week of your prescription medicines and a written list of them
WhistleSignal for help with no voiceOn a cord around your neck, not in the bag
Dust mask, plastic sheeting, duct tapeBad air, sealing a roomPre-cut sheets
Moist towelettes, garbage bags, plastic tiesSanitationA garbage bag is also a poncho and a ground sheet
Wrench or pliersTurning off utilitiesIn an apartment, mainly for the gas valve if told to
Manual can openerCanned foodCheap and forgotten
Local mapsPhone dead, streets closedA paper subway map and a borough map
Phone chargers and a backup batteryCalls, alerts, 311, bankingKeep the battery bank charged monthly

Add to the federal list: copies of your ID, lease, insurance and medical cards in a zip bag; a spare set of keys; cash in small bills (card readers fail when the power does); a change of underwear and socks; a light sleeping bag or emergency blanket; a notebook and pen with your key phone numbers written down; a photo of each family member and pet for reunification.

What stays out

  • Anything you cannot carry up six flights of stairs. If the bag is too heavy to jog with, it will be left behind.
  • Weapons. Do not bring them; centers screen bags and may refuse entry.
  • Glass jars, cans of food you have no opener for, anything that leaks.
  • Candles. A flashlight does the job without starting the fire you just escaped.
  • Originals of documents. Copies in the bag, originals in a fireproof box at home or with family.

Where people actually sleep in an evacuation

Sort your options now, best first. The bag is the same for all of them.

  1. Family or friends outside the danger zone. The best shelter is a couch in someone’s apartment in a higher zone. Agree the plan in advance and text them the moment an order is announced, not when you arrive.
  2. A hotel. Book early; rooms fill within hours of an order. Keep a card with room on it for this.
  3. A city evacuation center. Free, staffed, pet-friendly, accessible. Bring the go-bag, bedding if you can carry it, and patience; you will be sleeping on a cot in a gym with hundreds of others. Check which centers are open at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311. Confirm via 311 or the finder at the time; centers change with each emergency.
  4. Your car, if you have one, parked well outside the zone. Never in a garage, never below ground, never with the engine running while you sleep.
  5. A tent or tarp. Last resort, for a night, when everything above has failed.
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Evacuation orders are given by zone (zone 1 first). When your zone is ordered to leave, leave early and by public transit if you can; do not wait for the storm to start. Trains and buses may be suspended before the worst weather, and streets in the zone flood before the water reaches your building.

Evacuation centers are opened by the city when an order is issued and are shown on the finder at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane. They accept pets. Call 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115) if you cannot find one or cannot get there.

Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 now so the order reaches you by text. Text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts.

Tarp, cordage and a dry sleeping system

If you end up outdoors for a night, the enemy is not cold air; it is wet ground and wind. The order of protection is: something under you, something over you, something between you and the wind.

📊 FIGURE — Under, over and around: the improvised tarp shelter
Side view: a layer under you, dry layers over you, and the tarp raised on the sheltered side with its wind-side edge on the ground. The boxes list what the lesson names for each layer.
  • Under you: a garbage bag, a folded tarp, cardboard, a foam mat. Never bare ground or concrete; it drains heat all night.
  • Over you: an emergency blanket or sleeping bag, dry clothes, a hat.
  • Around you: a tarp tied to two fixed points with cordage, one edge on the ground on the wind side, the other edge raised. Practise tying two knots you can do in the dark: a bowline for a fixed loop and two half hitches to tie off.
  • Stay dry. Wet clothes are a hypothermia risk even in summer (Section 2 signs).
  • Stay near other people and lit areas. Ask a police officer or fire station where you can go; they will point you to a shelter.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Sleeping in a park because it seems simpler than a shelter. New York City parks are closed overnight and camping there is not permitted under the park rules as generally cited (confirm the exact hours below); you can be woken and moved, and you are alone in the dark with your belongings. A tent in a park is a last resort, for a night, when every option above has failed. It is never the plan.

The evacuation center is not a homeless shelter, not a police station and not a hospital. It is a gym with cots, food, charging and staff who can connect you to help. Go.

  • Put a backpack by the door tonight with a flashlight, a whistle, a bottle of water and your phone charger. Cost: nothing you do not already own.
  • Photograph your ID, lease, insurance card and prescription labels; print copies into a zip bag in the bag.
  • Text two people outside your zone and ask: if my zone is evacuated, can I come to you?
  • Withdraw 60 to 100 dollars in small bills and put it in the bag; do not spend it.
  • Add a week of your medicines, a manual can opener and a paper subway map.

Do this first: look up your home address at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane (or call 311) and write your zone number on the inside of your front door. It matters because the city orders evacuations by zone number, and the subway that would carry you out is shut down hours before the wind arrives. If you do not know your zone, you cannot know whether an order is about you.

\n

What the six zones mean

\n

New York City Emergency Management (NYCEM) divides the parts of the city that can flood from storm surge into six hurricane evacuation zones. The zones were changed from the old letters A, B and C to the numbers 1 to 6 in 2013. Zone 1 is the most likely to flood; zone 6 would flood only in the most severe and unlikely hurricane.

📊 FIGURE — The six evacuation zones from highest to lowest surge risk
Zone 1, nearest the water, floods in any hurricane and is evacuated first; zone 6 only in the most severe storm. Outside all six, storm surge is not the problem, so you stay home unless told otherwise.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ZoneRisk of storm-surge floodingWho is told to leave
1Highest — all low-lying coastal areas that could flood from any hurricane making landfall near the cityFirst, in any hurricane evacuation
2HighWhen the storm is stronger or the track is worse
3Moderate-highAs above
4ModerateAs above
5LowerOnly in a severe storm
6Lowest — only the most severe and unlikely hurricane scenariosLast
No zoneNot expected to flood from storm surgeStay home and shelter in place unless told otherwise
\n

The city decides which zones to evacuate for each real storm, from zone 1 upward, based on the strength and track of that storm. An order can cover zone 1 alone, or zones 1 to 3, or more. It is never \"everyone leave\".

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Hurricane evacuation zone: an area of New York City ranked 1 (highest risk) to 6 (lowest risk) by how likely it is to flood from storm surge — the wall of sea water a hurricane pushes on to land. The zones are about sea water, not rain. A street outside every zone can still flood from rain, as it did during Hurricane Ida in September 2021.

\n

Look up your address now

\n
    \n
  • Web: finder.nyc.gov/hurricane (the Hurricane Evacuation Zone Finder) or nyc.gov/knowyourzone. Type the address; it tells you the zone and shows evacuation centers.
    • \n
  • Phone: call 311. Video Relay Service users call 212-639-9675; TTY (text telephone) users call 212-504-4115.
    • \n
  • Look up three addresses: home, work, and the friend or relative you would go to. A friend who is also in zone 1 is not a safe place to go.
    • \n
  • Read the zone off the finder, not off memory of the old letter system. The letters A, B and C have not been used since 2013.
    • \n
\n

What an evacuation order means

\n

When a storm threatens, the city names the zones that must leave. The order comes through Notify NYC, the news, Wireless Emergency Alerts on your phone, and police loudspeakers. When your zone is named:

\n
    \n
  1. Leave as soon as the order is issued — not when the rain starts. The Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) hurricane plan shuts the subway and buses down before sustained winds of 39 mph arrive, and a full shutdown takes about eight hours. During Hurricane Sandy in October 2012 the shutdown began at 7 p.m. on the Sunday and all service had stopped by 3 a.m. Monday, before the storm reached the city.
    2. \n
  2. Go to a friend or relative outside every evacuation zone first. An evacuation center is for people with nowhere else to go.
    3. \n
  3. If you need accessible transport to get out, call 311 as soon as the order is issued; the city arranges it.
    4. \n
  4. Take your Go Bag (see the evacuation-center lesson), your medication, your phone charger and your pet.
    5. \n
\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Evacuation is ordered by zone number. Zone 1 leaves first. If your zone is not named, stay home unless the city says otherwise — roads and centers are needed for the people who must move.

\n

Why leaving early is the whole game

\n

Storm surge does not rise like a bathtub. It comes in fast, at night, with the power out. Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021 was not even a surge event, only rain, yet it killed 14 people in New York City; 10 of them drowned in basement apartments. Rain fell at 3.5 inches per hour, about double the 1.75 inches per hour the sewers were designed for. Water that fills a basement stairwell traps the door shut.

\n
    \n
  • Basement or ground-floor apartment in any zone: leave the moment an order is issued for your zone, and leave for heavy-rain warnings too, even with no order. Go upstairs to a neighbour if you cannot get out of the building.
    • \n
  • High-rise: during the 14 August 2003 blackout, high-rises lost water pressure because the pumps stopped. When the power fails you may have no water, no elevator and no working intercom. That is why the order says leave, not \"stay high up\".
    • \n
  • Elevators: do not use them once flooding or a power failure has started; you can be trapped between floors.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting \"to see how bad it gets\" is the mistake that kills people. By the time the water is in the street the subway has been closed for hours, the buses have stopped, the bridges may be closed to high winds, and rescue crews cannot reach you. Leave when the order is issued, in daylight if you can.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Your zone is not your neighbourhood name or your flood-insurance map; it is the number the finder gives for your exact address. Two buildings on the same block can be in different zones. NYCEM prints the zone map in a yearly hurricane guide (the 2025 edition is a PDF on nyc.gov) — the finder is always more current than a printed map.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

During Hurricane Sandy (2012) the city ordered the mandatory evacuation of what was then \"Zone A\", a little under 400,000 people, the day before the storm. I could not open the source pages today, so confirm before you rely on this figure — the lesson that matters is that the order came a full day early and people who waited were caught by the surge.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Look up your home, work and \"go-to\" addresses at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane and write the zone numbers on a card by the door (free, 5 minutes).
  • Save 311, 212-639-9675 (video relay) and 212-504-4115 (TTY) in your phone under \"NYC zone\".

Evacuation center, shelter, and what happens when you arrive

\n

The words matter. In New York City's plan a hurricane evacuation center is the building you walk or ride to; the NYC Open Data description says people who need shelter are \"processed at a hurricane evacuation center and then transported to a hurricane shelter\". Follow the arrows: the order names your zone, you find the center that is open now, pack, register at the center, and the city transports you on to a hurricane shelter if you need a bed.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Hurricane evacuation center: a public building, usually a school or college, that the city opens when it issues an evacuation order. You register there; if you need a place to sleep, the city moves you from the center to a hurricane shelter. All are pet-friendly and have accessible facilities.

Service animals and pets are welcome in all NYC shelters. Pets are kept in a separate area, so bring the carrier; a loose cat cannot be admitted to a shared room. Do this first: if your apartment is dangerously hot and you cannot cool it, or dangerously cold and the heat is off, call 311 and ask for the nearest open cooling center or, in winter, the nearest warm place. Heat and cold kill quietly, indoors, one person at a time. The city opens free, air-conditioned or heated public rooms for exactly this, but only during declared emergencies, so you must know how to find out whether they are open today.

📊 FIGURE — Cooling centers by day, Code Blue drop-in centers by night
Left column: the heat path, from the alert that opens cooling centers to the everyday refuges. Right column: the cold path, from Code Blue to a drop-in center or intake. The red bar is the 911 line for both.
\n

Cooling centers: when they open and how to find one

\n

Cooling centers are free, air-conditioned public spaces in all five boroughs — libraries, senior centers, community centers and some NYCHA (New York City Housing Authority) community rooms. They are not always open. They activate when the National Weather Service issues a Heat Advisory or an Excessive Heat Warning for the city, or when the city declares a heat emergency on its own.

\n\n\n\n\n
Way to find itHow
Cooling center finderfinder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters (also reached as nyc.gov/cooloptions) — updated during each heat event with the sites that are open and their hours
311Ask for the nearest cooling center to your address; the operator gives the closest open site and its hours
Notify NYCHeat alerts say when centers open (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692)
\n

Go in the afternoon, when apartments are hottest, and stay several hours; bring water, your phone charger and something to read. Take an elderly neighbour with you. The person who dies in a heat wave is usually alone, older, with no air conditioning, and did not think it was \"that bad\".

\n

Libraries, malls and other daytime refuges

\n

Even when no emergency is declared, a public library is a free, air-conditioned, heated, staffed room with bathrooms, outlets and Wi-Fi. The New York Public Library (Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island), Brooklyn Public Library and Queens Public Library branches are the everyday version of a cooling center; during declared heat emergencies many branches are listed as official cooling centers. Other daytime refuges: shopping malls, community and senior centers, hospital lobbies and large chain stores. None of these will let you sleep there. For the night, you need the section below.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Code Blue: a Department of Homeless Services (DHS) emergency notice in effect whenever the temperature, including wind chill, is at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m. During Code Blue no one who asks for shelter is turned away: drop-in centers take as many people as they can, shelter intake is simplified, and more than 50 hospitals keep an open-door policy for people who need to come in from the cold.

\n

Code Blue: a warm place for the night

\n

If your heat fails, your building is condemned, or you have to leave a violent home, and the temperature with wind chill is 32°F or lower, Code Blue is in effect and you can walk into a DHS drop-in center at any hour. Call 311 first if you can: 311 can also send an outreach team to someone you see sleeping outside.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n

\n

DHS intake centers: applying for shelter

\n

Shelter for more than one night goes through an intake center. Intake for single adults is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week, including holidays.

\n\n\n\n\n

\n

Hospitals: the door that is always open

\n

NYC Health + Hospitals, the public hospital system, runs 11 acute-care hospitals with emergency departments: Bellevue, Harlem and Metropolitan (Manhattan); Jacobi, Lincoln and North Central Bronx (the Bronx); Kings County, South Brooklyn Health and Woodhull (Brooklyn); Elmhurst and Queens (Queens). All 11 have emergency and trauma services for children as well as adults. During Code Blue, more than 50 hospitals across the city keep an open-door policy. If someone is confused, hot to the touch, or shivering and slurring their words, do not walk them anywhere: call 911.

\n\n\n\n\n
What you seeWhat it isWhat to do
Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool clammy skinHeat exhaustionCool place, loosen clothing, sip water; if no better in an hour, 911
Confusion, hot skin, temperature 103°F or above, may have stopped sweatingHeat strokeCall 911 now; cool the person at once; no fluids if confused or unconscious
Shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsinessHypothermiaWarmth, remove wet clothes, warm the chest, neck, head and groin first; warm drinks only if fully alert; 911
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Sleeping in a car, a stairwell or a basement with a gas stove or generator running for heat. Carbon monoxide has no smell; it kills in your sleep. A generator must run outdoors, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, never in a garage. On a Code Blue night the drop-in center is warm, free and open all night. Go there instead.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Under city rules, your landlord must supply heat from 1 October to 31 May; if your apartment is cold, 311 takes heat complaints and sends inspectors. In a heat wave, 311 is also the number for a cooling center, and the Cooling Assistance Benefit (a free air conditioner for some low-income households with a medical need) is applied for through the Human Resources Administration — ask 311 whether the season is open.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Three things I could not confirm today; confirm before you rely on them. (1) The exact indoor heat-season temperatures the landlord must keep (ask 311 or check nyc.gov/hpd). (2) Aging Connect, the Department for the Aging hotline, is listed on a third-party site as 212-244-6469 for senior cooling options; confirm with 311. (3) Whether every drop-in center address above is current — the DHS pocket guide PDF has no date I could see; ask 311 the night you need it.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Save finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters and the drop-in center nearest you in a phone note called HOT / COLD (free).
  • Find your nearest library branch and its hours; it is your everyday refuge with outlets and a bathroom.
  • Buy a battery-powered carbon monoxide detector if you do not have one; never heat a room with a stove.
  • Write down the one elderly or disabled neighbour you will check on in a heat wave or cold snap; tell them your apartment number.
  • Learn the three rows of the heat/cold table above until you can say them from memory.

Every evacuation order, cooling center opening, Code Blue notice, water-main break and subway shutdown reaches Notify NYC subscribers first. The rest of this lesson is the list of numbers a frightened person needs at 3 a.m., in the order she needs them.

The text service runs on a platform called Nixle; it does not track your location and does not share your details with third parties.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Notify NYC: New York City's official emergency information service, run by NYC Emergency Management. It sends alerts by text, email, app, social media and RSS about emergencies and major events, citywide or by neighbourhood. It is opt-in: you get nothing until you sign up.

\n

Alerts you get without signing up

\n
    \n
  • Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) are the loud, government-issued alerts that appear on nearly every phone in an area: evacuation orders, flash-flood warnings, AMBER alerts. Check your phone's notification settings and make sure \"Emergency Alerts\" and \"Public Safety Alerts\" are switched on. They do not need an app or a sign-up.
    • \n
  • NOAA Weather Radio (NOAA is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration). The New York City transmitter, call sign KWO35, broadcasts on 162.550 MHz from the top of the Empire State Building, programmed by the National Weather Service office in Upton, New York. All NOAA weather radio stations use one of seven frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz. In an emergency the forecasters interrupt the broadcast and send a tone that wakes a weather radio's alarm. A battery or hand-crank weather radio works when the cell network and the power are both gone.
    • \n
\n

911 or 311: choose in one second

\n\n\n\n\n\n
NumberUse it forExamples
911Life-threatening emergency, crime in progress, fireSomeone not breathing; smoke in the hallway; water rising in a basement apartment with a person inside; a downed wire sparking
311Everything else the city doesNearest open evacuation or cooling center; no heat; a flooded street with no one in danger; accessible transport during an evacuation; a homeless person who needs outreach; your evacuation zone
311 by Video Relay ServiceDeaf and hard-of-hearing callers212-639-9675
311 by TTYText-telephone users212-504-4115
\n

If you are not sure whether it is a 911 call, it is. Dispatchers would rather redirect you than find out later.

📊 FIGURE — Which number to use: 911, Text-to-911, 311, Notify NYC or the radio
Work down the questions on the left; the first yes gives the number on the right. 911 is for a life in danger, 311 for everything else the city does, 692-692 to hear first, and the radio when the phone is dead.
\n

Text-to-911: \"call if you can, text if you can't\"

\n

Text-to-911 has worked in all five boroughs since June 2020, in English and Spanish. A voice call is processed faster, so call if you can; text when you cannot speak safely (an intruder in the apartment, a domestic-violence situation), when you are Deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability, or when the line will not connect but texts are going through.

\n
    \n
  1. Enter 911 as the recipient, no spaces or hyphens.
    2. \n
  2. First message: what the emergency is, your full address with cross streets, and the borough. Location from a text is less exact than from a call, so type it.
    3. \n
  3. Use complete words and sentences, no abbreviations, no slang.
    4. \n
  4. Keep your phone on and answer the dispatcher's replies.
    5. \n
  5. Do not text 911 in a group chat, and do not send photos, videos, GIFs or emoji.
    6. \n
\n

The service is free and uses ordinary SMS through your carrier, so it needs a plan with texting.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

911 for a life in danger. 311 for the city. 692-692 to hear about it first. 162.550 MHz when the phone is dead.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Turning the phone's emergency alerts off because AMBER alerts woke you once. The same channel carries the evacuation order and the flash-flood warning. During Hurricane Ida people in basement apartments had minutes; the alert is the warning. Leave alerts on, and keep a battery radio for when the towers go down.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC Emergency Management also posts every alert on the Notify NYC web page, and 311 has an online portal and an app (NYC311) for non-urgent requests. When the whole network is congested, texts often go through when calls will not: that is why Notify NYC by text and Text-to-911 are your fallbacks, in that order.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Two details I could not confirm today; confirm before you rely on them. (1) Dialing 711 reaches a state telecommunications relay service for people who are Deaf or have speech disabilities, and 911 can be reached through relay; confirm on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) page or with 311. (2) The exact settings menu for Wireless Emergency Alerts differs by phone model; check yours tonight and confirm with your carrier that alerts are enabled.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 now, then reply with your ZIP code (free, 1 minute).
  • Open your phone settings and make sure Emergency Alerts and Public Safety Alerts are on.
  • Save 311, 212-639-9675 and 212-504-4115 as contacts; put 911 on your lock-screen emergency information with your address and any medical condition.

Do this first: decide today that when a hurricane evacuation is ordered you will travel before the MTA announces its shutdown, not after. The subway is the one thing in this city that moves a million people out of harm's way, and it stops early on purpose. Everything below is about what to do when it has stopped: how to know, where to walk, what a flooded street hides, and where to get information when your phone shows no bars.

\n

How the MTA shuts down before a storm

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Trigger or stepWhat happens
Forecast of sustained winds of 39 mph or moreThe MTA hurricane plan calls for suspending subway, bus and rail service before those winds arrive
Time neededAbout eight hours to suspend the subway: trains are moved to high ground, tunnels and yards are protected, staff are sent home
Winds above 60 mphSome bridges may be closed as well
Hurricane Sandy, October 2012Shutdown began 7 p.m. Sunday; all service stopped by 3 a.m. Monday. Service came back over days, not hours
\n

Read it backwards: if the storm is due Monday night, the last trains run Sunday evening. Anyone still at work in Manhattan on Monday morning is walking home. The MTA posts its storm procedures in its weather service guide at mta.info/guides/weather-service-guide; heavy rain alone can also suspend lines when tunnels and stations flood.

📊 FIGURE — How and when the MTA shuts the subway before a storm
Top: the four steps of the MTA storm plan, in order. Bottom: the Sandy timeline shows the eight-hour shutdown finishing about a day before the storm, so the last trains run the evening before.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Sustained wind: the average wind speed over a period of time, as opposed to a gust. The MTA acts on the forecast of sustained winds of 39 mph, which is the lower edge of tropical-storm strength, not on the first gust. That is why the shutdown always feels early: it is meant to.

\n

Bridges, ferries and walking between boroughs

\n

New York's boroughs are connected by bridges with pedestrian paths, tunnels that never allow walkers, and ferries that stop in high wind. During the 14 August 2003 blackout, with subways stopped in the tunnels, most of the city walked home across the bridges. Plan the walk before you need it.

\n
    \n
  • Trace your route from work to home on a map today. Note which bridges have walkways and where the stairs and ramps are. Walk it once on a nice weekend so it is not new in the dark.
    • \n
  • Wear or carry shoes you can walk five miles in. Keep them under your desk.
    • \n
  • Bridges close to pedestrians in high wind; if a police barrier is across the walkway, do not go around it.
    • \n
  • Tunnels (Lincoln, Holland, Queens-Midtown, Hugh L. Carey) are never open to pedestrians and are the first to flood.
    • \n
  • Ferries stop before the wind reaches storm strength; do not count on one as your evacuation route.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Distances and ferry rules I could not verify today; confirm before you rely on them. Commonly quoted walking lengths: Brooklyn Bridge about 1.1 miles, Williamsburg Bridge about 1.5 miles, Queensboro (59th Street) Bridge about 1.1 miles; the Staten Island Ferry is usually free and runs around the clock but suspends in storms. Check the NYC DOT and NYC Ferry websites, or 311, before you plan on any of these.

\n

What a flooded street hides

\n

Hurricane Ida put 3.5 inches of rain an hour on a sewer system built for 1.75. When that happens water flows up out of the sewers and manhole covers lift. A flooded street in New York is not a puddle; it is an opaque brown surface over:

\n
    \n
  • Open manholes and storm drains with covers pushed off. Step in one and you are gone.
    • \n
  • Live electrical wires and submerged Con Edison vaults. Water next to a downed wire or a humming grate is electrified for many feet around.
    • \n
  • Raw sewage. Any cut you get in flood water needs washing and a doctor.
    • \n
  • Subway stairs and cellar hatches. Water pouring into a station entrance is a river with a drop at the end.
    • \n
  • Cars that float. Do not sit in a car in rising water; get out and go to higher ground on foot.
    • \n
\n

Never enter a flooded basement or a flooded subway stairwell to save belongings. If a person is inside, call 911 and stay at the edge.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Walking or driving into moving water \"because it looks shallow\". Moving water knocks adults down at a depth well below the knee, and once you are down it carries you into the drain or the stairwell you could not see. Turn around. Find another street. Nothing in the water is worth it.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The National Weather Service \"Turn Around Don't Drown\" campaign says six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet and about twelve inches can carry away a small car; I could not open weather.gov today, so confirm before you rely on the numbers. The rule that does not need a number: do not enter moving water.

\n

Rallying points and a plan that works without a phone

\n
    \n
  1. Pick a near meeting place (outside your building, across the street) for a fire or a gas leak.
    2. \n
  2. Pick a far meeting place outside every evacuation zone: a friend's apartment, a specific library branch, a named evacuation center from the finder. Write it down for everyone in your household.
    3. \n
  3. Pick an out-of-city contact, someone in another state. When local circuits are jammed, a text to another state often gets through when a call across the street does not. Everyone checks in with that person.
    4. \n
  4. Agree on a time rule: \"if the subway is shut and we cannot reach each other, we both go to the far place by dark.\"
    5. \n
\n

Information when the network is down

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SourceWhat it gives youNeeds
NOAA Weather Radio KWO35, 162.550 MHzWarnings and official statements, with an alarm toneBattery or hand-crank radio
AM/FM news radioEvacuation orders, transit status, which bridges are openAny battery radio, or a car radio
Notify NYC by textShort official alerts; text often works when voice does notAny signal at all
311 by phoneOpen centers, transport, zone lookupsA working line
MTA alerts and mta.infoLine-by-line service statusData
Your building's front door and lobbyNotices from the super, the block association, NYPDNothing
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The MTA, NYC Emergency Management and Con Edison all put out alerts; Notify NYC gathers the ones that matter. In a citywide event the police also drive slowly through evacuation zones with loudspeakers. If you hear one, you are being told to leave. Do not wait for a text to confirm it.

\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Walk your work-to-home route once this month and time it; write the time on your evacuation card (free).
  • Put a pair of walking shoes and a small bottle of water at work.
  • Agree a near meeting place, a far meeting place and an out-of-state contact with your household or closest friend; text it to them today.
  • Buy a battery AM/FM radio if the weather radio you bought for the alerts lesson does not have one.

  • Look at a map of the bridge walkways nearest home and note which one is your backup if the first is closed.
\n

Before you touch anyone, look at the scene for two seconds: fire, smoke, traffic, a downed wire, a person who might hurt you. If it is not safe, you do not go in — you call 911 from the doorway. Then check the person, call 911 (or send a specific person to call), and give care until help arrives. That order — check, call, care — is the whole of first aid in three words. Everything else in this chapter hangs on it.

\n\n

1. The kit: what actually gets used

\n

A first-aid kit is not a pharmacy. It is the small set of things that stop bleeding, cover wounds and keep you from spreading germs. The American Red Cross publishes a minimum contents list; the items below come from it, cheapest and most-used first. Keep the kit where you can find it in the dark: one place, always the same place.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ItemWhy it matters
Nitrile or vinyl gloves (several pairs, latex-free)Blood carries disease. Gloves first, every time.
Gauze pads (3×3 and 4×4 inch) and two 5×9 inch trauma padsTo press on a bleeding wound and to pack a deep one.
Roller gauze (3 and 4 inch) and cloth tapeHolds a dressing on so you can free your hands.
Adhesive bandages, assorted sizesSmall cuts. The most-used item.
Two triangular bandages and safety pinsAn arm sling, or a tie for a splint.
Antiseptic wipes, triple-antibiotic ointment packetsClean small wounds after the bleeding stops.
Scissors, tweezers, instant cold pack, emergency blanketCut clothing, remove splinters, cool a sprain, keep someone warm.
CPR face shield with one-way valveLets you give rescue breaths safely.
Hand sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol)When there is no water to wash.
A printed first-aid guideYour phone may be dead.
\n

Add a tourniquet (a real one, such as a CAT or SOF-T, not a belt) once you have taken a Stop the Bleed class. Add your own daily medications (section 4) and a copy of your medical card. Check the kit twice a year; replace what you used the same week.

\n\n

2. Check, call, care

\n
    \n
  1. Check the scene. Is it safe for you? What happened? How many people are hurt?
    2. \n
  2. Check the person. Tap the shoulder and shout, “Are you OK?” Look for breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not breathing.
    3. \n
  3. Call 911. If you are alone with an adult who is not breathing, call first, put the phone on speaker, and start CPR. If others are there, point at one person: “You, in the red jacket, call 911 and come back.” Unassigned jobs do not get done.
    4. \n
  4. Care. The dispatcher will tell you what to do. Stay on the line. Do not hang up until they say so.
    5. \n
\n

Tell 911: the exact address, the floor and apartment number, the door buzzer code, and the nearest cross street. Then send someone to the lobby to hold the door and the elevator for the medics. In a high-rise the elevator ride is the slowest part of the rescue.

📊 FIGURE — Check, call, care, then the CPR numbers
Follow the arrows: look at the scene first, then check the person, call 911 and give care. The panel below gives the Hands-Only CPR numbers for an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Cardiac arrest means the heart has stopped pumping: the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. It needs CPR and an AED (automated external defibrillator) now. A heart attack is a blocked artery: the person is usually awake, with chest pressure, pain in the arm, jaw, back or stomach, shortness of breath, cold sweat or nausea. It needs 911 and rest, and it can turn into cardiac arrest. You treat what you see: awake and in pain, call 911 and stay with them; unresponsive and not breathing, call 911 and push on the chest.

\n\n

3. When it is 911, not a clinic

\n

Call 911 for anything that could kill or permanently disable someone in the next hour. Do not drive them yourself if any of these apply: the ambulance crew starts treatment on the way and the hospital is warned before you arrive.

\n
    \n
  • Not breathing, gasping, or unresponsive
    • \n
  • Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes, or that goes away and comes back
    • \n
  • Stroke signs — B.E. F.A.S.T.: sudden loss of Balance, Eye (vision) changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble; T is Time to call 911
    • \n
  • Bleeding that soaks through a dressing or spurts
    • \n
  • A severe allergic reaction: swelling of the lips or throat, trouble breathing, hives spreading fast
    • \n
  • Seizure that lasts more than a few minutes, or any seizure in someone who has never had one
    • \n
  • Sudden confusion, a bad headache with a stiff neck, a fever with a rash that does not fade when pressed
    • \n
  • Any burn, fall or injury you are not sure about in a baby, an older person or a pregnant woman
    • \n
\n

For a swallowed medicine, chemical or a suspected overdose where the person is awake and breathing, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222: free, 24 hours, nurses and pharmacists, help in 161 languages. If the person is unresponsive or struggling to breathe, it is 911.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Text-to-911 has worked in New York City since June 2020: call if you can, text if you can’t (for example if you are hiding, deaf, or cannot speak). 911 is for life-threatening emergencies; 311 is for everything else.

The public NYC Health + Hospitals system treats everyone regardless of ability to pay or immigration status, and does not record immigration status. Under the federal law EMTALA, every hospital emergency department must examine and stabilise anyone with an emergency condition. Do not let a missing insurance card stop a 911 call.

The American Red Cross runs first aid, CPR and AED classes in all five boroughs (redcross.org/take-a-class). One afternoon is enough to be useful for the rest of your life.

\n\n

4. CPR: push hard, push fast

\n

If an adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 911, then start compressions. The American Heart Association’s Hands-Only CPR is two steps: call 911, then push hard and fast in the centre of the chest. Rescue breaths are added only if you are trained and willing.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
WhatNumber
Hand positionHeel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone), other hand on top, arms straight, shoulders over hands
Rate100 to 120 compressions per minute
Depth (adult)2 to 2.4 inches (5 to 6 cm); let the chest come all the way back up
Ratio if giving breaths30 compressions, then 2 breaths, repeat
Stop whenThe person breathes or moves, an AED is ready to analyse, medics take over, or you physically cannot continue
\n

Compressions are tiring. Swap with another person when you tire, with as little pause as possible. If an AED is nearby (many lobbies, gyms, subway stations and offices have one), open it and follow the voice prompts; it will not shock someone who does not need it.

\n\n

5. Choking

\n

Ask, “Are you choking?” If the person can cough or speak, encourage them to keep coughing and do nothing else. If they cannot breathe, cough or speak, or their lips are turning blue, act: the Red Cross method is five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts, repeated until the object comes out or the person goes limp.

\n
    \n
  1. Five back blows. Stand to the side and slightly behind. Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward. Hit firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, each blow separate.
    2. \n
  2. Five abdominal thrusts. Stand behind, one foot between their feet. Find the navel with two fingers; make a fist with the other hand and place the thumb side just above your fingers. Cover the fist with your hand and pull sharply inward and upward, five times.
    3. \n
  3. Repeat five and five until they can cough, speak or breathe. If they become unresponsive, lower them to the floor, call 911, and start CPR — look in the mouth before giving breaths and remove anything you can see.
    4. \n
\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Babies under 1 year and pregnant or very large adults need a different technique (back blows with chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts). I could not verify the exact steps from a Red Cross page in this search, so confirm before you rely on this: read the Red Cross “Infant Choking” page at redcross.org or, better, take a class. If it happens now and you are unsure, call 911 and do what the dispatcher says.

\n\n

6. The recovery position

\n

Someone who is unresponsive but breathing (drunk, after a seizure, after fainting) can choke on vomit if left on their back. Roll them on their side so fluid drains out of the mouth. Kneel beside them, pull the far knee up so the foot is flat on the floor, put one hand on that knee and the other protecting the head, and gently pull the knee toward you to roll them onto their side. The bent knee keeps them from rolling onto their stomach. Check breathing every minute until help arrives. Do not use it if you suspect a neck or back injury (a fall from height, a car crash): keep the head still instead and wait for 911.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

“Let’s wait and see.” Brain cells start dying within minutes without oxygen. Bystander CPR started at once can double or triple the chance of surviving cardiac arrest; every minute of waiting for someone more qualified takes that away. Fear of doing it wrong, of breaking a rib, of the ambulance bill or of a cough that turns out to be nothing has killed more people than bad CPR ever has. If in doubt, call 911 and push on the chest.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS
  • Check, call, care — in that order.
  • Not breathing: 911, then 100–120 pushes a minute, 2–2.4 inches deep, and do not stop.
  • Choking and cannot speak: 5 back blows, 5 abdominal thrusts, repeat.
  • Breathing but unresponsive: recovery position, watch the breathing.
  • Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 for anyone awake and breathing; 911 for everyone else.
\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Save 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Control) in your phone as “Poison” tonight. Free.
  • Write your building address, floor, apartment and buzzer code on a card by the door, so a visitor can read it to 911.
  • Watch the American Heart Association’s 90-second Hands-Only CPR video and press on a cushion at 100–120 a minute until it feels natural.
  • Buy or build the kit above (about $25–$40); add gloves and two trauma pads first if the budget is tight.
  • Find the nearest AED: your lobby, gym, office and the station you use. Ask the super.
  • Book a Red Cross first aid/CPR/AED class this month.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Checked 26 September 2026.

  • American Red Cross, “CPR Steps” — redcross.org/take-a-class/cpr/performing-cpr/cpr-steps
  • American Heart Association, “Hands-Only CPR” — cpr.heart.org/en/cpr-courses-and-kits/hands-only-cpr
  • American Red Cross, “Adult & Child Choking” — redcross.org … adult-child-choking
  • American Red Cross, “Unresponsive and Breathing Person” — redcross.org … unresponsive-and-breathing-person
  • American Red Cross, “Anatomy of a First Aid Kit” — redcross.org … anatomy-of-a-first-aid-kit.html
  • American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” — heart.org; American Stroke Association, “Stroke Symptoms” — stroke.org
  • New York State Department of Health, “New York Regional Poison Control Centers” — health.ny.gov
  • NYC Health + Hospitals / NYC Health, “Open Letter to Immigrant New Yorkers” — nyc.gov/site/immigrants/city-services/health-services.page
  • FACTS.md: text-to-911 in NYC since June 2020; 911 versus 311.
