Severe bleeding can kill in under five minutes, before any ambulance arrives, so the first thing is always the same: find the wound and press on it hard with both hands. Everything else — gloves, dressings, tourniquets, the burn under the tap, the splint — comes after the pressure is on. This section follows the Stop the Bleed course from the American College of Surgeons, then the Red Cross rules for wounds, burns, broken bones and sprains.

\n\n

1. Stop the Bleed: press, pack, tourniquet

\n

Call 911 or have someone call. Put on gloves if they are within reach; if not, use a plastic bag or just your hands and wash afterwards. Open or cut away clothing so you can see where the blood is coming from.

📊 FIGURE — Press, pack, tourniquet, and where the tourniquet goes
Left: the three Stop the Bleed steps in order; go down only when the step above fails. Right: a tourniquet sits 2 to 3 inches above the wound on the limb, never over the knee or elbow.
\n\n\n\n\n
StepWhat to doUse it when
1. Direct pressureGauze or the cleanest cloth available over the wound. Press hard with both hands, arms straight, using your body weight. Do not lift to look. If blood soaks through, add more on top and press harder.Every wound, first.
2. Wound packingFor a deep wound in the neck, shoulder, groin or armpit (where a tourniquet cannot go): push gauze or clean cloth into the wound until it is full, then press on top and hold.Deep wounds in the trunk and junctions.
3. TourniquetFor a limb wound that pressure does not control: place it 2 to 3 inches above the wound, never on a joint (knee or elbow). Tighten until the bleeding stops — it will hurt. Write the time on it or on the skin. Do not loosen or remove it; only a hospital does that.Arm or leg bleeding that pressure cannot stop, or an amputation.
\n

If bleeding stops with the tourniquet but starts again, tighten it further, or add a second one above the first. Keep the person lying down and warm: a bleeding person gets cold fast, and cold blood clots badly. Cover them with a blanket or coat while you wait.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Life-threatening bleeding is blood that spurts, pools on the ground, soaks through clothing or dressings, or comes with a lost limb; or any bleeding in someone who becomes pale, confused or sleepy. That is a 911 call and a Stop the Bleed response. A cut that oozes and stops under a fingertip in a minute or two is not.

\n\n

2. Small cuts and scrapes: clean, cover, watch

\n
    \n
  1. Wash your own hands. Put on gloves.
    2. \n
  2. Press with clean gauze until the bleeding stops (a few minutes).
    3. \n
  3. Rinse the wound under clean running water. Pick out visible dirt with clean tweezers. Do not scrub or pour bleach, alcohol or peroxide into the wound.
    4. \n
  4. Thin layer of antibiotic ointment if you have it; cover with a clean dressing; change it daily or when wet.
    5. \n
  5. Over the next days watch for infection: spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus, red streaks running from the wound, fever. Any of those means a clinic today; red streaks or fever with confusion means 911 (section 5).
    6. \n
\n

A wound needs a clinic or emergency department, not home care, if it gapes open, is deeper than a quarter inch, is on the face or over a joint, is an animal or human bite, is a puncture from a dirty object, or was made by a rusty nail and you have not had a tetanus booster in the last 10 years (the CDC recommends adults get one every 10 years).

\n\n

3. Burns: cool water, then cover

\n

First, stop the burning: move the person from the heat, put out flames (stop, drop and roll, or smother with a blanket), take off hot or wet clothing and jewellery unless it is stuck to the skin. Then:

\n
    \n
  • Cool the burn under cool (not cold) running water for about 10 minutes. Cooling limits the depth of the burn and eases pain. The tap is your best tool.
    • \n
  • Cover loosely with a clean, dry, non-stick dressing or plastic wrap. Do not wrap tightly.
    • \n
  • Do not put ice, butter, oil, toothpaste, mayonnaise, petroleum jelly or any greasy thing on a burn: grease seals in the heat and ice damages the skin further.
    • \n
  • Do not break blisters.
    • \n
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Call 911 for a burn that…
Goes through all layers of skin: dry, leathery, charred, or with white, brown or black patches
Is larger than about 3 inches (8 cm) across
Is on the face, hands, feet, genitals, buttocks or across a major joint
Was caused by electricity, lightning or a strong chemical
Comes with trouble breathing, a hoarse voice or soot around the nose and mouth (smoke inhalation, section 3)
Is on a baby or an older person, or on someone who is not fully alert
\n

For a chemical burn, brush off dry powder first, then flush with running water and keep flushing while someone calls 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, until they tell you to stop. For an electrical burn do not touch the person until the power is off.

\n\n

4. Broken bones: do not move it

\n

Signs of a fracture: the limb looks bent or shortened, the person heard or felt a snap, there is swelling and bruising and they cannot put weight on it or use it, or bone is showing (an open fracture). You cannot tell a bad sprain from a break without an X-ray, so treat a doubtful injury as a break.

\n
    \n
  1. Call 911 for an open fracture, an obvious deformity, a broken thigh, hip, pelvis or back, any head, neck or spine injury, or a person you cannot move safely down the stairs. For a wrist or ankle you can get to a clinic or emergency department by taxi with the limb supported.
    2. \n
  2. Control bleeding around an open fracture with pressure beside the bone, not on it. Cover the wound.
    3. \n
  3. Support the limb in the position you found it. Do not straighten it. Splint only if you must move the person before help arrives: a rolled magazine, a piece of cardboard or a folded towel along the limb, tied above and below the injury with triangular bandages or strips of cloth, snug but not tight. Check that fingers or toes stay warm and pink.
    4. \n
  4. Cold pack wrapped in cloth on the swelling, 20 minutes at a time.
    5. \n
  5. Nothing to eat or drink: they may need surgery.
    6. \n
\n\n

5. Sprains and strains: RICE

\n

A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament (usually ankle, wrist, knee); a strain is a pulled muscle or tendon. For the first two days the Red Cross advice is RICE:

\n
    \n
  • Rest — stop the activity; do not “walk it off”.
    • \n
  • Ice (immobilise and cool) — a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for 20 minutes, off for at least 20, repeat. Never ice directly on skin.
    • \n
  • Compression — an elastic bandage, snug, loosened if the toes or fingers go numb or pale.
    • \n
  • Elevation — the injured part above the level of the heart when sitting or lying.
    • \n
\n

Get it checked if you cannot bear weight after a day, if the joint looks deformed, if numbness or tingling does not go away, or if it is not clearly better in a few days.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The Stop the Bleed course (short, and often free) is taught across the city by hospitals including NYC Health + Hospitals and by the Red Cross; find a class at stopthebleed.org. Some buildings mount a bleeding-control kit next to the AED — look for one where you see the AED sign.

In a walk-up or during a blackout the medics may take 20 minutes to reach the fifth floor. Send someone down to hold the street door open and to tell them the apartment number; every minute you save them is a minute of blood the person keeps.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Peeking. Lifting the dressing every 30 seconds “to see if it stopped” tears the clot that was forming and starts the bleeding again. Once the pressure is on, it stays on — add more gauze on top and keep pressing until the medics take over. The second deadly mistake is loosening a tourniquet “to let some blood through”. It is tight because it is working. Note the time and leave it.

\n\n
🦺 SAFETY

Blood on your skin: wash with soap and water at once. Blood in your eyes or mouth, or a needle-stick: rinse and go to an emergency department today for a blood-borne disease check. Say what happened; it is routine for them.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Put two 5×9 inch trauma pads and a roll of gauze in your kit (under $10) — enough to pack one bad wound.
  • Practise direct pressure on a cushion: both hands, arms straight, lean in with your body weight, for a timed five minutes. Notice how tiring it is; that is why you swap with someone.
  • Sign up for a free Stop the Bleed class at stopthebleed.org; buy a real tourniquet only after you have been shown one.
  • Check your last tetanus booster date with your doctor or pharmacy; if it was more than 10 years ago, get one.
  • Write on the inside of your kit lid: “Burns: cool water 10 min, cover, no butter, no ice.”
  • Put a triangular bandage (or a large square scarf) in the kit: sling, splint tie, or head cover.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Checked 26 September 2026.

  • Stop the Bleed (American College of Surgeons): direct pressure, wound packing, tourniquet 2–3 inches above the wound, not on a joint, note the time, do not remove — stopthebleed.org (FACTS.md)
  • American Red Cross, “Burns: Types, Symptoms, and How To Help” — redcross.org … learn-first-aid/burns; Red Cross Scientific Advisory Council, “Burn Cooling” advisory (2019)
  • Mayo Clinic, “Burns: First aid” (911 criteria: full-thickness, larger than 3 inches, face/hands/feet/genitals/joints, electrical or chemical) — mayoclinic.org
  • American Red Cross, “Muscle, Bone and Joint Injury” — redcross.org … muscle-bone-joint-injury
  • CDC, “Tetanus Vaccination” (adults: booster every 10 years) — cdc.gov/tetanus/vaccines
  • Banner Health, “Signs a Wound Is Infected and When to Get Care” — bannerhealth.com
  • New York State Department of Health, Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 — health.ny.gov

Heat, cold and bad air kill quietly, and they kill the people who are alone: the older neighbour in a top-floor apartment in July, the person warming a flat with the oven in a January blackout, the family running a generator in the hallway. The fix in every case starts the same way: get the person out of the heat, the cold or the air, and if they are confused, call 911. Confusion is the sign that separates “rest and sip water” from “this person is dying”.

\n\n

1. Heat: exhaustion or stroke?

\n

The difference is the brain. Heat exhaustion is a body working hard to cool itself; heat stroke is a body that has lost the ability to. Look at the skin and ask a question.

📊 FIGURE — Heat exhaustion vs heat stroke, row by row
Read across each row: the left column is a body still cooling itself, the right column is a body that has lost that ability. Hot skin plus confusion moves the person to the 911 column.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
Heat exhaustionHeat stroke (911)
SkinCool, pale, clammy, heavy sweatingHot, red; may be dry or still sweating
MindTired, weak, dizzy, nauseous, headache, crampsConfused, slurred, agitated, seizure or unconscious
TemperatureRaised103°F (39.4°C) or above
What you doMove to a cool place (air conditioning, shade, a cool shower), loosen clothing, cool wet cloths, sip water. If not better in an hour, or vomiting, get medical help.Call 911 first. Cool the person immediately and aggressively: cool water on the skin, fan, ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin, or a cool bath if you can do it safely. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious.
\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

During a declared heat emergency the city opens cooling centers (libraries, community centers, senior centers). Find one at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or call 311; confirm at the time, as the list changes with each emergency. Heat kills people at home, alone, without air conditioning. The single most useful thing you can do in a heat wave is knock on that door on your floor twice a day.

In a cold snap, Code Blue is in effect when the temperature including wind chill is at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m.: Department of Homeless Services drop-in centers and shelters take walk-ins, and more than 50 hospitals keep an open door. If your heat fails, call 311 (heat is required by law in the heating season) and, if the apartment is dangerously cold and the person is elderly or ill, do not wait: go somewhere warm.

\n\n

2. Dehydration and the rehydration drink

\n

Thirst comes late. Signs to act on: dark urine or very little urine, dry mouth, no tears in a child, dizziness on standing, headache, fast pulse. In heat, illness with vomiting or diarrhoea, or a blackout without cold water, an adult can slide from “a bit off” to confused in a day.

\n

If plain water is not staying down or the person is losing a lot of fluid, an oral rehydration solution (ORS) replaces both water and salts. Buy packets (pharmacy, a few dollars) or, if you have none, use the CDC recipe:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
Home ORS (CDC)
1 litre (about 4¼ cups) of clean, safe water
6 level teaspoons of sugar
½ level teaspoon of salt
Stir until dissolved. Sip small amounts often. Make it fresh each day.
\n

Measure exactly: too much sugar makes diarrhoea worse and too much salt is dangerous, especially for a child. Get medical help for no urine in more than 8 hours, blood in the stool or vomit, dizziness or confusion on standing, a fever over 102°F, or any diarrhoea in a baby under 12 months (section 5).

\n\n

3. Cold: hypothermia and frostbite

\n

Hypothermia is a body temperature below 95°F (35°C). It happens indoors, in a cold apartment, to older people and babies, and after getting wet. Signs: shivering (which may stop as it gets worse), exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness. A person who is very cold and stops shivering is in danger, not recovering.

\n
    \n
  1. Call 911.
    2. \n
  2. Move the person somewhere warm. Take off wet clothes.
    3. \n
  3. Warm the core first: chest, neck, head and groin. Use blankets, skin-to-skin contact under a blanket, warm (not hot) compresses. Do not put them in a hot bath and do not rub the arms and legs: that pushes cold blood to the heart.
    4. \n
  4. Warm sweet drinks only if they are fully awake and can swallow. No alcohol.
    5. \n
  5. Handle them gently; a very cold heart can stop with rough movement. If they stop breathing, start CPR.
    6. \n
\n

Frostbite is frozen skin, usually fingers, toes, ears, nose and cheeks. First sign is redness or pain, then a white or greyish-yellow patch, skin that feels unusually firm or waxy, and numbness. Get indoors. Treat hypothermia first if both are present. Then:

\n
    \n
  • Put the frozen part in warm, not hot, water — comfortable to the touch of an unaffected hand. For the nose or ears, warm wet cloths for about 30 minutes.
    • \n
  • Do not rub or massage the area, and do not rub it with snow. Do not use a heating pad, stove, radiator or fire: the skin is numb and will burn.
    • \n
  • Do not thaw it if there is any chance it will refreeze before you reach care. Do not walk on frostbitten feet if you can avoid it.
    • \n
  • Get medical care: frostbite that blisters, or any that is white and hard, needs a doctor today.
    • \n
\n\n

4. Smoke inhalation

\n

Most people who die in fires die of smoke, not flames. Get low and get out (smoke rises; the cleanest air is near the floor), and get the person into fresh air only if you can do so safely. Then look for: coughing, hoarse voice, wheezing, shortness of breath, soot around the nostrils or mouth, singed nose hairs or eyebrows, headache, confusion. A hoarse voice or soot in the nose means the airway itself was burned and can swell shut hours later — call 911 even if they say they feel fine. Sit them up if they are awake and breathing; on their side if drowsy. Loosen tight clothing. Do not send them back in for anything.

\n\n

5. Carbon monoxide: the flu that is not flu

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas you cannot see, smell or taste, made by anything that burns fuel: a generator, a car, a gas stove or oven, a charcoal or propane grill, a kerosene heater, a boiler with a blocked flue. It replaces the oxygen in your blood. People who are asleep, drunk or sedated can die from it before they notice a single symptom.

\n

The CDC lists the most common symptoms of CO poisoning as headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, and notes they are often described as “flu-like”. The tell-tale differences from flu: no fever, everyone in the apartment (including the cat) is ill at the same time, it gets better when you go out and worse when you come home, and it started when a fuel-burning appliance was turned on.

\n
    \n
  1. Get everyone out into fresh air immediately. Do not stop to open windows or to find the cause.
    2. \n
  2. Call 911 from outside. Say “possible carbon monoxide”. The Fire Department will meter the apartment.
    3. \n
  3. Do not go back in until they say it is safe. Anyone with symptoms goes to the emergency department; treatment is oxygen, and severe cases need a pressure chamber.
    4. \n
\n\n\n\n\n
NeverBecause
Run a generator indoors, in a basement, garage, hallway or on a balcony under a windowOutdoors only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away (CDC/CPSC). Even with the doors open.
Heat the apartment with the gas oven or a charcoal or propane grillPeople die this way in every long blackout. Extra blankets and one warm room instead.
Ignore a chirping CO alarm as “low battery”Replace the battery at once; if the alarm sounds continuously, treat it as real: out, then 911.
\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

New York City Local Law 7 of 2004 requires the building owner to install at least one working carbon monoxide alarm in every apartment, within 15 feet of the entrance to each sleeping room. If yours is missing or dead, tell the landlord in writing and call 311 (HPD enforces it). You can also buy a battery-powered CO alarm for about $20–$30 — the price of one Sunday brunch — and it is the one item in this chapter that works while you sleep.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Treating a heat-stroke or CO victim like someone with a cold. “She’s just tired, let her sleep it off” is how a confused, overheated or gassed person dies in the next room. Confusion is never a symptom you wait out. Sleepiness in a hot apartment, or after the generator or oven went on, is a 911 call.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS
  • Hot and confused: 911, cool them now, no drinks.
  • Cold and no longer shivering: 911, warm the core first, gently.
  • Frostbite: warm water, never rub, never a radiator.
  • Hoarse voice or soot in the nose after smoke: 911 even if they feel fine.
  • Headache, dizziness and nausea in everyone at home at once: it is CO until proven otherwise. Out, then 911.
  • ORS: 1 litre water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, ½ level teaspoon salt.
\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Test your CO alarm today (press the button). None? Text your landlord and call 311; buy a $20–$30 battery one tonight regardless.
  • Buy two packets of oral rehydration salts at the pharmacy and tape the CDC recipe inside a kitchen cupboard.
  • Save finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters and 311 in your phone; note which neighbour on your floor is over 65 or lives alone.
  • Keep a spray bottle and a small battery fan with your blackout supplies: cool water on skin plus moving air is how you cool a person without electricity.
  • Decide now, in writing, where you would go if your heat failed for 48 hours in January (a friend, family, or a warming center via 311).
  • Put an instant cold pack and an emergency blanket in the kit if they are not there already.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Checked 26 September 2026.

  • FACTS.md (NYC Emergency Management / NYC Health / American Red Cross): heat exhaustion versus heat stroke (103°F, confusion, no fluids if confused), hypothermia signs and core-first warming, cooling center finder, Code Blue
  • CDC, “Preventing Hypothermia” and “Cold-related Illnesses” (frostbite signs, warm water, do not rub, below 95°F get help) — cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention
  • American Red Cross, “Hypothermia and Frostbite” — redcross.org … hypothermia-and-frostbite.html
  • CDC, “Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics” (symptoms, flu-like, generator 20 feet from openings) — cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about
  • CDC, “How to make oral rehydration solution” (1 litre water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, ½ level teaspoon salt) — cdc.gov … ors_seasia_508.pdf
  • NYC Department of Buildings, “Local Law 7 of 2004” (CO alarm within 15 feet of each sleeping room entrance) — nyc.gov … locallaw07of04.pdf
  • Cleveland Clinic, “Smoke Inhalation: Symptoms & When To Be Concerned” — my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/smoke-inhalation

In a disaster the pharmacy is closed, the fridge is warm and the elevator is dead. The people who get through it are the ones who did three boring things beforehand: kept a 30-day reserve of every medication they cannot skip, wrote down what they take and why, and told the power company about any machine that keeps them alive. This section is about you, and about the neighbour with insulin in a dead fridge or an oxygen concentrator with no outlet — because in a blackout, you may be the only one who checks.

\n\n

1. The 30-day reserve

\n

Which medications matter? The ones where missing three days lands you in hospital: insulin and other diabetes drugs, heart and blood-pressure drugs, blood thinners, seizure drugs, asthma inhalers, thyroid, psychiatric medications, HIV drugs, transplant drugs, and anything the label says never to stop suddenly. Write that list first. Then build the reserve, one of these ways:

\n\n\n\n\n\n
HowWhat to say
Ask for a 90-day supply“Can this be written and filled as a 90-day prescription?” Many insurers allow it and it is often cheaper. A 90-day fill gives you a rolling reserve by itself.
Refill early, every timeMost plans let you refill a few days before you run out. Refill on the first allowed day, every month, and the extra days accumulate into a reserve within a year.
Ask for an emergency or “vacation” supply“I am building an emergency supply as recommended by Ready.gov. Can you give me an extra month, or an early fill?” Pharmacists hear this often; the answer is frequently yes for non-controlled drugs.
RotateUse the oldest bottle first and put the new one at the back, so the reserve never expires.
\n\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

New York law lets a pharmacist give a one-time emergency refill of up to 30 days of a non-controlled medication needed to keep you alive or keep a chronic condition stable, when they cannot reach your prescriber; and a similar emergency supply of insulin and supplies. I saw this described on the New York State Senate’s bill page and in a state pharmacy regulation excerpt, not on the enacted law itself, so confirm before you rely on this: ask your pharmacist, “If I run out and my doctor cannot be reached in an emergency, can you give me an emergency refill under New York law?” Their answer, for your specific drug, is what counts.

\n\n

Keep the reserve in the original labelled bottles (a pharmacy will refill from a label; nobody will refill from a pill organiser). Keep a photo of every label on your phone and a printed list in the kit. After an evacuation, the free Rx Open map from Healthcare Ready (healthcareready.org/rxopen) shows which pharmacies in a disaster area are open, closed or on restricted hours; it also shows open Red Cross shelters. Chain pharmacies can usually see your prescription at any of their stores, so an open branch in another borough can fill it.

\n\n

2. Insulin and the dead fridge

\n

This is the one people get wrong in both directions: throwing out insulin that was still good, or injecting insulin that has been cooked. The FDA guidance for emergencies:

📊 FIGURE — Insulin temperature limits and the blackout clock
Top: the three temperature bands the FDA describes; the green band is where insulin still works for up to 28 days. Bottom: what to do in the hours after the fridge dies.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
Rule (FDA)
Insulin in vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, can be kept unrefrigerated between 59°F and 86°F for up to 28 days and will still work.
Never freeze it and never use insulin that has been frozen. If you use ice or a cooler, keep the insulin out of direct contact with the ice.
Above 86°F it loses strength; the longer and hotter, the weaker. In a true emergency you may still have to use warm insulin rather than none — keep it as cool as you can and watch blood sugar closely.
Exact limits vary by product. Check the package insert for your insulin; when power returns, replace any insulin that was exposed to extreme heat as soon as you can.
\n

So in a blackout in July: the fridge is fine unopened for about four hours; after that, move the insulin to an insulated bag with a cold pack wrapped in a towel (not touching the vial), or the coolest room in the apartment away from windows. A 28-day clock has started, which is why you also keep an unopened reserve. The same “keep cool, do not freeze” rule applies to many refrigerated drugs (some eye drops, injectable biologics, some antibiotics): the label or the pharmacist tells you how long each can stay out.

\n\n

3. Oxygen, CPAP, ventilators, dialysis: machines that need the grid

\n

An oxygen concentrator makes oxygen from room air using electricity. When the power goes, so does the oxygen. Anyone using one needs, in advance:

\n
    \n
  • Backup oxygen cylinders from the supplier that do not need electricity, and a written note of how many hours they last at the prescribed flow. Ask the supplier for them — the American Lung Association says suppliers should provide stand-alone tanks. Watch the gauges and order refills early.
    • \n
  • For a portable concentrator: extra charged batteries and a car charger.
    • \n
  • A plan to leave: a friend or family member with power, or a hospital, before the cylinders run out. If the oxygen is about to run out and there is nowhere to go, call 911; do not wait until the person is blue.
    • \n
  • Never smoke or have an open flame near oxygen.
    • \n
\n

The same planning applies to home dialysis, ventilators, feeding pumps, power wheelchairs, electric hospital beds and nebulisers. People on in-center dialysis should know their unit’s emergency plan and the backup unit; missing sessions is dangerous, and the Rx Open map lists dialysis centers that are open after a disaster.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Register with Con Edison’s Life-Sustaining Equipment program: online through My Account, by mail, or by calling 1-877-582-6633. A doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or local board of health official must certify the equipment (Con Edison’s page says within 30 days of their receiving your form) and the certification is renewed every year. Registration gets you outreach from Con Edison during outages; it does not guarantee faster restoration and it does not replace backup cylinders and a plan to leave. Also tell the building super and the local firehouse that a person on your floor uses oxygen, and put it on the 911 call: “patient is oxygen-dependent and the power is out.”

In a blackout the elevators stop. Someone on oxygen on the 14th floor cannot walk down — which is one more reason the firehouse, the super and Con Edison should know the apartment exists before the night it matters.

\n\n

4. Medications after flood, fire or heat

\n
    \n
  • Pills that got wet with flood or contaminated water are contaminated: discard them, even in the original bottle, and replace them. If the container got wet but the pills inside look completely dry and unchanged, the FDA says you may use them until you get a replacement.
    • \n
  • Drugs exposed to the heat of a fire, or left in a hot car or sunlit window for days, may no longer work; replace them as soon as you can. For a life-saving drug with no replacement in reach, use what you have and replace it at the first chance.
    • \n
  • Powders that must be mixed (some antibiotics for children) are mixed only with bottled or purified water, never tap water under a boil-water notice.
    • \n
  • Insulin, epinephrine auto-injectors and inhalers left in a hot apartment: check the label’s storage temperature and replace if it was exceeded.
    • \n
\n\n

5. The medical card

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A medical card is one sheet, printed, that lets a stranger keep you alive when you cannot speak. It lives in your wallet, in the kit, on the fridge door and as a photo on your phone’s lock screen or medical ID. It holds: full name and date of birth; conditions (diabetes, epilepsy, heart failure, pregnancy, a pacemaker); every medication with dose and time; allergies, especially to drugs; blood thinners (medics need to know before they treat bleeding); your doctor and pharmacy phone numbers; two emergency contacts; insurance ID; and any device you depend on. Date it and redo it every time something changes.

\n

Phones have a medical ID that medics can read from the lock screen without your passcode; fill it in, but do not rely on it alone, because the phone will be the first thing to die. For an older neighbour, offer to type theirs and print two copies.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

“I’ll get my refill tomorrow.” The reserve exists because tomorrow the pharmacy is flooded, the doctor’s office is closed and the bridge is shut. Insulin, seizure drugs, heart drugs and blood thinners are not things you go without for a weekend; stopping some of them suddenly can kill within days. Equally: never share, borrow or “split” a prescription drug with a neighbour to bridge a gap. The pharmacist, Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) or the NYC Health + Hospitals virtual ExpressCare line can tell you what to do instead.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS
  • 30 days of every drug you cannot skip, in labelled bottles, rotated.
  • Insulin: 59–86°F for up to 28 days out of the fridge; never frozen; cooler than 86°F if at all possible.
  • Oxygen: backup cylinders, know the hours, a place to go, 911 before it runs out.
  • Con Edison Life-Sustaining Equipment: 1-877-582-6633, doctor certifies, renew yearly.
  • Wet pills are contaminated pills. Replace.
  • A printed medical card in the wallet, the kit and on the fridge.
\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Write your medication list tonight: drug, dose, why, prescriber, pharmacy. Photograph every label. Free.
  • At your next refill, ask two questions: “Can this be a 90-day supply?” and “What is the earliest day I can refill each month?”
  • Print the medical card (template: a plain table in any notes app). Wallet, kit, fridge door. Fill in your phone’s medical ID.
  • Buy an insulated lunch bag and two freezer packs ($10–$15) and label them “medications” even if you take none: the neighbour might.
  • Knock on doors: who on your floor uses oxygen, insulin, dialysis or a power wheelchair? Write their apartment numbers on your emergency card and give them Con Edison’s number.
  • If you or anyone at home uses a powered medical device, register with Con Edison this week and ask the supplier about backup cylinders or batteries.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Checked 26 September 2026.

  • FDA, “Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency” (59–86°F up to 28 days; never freeze; above 86°F loses strength) — fda.gov … insulin-storage
  • FDA, “Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster” (discard drugs touched by flood water; heat-exposed drugs; reconstitute only with purified or bottled water) — fda.gov … safe-drug-use-after-natural-disaster
  • Con Edison, “Special Services and Protections” (Life-Sustaining Equipment: 1-877-582-6633, medical certification within 30 days, updated annually) — coned.com … special-services; Con Edison news, “Using Life-Support Equipment? Con Edison Needs to Know” (June 2023)
  • American Lung Association, “Preparing for a Power Outage as a Medical Device User” and “Using Oxygen Safely” (backup tanks from supplier, tell the power company) — lung.org/blog/power-outage-preparation
  • Healthcare Ready, “Rx Open” (map of open/closed pharmacies, dialysis centers and Red Cross shelters in a disaster) — healthcareready.org/rxopen
  • FACTS.md (FDA): a closed refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours in an outage.

When the hospitals are overloaded — a heat wave, a flu winter, a hurricane, a blackout — the person who keeps her hands clean, treats a fever and a stomach bug at home correctly, and knows the three or four signs that mean “this is beyond home care” keeps herself and her neighbours out of a 12-hour emergency-room queue, and gets there fast when it truly matters. Wash your hands, watch the danger signs, and know which door to walk through.

\n\n

1. Hands and masks: the cheapest medicine there is

\n
    \n
  • Soap and water for at least 20 seconds (hum “Happy Birthday” twice): before eating or preparing food, after the toilet, after handling a sick person, garbage or a wound, after coming in from outside. Soap and water beat sanitizer for norovirus and other stomach bugs.
    • \n
  • No water? Hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, rubbed over every surface until dry. It does not work on visibly dirty hands.
    • \n
  • In a water outage, keep a jug and a bar of soap by a bowl; pour to wash. Save the sanitizer for when the jug is empty.
    • \n
  • A well-fitting mask on the sick person and on whoever cares for them cuts the spread of coughs and flu inside a small apartment. Open a window when you can; keep the sick person in one room with the door closed if you have the space.
    • \n
  • Do not share towels, cups or utensils with someone who is ill. Wipe door handles, the toilet flush and the tap with a household disinfectant daily.
    • \n
\n\n

2. Fever: who needs a doctor now

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A fever is the body fighting an infection, and in a healthy adult it is usually not dangerous by itself. What matters is who has it and what comes with it. The very young and the very old get seriously ill fast and show it late.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
WhoAct now
Baby under 3 monthsAny temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is an emergency: call the paediatrician immediately, and if you cannot reach one, go to an emergency department. Do not give fever medicine first and wait.
Any childTrouble breathing, a seizure, a stiff neck, constant vomiting or diarrhoea, unusual drowsiness or floppiness, a rash that does not fade when you press a glass on it, or signs of dehydration (no urine in 8 hours, no tears, sunken soft spot, very dry mouth): 911 or an emergency department.
Older adultOlder people may have a serious infection with little or no fever. Sudden confusion, a fall, not eating or drinking, new weakness, or fast breathing in a person over 65 is a same-day medical visit, and 911 if they are confused or hard to wake.
Any adultFever with a stiff neck and severe headache, with confusion, with trouble breathing, with a spreading rash, after a recent surgery or in someone on chemotherapy, or a fever over 102°F with vomiting and diarrhoea: emergency department. Fever with a cough and aches, drinking well, thinking clearly: rest, fluids, a clinic or a virtual visit if not better in three days.
\n

Fever medicines (acetaminophen or ibuprofen) are used only as the package label directs, for the age and weight on the label. Never give aspirin to a child or teenager for a fever. If in doubt about a dose for a child, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222: they answer dosing questions, free, at any hour.

\n\n

3. Diarrhoea and vomiting: the fluid problem

\n

In a disaster, stomach bugs spread through shared toilets, dirty water and unwashed hands, and the danger is dehydration, not the bug. Small sips of water or oral rehydration solution every few minutes (the CDC recipe: 1 litre clean water, 6 level teaspoons sugar, ½ level teaspoon salt; or bought packets) are the treatment. Plain food when they can eat. Wash hands like a surgeon after every trip to the toilet.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Get medical care for
Blood in the stool or vomit
No urine for more than 8 hours, or dizziness or confusion on standing
A fever over 102°F (38.9°C)
Diarrhoea in a baby under 12 months, in someone born prematurely, or in anyone with a serious medical condition
Not able to keep any fluid down for a day, or diarrhoea lasting more than a few days
\n\n

4. Is this wound infected?

\n

Every wound is a little red and sore on day one. Infection is what gets worse after day two. Look daily when you change the dressing:

\n
    \n
  • Redness spreading outward, swelling, warmth, increasing pain
    • \n
  • Thick yellow or green pus, or a bad smell
    • \n
  • Red streaks running from the wound up the limb toward the heart
    • \n
  • Fever or chills
    • \n
\n

Spreading redness, pus or increasing pain: a clinic or urgent care today. Red streaks, fever with a wound, or a wound infection in someone with diabetes or a weak immune system: an emergency department today. Confusion, fast breathing or a very fast pulse with any infection: 911 — that is how sepsis looks, and hours matter.

\n\n

5. Which door: home, clinic, emergency department, or 911

📊 FIGURE — Which door: home, clinic, emergency department or 911
Four doors from least to most urgent, left to right, with the examples the lesson gives for each. Pick the leftmost column that fits, and move right the moment breathing, bleeding or confusion appears.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
Go toFor
Home care (plus a phone or video visit)Cold and flu with normal breathing, mild fever in an adult, a stomach bug that is staying hydrated, a small clean cut, a mild sprain, a rash without fever.
Clinic or urgent care (same day)Something that is not life-threatening but should be seen within 24 hours: a cut that may need stitches, a wound with early infection, an ear or urinary infection, a fever that is not settling, a sprain you cannot walk on, a minor burn, a prescription that ran out.
Emergency department (go now, by taxi if the person can sit up and breathe normally)A fever in a baby under 3 months, a deep or gaping wound, a broken wrist or ankle, a burn on a hand or face, dehydration you cannot reverse at home, an infection with red streaks or fever.
911Trouble breathing, chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, unresponsive or confused, seizure, severe allergic reaction, a fall from height, a suspected overdose with slowed breathing, anyone you could not safely get down the stairs. The crew treats on the way; you cannot.
\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC Health + Hospitals runs the city’s public hospitals and its emergency departments treat everyone regardless of ability to pay or immigration status; by federal law (EMTALA) every hospital emergency department in the city must examine and stabilise anyone with an emergency. They do not record immigration status. If you cannot pay, ask for the financial assistance office afterwards.

For the not-life-threatening layer, NYC Health + Hospitals Virtual ExpressCare is a 24/7 phone or video urgent-care visit for cold and flu, minor infections, rashes, headaches and reproductive and mental health questions, and its walk-in ExpressCare clinics sit inside several public hospitals. Search “NYC Health + Hospitals ExpressCare” or ask 311 for the current number; confirm at the time. In a disaster this is how you reach a clinician when the streets are flooded and the clinics are dark. 311 also answers “which pharmacies and clinics are open near me” during an emergency.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

“The ER will be packed, let’s wait until morning.” In an overloaded system the queue is for the people who can wait; a baby under three months with a fever, an older person who is suddenly confused, a wound with red streaks and a fever, or anyone struggling to breathe is not in that queue — they are triaged first. Waiting because the hospital is busy is how a treatable infection becomes sepsis overnight. The other side of the same mistake is calling 911 for a cold: an ambulance tied up on a fever is an ambulance not at a cardiac arrest.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS
  • 20 seconds of soap; 60% alcohol when there is no water.
  • Baby under 3 months, 100.4°F or more: emergency, now.
  • Older person suddenly confused: infection until proven otherwise; same day, 911 if hard to wake.
  • Stomach bug: sips of ORS; blood, no urine 8 hours, or confusion means care today.
  • Wound worse after day two, pus, red streaks, fever: get it seen; confusion or fast breathing with infection: 911.
  • NYC public emergency departments treat everyone; cost and papers are never a reason not to go.
\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Put a bar of soap and a 1-gallon jug of water under the bathroom sink as the “no-water handwashing station”. Free.
  • Buy a digital thermometer ($8–$12) and check it works; write 100.4°F / 38°C on the box.
  • Buy two packets of oral rehydration salts and a bottle of 60%+ hand sanitizer for the kit.
  • Look up and save the NYC Health + Hospitals Virtual ExpressCare number and the nearest public hospital emergency department; write both on your medical card.
  • Note the birthdays of any baby and any neighbour over 65 on your floor; they are the ones you check on first in a heat wave or a blackout.
  • Read the label on the fever medicine you own and write the correct adult dose and the maximum per day on the lid.
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED

Checked 26 September 2026.

  • CDC, “About Handwashing” and “Hand Sanitizer Facts” (at least 20 seconds; sanitizer at least 60% alcohol; soap beats sanitizer for norovirus) — cdc.gov/clean-hands/about
  • HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics), “Fever: When to Call the Pediatrician” (under 3 months, 100.4°F; danger signs; dehydration signs) — healthychildren.org … When-to-Call-the-Pediatrician.aspx
  • CDC, “How to make oral rehydration solution” — cdc.gov … ors_seasia_508.pdf; CDC Yellow Book / food-safety guidance on when diarrhoea needs care (blood, no urine 8 hours, dizziness, fever over 102°F, infants under 12 months)
  • Banner Health, “Signs a Wound Is Infected and When to Get Care” (spreading redness, pus, red streaks, fever; urgent care versus emergency) — bannerhealth.com
  • NYC Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs, “Health Services” (NYC Health + Hospitals treats regardless of ability to pay or immigration status; EMTALA) — nyc.gov … health-services.page
  • NYC Health + Hospitals, ExpressCare (24/7 virtual urgent care; walk-in clinics) — nychealthandhospitals.org … expresscare
  • New York State Department of Health, Poison Control 1-800-222-1222 — health.ny.gov

The moment the water stops, do two things: fill every bucket, pot and the bathtub with whatever still comes out of the tap, and decide whether your toilet can still be flushed. A toilet that is not managed becomes the fastest way for a household to get sick. Diarrhoea from dirty hands and dirty surfaces spreads inside a small apartment in days. Everything below is cheap, fits in a closet, and takes one evening to set up.

1. First: can you still flush?

A toilet does not need the tank to work. It needs water poured into the bowl fast enough to start the siphon. If the sewer under your building is intact, you can keep using your normal toilet for as long as you have non-drinking water.

StepWhat to do
1Fill a bucket with 1–2 gallons of water you would not drink: bathtub water, melted ice, rain caught in a bucket. Older toilets may need 3–5 gallons.
2Pour it straight into the bowl (not the tank): slowly for the first second, then fast and all at once. The rush of water is what makes it flush.
3Do not flush for urine alone. Save flush water for solids. Keep the lid closed.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Never flush with drinking water. One flush is one to two gallons, which is one to two days of drinking water for one person (Ready.gov: 1 gallon per person per day). Flush only with water you cannot drink.

Never flush if water is coming back up. If water rises in the tub, sink or a floor drain when someone upstairs flushes, the sewer line is blocked or full. Every flush then comes up in your apartment or a neighbour’s. Stop, switch to the bucket toilet below, and call 311.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Tall buildings pump water up to the upper floors. When the power fails the pumps stop, so your tap can go dry even when the street mains are fine. In the blackout of 14 August 2003, high-rise apartments in New York City lost water pressure this way. If you live above the sixth floor, assume every blackout is also a water outage and fill the tub the minute the lights go out.

Basement and ground-floor apartments have the opposite problem: they are the first place a blocked sewer backs up into. During Hurricane Ida (1–2 September 2021) rain fell at about 3.5 inches an hour, double what the sewers were built for. If sewage is rising through a drain, leave the room and call 311; call 911 if water is rising fast enough to trap you.

2. When you cannot flush: the twin-bucket toilet

📘 DEFINITION

Twin-bucket toilet: two 5-gallon buckets. One, lined with a heavy plastic bag and dosed with absorbent material, takes solid waste. The other takes urine. Keeping them separate keeps the solid-waste bag dry, light and far less smelly, because urine is most of the volume. A snap-on toilet seat lid made for a 5-gallon bucket turns it into something you can actually sit on.

📊 FIGURE — The twin-bucket toilet and where the bags go
Two 5-gallon buckets: solids go in the bagged, littered bucket with the snap-on seat; urine goes in the other. Tied, double-bagged waste moves to the lidded can along the arrow.

Buy the kit this week. Every item is sold at a hardware store, pet store or online, and the whole set is cheap enough to fit a small budget.

  • Two 5-gallon buckets with lids (hardware store). Mark one SOLIDS and one LIQUIDS with a marker.
  • One snap-on bucket toilet seat.
  • A roll of heavy-duty trash bags (thick contractor bags are best) plus a roll of ordinary kitchen bags for double-bagging.
  • Absorbent material: one large bag of plain clay cat litter is the simplest. Sawdust, peat moss, wood ash, shredded paper or garden lime also work.
  • A scoop or old cup kept only for the litter.
  • Toilet paper, wet wipes, nitrile gloves, hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.
  • A third lidded container (a large lidded trash can or plastic tote) to hold the tied bags.
AbsorbentHow muchNotes
Clay cat litterHalf a cup in the bottom of the bag, then half a cup after every useCheap, sold everywhere, absorbs liquid and cuts smell
Sawdust, peat moss, shredded paperA generous scoop after every useFree or nearly free; cover the waste completely
Wood ash or garden limeA generous sprinkle after every useReduces smell and flies. Lime is caustic: gloves on, keep it out of eyes, follow the bag label

Using it, in order:

  1. Line the SOLIDS bucket with a heavy bag, fold the edge over the rim, and put half a cup of litter in the bottom.
  2. Snap the seat on. Use it for solids and toilet paper only.
  3. Cover every deposit with litter until nothing is visible. Close the lid.
  4. Urine goes in the LIQUIDS bucket. If your normal toilet still drains, pour the urine bucket into it once or twice a day and give it one bucket flush. If it does not drain, put litter in the liquids bucket too and bag it the same way.
  5. When the solids bag is a third full, or at the end of each day, twist it shut, tie it, put it inside a second bag, tie that, and move it to the lidded storage container. A bag that is more than a third full is heavy and splits.
  6. Sanitize or wash your hands every single time. No exceptions, no matter how tired you are.
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Set the toilet up before the water stops. Practise once, with clean litter, so that at 3 a.m. in the dark you are not reading instructions. A bucket, a seat, bags and litter cost less than one week of takeout and will keep you healthy for a month.

3. Where the waste actually goes for two weeks

In the countryside the answer is a pit at least 12 inches deep and far from any water. In a New York apartment there is no pit. Your plan is bag, seal, store, hand over.

  • Bag and seal: every bag is tied, double-bagged and tied again. Air-tight is what stops smell and flies.
  • Store: in a hard container with a tight lid, away from food, out of reach of children and pets, and off the fire escape and hallway (blocked exits are a fire hazard and your neighbours’ problem). A lidded trash can in the bathroom or a plastic tote in a closet works. Cooler places smell less.
  • Count it: one person, two weeks, roughly one solids bag a day is about 14 small bags. A 20-gallon lidded can holds them. Two people, two cans.
  • Hand over: in a declared emergency the city may announce that bagged human waste can go out with regular trash. Only do this when it has been announced. Until then, hold it. Ask 311 or watch Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692) for the instruction.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Do not tip a bucket into a street drain, a park, a sink or a toilet that will not flush. A blocked sewer sends it straight back into the lowest apartment in the building, which may be a family in a basement unit. Loose waste on the street feeds rats within hours.

Do not put a waste bag in a household trash chute or a shared bin without double-bagging: a split bag in a chute contaminates the whole building’s trash room.

4. Handwashing with almost no water

Soap and water is the best way to remove germs. You need much less water than you think. Make a hands-only station on day one, in the bathroom, next to the bucket toilet, and use it every time.

  1. Take a plastic bottle or a jug with a spout. Poke one small hole near the bottom or loosen the cap a quarter turn so a thin stream runs.
  2. Wet hands with the stream, close the cap, lather with a bar of soap for at least 20 seconds (hum “Happy Birthday” twice), then open the cap and rinse. A whole wash uses a cup or two of water.
  3. Catch the rinse water in a basin. That grey water is your next flush water.
  4. Dry on a clean towel kept only for hands, or air-dry.

When there is no water at all, use hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol (the percentage is printed on the label) and rub until dry, or wet wipes followed by sanitizer. Soap and water are still better; go back to them as soon as you can.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Hand sanitizer is widely reported by CDC to work poorly on hands that are visibly dirty or greasy, and against some stomach bugs such as norovirus. That matches how sanitizer is used in hospitals, but the page could not be opened today: confirm before you rely on this on cdc.gov/clean-hands or ask a pharmacist. Practical rule regardless: after the bucket toilet, if your hands look dirty, wipe first, then sanitize, and wash with soap the moment you have water.

Garden lime and quicklime can burn skin and eyes. This course could not open a safety sheet today: confirm before you rely on this by reading the label on the bag. Plain clay cat litter has no such risk and is the safer default.

5. Trash and rats when collection stops

Rats eat garbage. When the Department of Sanitation (DSNY) stops collecting for a few days, the food waste on your block is a rat buffet. The city’s own rules for rat prevention are exactly what you should follow at home during an outage.

  • Store all garbage in hard plastic, rat-resistant containers with tight-fitting lids, not in loose bags on the floor.
  • Wrap food waste (peels, bones, packaging with food on it) in a bag and tie it before it goes in the can. Rinse cans and containers with a splash of grey water if you can spare it.
  • Bring garbage to the curb as close to pick-up time as possible. Trash left out too long attracts rats. The city moved the residential set-out time to 8 p.m. in April 2023.
  • See rats or droppings in the building? Building owners must keep the property pest-free under the New York City Health Code. File a rodent complaint through 311 with the address and a description; it goes to the Health Department.
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Buy two 5-gallon buckets, a snap-on seat, a box of contractor bags and a bag of clay cat litter. Store them together with gloves, wipes and sanitizer.
  • Buy one lidded 20-gallon trash can or plastic tote to hold used bags. Label it.
  • Make a tippy-tap handwashing bottle and put a bar of soap and a hand towel next to the toilet tonight.
  • Find the drain in your bathroom floor or tub and check it after any heavy rain: rising water there means the sewer is backing up.
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 so you receive the city’s instructions on waste disposal in an emergency.
  • Practise one bucket flush and one dry run of the twin-bucket toilet with clean litter, so you have done it once.
✅ VERIFIED
  • Ready.gov, “Water” — 1 gallon per person per day — ready.gov/water, checked 26 Sep 2026 (via FACTS.md).
  • Washington State Department of Health, “Toilet Use During an Emergency” — bucket lined with plastic bag, kitty litter/peat moss/lime/sawdust/wood ash, storing tied bags away from children and pets until disposal is announced — doh.wa.gov, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • King County (WA) Public Health, “How to create an emergency toilet” — half a cup of kitty litter in the bag and half a cup after each use; bagged waste may go with regular garbage only when authorities announce it — kingcounty.gov, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • Roto-Rooter, “Can I collect water in a bucket to flush the toilet?” and Mr. Rooter, “3 Ways to Manually Flush a Toilet” — 1–2 gallons poured quickly into the bowl; older toilets 3–5 gallons — rotorooter.com, mrrooter.com, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • CDC, “About Handwashing” — scrub at least 20 seconds; sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol when soap and water are not available — cdc.gov/clean-hands, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • NYC Health, “Rats” and “Rats: Information for Tenants and Property Owners” — hard plastic rat-resistant containers with tight lids; 311 rodent complaints; Health Code duty on owners — nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/rats.page, checked 26 Sep 2026.

  • NYC Emergency Management, Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692); Hurricane Ida rainfall and basement deaths; 2003 blackout high-rise water loss — from FACTS.md, checked 26 Sep 2026.

After a flood, a sewer backup or a long outage, the danger moves from the water to the weeks after it: mixed cleaning chemicals, mold growing inside the walls, spoiled food and pests. Your first act is simple: gloves on, windows open, and one product at a time, never two. This lesson gives you the bleach table, the 24–48 hour mold rule, and the New York City rules for rats and mosquitoes, so that the clean-up does not hurt you more than the flood did.

1. The bleach table: one bottle, three jobs

📘 DEFINITION

Cleaning removes dirt with soap and water. Disinfecting kills germs with a chemical after the dirt is gone. Bleach does not work well on a dirty surface, so it is always clean first, then disinfect.

📊 FIGURE — How much bleach per gallon for water, surfaces and mold
Three jobs, three strengths, left to right from weakest to strongest; the bold line in each box is the amount per gallon of water. The red band is the rule that must never be broken.

Contact time: the minutes a surface must stay visibly wet with disinfectant for it to work. Wiping it dry at once wastes the bleach.

Use regular, unscented household bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite on the label). Never scented, colour-safe or splash-less bleach with added cleaners. Mix with room-temperature water in a clearly labelled bottle or bucket, and make a fresh batch every day: the diluted solution loses its strength after 24 hours.

JobBleach per gallon of waterThen
Make clear water safe to drink8 drops (about 1/8 teaspoon); 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) if the water is cloudyStir, wait 30 minutes before drinking
Disinfect counters, door handles, the bucket toilet, the floor5 tablespoons (1/3 cup); or 4 teaspoons per quartClean with soap first, apply, keep wet at least 1 minute, air dry
Mold on a hard surface (tile, metal, sealed wood)No more than 1 cupOr plain soap and water; scrub, rinse, dry completely
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Never mix bleach with ammonia or with any other cleaner. The gas that forms can cause serious injury or death, and it happens in seconds in a small bathroom. Ammonia is in many glass cleaners; acids are in toilet-bowl cleaners and vinegar. One product, rinse, then the next, if you must.

Open a window, wear gloves, and if you start coughing or your eyes burn, leave the room and get fresh air. If breathing becomes hard, call 911.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

One bottle of unscented bleach, one measuring spoon set, and the three rows above cover drinking water, surfaces and mold. Write the table on a label and stick it to the bottle today.

2. After a flood: the 24–48 hour mold rule

Mold needs only moisture and time. CDC’s rule is plain: clean up and dry out everything within 24 to 48 hours. If you could not dry your home and belongings in that window, assume you have mold growth, even where you cannot see it. Hidden mold makes people cough and wheeze, and can make people with asthma seriously ill.

  1. Get air moving. Open windows and doors. If you have power, run fans pointing out of the window and a dehumidifier.
  2. Remove what will not dry. Anything porous that stayed wet more than 48 hours goes out: carpet and carpet padding, upholstered furniture, mattresses, insulation, drywall (sheetrock), wallpaper, cardboard, books. It cannot be cleaned and will grow mold from inside.
  3. Clean hard surfaces. Soap and water, or bleach at no more than 1 cup per gallon. Scrub, rinse, dry.
  4. Measure the damage. If the moldy area is bigger than about 10 square feet (a patch roughly 3 feet by 3 feet), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guide for large jobs applies and this is a professional job, not a weekend one.
  5. Do not paint or caulk over mold. Fix the water source first, dry, then finish.
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Basement and cellar apartments are where New York floods land. During Hurricane Ida (1–2 September 2021), 10 of the 14 people killed in the city drowned in basement units, and the apartments that survived were wet for days. If your apartment flooded, photograph everything before you throw it out, for insurance and for the landlord.

Renters do not fix walls alone. Report a flooded or moldy apartment to your landlord in writing and to 311, and search “mold” on the NYC Health site for the current guidance.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

CDC and EPA are widely reported to advise an N95 respirator, non-porous gloves and goggles for anyone cleaning mold or flood debris, and to keep children, pregnant women, older adults and people with asthma or weak immune systems away from the clean-up. Those pages could not be opened today: confirm before you rely on this on cdc.gov/mold-health or ask your doctor. Wearing that gear is cheap and harmless, so wear it anyway.

New York City is reported to require landlords to correct mold (Local Law 55 of 2018 is the usual citation) and to let tenants file a complaint with the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) through 311. Confirm before you rely on this by calling 311 and asking how to file a mold complaint for your building.

3. Rats, mosquitoes and standing water

Rats

  • Garbage in hard plastic rat-resistant containers with tight-fitting lids; never loose bags on the sidewalk or in the hallway.
  • Put trash out as close to pick-up as you can. Residential set-out is after 8 p.m.
  • Bagged toilet waste (lesson 1) counts as garbage to a rat. Keep it in a hard lidded container, not a bag on the floor.
  • Rats, droppings or burrows on your property: 311 rodent complaint. The owner is required by the Health Code to keep the building pest-free.

Mosquitoes and West Nile virus

  • Mosquitoes breed in still water. Empty standing water at least once a week from buckets, flowerpots and plant saucers, bird baths, children’s toys, tarps, clogged gutters and any container.
  • Your own stored flush water counts. Keep every bucket and tub covered with a lid, a board or a sheet of plastic.
  • Chronic standing water on private or public land, and water in the street from a clogged catch basin: report it through 311.
  • In 2026 the number of mosquito pools testing positive for West Nile virus in the city nearly doubled against the same period of 2025. Wear long sleeves at dusk and use an EPA-registered repellent per its label. The Health Department’s page is nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/mosquitoes.page.

4. Food hygiene without a working kitchen

Most emergency stomach illness comes from the food and hands, not from the water. Keep the fridge shut and count hours.

SituationRule (FDA)
Refrigerator, door kept shutFood stays safe about 4 hours
Full freezer, door kept shutAbout 48 hours; half-full about 24 hours
Perishable food above 40°FThrow it out after 2 hours (1 hour if the room is above 90°F)
Not sureWhen in doubt, throw it out
  • Wash or sanitize hands before touching food, every time, and again after the toilet.
  • Wipe the top of every can before opening. Use a clean spoon for each food; do not eat from the pot and put it back.
  • Eat from the fridge first, then the freezer, then cans and dry food. Eat straight from the can to save wash water.
  • Keep a small bowl of the surface-strength bleach mix (1/3 cup per gallon) to disinfect the one knife, one spoon and one plate you use, after washing them with soap. Let them air dry.
  • Food waste is tied in a bag and goes into the hard lidded can at once; it is what draws rats and flies.
❓ NOT VERIFIED

CDC is widely reported to say that any food that touched floodwater or sewage must be thrown away, including packages with screw caps, snap lids and cardboard, while undamaged sealed metal cans can be kept after the labels are removed and the cans are washed and disinfected. This page could not be opened today: confirm before you rely on this on cdc.gov (search “food safety after a flood”) or call 311. Until then, the safe rule is simpler: if floodwater touched it and it is not a sealed metal can, throw it out.

5. Cleaning your body without a shower

Skin infections, rashes and foot problems start on day three or four of no washing. A daily wash with a basin uses about a quart of water and keeps you working.

  1. Warm a little water if you can. Use one basin, one washcloth, one small towel, kept only for this.
  2. Wash in order, cleanest to dirtiest: face, hands and arms, armpits, torso, groin, feet. Rinse the cloth between areas.
  3. Dry completely, especially between toes and skin folds; damp skin is where rashes and fungus start.
  4. Change socks and underwear daily even if you cannot wash the rest. Hang used ones to air.
  5. Brush teeth with a mouthful of drinking-safe water; spit into the liquids bucket.

Clothes that touched floodwater or sewage should be kept in a tied bag apart from other laundry until you can wash them in hot water with detergent, separately from everything else.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Write the three-line bleach table on masking tape and stick it to your bleach bottle; put a set of measuring spoons and a marker next to it.
  • Check that you own unscented 5–9% bleach, not the scented or splash-less kind, and check the date on it.
  • Buy nitrile gloves, goggles and two N95 masks and keep them with the bleach.
  • Walk your apartment: where would water come in, and which items are porous and would have to go? Move the important ones off the floor.
  • Put a lid, board or plastic sheet over every bucket and tub you plan to use for stored water.
  • Save 311 in your phone and write down your landlord’s email or mailing address, so a mold or flood report can be made in writing the same day.
  • Set a weekly phone reminder: “dump standing water”.
✅ VERIFIED
  • CDC, “Cleaning and Disinfecting with Bleach” (Water, Sanitation and Environmentally Related Hygiene) — 5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) per gallon or 4 teaspoons per quart of room-temperature water; contact time at least 1 minute; solution effective up to 24 hours; never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleanser — cdc.gov/hygiene/about/cleaning-and-disinfecting-with-bleach.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • CDC, “Mold” — dry within 24–48 hours or assume mold; discard porous items wet more than 48 hours (carpet, padding, upholstery, insulation, drywall, wallpaper); hard surfaces with soap and water or no more than 1 cup of bleach per gallon; areas over 10 square feet use the EPA guide “Mold Remediation in Schools and Commercial Buildings” — cdc.gov/mold-health/about/index.html, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • EPA, “Mold Course Chapter 4” — the 10 square feet threshold — epa.gov/mold/mold-course-chapter-4, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • CDC, “Making Water Safe in an Emergency” — 8 drops per gallon of clear water, 16 if cloudy, wait 30 minutes; unscented 5–9% bleach — cdc.gov/water-emergency, checked 26 Sep 2026 (via FACTS.md).
  • FDA, “Food and Water Safety During Power Outages” — fridge 4 hours, full freezer 48 hours, half-full 24 hours; discard after 2 hours above 40°F (1 hour above 90°F) — fda.gov, checked 26 Sep 2026 (via FACTS.md).
  • NYC Health, “Rats” and “Rats: Information for Tenants and Property Owners” — rat-resistant lidded containers, 311 complaints, Health Code duty on owners — nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/rats-tenants-property-owners.page, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • NYC Department of Sanitation press release 24-015 — set-out time 8 p.m. since April 2023 — nyc.gov/site/dsny/news/24-015, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • NYC Health, “Mosquitoes” and 2026 press release “NYC Health Department Detects Increase in Mosquitos with West Nile Virus” — empty standing water at least once a week; report standing water via 311; positive mosquito pools nearly doubled versus 2025 — nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/mosquitoes.page, nyc.gov press release 2026, checked 26 Sep 2026.
  • NYC Emergency Management / FACTS.md — Hurricane Ida deaths in basement apartments, checked 26 Sep 2026.

When the lights go out, reach for the flashlight you keep in one fixed place, not for a candle. Then switch off the stove, the iron, the space heater and anything else that makes heat, and unplug the electronics you care about. Leave one lamp switched on so you know the moment power returns. Do it in that order because the blackout itself rarely hurts anyone; the fire that follows it does. Candles knocked over in the dark, batteries charged on a bed, and generators run in the wrong place are what kill people in a power outage.

\n\n

1. The first minute after the lights go out

📊 FIGURE — The first minute after the lights go out, in order
Five actions in the order the lesson gives them, ending with the window check that decides whether you reset a breaker, call the super or call Con Edison.
\n
    \n
  • Get light in your hand. A headlamp or flashlight lives in the same drawer every day, so your hand finds it in the dark. Use the phone flashlight only if you must: it drains the one battery you need most.
    • \n
  • Turn off everything that heats. Stove burners, oven, toaster, iron, hair tools, space heater. If they were on when the power failed, they will come back on by themselves when power returns, possibly while you are asleep or out.
    • \n
  • Unplug the electronics you cannot replace. New York City Emergency Management and Ready.gov both warn that power can come back with surges or spikes that damage equipment. Unplug the laptop, the TV, the router.
    • \n
  • Leave one lamp or radio on. That is the city's own tip: a single switched-on lamp tells you when service is back.
    • \n
  • Look out of the window. Is it only your apartment (check your circuit breakers), your building, or the whole block? That decides whether you call the super or Con Edison (covered in section 3).
    • \n
\n\n

2. Light that will not burn the apartment down

\n

Ready.gov's rule is short: have flashlights for every member of the household, and use only flashlights for emergency lighting, because candles cause fires. NYC Emergency Management adds gas lanterns to the list of things not to use indoors. Cheapest useful options, in the order to buy them:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ItemWhyNotes
LED headlampHands free: you can carry water, hold a rail on the stairs, help a neighbourCheapest single item that changes the outcome; keep one by the door and one by the bed
LED lanternLights a whole room from a table, no flameSet it in the room where everyone gathers
Flashlight per personReady.gov: one for every household memberSame battery size as the lantern (see below)
Glow sticksNo heat, no battery, safe for a child or a bathroom overnightLast one night each; keep a few in the kit
Phone flashlightLast resortEvery minute of light is a minute of phone you lose later
\n

If you have no other light and must use a candle, follow the FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) rules exactly:

\n
    \n
  • Never leave a burning candle unattended. Put it out before you leave the room and before you lie down.
    • \n
  • Keep it at least 4 feet from anything that burns: curtains, blinds, bedding, papers, books, decorations.
    • \n
  • Use a sturdy metal, glass or ceramic holder; a holder with a non-combustible shade or globe is best.
    • \n
  • Put it out when the flame burns within 2 inches of the holder.
    • \n
  • FDNY reports that more than 33 percent of candle fires start when the candle was left unattended.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

The blackout candle you fall asleep next to. The outage happens at night, you light a candle to feel less alone, and you doze off. A tipped candle on a bedside table, a blanket, a curtain, and there is no smoke alarm sounding if its battery was dead too. In a building with one dark stairwell, a fire that starts on your floor is a fire everyone above you must pass.

Use battery light. If a candle is truly all you have, it goes in a glass or metal holder on a bare table, 4 feet from anything, and it is out before your eyes close.

\n\n

3. Batteries: one size, rotated, checked

\n
    \n
  • Pick one battery size for everything. If the headlamp, the lantern, the flashlights and the radio all take AA, any spare battery fits any device, and you only need to stock one kind. When you buy a new device, check the battery size before the price.
    • \n
  • Stock spares in the kit, in the original pack, and read the \"best before\" date printed on it. Ready.gov's basic kit lists extra batteries as a standard item.
    • \n
  • Test on a schedule. Twice a year, when the clocks change, switch on every light and radio in the kit and swap out any battery that is weak or has passed its date.
    • \n
  • Rechargeable cells save money over years, but they only help if they are charged when the power fails. Charge them the same day you charge the power bank (below).
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Battery packs print a shelf life, and lithium single-use cells are commonly sold as lasting far longer in storage than alkaline ones, but no figure was verified for this lesson. Confirm before you rely on this: read the date and the storage temperature printed on the pack you actually buy.

\n\n

4. Keeping a phone alive for a week

\n

In a long outage the phone is your map, your radio, your link to the out-of-area contact and, if calls are jammed, your only way to text 911. Treat its battery as drinking water: rationed, not spent.

\n
    \n
  • A charged power bank is the single cheapest upgrade. Ready.gov lists phone chargers and a backup battery in the basic kit. Charge it fully now and top it up on the first of every month; a power bank that has sat empty for a year is a paperweight.
    • \n
  • A car charger turns any friend's car or a rideshare into a charging point.
    • \n
  • A small folding solar panel (the kind that hangs in a window) charges slowly and only in direct sun, but it is the only source that refills itself. Never hang anything on a fire escape: it must stay clear.
    • \n
  • A hand-crank radio with a USB output gives a trickle of charge and a radio in one item (more on radios in section 2).
    • \n
  • Charging etiquette in a blackout: charge from the power bank only when the phone is nearly empty, and turn the phone fully off overnight rather than leaving it searching for a signal.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Common battery-saving settings: Low Power (or Battery Saver) mode on, screen brightness down, background app refresh off, and Airplane Mode when there is no signal at all so the phone stops hunting for a tower. These are general practice, not verified against a public safety source for this lesson.

Confirm before you rely on this: open your phone's Battery settings and check what each option actually does on your model.

\n\n

5. Lithium-ion batteries: the fire that follows the charge

\n

Power banks, phones, laptops, e-bikes and scooters all run on lithium-ion batteries. FDNY's safety rules, which matter more in a blackout because everyone is charging everything the moment power returns:

\n
    \n
  • Buy devices and batteries that carry the UL (Underwriters Laboratories) mark, which shows they were tested to a recognised safety standard.
    • \n
  • Use only the manufacturer's cord and power adapter made for that device.
    • \n
  • Do not charge overnight or leave a charging battery unattended, and do not overcharge.
    • \n
  • Keep batteries at room temperature, out of direct sunlight, and away from anything flammable.
    • \n
  • Never let an e-bike or scooter block your exit: if it burns, the way out is gone.
    • \n
  • If a battery gets hot, smells strange or swells, stop using it. If there is smoke or fire, get out and call 911.
    • \n
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The numbers behind the rules. New York City reported 268 fires caused by lithium-ion batteries in 2023, killing 18 people. In that year, 133 of the fires started from batteries that were not even charging, against 91 that were: a damaged or cheap battery is a hazard sitting still.

What the city tells you to do when power fails: use flashlights rather than candles or gas lanterns; turn off switches and unplug appliances so they are not damaged when service returns; leave a single lamp or radio on so you know when power is back; keep the refrigerator and freezer shut; stay away from downed or hanging wires; never use a generator indoors.

Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 for the city's official alerts, or text your ZIP code to 692-692 for your own neighbourhood.

\n\n

6. Generators: the machine that kills in the dark

\n

You almost certainly cannot run a generator from an apartment, and you should not try. The rule still matters, because the neighbour with the extension cord through the window, the relative in a house upstate, and the friend with a \"quiet\" generator on a balcony are the cases that end in an ambulance. Carbon monoxide (CO) is the exhaust gas from anything that burns fuel. You cannot see it or smell it.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Rule (CDC and CPSC)Number
Where a generator may runOutdoors only, more than 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away from the building
Where it may never runInside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, even with fans on or doors and windows open
Deaths in the United StatesAbout 100 people a year die of CO from portable generators (CPSC)
How close is too closeNearly half of non-fatal CO poisonings during hurricanes were linked to generators run within 7 feet of the home (CDC)
After it is switched offCO can linger for hours indoors, even after the generator has stopped
The alarmA battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas (CPSC)
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colourless, odourless gas produced when fuel burns without enough air: generator engines, car engines, charcoal, gas. It replaces oxygen in the blood. Because you cannot sense it, the only warning you get is a battery-powered CO alarm, which is why one belongs in every home that ever runs a generator, and every apartment above a garage.

🦺 SAFETY

If a CO alarm sounds, or anyone feels dizzy, sick or confused while a fuel-burning device is running nearby, get everyone outside into fresh air first and then call 911. Do not go back in to switch the machine off.

Anything with an engine or a flame belongs outside: never bring a generator, a charcoal grill or a camping stove indoors to cook or to keep warm.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

The classic symptoms of CO poisoning are usually described as headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, easy to mistake for flu. That list was not re-checked against the CDC page for this lesson.

Confirm before you rely on this: read the CDC carbon monoxide page linked below, and treat any \"flu\" that strikes everyone in the home at once, while a fuel device runs, as CO until proven otherwise. Call 911.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Flashlight, not candle. Unplug, and leave one lamp on. One battery size. Power bank charged on the first of the month. Generators, grills and stoves stay outdoors, 20 feet from any opening, with a battery CO alarm inside.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Put one flashlight or headlamp in the drawer nearest your bed and one by the front door. Tell your hand where they are.
  • Check the battery size of every light and radio you own, choose one size, and buy one pack of spares for the kit. Write the \"best before\" date on the outside of the kit.
  • Charge your power bank to full tonight. Set a phone reminder for the first of every month: \"charge the bank\".
  • Press the test button on your smoke alarm and, if you have one, your CO alarm. If nothing sounds, replace the battery today.
  • Move any candles into a box with a lighter, matches and a glass holder, and put the box away from the bed. Better: buy two more LED lights instead.
  • Read the FDNY lithium-ion tips once, then move any charger off the bed, sofa or carpet and onto a hard surface.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources checked for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • CDC, \"Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics\" (generator distance, never indoors, CO lingers, battery CO detector): cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about
  • CPSC, \"Carbon Monoxide Information Center\" and 2022 generator report (about 100 deaths a year, 20 feet, alarms on every level): cpsc.gov
  • CPSC, \"Portable Generator Safety Alert\" (PDF): cpsc.gov
  • Ready.gov, \"Power Outages\" (flashlights for every household member, candles cause fires, surges on restoration): ready.gov/power-outages
  • Ready.gov, \"Build A Kit\" (extra batteries, chargers, backup battery; via FACTS.md): ready.gov/kit
  • FDNY Smart, \"Be #FDNYSmart with Candles\" and \"Never Leave Candles Unattended\": fdnysmart.org
  • FDNY, \"Lithium-Ion Battery Safety\": nyc.gov/fdny; FDNY Smart tips: fdnysmart.org
  • City of New York, \"New Actions To Prevent Deadly Lithium-Ion Battery Fires\" (2023: 268 fires, 18 deaths): nyc.gov
  • NYC Emergency Management, \"Notify NYC: Con Edison Power Outage\" (flashlights not candles or gas lanterns, one lamp on, unplug): nyc.gov/em
