When the network is jammed, send a text, not a call. Your first message goes to your out-of-area contact and says three things: where you are, that you are safe or not, and where you are going. Then put the phone down. FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) says it plainly: after a disaster, phone systems are overloaded or damaged, and a text message needs far less of the network than a call, so it is much more likely to get through. Everything else in this section is about having a second and third way to hear and be heard when the phone is dead or the towers are gone.

\n\n

1. Text first, and keep it short

\n
    \n
  • Text, do not call. Mobile networks become overwhelmed in emergencies. Texts use less bandwidth and are transmitted more reliably when everyone is trying to use their phone at once (FEMA and FCC guidance).
    • \n
  • Text 911 if you cannot call. New York City has had Text-to-911 since June 2020. The rule is \"call if you can, text if you can't\". Give your location first, in words, then what is wrong.
    • \n
  • One message, then silence. Every message you send or receive uses battery. Agree with your people that one check-in means \"safe\" and nobody needs a reply until the next agreed time.
    • \n
  • Save the emergency calls for emergencies. 911 is for life-threatening situations; 311 is the city's line for everything else, including outage questions and where to find help.
    • \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Out-of-area contact: one relative or friend who lives outside the region, whom every member of your household texts with their status. FEMA recommends an out-of-state contact because local networks jam while long-distance messages often still get through, and because one person collecting everyone's check-ins means nobody has to reach everybody. Pick someone who answers their phone.

\n\n

2. The paper card: the plan that works when the phone is dead

\n

You do not know your own contact's number by heart. Nobody does any more. Write it down. A card in your wallet, a copy taped inside a kitchen cupboard, a copy in the go-bag. It should carry:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Line on the cardWhat to write
Out-of-area contactName, mobile, a second number if they have one
Emergency911 (call or text); 311 for city services
Con Edison1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633); text OUT to 688243 to report an outage
Notify NYCText NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or your ZIP code to 692-692
Building super and a neighbourNames, apartment numbers, phones
Doctor and pharmacyPhone numbers; your medications and doses
Meeting placesOne near home, one outside the neighbourhood, written as addresses
Walking route home from workStreet by street, including which bridge
\n

Set up the free official alerts now, while the network is calm:

\n
    \n
  • Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA). These are the loud text-like messages the government pushes to phones in a specific area: extreme weather, evacuation orders, AMBER alerts and national emergencies. They need no app or sign-up, cost nothing, and are broadcast by cell towers in a way that does not get stuck in congestion the way ordinary texts and calls do. Check your phone's notification settings and make sure they are switched on.
    • \n
  • Notify NYC. Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood-level alerts; there is also an app and a website.
    • \n
  • Con Edison text alerts. Text REG to OUTAGE (688243) and follow the prompts; you will need your account number and ZIP code. Once registered, text OUT to 688243 when you lose power.
    • \n
\n\n

3. Radio that receives: NOAA weather radio and the local station

\n

When cell service and the internet are gone, broadcast radio still works, because one transmitter reaches a million radios without anybody's network. Ready.gov's basic kit includes a battery-powered or hand-crank radio and a NOAA weather radio, and the city's own outage advice is to tune a battery radio to local stations for restoration updates.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards is a network of more than 1,000 transmitters run by NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) broadcasting warnings and emergency information around the clock on seven frequencies: 162.400, 162.425, 162.450, 162.475, 162.500, 162.525 and 162.550 MHz. An ordinary AM/FM radio cannot pick them up; you need a receiver built for them. Receivers with SAME (Specific Area Message Encoding) let you program your own county so the alarm sounds only for warnings that cover you, instead of every warning in the state.

\n
    \n
  • A hand-crank or battery NOAA radio with SAME is the single item that wakes you for a warning at 3 a.m. when the phone is off to save battery.
    • \n
  • Program it for your county (in NYC, each borough is a county) the day you buy it, and write the local NOAA frequency you receive on a strip of tape on the radio.
    • \n
  • Find a local AM or FM news station now and write its frequency on the same tape. In a blackout you do not want to be scanning.
    • \n
\n\n

4. Radio that talks: FRS and GMRS handhelds, and their real range in the city

\n

Walkie-talkies let two people speak with no tower in between. They are cheap, but the range printed on the box is a fantasy in Brooklyn.

📊 FIGURE — FRS vs GMRS handhelds, and their real range in the city
The rows compare the two walkie-talkie services on licence, power and channels. The two bars at the bottom draw the box claim of 35 miles against the half-mile to a mile you get between buildings.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
FRS (Family Radio Service)GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service)
LicenceNone neededFCC licence required: $35, valid 10 years, no test; the licensee's immediate family may use it
Power2 watts or lessHigher power allowed; any radio over 2 watts or with a detachable antenna counts as GMRS
ChannelsFRS is limited to 2 watts on channels 1–7 and 15–22 (FCC)Shares channels with FRS; transmitting on GMRS power or channels without a licence is illegal
Box says\"Up to 35 miles\"\"Up to 35 miles\" or more
Real rangeLine-of-sight in the open, hilltop to hilltop, can reach tens of miles. With buildings in the way: about half a mile to a mile in a city, and roughly 0.5–1.5 km (a third of a mile to under a mile) once a few buildings or trees block the path.
\n

What that means in practice: an FRS pair connects you with a neighbour two floors down, a friend in the building across the street, or a walking partner half a block ahead. It will not reach your sister in Queens. Plan for what it can do:

\n
    \n
  • Buy a pair of FRS radios that take the same battery size as your lights. Give one to the neighbour you would check on.
    • \n
  • Agree a channel and check-in times (for example, on the hour) and keep the radios off in between, so batteries last days rather than hours.
    • \n
  • Stand near a window or on the roof landing when you transmit; a few floors of height beats a bigger battery.
    • \n
  • If you want more range, get the GMRS licence first. Using GMRS power without it is illegal, and the licence covers your household.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Believing the phone will be there. A person who has never written a number down, never downloaded a map, and never owned a radio spends the first hour of a blackout redialling, watching the battery fall from 40 percent to 12, and then has no map, no contact and no news for the next three days.

The phone is a tool with a small tank of fuel. The paper card, the offline map and the radio are what let you turn it off.

\n\n

5. Offline maps and the walk home

\n
    \n
  • Download an offline map of the whole city now. Most map apps let you save an area for use without signal. Save Manhattan, your borough and the borough you work in.
    • \n
  • Keep a paper map in the kit (Ready.gov lists local maps as a kit item) and a printed subway map. In the 2003 blackout, the subway stopped and most New Yorkers walked home; a paper map does not need charging.
    • \n
  • Walk your route once, from work to home, on an ordinary weekend, and write the turns on the paper card. Note the bridge you would use and where you could rest.
    • \n
  • Keep walking shoes at work if you ever wear anything else. Miles on concrete in the wrong shoes end a walk early.
    • \n
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Why the walk home matters here: on 14 August 2003 the blackout began just after 4:10 p.m. on a working day. The MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority) shut down with up to 400,000 people in subway cars, limited service came back only around 8 p.m., and most people got home on foot. A New Yorker's communication plan therefore includes a walking route and a meeting place, not just a phone number.

Text-to-911 works across the city (since June 2020). Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692) and Con Edison alerts (text REG to 688243) are free and take two minutes to set up. Both stop working the moment your phone is dead, which is why the radio and the paper card come first.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Often-repeated tips that were not confirmed against the FCC or FEMA page for this lesson: wait about 10 seconds before redialling a call that fails, so the network is not flooded with repeat attempts; keep a corded (non-cordless) landline phone if you have a landline, because it may work without building power; and choose an out-of-area contact who lives at least 100 miles away.

Confirm before you rely on this: read the FCC \"Emergency Communications\" page linked below and ask 311 about local guidance.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Text, do not call. One contact out of the region. The card in your wallet has the numbers your phone would have had. NOAA radio wakes you; FRS radio reaches the block, not the borough; the paper map gets you home.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Pick your out-of-area contact and text them today: \"If something happens in NYC, you are my check-in person. I will text, not call.\"
  • Write the paper card with the numbers in the table above. Put one in your wallet and one in the kit.
  • Switch on Wireless Emergency Alerts in your phone settings. Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692. Text REG to 688243 to register with Con Edison.
  • Download an offline map of your borough and Manhattan. Print a subway map for the kit.
  • Buy a hand-crank NOAA weather radio with SAME and program your county. Tape the frequency on it.
  • When budget allows, buy a pair of FRS radios and test them with a neighbour from inside your apartments, so you know the real range before the day you need it.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources checked for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • FEMA, \"Text Don't Call\" and \"What's the best way to communicate after a disaster?\": fema.gov; fema.gov
  • FCC, \"FCC/FEMA Emergency Communications Tips\" (text instead of call; out-of-state contact): fcc.gov/emergency
  • FCC, \"Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA)\": fcc.gov
  • FCC, \"Personal Radio Services\" and \"General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS)\" (FRS 2 watts, no licence; GMRS licence, 10 years, family use): fcc.gov; fcc.gov
  • Midland Radio, \"FRS and GMRS 101\" and REI, \"How to Choose Two-way Radios\" (real-world range in cities): midlandusa.com; rei.com
  • NOAA / National Weather Service, \"NOAA Weather Radio\" (seven frequencies, SAME, more than 1,000 transmitters): weather.gov/nwr
  • Con Edison, \"Sign Up For Con Edison Text Alerts\" and \"Report an Outage\": coned.com; coned.com
  • NYC Emergency Management, Notify NYC and Text-to-911 (via FACTS.md): a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov
  • Ready.gov, \"Build A Kit\" (radio, NOAA weather radio, local maps): ready.gov/kit
  • Northeast blackout of 2003 (start time, 400,000 in subway cars, service around 8 p.m.): wikipedia.org; history.com

If the lights flicker, the hallway goes dark, or anyone says the power is \"unstable\", take the stairs. Then report the outage to Con Edison yourself (text OUT to 688243 or call 1-800-75-CONED), keep the refrigerator shut, fill the bathtub while the taps still run, and knock on the door of the neighbour who uses an oxygen machine. Those four actions cover the ways a blackout hurts people in a tall building: trapped in a box, without water, eating spoiled food, or losing the machine that keeps them breathing.

\n\n

1. Elevators: why the stairs are the rule

\n

An elevator is a steel room that only opens when the building has power and the controller is happy. In the Manhattan blackout of July 2019, FDNY reported that more than 400 elevators got stuck; everyone was removed safely, but each rescue took a crew and time. In the brief citywide outage of December 2023, people were trapped in elevators even though the power was back within moments. The reason, as reported then: elevators are sensitive to momentary fluctuations, and after a flicker the system often needs to be reset before it will move.

\n
    \n
  • Flickering lights, a brownout, a storm warning, or power \"just restored\": stairs. Do not ride until the building confirms the elevators have been reset.
    • \n
  • Carry the headlamp. Stairwells in many buildings have emergency lights that last only a short time on battery; after that they are pitch black.
    • \n
  • Know both stairwells and count the floors as you go. In the dark, floor numbers are hard to read.
    • \n
  • Neighbours who cannot manage stairs (wheelchair, oxygen, heart condition, small children) need a plan made with them in advance: who checks on them, who brings water up.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

If you are ever trapped in an elevator: the usual guidance is to press the alarm button, use the emergency phone in the car, call 911 from your mobile, and then wait; do not try to force the doors or climb out, because cars can move without warning. This is standard fire-service advice but was not confirmed from an FDNY page for this lesson.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask your building management what the alarm button in your elevator actually connects to, and check with 311 or FDNY guidance.

\n\n

2. High-rise water: the tap can go dry

\n

City water pressure alone lifts water only so far. Taller buildings use electric pumps to push water up to a roof tank or straight to the upper floors. When the power fails, the pumps stop. A roof tank gives the building whatever is in it, and then the taps on the upper floors run dry and the toilets stop refilling. FACTS.md records that in the 2003 blackout New York high-rises lost water pressure.

\n
    \n
  • The moment the power fails, fill the bathtub, every pot and every bottle, while water still comes out. Bathtub water is for flushing and washing; drinking water is the stored supply from the water chapter (1 gallon per person per day, 14 gallons for two weeks).
    • \n
  • Flush with a bucket. Pouring water quickly into the bowl flushes a toilet with no tank refill.
    • \n
  • Ask the super today (see the NOT VERIFIED box): does our water depend on a pump, is there a backup generator for it, and how long does the tank last?
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Which floors lose water depends on the building. It is often said that street pressure reaches roughly the sixth floor and that everything above needs a pump, but no figure was verified for this lesson and your building may differ.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask the superintendent or management company how water reaches your apartment in a blackout, and whether the building's fire pump and domestic pump have generator backup. If nobody knows, assume your taps will stop and store water accordingly.

\n\n

3. The refrigerator: the clock starts when the door opens

\n

The FDA (Food and Drug Administration) rules are simple and the numbers are worth memorising:

📊 FIGURE — How many hours food stays safe once the power fails
Each bar is the FDA time limit for food with the door kept shut, drawn to the same hour scale. The shortest bar is the one that matters most: perishables above 40 F are gone after two hours.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SituationRule
Refrigerator, door kept shutKeeps food safe about 4 hours
Full freezer, door kept shutAbout 48 hours
Half-full freezer, door kept shutAbout 24 hours
Perishable food above 40°FDiscard after 2 hours (after 1 hour if the room is above 90°F)
Not sure\"When in doubt, throw it out.\" Never taste food to decide.
\n
    \n
  • Every time the door opens, cold falls out. Decide what you want before you open it, take it, shut it.
    • \n
  • Eat in this order: refrigerator first (it fails first), then freezer, then shelf-stable food from the kit.
    • \n
  • A cheap refrigerator thermometer, bought now, tells you the truth about 40°F instead of a guess.
    • \n
  • Meat, fish, dairy, eggs, cooked leftovers and cut fruit are the perishables. Unopened cans, dry pasta, peanut butter and crackers are not.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

\"It still smells fine.\" Food that has been above 40°F for more than 2 hours can carry bacteria you cannot smell or taste. In a blackout, with no water pressure and no working toilet, food poisoning is not an inconvenience; vomiting and diarrhoea dehydrate you fast, and 911 and the hospitals are already overloaded.

Follow the table. The cost of a thrown-out chicken is nothing next to two days of illness in a dark apartment.

\n\n

4. Medical devices and Con Edison's Life-Sustaining Equipment list

\n

If you or anyone in your household depends on electrically powered equipment (oxygen concentrator, ventilator, dialysis machine, powered wheelchair, CPAP for severe sleep apnea, electric feeding pump), do two separate things: register with Con Edison, and build your own backup, because registration does not keep the power on.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Con Edison Life-Sustaining Equipment (LSE) programDetail
WhoAnyone who depends on Con Edison electricity to run life-support equipment, or for whom a service disruption would be a medical emergency
Even if electricity is in your rentYes: register even if you never see a Con Edison bill
Howconed.com/SpecialServices (log in to My Account), or call 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633)
CertificationA medical doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or local board of health official must certify the equipment within 30 days of your registration; the certification must be renewed every year
What you getCon Edison contacts registered customers in an emergency; priority in outage restoration; alerts for planned outages; extra protections before any shut-off
\n

Your own backup, made with your clinician and equipment supplier:

\n
    \n
  • The FDA advises people who use oxygen concentrators to prepare for outages with an alternate power source. Ask the oxygen supplier whether you need extra portable-concentrator batteries, compressed oxygen tanks that need no electricity, or both.
    • \n
  • CPAP users: ask the sleep-medicine provider now what to do on nights without power, especially with severe sleep apnea, and whether a battery is worth buying.
    • \n
  • Write the plan on the paper card: how many hours the battery gives, where the spare tank is, which relative or hospital you go to when it runs out.
    • \n
  • If a device fails and the person is struggling to breathe, call 911. Do not wait for the power to return.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Refrigerated medicines such as insulin have a limit on how long they stay effective at room temperature, and it differs by product. No figure was verified for this lesson.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask your pharmacist or the printed package insert how long your own medicine may stay out of the fridge, and write the answer on the paper card.

\n\n

5. Reporting the outage and getting real information

\n

Con Edison learns about many outages from customers. Do not assume the neighbours reported it.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Do thisHow
Report the outageText OUT to OUTAGE (688243) if registered; call 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633); coned.com/reportoutage; or the Con Edison app
Register for text alerts in advanceText REG to 688243; have your account number and ZIP code ready
Check restoration statusoutagemap.coned.com, or the app
City alertsText NOTIFYNYC to 692-692; questions to 311; life-threatening emergencies to 911
Downed or hanging wiresStay away and report them; treat every wire as live
Before power returnsSwitch off appliances and unplug electronics; leave one lamp or radio on to show when service is back
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Outage vs. your own breaker. If only your apartment is dark and the hallway lights work, check your circuit-breaker panel first and call the super; that is not a Con Edison outage. If the hallway, the block or the street lights are out, it is, and it needs reporting.

\n\n

6. What 14 August 2003 taught the city

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
FactLesson
Started just after 4:10 p.m. on a Thursday; about 50 million people in the Northeast and Ontario lost powerThe big one comes on a working afternoon, not a convenient weekend
Up to 400,000 people were in subway cars when the MTA stopped; limited service returned around 8 p.m.Have a walking route and shoes; never assume the train
All 11,600 NYC traffic signals went darkCross streets as if every car cannot see you
Outages lasted from 2 hours to 4 days by area; full power returned to NYC on 16 AugustPlan for days, not hours: water, food, phone battery, medication
High-rises lost water pressure (general history, FACTS.md)Fill the tub at minute one; store drinking water in advance
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Your building, not the city, decides your blackout. A walk-up with a gas stove and street-pressure water rides out a long outage with a flashlight and a fridge rule. A 20th-floor apartment with electric everything, pumped water and one dark stairwell is a different emergency, and the difference is decided before the lights go out: water stored, tub filled at minute one, headlamp by the door, neighbour plan agreed.

Cash matters: card readers and ATMs run on electricity. Keep enough small bills in the kit for a few days of food and a bus.

Report your outage to Con Edison every time (1-800-75-CONED or text OUT to 688243), register life-support equipment on the LSE list, and use 311 for questions, 911 only for danger to life.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Flicker means stairs. Fill the tub at minute one. Fridge 4 hours, full freezer 48, half freezer 24, throw out anything above 40°F for 2 hours. Register the machine with Con Edison and still own a backup. Report the outage yourself.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Put a bucket under the kitchen sink. It flushes the toilet and carries water up the stairs.
  • Write on the paper card: 1-800-75-CONED, \"text OUT to 688243\", and your Con Edison account number if you have one. Text REG to 688243 to register.
  • Tape the fridge numbers (4 h / 48 h / 24 h / 40°F for 2 h) inside a kitchen cupboard door. Buy a fridge thermometer.
  • Ask the super three questions: does our water depend on a pump, is there a generator, and how are the elevators reset after an outage. Write the answers on the card.
  • Walk both stairwells once with the headlamp and count the floors to the exit.
  • Knock on the doors on your floor and find out who uses oxygen, a ventilator, a powered wheelchair or cannot manage stairs. Agree who checks on whom. If anyone uses life-support equipment, help them register with Con Edison today.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources checked for this lesson (checked 26 Sep 2026):

  • NBC New York, \"More Than 400 Elevators Got Stuck During Manhattan Blackout, FDNY Says\" (July 2019): nbcnewyork.com
  • ABC7 New York, \"Fault in electrical transmission line causes brief power outage across NY\" (December 2023; elevators sensitive to fluctuations, need reset): abc7ny.com
  • FDA, \"Food and Water Safety During Power Outages\" (4 h, 48 h, 24 h, 40°F for 2 h; via FACTS.md): fda.gov
  • Ready.gov, \"Power Outages\" (fridge about four hours, full freezer about 48 hours, disconnect appliances): ready.gov/power-outages
  • Con Edison, \"Special Services and Protections\" and \"Using Life-Support Equipment? Con Edison Needs to Know\": coned.com; coned.com
  • Con Edison, \"Life-Support Equipment / Medical Emergency Survey\" (PDF; 1-800-75-CONED, register even if electricity is in your rent): coned.com
  • NYCHA Journal, \"Register Your Life-Support Equipment with Con Edison\" (certification within 30 days, annual renewal, priority restoration): nychajournal.nyc
  • Con Edison, \"Report an Outage\", \"Text Alerts\" and \"Outage Map\": coned.com; coned.com; outagemap.coned.com
  • NYC Emergency Management, \"Notify NYC: Con Edison Power Outage\" (unplug, one lamp on, downed wires): nyc.gov/em
  • American Lung Association, \"Preparing for a Power Outage as a Medical Device User\" (FDA oxygen-concentrator advice; ask supplier about tanks and batteries): lung.org
  • Northeast blackout of 2003 (4:10 p.m., 400,000 in subway cars, 11,600 signals, 2 hours to 4 days, restored 16 August): wikipedia.org; history.com; energy.gov

If the smoke alarm sounds, do not stop to investigate, dress or gather things. Get low, feel your apartment door with the back of your hand, and if it is cool, get out and close every door behind you. Smoke, not flame, is what kills most people in apartment fires, and the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) says you may have less than 2 minutes from the first beep to get everyone out. In New York City the right move also depends on one thing you must learn tonight, while nothing is burning: whether your building is fireproof or non-fireproof.

1. Know your building before anything burns

FDNY (the Fire Department of the City of New York) divides apartment buildings into two kinds, and the survival rule is different for each. Owners of buildings with three or more apartments must post an Emergency Preparedness Notice on the inside of every apartment entrance door and in the lobby, and must hand out the FDNY Fire and Emergency Preparedness Annual Bulletin every year. Your notice tells you which kind of building you are in. Read it today.

Building typeFDNY guidance if the fire is NOT in your apartment
Non-fireproofUsually safer to leave immediately. Fires in non-fireproof buildings are not easily contained to one part of the building and spread quickly. Feel the door and knob; if not hot, open slightly, check the hallway, and exit if you can do so safely.
FireproofUsually safer to stay inside your apartment than to enter a smoke-filled hallway. Stay in, keep your door shut, and listen for instructions from firefighters, unless conditions in your apartment become dangerous.
📘 DEFINITION

Fireproof building: a building whose structure is built to contain a fire to the apartment where it started, so FDNY advises residents in other apartments to stay put behind a closed door. Non-fireproof building: a building where fire and smoke can spread quickly from one part to another, so FDNY advises leaving at once if you can do so safely.

Which one you live in is printed on the fire safety notice on your apartment door. If there is no notice, ask the superintendent or management in writing, and call 311 if they will not answer.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The FDNY \"Close the Door\" notice must be posted on the hallway side of every stairwell door in your building. The reason is simple: a closed door keeps a fire inside one apartment and keeps the public hallway clear of flames, heat and smoke long enough for the neighbours to get out and firefighters to get in.

New York City law also requires the owner to install at least one approved, working smoke detecting device in each apartment, within 15 feet of the primary entrance to every room used for sleeping. If yours is missing or dead, tell the owner in writing and call 311.

2. Alarms: the cheapest thing that will ever save your life

A working alarm turns a fire you sleep through into a fire you walk away from. NFPA and the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) give the same rules:

RuleDetail
WhereInside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area (the hallway), and on every level of the home
TestPress the test button once a month
BatteriesReplace at least once a year in alarms with replaceable batteries
Replace the whole alarmEvery 10 years (the date is printed on the back)
InterconnectedBest practice: when one sounds, they all sound
Carbon monoxide (CO) alarmReplace per the manufacturer or every 5 years (CDC). Lesson 2 covers CO.

A chirp every minute means a dying battery: change it that day. Never pull the battery because cooking sets it off.

3. Fire in your apartment: get out and close the door

FDNY gives the same four steps for every building type when the fire is in your own apartment:

  1. Get everyone out. Shout, do not search for valuables or pets that are hiding.
  2. Stay low as you go. Smoke and heat rise; the air near the floor is cleaner and cooler.
  3. Use your safest and most accessible exit. Know both of them now: the front door and the fire escape or second stair.
  4. Close all doors as you leave, including the apartment door behind you.

Call 911 once you reach a safe place. Give the address, floor and apartment number, and say if anyone is still inside. Then stay out.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Leaving the apartment door open. An open door turns the hallway and stairwell into a chimney. The smoke that fills the stairs is what kills the neighbours who never saw the flames. Close the door behind you every time, even if you think you will be back in a minute.

Going back in. People die returning for a phone, a bag or a pet. Once out, stay out and tell the firefighters what is still inside.

4. Fire somewhere else in the building: stay or go?

Before you ever open your door in a fire, feel the door and the doorknob with the back of your hand. If either is hot, do not open it. Then use the table in part 1:

📊 FIGURE — Stay or go: the FDNY decision when the alarm sounds
Start at the top and answer each question. A fire in your own apartment or a hot door ends in the red boxes; otherwise the building type printed on your door notice decides whether you leave or stay put.
  • Non-fireproof building, door cool, hallway clear: leave now, closing doors behind you, and call 911 from outside.
  • Fireproof building, fire not in your apartment: stay inside with the door shut. Call 911, tell them your exact apartment number and that you are staying put, and wait for firefighters. Leave only if your own apartment becomes dangerous.
  • Any building, door hot or hallway full of smoke: keep the door shut. Call 911 and say where you are. Get to a window and make yourself visible.
❓ NOT VERIFIED

These points are widely taught by fire departments but I could not open the FDNY or NFPA pages that state them today; confirm before you rely on this by reading the fire safety notice on your apartment door and the FDNY guides linked below.

Never use an elevator during a fire; use the stairs. Elevators can stop between floors or open onto the fire floor.

If you are trapped: stuff wet towels or clothing along the bottom of the door to slow smoke, open a window a little for air only if smoke is not coming in from outside, and wave a bright cloth or phone light so firefighters can see you.

Fire escapes: it is your exit. Never store anything on it, and only a gate the FDNY approves (one that opens from inside without a key) may cover a fire escape window. Ask 311 if in doubt.

5. Extinguishers: P.A.S.S., and when not to fight

USFA says extinguishers can be useful for small fires, but alarms, a CO alarm and an escape plan are the foundation of home safety. A fire that has grown beyond the pan or bin it started in is a leave-now job, not an extinguisher job. The USFA method is P.A.S.S.:

LetterAction
P — PullPull the pin; this also breaks the tamper seal
A — AimAim low, at the base of the fire, not the flames
S — SqueezeSqueeze the handle to release the agent
S — SweepSweep side to side at the base until the fire is out
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Confirm before you rely on this, on the extinguisher label and the USFA page linked below: for a home, buy a multipurpose ABC extinguisher and keep it by the kitchen exit, not next to the stove.

Fight a fire only if all of these are true: it is small and contained, everyone else is out, 911 has been called, the room is not filling with smoke, and your exit is at your back.

For a small pan fire on the stove: turn off the burner and slide a lid over the pan; never throw water on burning oil. If the fire is inside the oven, keep the oven door closed and turn it off.

6. E-bikes and lithium-ion batteries: the fire that blocks the door

A failing lithium-ion battery erupts rather than smoulders, usually while charging. In NYC these fires became a top cause of fire deaths:

YearNYC lithium-ion battery fires and deaths
2023268 fires, 18 deaths
2024Deaths fell to 6
20251 death reported (UL Standards & Engagement)

FDNY safety tips for any device with a lithium-ion battery (e-bike, e-scooter, power bank, laptop):

  • Never charge near an exit or a path to one: not by the apartment door, a bedroom door, or a window, especially a window that leads to the fire escape. A battery fire between you and the door is a trap.
  • Do not charge in your bedroom and do not charge overnight; do not overcharge.
  • Use only the manufacturer’s cord and power adapter made for that device.
  • Buy devices and batteries with the UL Mark (Underwriters Laboratories), which shows testing to a national safety standard.
  • Never repair a damaged battery; replace it.
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC Local Law 39 requires e-bikes, e-scooters and their batteries to meet UL safety standards before they can be sold, leased or rented in the city. UL Standards & Engagement reports that deaths from e-mobility fires fell from 18 in 2023 to 1 in 2025 after the law took effect. If a shop or a delivery employer hands you an uncertified battery, that is the one to refuse.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Widely taught but not confirmed on an FDNY page today; confirm before you rely on this with FDNY or the product label: if a battery hisses, smells strange, gets hot, swells or smokes, stop using it, move away from it and call 911. Do not try to put out a burning battery yourself; get out and close the door.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Tonight: read the fire safety notice on the inside of your apartment door and write down \"fireproof\" or \"non-fireproof\" in your phone notes. No notice: ask the super and 311.
  • Tonight: press the test button on every smoke alarm; note the date on the back and replace any alarm older than 10 years.
  • This week: walk both ways out with your eyes closed once, counting doors to the stairwell.
  • This week: move every charger for an e-bike, scooter or power bank away from the door and the fire-escape window, and stop charging overnight.
  • This week: buy a multipurpose extinguisher for the kitchen if you do not have one, and read its label.
  • This month: put a new battery in every alarm with a replaceable battery and set a yearly phone reminder.
✅ VERIFIED

If you smell gas, leave now. Do not flip a light switch, do not ring a doorbell, do not touch your phone or any appliance until you are outside, and only then call 911 or your gas company. A spark from a switch is enough to set off an explosion, and the smell does not have to be strong to be dangerous. Two other dangers in this lesson give no smell at all: carbon monoxide, which kills people in their sleep, and wildfire smoke, which in June 2023 turned the New York sky orange and sent people to emergency rooms. Each has one simple rule, and each rule is below.

1. Gas: leave, then call from outside

Natural gas is made to smell bad on purpose so you notice a leak. Con Edison’s instructions, word for word in meaning:

📊 FIGURE — Gas leak: leave first, call second, spark nothing
Three steps left to right: smell it, leave, then call from outside. The red band lists what must not be touched on the way out, and the bottom row gives the number for each part of the city.
  1. Leave the area immediately and take others with you. If the leak is outside, move far away from it.
  2. Do not light a match, smoke, flip a switch, ring a doorbell, or touch appliances or electronics, including your phone, until you are away from the gas. Any of them can make a spark.
  3. Once you are safe, call 911 or your gas company. You do not have to give your name.
  4. Leave even if the odour is faint. Do not go back in to open windows or find the source.
Where you liveGas company24-hour gas emergency number
Manhattan, the Bronx and the parts of Queens Con Edison servesCon Edison1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633)
Brooklyn, Queens (National Grid areas) and Staten IslandNational Grid (gas only; electricity is still Con Edison)1-718-643-4050, 24 hours a day, every day
Anywhere, if you are not sure who your gas company is—911
📘 DEFINITION

Gas emergency: any smell of gas, a hissing sound at a pipe or appliance, or dead plants and bubbling water over a buried line. Con Edison and National Grid both say: leave first, call second, and 911 always works.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

The light switch. Reaching for the switch to see where the smell is coming from is the classic fatal reflex. Gas in the air plus one spark is an explosion. Walk out in the dark; your phone flashlight counts as an electronic device, so do not use it either until you are outside.

Staying to air the place out. Opening windows is not your job. Leave, call, and let the crew with a meter decide when it is safe.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC Local Law 157 requires natural gas detectors in residential buildings. The Department of Buildings finalised its rules on 14 February 2024 and the compliance deadline has been extended to 1 January 2027. If your building has not installed one by then, ask the owner in writing and call 311. Con Edison also publishes a page on natural gas detectors and a map of reported gas leaks at coned.com.

Save both gas numbers in your phone tonight under \"GAS\", so you are not searching for them on the sidewalk.

2. Carbon monoxide: the killer you cannot smell

Carbon monoxide (CO) is an odourless, colourless gas that the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) says \"kills without warning\". It comes from anything that burns fuel: a gas stove or oven, a boiler, a generator, a charcoal grill, a car engine. You cannot see, smell or taste it. The only warning you get is a CO alarm, or symptoms that feel like the flu:

CO symptoms (CDC)What to do
Headache, dizziness, weaknessGet everyone into fresh air now; call 911
Upset stomach, vomiting, chest painDo not lie down \"to feel better\"; leave the apartment
Confusion, passing outCall 911 from outside; the person cannot rescue themselves

The CDC warns that people who are asleep, drunk or under the influence of other substances can die from CO before they feel any symptom. That is why the alarm matters more than your senses. Replace a CO alarm per the manufacturer’s instructions or every 5 years, and use a battery-powered or battery-backup unit so it works in a blackout. If the CO alarm sounds, treat it like a fire alarm: everyone out, call 911, do not go back until the fire department says so.

🦺 SAFETY

A generator runs outdoors only, at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away, never in a garage, hallway or on a fire escape (CDC and the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission). Keep a battery-powered CO alarm indoors whenever one is running nearby.

Two clues that point to CO rather than a virus: everyone in the apartment feels sick at the same time, and you feel better when you go out and worse when you come home.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Widely taught but not opened on a CDC page today; confirm before you rely on this with the CDC page linked below or NYC Health: never use a gas oven or stove burners to heat the apartment during a heating outage, and never bring a charcoal or gas grill or a camp stove indoors. Both are common causes of CO deaths in cold snaps.

3. Wildfire smoke and the Air Quality Index

Smoke from wildfires hundreds of miles away can settle over New York City for days. The tool that tells you how bad the air is today is the Air Quality Index (AQI) published by AirNow.gov (a U.S. government site run with the Environmental Protection Agency). The higher the number, the more polluted the air and the greater the health concern. What AirNow states directly:

AQI valueAirNow meaning
50 or belowGood air quality
100 or belowSatisfactory for almost everyone
Above 100Air quality is unhealthy; the higher the value, the greater the concern
Over 300Hazardous
📘 DEFINITION

Air Quality Index (AQI): a colour-coded scale from AirNow.gov that turns pollution measurements into one number and a plain-English category, so you can decide whether to go out, exercise or wear a mask without reading science. Check it at airnow.gov or type your ZIP code into the AirNow site.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

AirNow’s full category breakpoints and its mask advice could not be opened today; confirm before you rely on this at airnow.gov/aqi/aqi-basics/ and NYC Health (call 311):

Breakpoints as commonly published: 51–100 Moderate; 101–150 Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups; 151–200 Unhealthy for everyone; 201–300 Very Unhealthy; 301 and above Hazardous.

Sensitive groups usually named: children, older adults, pregnant people, and anyone with asthma, other lung disease or heart disease.

Mask: during smoke, a properly fitted N95 (or KN95/P100) respirator with both straps on and no gap at the nose is the mask that helps; a cloth or loose surgical mask does not filter fine smoke particles. Anyone with heart or lung disease should ask a doctor before wearing one for long periods, because it makes breathing harder.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Sign up for Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts) so an air quality health advisory reaches your phone before you smell the smoke. Non-emergency questions, including where to find a mask distribution, go to 311.

4. Make one clean room

The action that helps most is to stay inside and stop bringing smoke in. When the AQI is high, close the windows, keep the front door shut, and pick one room to keep as clean as possible: a bedroom with the fewest windows is ideal. Postpone outdoor exercise, and put off the errands that can wait. Drink water and rest; smoke tires the body.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Not opened on an EPA or AirNow page today; confirm before you rely on this at airnow.gov and the EPA \"clean room\" guidance, or ask 311 for NYC Health advice:

If you have a window or wall air conditioner, run it on the setting that recirculates indoor air and close its fresh-air vent; a portable air cleaner with a HEPA filter sized for the room is the best single purchase, and a box fan with a furnace filter (MERV 13) taped to it is the cheap version.

Do not add smoke of your own: no candles, incense, frying, vacuuming without a HEPA filter, or smoking indoors while the air is bad.

5. Who is most at risk, and when it is a 911 call

In each of these three dangers, the people who die are the ones who cannot get themselves out: the sleeping, the drunk, the very young, the very old, and anyone already struggling to breathe. If you live alone, tell one neighbour or friend that you will text them each morning during a smoke event or a heating outage, and agree that no text means they call you and then 911.

  • Gas smell: everyone out, call from outside. 911 if anyone is dizzy or you hear a loud hiss.
  • CO alarm or flu-like symptoms in several people at once: everyone out, 911.
  • Smoke day: 911 for chest pain, trouble breathing, or an asthma attack that the usual inhaler does not stop.
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Gas: leave, then call. Carbon monoxide: the alarm is your only warning. Smoke: check the AQI, stay in, close up, one clean room.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Tonight: save 1-800-752-6633 (Con Edison) and 1-718-643-4050 (National Grid) in your phone under \"GAS\", plus 911.
  • Tonight: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and bookmark airnow.gov with your ZIP code.
  • This week: buy a battery-powered CO alarm if you have none, and write the install date on it; replace it in 5 years.
  • This week: buy a small box of N95 respirators and try one on so you know how the straps fit (confirm with a doctor if you have a heart or lung condition).
  • This week: choose your clean room and check which window air conditioner setting recirculates air.
  • This month: ask the owner in writing whether a natural gas detector is installed for Local Law 157.
✅ VERIFIED

Leave early. That is the whole skill. Almost every street attack, crowd crush and blackout injury happens to someone who stayed to watch, argue, film or protect a bag. The moment a place or a person makes you uneasy, move toward an exit, put space between you and the problem, and only then decide whether it was nothing. Being wrong costs you five minutes. Being right saves your life. This lesson gives you the reading skills, the de-escalation words, the crowd rules, and the honest facts about guns and looting in New York City.

\n\n

1. Read the situation before it reads you

\n

Situational awareness is not paranoia. It is a short habit you run every time you enter a new space.

\n
    \n
  • Find two exits the moment you enter a subway car, a bar, a rally, a store or a stairwell. One is the door you came in. The other is the one you would use if that door were blocked.
    • \n
  • Take one earbud out at street corners, on platforms and at building entrances. Most of your warning comes through your ears.
    • \n
  • Phone in the pocket, not in the hand, when you are moving through a crowd or a dark block. A lit screen tells everyone you are not watching.
    • \n
  • Notice the baseline. Every place has a normal noise, speed and mood. When the mood changes — voices rise, people start moving the same direction, a space empties fast — that change is your signal. You do not need to know why. You need to move.
    • \n
  • Stand back from the platform edge and behind a pillar or bench when the platform is crowded. Let the first train go if you cannot board without pushing.
    • \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Situational awareness means knowing where you are, who is around you, where the exits are and what \"normal\" looks like here, so that you notice change early enough to leave calmly. The measure of success is that nothing happens to you, because you were already gone.

\n\n

2. De-escalate: your goal is distance, not victory

\n

When a stranger is shouting, threatening or blocking your way, the winning move is the one that ends with you further away and unhurt. Nothing you own is worth a fight in a city where help may be twenty minutes out.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
DoDo not
Keep your hands visible and open, palms slightly outPoint, jab a finger or square up
Speak low, slow and short: \"Okay. I hear you. I'm leaving.\"Argue about who is right or correct their facts
Turn your body at an angle and keep stepping back toward people and lightTurn your back and run unless you have a clear, close exit
Hand over the phone, wallet or bag if demanded. Toss it slightly to one side so they have to step for it while you move awayChase anyone who takes something from you
Say a neighbour's or doorman's name loudly if you are near home (\"Luis, call it in\") even if nobody is thereThreaten to call the police in a way that sounds like a challenge
Once safe, call 911 for an emergency in progress; text 911 if you cannot speak safelyPost the incident on social media before you have reported it
\n

If someone follows you, do not go home. Walk into a bodega, pharmacy, hotel lobby or subway booth — anywhere with staff and cameras — and say, \"Someone is following me, I need to stay here and call 911.\"

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

911 is for a life-threatening emergency or a crime in progress. 311 is for everything else. Text-to-911 has worked in NYC since June 2020: call if you can, text if you can't. Texting is the right choice when speaking out loud would make you a target, for example while you are hiding.

Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) reach every capable phone near a cell tower, free and with no sign-up, when the government issues a warning. Sign up for Notify NYC as well: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts.

\n\n

3. Crowd crush: how people really die, and how to stay alive

\n

People in a crowd crush do not die by being trampled. They die standing up, pressed so tightly from every side that their chests cannot expand to breathe. The crowd does not have to be angry or running. It only has to be dense. Crowd scientists put the danger point at about six people per square metre. Above that, the slightest movement sends waves through the packed bodies, people fall, and the pressure on those still standing becomes crushing. Times Square on New Year's Eve, a stadium exit or a protest funnelled into a narrow street can all reach that density.

📊 FIGURE — Crowd crush: what to do at each stage as density rises
The bar shows a crowd getting denser toward the six-per-square-metre danger point. The six boxes, in order, give the one action for each stage, from arrival to being on the ground.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
WhenWhat to doWhy
On arrivalSpot the exits and the edges of the space. Stay near an edge or an exit, not in the middle.The middle is where pressure builds and where you cannot move.
When you first feel uncomfortableLeave. That feeling is the signal. Do not wait for a surge.Once a surge starts, nobody can leave.
If the crowd starts to pack inBring your arms up in front of your chest like a boxer, elbows out.This holds a pocket of space so your ribs can move and you can breathe.
If you are being carriedStay on your feet. Move with the wave, then diagonally toward an edge between waves. Never push against the flow.Fighting the wave uses the oxygen you need.
If you drop somethingLeave it. Even a phone. Even a shoe.Bending down is how people fall and are buried by others.
If you fall and cannot get upCurl on your side, knees to chest, arms over your head and neck.Protects your airway and skull until the pressure moves on.
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Stopping to pick up a dropped phone in a packed crowd. Bend down at six people per square metre and you go under. The people behind you cannot see you and cannot stop. Your phone is replaceable; leave it.

Staying because you paid for the ticket. The exit you take when it first feels wrong is the only exit that is still open ten minutes later.

\n\n

4. Home security when police are stretched

\n

During a citywide emergency, officers are pulled to rescues, fires and traffic. Your building becomes your own responsibility. The good news is that the real dangers to a New York apartment in a disaster are almost never intruders. They are fire, carbon monoxide, heat, cold and floodwater. Keep that ranking in your head when you decide what to worry about.

\n
    \n
  • Lock the door, use the chain, and open it to nobody you have not verified. \"Building inspector\", \"Con Ed\", \"FEMA\", \"the city\" — anyone in a real job has an ID and can wait while you call the company or 311 to check. Lesson 3 covers this in detail.
    • \n
  • Keep a flashlight, whistle and phone by the bed. A whistle carries further than a voice and costs less than a coffee.
    • \n
  • Do not post that you have evacuated or that your building is empty. Tell the people who need to know directly.
    • \n
  • Do not let fear of crime shut your windows in a heat wave. In the 1995 Chicago heat wave, 739 people died. Many of the elderly who died were alone and had kept their windows shut for fear of break-ins. Fear of a burglar killed far more people that week than burglars did. If you cannot open a window safely, go to a cooling center (finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or 311).
    • \n
  • Know your neighbours' names. A floor where people know each other is the best security system in the city, and it is free. Lesson 2 builds it.
    • \n
\n\n

5. Why a gun is not the plan, and what is legal instead

\n

In New York, carrying a concealed handgun requires a New York Pistol License. You must be 21 or older, apply, pass a background check and complete the state's requirements before you may carry. Owning one without that licence is a serious crime. Beyond the law, a handgun in a small apartment on a chaotic night, with neighbours behind thin walls, is far more likely to hurt someone you love than to stop a stranger. This course does not recommend it.

\n

Vigilantism is illegal. Do not join or form armed patrols, do not \"guard\" a store, and do not confront people you think are looters. Report and step back. The people you confront may be neighbours looking for water, and the person who gets hurt may be you.

\n

Pepper spray is the one carried self-defence tool that New York law allows an ordinary adult, with strict conditions:

\n
    \n
  • You must be 18 or older and have no felony or assault convictions.
    • \n
  • You must buy it in person, inside New York State, from a licensed firearms dealer or a pharmacist, and fill in a form at the counter.
    • \n
  • Ordering it online from an out-of-state seller is illegal. Do not do it.
    • \n
  • It is for escape, not for winning: spray, turn, leave, call 911.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Vendor pages say New York limits the size and strength of a legal pepper spray canister and that only certain models qualify. I could not read the state rule itself today, so confirm before you rely on this: ask the pharmacist or licensed dealer at the counter which models are legal in New York and read the product label before you buy.

\n\n

6. Looting: the myth that keeps people in flooding basements

\n

Decades of research from the Disaster Research Center at the University of Delaware and a 2025 systematic review in BMC Public Health reach the same conclusion: after a natural disaster, looting is rare, the exception rather than the rule. Disasters mostly trigger cooperation and altruism. Where people do enter damaged buildings, it is usually to find water, food, clothes or the belongings of family and friends. Widespread looting belongs to riots, which are conflicts, not to storms and floods, which pull people together.

\n

Why does this matter for your survival? Because fear of looting is one of the reasons people refuse to evacuate. During Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021, 14 people died in New York City and 10 of them drowned in basement apartments, as rain fell at 3.5 inches an hour into sewers built for about 1.75. Nobody can guard a television from under water. When the city issues an evacuation order for your zone, your possessions are not a reason to stay.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Fear of other people kills more New Yorkers in a disaster than other people do. Shut windows in a heat wave, a basement not evacuated, a fight over a bag: each is a death that a calm decision would have prevented. Leave early, lock up, and trust the neighbours you have met.

🦺 SAFETY

If you are ever inside a store or building when others are breaking things, walk out the nearest exit, do not film, do not intervene, and call 911 from a safe distance. Report; never confront.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Tonight: put a whistle and a small flashlight on your keys and another by your bed (under $10 for both).
  • This week: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and check that Wireless Emergency Alerts are switched on in your phone's notification settings.
  • Next time you enter the subway: practise finding two exits and standing behind a pillar, away from the edge, without looking at your phone.
  • Write out your de-escalation line and say it aloud once: \"Okay. I hear you. I'm leaving.\" A rehearsed sentence comes out under stress; an unrehearsed one does not.
  • If you want pepper spray, go to a licensed pharmacy or firearms dealer in New York State this month, ask what is legal, and sign the form. Do not order it online.
  • Tell one neighbour that you will evacuate when your zone is called, whatever is in the apartment.
✅ VERIFIED

The Conversation, \"Ten tips for surviving a crowd crush\" (arms up like a boxer, move with the wave then diagonally, do not pick up dropped items, leave when you first feel uncomfortable, six people per square metre) theconversation.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NPR / KQED, \"8 tips to follow if you're trapped in a crushing crowd\" (if you fall: knees to chest, cover head and neck) npr.org (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Next City, \"The Myth of Disaster Looting\" (Disaster Research Center, University of Delaware: looting rare, fear of looting deters evacuation) nextcity.org (checked 26 Sep 2026)

BMC Public Health 2025, \"Looting and antisocial behavior after disasters: a systematic review\" pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

University of Chicago Press, Klinenberg, \"Heat Wave: A Social Autopsy of Disaster in Chicago\" (739 deaths, isolated elderly, windows kept shut from fear) press.uchicago.edu (checked 26 Sep 2026)

USCCA, \"New York Concealed Carry Gun Laws\" (New York Pistol License required, age 21) usconcealedcarry.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)

SABRE, \"Pepper Spray and New York: The Laws and Where to Buy\" (18+, in-person purchase from licensed firearms dealer or pharmacist, form at point of sale, no out-of-state online orders) sabrered.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NYC Emergency Management, \"Know Your Zone\" and Hurricane Ida figures; Notify NYC; text-to-911 — from FACTS.md verified 26 Sep 2026 nyc.gov

Ready.gov, \"Emergency Alerts\" (Wireless Emergency Alerts are free, automatic, no sign-up) ready.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Knock on three doors this week and learn three names. In the first hours of a New York emergency, when 911 is flooded and the streets are blocked, the people who will pull you out of a smoke-filled hallway, notice that you have not come out of your apartment in a heat wave, or share a charged phone are the people on your floor. This is not a nice idea. It is what the death records from every major disaster show. This lesson turns your building into a team before you need one.

\n\n

1. Why the people on your floor are your first responders

\n

In July 1995 a heat wave killed 739 people in Chicago. The sociologist Eric Klinenberg went through the deaths one by one. The victims were mostly elderly people who lived alone, could not afford to run an air conditioner, kept their windows shut out of fear of crime, and had nobody who checked on them. His conclusion was blunt: living alone led to dying alone. Elderly women died at lower rates than elderly men, and the likely reason was that the women had kept up friendships and were missed sooner.

\n

New York City's own health department says the same thing in the present tense: most heat-stroke deaths in the city happen to people at home without air conditioning. The city's advice is to contact elderly or heat-sensitive friends, neighbours and relatives at least twice a day during a heat wave. A neighbour who knocks is the difference.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Mutual aid is neighbours organising to meet each other's needs directly — checking doors, sharing water, charging phones, carrying groceries up dark stairs — without waiting for an agency. It is the oldest emergency service in the city and it works because it is already there when the storm hits.

\n\n

2. Build the building contact sheet

\n

One sheet of paper, on the fridge and photographed on your phone, that answers: who lives here, who needs help, who can help, and how to reach the people who run the building. Start with your own floor. Grow it to the building if you can.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ColumnWhat to writeWhy it matters at 3 a.m.
Apartment and namesEvery adult, and how many children and petsSearchers need to know how many people should be coming out
Phone and a second contactCell, plus a relative outside the cityLocal lines jam; out-of-town texts often get through
Needs help to leaveUses a wheelchair, walker, oxygen, dialysis, is blind or deaf, has an infant, is over 75, lives aloneThese are the doors you knock first, and the people who cannot use stairs when the elevator is dead
Can helpNurse, doctor, EMT, CERT member, speaks a second language, has a car, strong enough to carrySkills you did not know were behind the next door
Has kitFire extinguisher, first-aid kit, NOAA weather radio, battery bank, tools, a spare key to a neighbour's doorOne radio per floor is enough if everyone knows where it is
BuildingSuper's cell, management company, where the gas, water and electric shutoffs are, where the roof and basement doors leadThe super may not be there; the shutoffs do not move
Outside911, 311, Notify NYC 692-692, Con Edison, your evacuation zone number (1–6), nearest cooling center once the finder shows itNobody should be searching for a number by candlelight
\n

Ask the super to walk you to the shutoffs once. Ask which neighbours hold spare keys for each other. Ask who on the floor is a nurse, an electrician, a Spanish or Cantonese or Bengali speaker. Write it down while it is still ordinary.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Your evacuation zone is at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115). Zone 1 is evacuated first; zone 6 last. Put the zone number of your building on the sheet. Neighbours in a basement apartment are in the highest-risk position in any flood: 10 of the 14 people who died in New York City during Hurricane Ida in 2021 drowned in basements.

Cooling centers: finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or 311. Code Blue in winter: when the temperature including wind chill is at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m., Department of Homeless Services drop-in centers and shelters accept walk-ins, and more than 50 hospitals keep an open door. Confirm any location via 311 or the official finder at the time — centers change with each emergency.

\n\n

3. Checking on an elderly or disabled neighbour

\n

Heat kills quietly. The person does not call for help because confusion is one of the first symptoms. So you go to them. In a heat emergency, knock twice a day: once in the late morning and once in the early evening, when apartments are hottest.

📊 FIGURE — Checking a neighbour in a heat wave: see, meaning, action
Read each row left to right: what you see at the door, what it means, and what you do. Red rows are 911 calls; the confused person is the one who will not call for help themselves.
\n\n\n\n\n\n
What you seeWhat it meansWhat you do
Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool clammy skin, headacheHeat exhaustionMove them somewhere cooler, loosen clothing, give sips of water, stay with them; if it does not improve, call 911
Confused or \"not themselves\", skin hot to the touch, may have stopped sweating, temperature 103°F or aboveHeat stroke — a medical emergencyCall 911 now. Cool them immediately: cool wet cloths, a fan, move them out of the hot room. Do not give drinks to someone who is confused or unconscious.
Shivering, slurred speech, drowsy, confused in a cold apartmentHypothermiaCall 911. Move them to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm the chest, neck, head and groin first; warm drinks only if fully alert
No answer, but you know they are homePossible collapseKnock hard and call their phone. Ask the super or a key-holder to open the door. If you believe someone inside is in danger, call 911 and say so
\n

If the apartment is hot and they have no air conditioner, the goal is to get them to a cooler place for a few hours: a neighbour's unit with a working AC, the lobby, a library, or a cooling center. Offer to walk with them. Many older people will not go alone.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Assuming silence means fine. The elderly man who does not answer the door on the third day of a heat wave is not \"keeping to himself\". Heat stroke starts with confusion, so the sick person is the last one who will call for help. Knock, call, get the door opened.

Giving water to a confused person. Someone who is confused or unconscious can choke. Cool the body, call 911, and let paramedics manage fluids.

\n\n

4. Mutual aid groups, tenant associations and \"Be a Buddy\"

\n

You do not have to build everything alone. New York already has structures you can plug into.

\n
    \n
  • Tenant associations exist in many rent-stabilised buildings and every NYCHA development. If your building has one, join it and ask for an emergency committee: one person per floor who holds the contact sheet. If it does not, three neighbours and a shared group chat is enough to start.
    • \n
  • Block associations and community boards know which corner store has a generator, which church opens as a warming room, and who has a van. Your community board's office can tell you what groups are active nearby.
    • \n
  • Mutual aid groups that formed during Hurricane Sandy and the pandemic still run in many neighbourhoods. Search your neighbourhood name with \"mutual aid\", or ask at the library.
    • \n
  • Be a Buddy is a NYC Health-funded pilot in Hunts Point, run through The Point Community Development Corporation, that trains residents of all ages to check on a specific vulnerable neighbour during floods, heat or cold. You do not need the programme to copy its method: pick one person, and be their buddy.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Tenants in New York are widely reported to have a legal right to organise a tenant association and to meet in the building's common areas without landlord interference. I could not read the statute today, so confirm before you rely on this: ask 311 for the Tenant Helpline or the New York State Attorney General's tenant resources before you challenge a landlord on it.

\n\n

5. NYC CERT: free training to become a real responder

\n

The Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) programme, run by NYC Emergency Management, trains volunteers to support their neighbourhood before, during and after an emergency. Members learn the same basics professionals rely on, and they are the people the city calls to staff shelters and help at scenes.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
RequirementDetail
Age18 or older
ResidencyLive or work in New York City
BackgroundPass an NYC Emergency Management background check
Before trainingComplete the free online FEMA course IS-100.c (Introduction to the Incident Command System) and attend a virtual orientation
Basic training11 sessions: basic fire safety, search and rescue, traffic management, first aid and triage
After graduating6-month probationary credentials; attend team meetings and events; at least one year of service
Applynyc.gov/cert or call 311
\n

Even if you never finish the course, the free FEMA IS-100.c course teaches you how emergency responders organise a scene, which makes you the calm person on the floor who knows what \"incident command\" means when a firefighter says it.

\n\n

6. The first hour: what a prepared floor does

\n
    \n
  1. Check yourself and your apartment first. You cannot help anyone with a bleeding hand or a gas leak behind you.
    2. \n
  2. Pair up. Nobody searches alone. Two people per hallway.
    3. \n
  3. Knock in order: the \"needs help\" apartments on the sheet first, then everyone else. Say your name and apartment number through the door.
    4. \n
  4. Use the stairs, never the elevator, when there is fire, smoke or a blackout. Hold the rail; count landings.
    5. \n
  5. Put one person on information. They hold the radio and the phone, check Notify NYC and 311, and tell the others. Everyone else stays off their phones and works.
    6. \n
  6. Report the count. If firefighters or police arrive, hand them the sheet: who is out, who is not, which apartments to check.
    7. \n
\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Knock first, then call. In a heat wave, knock twice a day on the doors marked \"needs help\". A contact sheet on the fridge and three neighbours who know your name will do more for your survival than any single item you can buy.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Tonight: write your own row of the contact sheet (names, phone, out-of-town contact, needs, skills, kit) and put it on the fridge. Free.
  • This week: knock on three doors, introduce yourself, and ask for one phone number each. Offer yours.
  • Ask the super to show you the gas, water and electrical shutoffs and where the roof and basement doors go. Photograph them.
  • Find your evacuation zone at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane and write the number on the sheet. Ask basement neighbours whether they know theirs.
  • Pick one elderly or disabled neighbour and agree with them that you will knock in a heat wave, a Code Blue night or a blackout. Save their number under \"Buddy\".
  • Start the free FEMA IS-100.c course online this month; if you like it, apply to NYC CERT at nyc.gov/cert or through 311.
  • Search your neighbourhood name plus \"mutual aid\" or \"tenant association\" and join one group chat.
✅ VERIFIED

NYC Emergency Management, \"NYC CERT: Join\" (18+, live or work in NYC, background check, IS-100.c, virtual orientation, one year of service, 6-month probation) nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NYC311, \"Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) Program\" (11 sessions; fire safety, search and rescue, traffic management, first aid and triage; apply via 311 or NYC.gov/cert) portal.311.nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NYC Health, \"Be a Buddy: Preparing for Hot Weather\" (most heat-stroke deaths at home without AC; contact heat-sensitive people at least twice a day) nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NY1, \"'Be a Buddy' and help your neighbors during severe weather\" (NYC Health-funded pilot at The Point CDC, Hunts Point) ny1.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)

University of Chicago Press, Klinenberg, \"Heat Wave: A Social Autopsy of Disaster in Chicago\" (739 deaths; isolation; windows shut from fear; women less vulnerable than men) press.uchicago.edu (checked 26 Sep 2026)

NYC Emergency Management, \"Extreme Heat\" nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Heat exhaustion, heat stroke and hypothermia signs (American Red Cross); cooling centers, Code Blue, Know Your Zone, Hurricane Ida figures, Notify NYC — from FACTS.md verified 26 Sep 2026 nyc.gov
