Before you act on any alarming message — \"evacuate now\", \"the water is poisoned\", \"FEMA is giving $500 to anyone who texts this number\" — spend sixty seconds finding the same information on an official source yourself. Not by tapping the link you were sent. By opening Notify NYC, the National Weather Service or 311 on your own. A real order will be there. A fake one will not. After a disaster the second wave is always people: fake contractors, fake inspectors, fake charities, and rumours that keep frightened people from getting help. This lesson gives you the short list of where the truth comes from and the checks that take less than a minute.

\n\n

1. Where the truth comes from

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
SourceWhat it gives youHow to reach it
Notify NYC (NYC Emergency Management)The city's official alerts: evacuation orders, cooling and evacuation center openings, transit and utility emergenciesText NOTIFYNYC to 692-692; text your ZIP code to 692-692 for local alerts; app; a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov
Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA)Short government warnings pushed to every capable phone near a cell tower, with a loud tone and vibration repeated twice. Free, automatic, no sign-upAlready on your phone; check that emergency alerts are enabled in notification settings
National Weather Service (NWS) New YorkOfficial weather watches and warnings for the city. NWS issues WEAs for tornado, flash flood, hurricane, extreme wind, blizzard and ice storm warnings, among othersweather.gov/okx; NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts 24 hours a day, even in a power outage
311Confirms any city order, opens a case, tells you what is openCall 311; video relay 212-639-9675; TTY 212-504-4115
911Life-threatening emergencies onlyCall if you can, text if you can't
FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency)Federal disaster assistance after a declared disaster, and a rumour-response page during big eventsfema.gov/disaster/recover/rumor-response
\n

Notice what every one of those addresses has in common: nyc.gov, weather.gov, ready.gov, fema.gov. The evacuation order that matters to you comes from the city, is delivered through Notify NYC and Wireless Emergency Alerts, and names your zone number (1 to 6). A screenshot in a group chat is not an alert. A message that does not name a zone, a time and a source is not an order.

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A Wireless Emergency Alert is a short warning sent by an authorised government agency through your mobile carrier to every capable phone in the area, using the cell tower like a radio broadcast. Nobody can send you one by text, email or social media. If a \"WEA\" arrived as a forward, it is not a WEA.

\n\n

2. The 60-second check

\n
    \n
  1. Who is actually saying this? Not who forwarded it. Is there an agency name, a date and a time? \"They said\" and \"a cop told my cousin\" are not sources.
    2. \n
  2. Open the official source yourself. Do not tap the link. Type nyc.gov/em, open the Notify NYC app, or open weather.gov/okx. If it is real and urgent, it is on the front page.
    3. \n
  3. Look for a second official channel. A real evacuation order or boil-water notice appears on Notify NYC and on 311 and, if it is weather, on the NWS. One source alone, especially a social media account, is not enough.
    4. \n
  4. Call 311. Say: \"Is there an evacuation order for zone 3 right now?\" They will tell you.
    5. \n
  5. Check the date. Old alerts from past storms are recirculated every time the sky darkens.
    6. \n
  6. If it passes, act. If it fails, do not forward it. Reply to the sender with the official link instead.
    7. \n
\n

A fake evacuation order sends people into flooded streets in the dark. A fake \"all clear\" keeps them in a basement. Either can kill.

📊 FIGURE — The 60-second check before acting on an alarming message
Run the five checks from top to bottom. Only a message that passes all of them is acted on; anything that fails is not forwarded, and the sender gets the official link instead.
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The city opens evacuation centers only when an evacuation order is issued, and the finder at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane shows which ones are open. They are pet-friendly and accessible. Any address you see printed, including in this course, must be confirmed via 311 or the official finder at the time — centers change with each emergency.

New York State's price-gouging law (General Business Law § 396-r) forbids selling goods or services at an \"unconscionably excessive price\" during an abnormal disruption of the market. Essential goods include food, water, gasoline, generators, batteries and flashlights, hotel lodging and transportation. The New York Attorney General enforces it; report gouging through ag.ny.gov.

\n\n

3. Contractor fraud after a flood

\n

The day the water goes down, vans appear. Some are honest. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says the dishonest ones share the same tells.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
Red flagWhat it meansYour move
Wants cash up frontNothing stops them leaving with itWalk away
\"You don't need a licensed contractor for this\"They are not licensedCheck the licence with the city or state before signing
\"This discount is only if you sign right now\"Pressure replaces a written estimateNever sign the same day; get it in writing
Insists on wire transfer, gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency or cashUntraceable and unrecoverablePay by credit card or check only
Wants the final payment before the work is doneThe work will not be doneFinal payment only when finished and you are satisfied
\n

Hire only contractors who are licensed and insured, and confirm the licence yourself with the government body that issues it rather than trusting a card they hand you. In New York City, 311 can direct you to the right agency to check a home-improvement licence.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Search results name the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection as the agency that licenses home-improvement contractors and offers an online licence lookup. I could not open the city page today, so confirm before you rely on this: call 311 and ask how to verify a home-improvement contractor's licence before you sign anything.

\n\n

4. Fake FEMA, fake inspectors, fake charities

\n

FEMA's own rules make the impostors easy to spot:

\n
    \n
  • FEMA never charges for disaster assistance, for an application or for an inspection, and never solicits or accepts money. Nor does any other federal, state or city agency. Anyone asking for a fee to \"file your claim\" is a thief.
    • \n
  • FEMA does not license, endorse or certify contractors. \"FEMA-approved contractor\" is a lie.
    • \n
  • A real FEMA inspector has an official ID badge and will never ask you for your nine-digit registration number, because they already have it.
    • \n
  • Scammers apply for FEMA aid in your name using stolen names, addresses and Social Security numbers. If a FEMA letter arrives that you did not apply for, report it.
    • \n
  • Report fraud to the FEMA Disaster Fraud Hotline: 1-866-720-5721.
    • \n
\n

The same door-check works for a \"Con Edison\" worker or a \"building inspector\": chain on, ask for ID, call the company or 311 on a number you look up yourself. A real worker will wait.

\n

Charities: give to organisations you already know with a track record. Be wary of any charity that seems to have sprung up overnight around this disaster. The FTC points to four independent checkers: BBB Wise Giving Alliance (Give.org), Charity Navigator, CharityWatch and GuideStar. Never donate by gift card, wire or cryptocurrency, and never to someone who knocks or calls and will not let you look them up first.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The New York State Attorney General runs a Charities Bureau with a public registry of charities that may solicit in New York. I could not open it today, so confirm before you rely on this: search \"New York Attorney General Charities Bureau\" yourself, or ask 311, before giving to a charity you do not already know.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Paying anyone anything to receive government help. Government disaster aid is free to apply for. The moment money is requested, you are talking to a criminal. Hang up, close the door, and call 1-866-720-5721.

Acting on a forwarded \"evacuation order\" or \"all clear\" without checking. Sixty seconds on Notify NYC or a call to 311 tells you whether it is real. Moving on a rumour has put people in floodwater and kept people in basements.

\n\n

5. Helping others without spreading panic

\n

FEMA's guidance during every large disaster is three sentences long: find trusted sources, share information from trusted sources, and discourage others from sharing information from unverified sources. Rumours are not harmless. FEMA has had to publicly deny claims that it confiscates property, runs camps, or diverts funds, because people who believed those rumours did not apply for help they needed.

\n

How to be the calm one in the group chat:

\n
    \n
  • Share the link, not the screenshot. \"Here is the Notify NYC page\" beats \"someone said\".
    • \n
  • Tell people what to do, not how bad it is. \"Zone 1 is ordered to evacuate; centers are listed at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane; who needs a ride?\" is useful. \"It's going to be a catastrophe\" is not.
    • \n
  • Say \"I don't know yet\" out loud. It is the most trust-building sentence in a crisis.
    • \n
  • Correct gently and privately when a neighbour shares something false. Send them the official link; do not shame them in the group.
    • \n
  • Call 311 for a boil-water rumour before you spend your last money on bottled water. Real notices are issued; they are not whispered.
    • \n
\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Official, then act. If it is not on Notify NYC, the NWS, 311 or a .gov page you opened yourself, it is not yet true for you. Aid is free; anyone charging is a scammer; anyone insisting on cash, wire, gift card or crypto is a scammer; anyone who will not wait while you check is a scammer.

🦺 SAFETY

Never let a stranger into your apartment to \"inspect\" damage while you are alone. Ask them to wait outside the locked door, call the company or 311 on a number you find yourself, and only then decide. If they push, close the door and call 911.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Now: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and your ZIP code to 692-692. Free. Then open your phone's notification settings and confirm emergency alerts are on.
  • Save three numbers in your contacts under \"OFFICIAL\": 311, the FEMA Disaster Fraud Hotline 1-866-720-5721, and the video relay 212-639-9675 if you use it.
  • Bookmark weather.gov/okx, nyc.gov/em and finder.nyc.gov/hurricane on your phone and iPad.
  • Buy a battery or hand-crank radio with NOAA Weather Radio (the kit item from Chapter 1) so you have an official channel when the phone network is gone.
  • Write the 60-second check on a sticky note by the door: Source? Official page? Second channel? 311? Date? Then act.
  • Ask 311 how to verify a home-improvement contractor's licence before you ever need one.
✅ VERIFIED

Federal Trade Commission, \"How To Avoid Scams After Weather Emergencies and Natural Disasters\" (cash up front, licence, sign-now discounts, wire/gift card/app/crypto, final payment, charity checkers) consumer.ftc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

FEMA, \"Disaster Fraud\" (FEMA never charges or accepts money; does not license contractors; inspectors carry ID and never ask for the registration number; hotline 1-866-720-5721) fema.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

FEMA, \"Common Disaster-Related Rumors\" (find, share and encourage trusted sources; rumours about vouchers, camps, confiscation) fema.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Ready.gov, \"Emergency Alerts\" (WEA, EAS, NOAA Weather Radio, IPAWS) ready.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

National Weather Service, \"Wireless Emergency Alerts\" (cell broadcast, free and automatic, tone and vibration repeated twice, warning types) weather.gov; NWS New York office weather.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

New York State Attorney General, \"Price gouging\" (General Business Law § 396-r, covered goods, how to report) ag.ny.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Notify NYC, 311, text-to-911, Know Your Zone, evacuation-center finder — from FACTS.md verified 26 Sep 2026 nyc.gov

"}, "SURVIVE/garden/s1": {"body": "

Before you buy a single seed, stand at each window in your apartment on a clear day and count how many hours of direct sun reach the sill. Light is the one thing in an apartment you cannot buy cheaply, and it decides what will grow. Do this first, because a pot of tomatoes in a shaded north window will use your water and your money and give almost nothing back.

\n\n

Be honest about what a windowsill can do

\n

A container garden will not feed you. It adds fresh food to a pantry that is otherwise all cans, rice and beans: leaves with vitamins, herbs that make plain food eatable, a few radishes, a handful of cherry tomatoes in August. That matters for health and for morale in a long emergency, but the calories come from the stored food. Plan the garden as a supplement, never as the plan.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Rough calorie picture, from memory and not checked today: a cup of raw lettuce or spinach is well under 20 calories; a cup of bean sprouts is around 30; a whole summer of cherry tomatoes from one pot is a few hundred calories in total. A working adult needs on the order of 2,000 calories a day. Confirm before you rely on this: look the food up on USDA FoodData Central (fdc.nal.usda.gov) on your phone. The point stands either way: greens are vitamins, not fuel.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Calories come from the pantry. The garden gives vitamins, freshness, flavour and something useful to do with your hands while you wait.

\n\n

Light: count the hours before you buy anything

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Full sun means at least six hours of direct sunlight a day. University extension guides say most vegetables need full sun. Leafy vegetables (lettuce, spinach, chard, herbs) tolerate less light than fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, eggplant), but every plant grows faster with more.

\n\n\n\n\n
Crop groupLight it needsExamples
Fruiting cropsFull sun: at least 6 hours of direct sun, more is betterCherry tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, eggplant, beans
Leafy and root cropsTolerate less than fruiting crops; still give them your brightest windowLettuce, spinach, arugula, chard, radish, scallions, herbs
SproutsNo sun at all (section 2)Mung bean, lentil, alfalfa, broccoli
\n

How to count: check the sill at about 9 a.m., noon and 3 p.m. and note when direct sun (not just daylight) is on it. In New York a south-facing window is the best you can get, an east or west window gives a few hours, and a window facing a taller building across the street may get none. A window with two or three hours of sun grows lettuce and herbs slowly; it will not ripen a tomato. If no window gets real sun, skip pots and go straight to sprouts and to a community garden plot (section 2).

\n\n

The fire escape is not a garden

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Putting pots, planters or a chair on the fire escape. In a fire the escape is the way out for you and for the people above you, at night, in smoke. A row of pots on the landing or a planter hooked on the railing can trip a person or fall on a firefighter below.

It is also illegal. Keep the sill inside the window, a shelf or rolling cart in front of the window, or a balcony if you have one.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The New York City Fire Code (section 1027, enforced by the FDNY, the Fire Department of the City of New York) makes it unlawful to obstruct or impede access to any required means of egress, and requires fire escape stairways to be kept clear and unobstructed at all times. Inspectors treat plants, furniture, grills and storage on a fire escape as a violation, and the fine can land on the tenant as well as the building owner.

Anything on the outside of a window sill hangs over a public sidewalk. Do not put a window box outside the glass unless your lease allows it and it is bolted, not balanced. A falling planter is a head injury for a stranger.

\n\n

Containers, soil and drainage

\n

Any container works if it holds soil, drains, and is big enough for the plant. The two mistakes are no drainage holes (roots rot in standing water) and the wrong soil.

\n\n\n\n
PlantContainerNotes
Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, cucumbersAt least 8–10 gallons of potting mix, 12–16 inches deep (University of Maryland Extension)A standard 5-gallon bucket is too small for a full-size tomato; use it for greens, or grow a dwarf or patio variety
Lettuce, spinach, arugula, radish, herbsSmaller and shallower pots are fine; deeper is still betterWindow boxes, yoghurt tubs, cut-down milk jugs, a 5-gallon bucket with holes drilled in the bottom
\n
    \n
  • Drainage: check every pot for holes before you plant; many decorative pots have none. Drill or punch several holes in the bottom. Put a saucer or tray under every pot so the floor and the neighbour downstairs stay dry.
    • \n
  • Soil: use bagged potting mix (a light mix of peat or coir with perlite or vermiculite). Extension guides say garden soil is too heavy for containers: it packs down, drains badly and drowns roots.
    • \n
  • Never dig soil from a New York yard, tree pit, lot or park for a pot. The reason is lead, below.
    • \n
\n
🦺 SAFETY

Lead is in much of New York City soil from old paint and leaded gasoline. The New York State Department of Health studied NYC community garden soils and found: beds amended with clean soil and compost had lower lead than non-growing areas; raised beds had lower lead than beds dug into the ground; fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, beans, squash) carry by far the least lead, leafy and root crops more; washing or peeling produce removes soil and dust that carry it.

The biggest exposure is not the vegetables. It is swallowing soil: children playing in bare dirt, and dust tracked into the home on shoes. The state estimated about 10 percent of gardeners and about 40 percent of visiting children exceeded health-based lead recommendations.

So: bagged potting mix in pots; if you garden in the ground, a raised bed filled with clean soil; cover bare soil with mulch or fabric; shoes off at the door; wash hands and produce.

\n\n

What to plant for the fastest food

\n

In an emergency you want crops that are ready in weeks, not months. Sow small amounts every week or two so something is always ready, and cut only the outer leaves of lettuce, chard and herbs so the plant keeps producing.

📊 FIGURE — Fastest crops: days from sowing to harvest, side by side
Each row is a crop on the same day scale: the diamond marks when baby leaves can be cut, the green bar is the mature harvest window. Tomatoes and peppers run off the chart into months.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
CropDays from sowing to harvestSource
Radish25–35 daysUniversity of Maryland Extension
ArugulaBaby leaves about 20 days; mature 40–50 daysExtension and seed-company figures seen in search
SpinachBaby leaves about 25 days; mature about 40 daysExtension and seed-company figures seen in search
Leaf lettuceBaby leaves 25–30 days; mature 30–45 daysExtension and seed-company figures seen in search
Cherry tomato, peppersMonths, not weeks, and only with full sunRead the packet
\n

The days-to-maturity number printed on your seed packet overrides this table. Herbs (basil, parsley, chives, cilantro, mint) grow well in a bright window and are the best return per inch of sill because one leaf changes a whole pot of rice. Scallions regrow from the white root ends of store-bought ones stood in a jar of water.

\n\n

Watering, and what to do when water is scarce

\n
    \n
  • Push a finger into the mix. Water when the top is dry, until water runs out the bottom. Small pots in a hot July window can need water every day.
    • \n
  • Water the soil, not the leaves, in the morning. Empty saucers so roots do not sit in water.
    • \n
  • Cover the soil surface with a mulch (shredded paper, straw, dry leaves) to slow evaporation.
    • \n
\n

If the water is off (a high-rise pump failure in a blackout, a main break, a boil-water order), the order is fixed: drinking first, at least 1 gallon per person per day (Ready.gov); cooking and hygiene second; plants last. Then stretch what you have:

\n
    \n
  1. Reuse clean rinse water from washing vegetables, rice or pasta, cooled. Never use water with soap, bleach or dish detergent on food plants.
    2. \n
  2. Move pots out of afternoon sun and group them together so they shade each other.
    3. \n
  3. Let the thirsty fruiting crops go first and keep the greens and herbs. Sprouts (section 2) need only a small rinse and no soil.
    4. \n
  4. When the tap comes back under a boil-water order, water your plants with tap water, but treat the water you drink and rinse eaten leaves with treated water.
    5. \n
\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Today: count hours of direct sun at each window at 9, 12 and 3. Write it on the window frame with tape.
  • Take everything off the fire escape.
  • Buy one bag of potting mix and two packets of seed: radish and a leaf lettuce or arugula (a few dollars each).
  • Turn two empty containers into pots: punch drainage holes, add a saucer.
  • Stand scallion root ends in a jar of water on the sill: free, and green in days.
  • Put shoes-off-at-the-door into practice if you visit any garden or park.
\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • University of New Hampshire Extension, “Growing Vegetables in Containers” fact sheet (full sun at least six hours; leafy crops tolerate less; garden soil too heavy for containers): extension.unh.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • University of Maryland Extension, “Growing Vegetables in Containers” and “Types of Containers for Growing Vegetables” (8–10 gallons and 12–16 inches for tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, cucumber; check for drainage holes): extension.umd.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • University of Maryland Extension, “Growing Radishes in a Home Garden” (25–35 days): extension.umd.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NC State Extension Horticultural Science and Hobby Farms, quick-growing vegetables (arugula, spinach, lettuce days to harvest): cals.ncsu.edu, hobbyfarms.com, checked 26 Sep 2026

Sprouts are the only crop that needs no sun, no soil and no season: a jar on the counter gives fresh food in days. They are also the raw food most often tied to outbreaks of food poisoning. Learn the rules before the first jar, decide who in your home may eat them raw, and cook them for anyone who may not.

\n\n

Sprouts: fast food, real risk

\n
📘 DEFINITION

Sprouts are seeds (mung bean, lentil, alfalfa, broccoli, radish) germinated in water and eaten whole, root and all, a few days after they start to grow. Microgreens are seedlings grown in a thin layer of soil under light and cut above the soil when the first leaves open. Sprouts need no light; microgreens do.

\n

Food-safety extension services (Virginia Tech, University of Connecticut) and the FDA (U.S. Food and Drug Administration) say the same things:

\n
    \n
  • The warm, wet conditions that make seeds sprout are ideal for bacteria too: E. coli, Salmonella and Listeria.
    • \n
  • Many outbreaks have been traced to raw sprouts, mostly E. coli and Salmonella. In most of them the source was contaminated seed, not dirty kitchens.
    • \n
  • Bacteria can sit under the seed coat. Rinsing the finished sprouts thoroughly does not make contaminated sprouts safe.
    • \n
  • The FDA advises children, older adults, pregnant people and anyone with a weakened immune system to avoid raw or lightly cooked sprouts. Cooking sprouts thoroughly reduces the risk.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Serving raw sprouts to a child, a pregnant person, an older neighbour or someone on chemotherapy because “I rinsed them well.” Rinsing does not remove bacteria trapped in the seed. In an emergency, with no doctor reachable and no clean water to spare for diarrhoea, a Salmonella infection can kill.

Raw sprouts are a healthy adult’s choice. For everyone else, stir-fry or boil them, or give them greens instead.

\n\n

How to sprout in a jar

\n

The method is simple: a wide-mouth jar, a piece of clean cloth or mesh held on with a rubber band, seed, and water. Soak the seed, drain it, then rinse and drain again morning and night, keeping the jar tipped so it drains and out of direct sun. When the sprouts are the length you want, rinse a last time, drain well, refrigerate and eat within a few days. Discard any batch that smells sour or musty, is slimy, or shows mould: when in doubt, throw it out.

📊 FIGURE — Sprouting in a jar, from soaking to the fridge, and who eats them raw
Follow the five steps left to right, rinsing twice a day until the sprouts are ready. The split at the bottom is the safety rule: only healthy adults get them raw; everyone else gets them cooked.
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The numbers I could not check today: buy seed sold for sprouting (not garden or bird seed, which may be treated); soak 8–12 hours; rinse two to three times a day; most sprouts are ready in 3–5 days; keep the finished sprouts in the fridge and eat within about 3 days. Some guides tell home sprouters to sanitise seed in a dilute bleach or vinegar solution before soaking, but the strength and time vary and a wrong dose is its own hazard.

Confirm before you rely on this: follow the instructions printed on the sprouting-seed packet, and read the Virginia Tech “Sprout Safety” sheet linked below on your phone. Seed packets from a reputable sprouting supplier are the label you follow.

\n

Why sprouts matter in a blackout: they need no light, no heat and only a cup or two of water a day. In January, with the power out, a jar of lentil sprouts is the only fresh food you can make. Dry lentils and mung beans from the pantry will sprout; keep one packet of seed meant for sprouting as well, because it is cleaner and it germinates reliably.

\n\n

Microgreens on a windowsill

\n

Microgreens are the middle step between a sprout and a salad. Fill a shallow tray (a takeout container with holes punched in it) with an inch or two of potting mix, sow seed thickly, press it in, keep it moist and put it in your brightest window. Cut the seedlings with scissors just above the soil when the first true leaves show; they do not regrow, so sow a new tray every week. Because they grow in soil and under light rather than in a wet jar, they are not tied to the same outbreak record as sprouts, but wash them like any salad.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Timing from memory: most microgreens (radish, pea, sunflower, broccoli, mustard) are ready in about 1–3 weeks. Confirm before you rely on this: the seed packet gives the days for your variety.

\n\n

GreenThumb community gardens: real soil, real sun

\n

If your windows get no sun, the way to real growing space in this city is a community garden. New York City Parks runs GreenThumb, the program that registers and supports the city’s community gardens. Most have shared beds, tool sheds, a water supply and experienced gardeners who will teach you. In a long emergency a garden is also a place where neighbours already know each other, which is worth more than the tomatoes.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

More than 550 community gardens and farms are registered with NYC Parks GreenThumb. To join: open the GreenThumb garden map at nycgovparks.org/greenthumb/join-a-garden, walk to the gardens near you, visit during their posted open hours and ask how to become a member or volunteer. If you cannot reach a garden directly, call GreenThumb at (212) 602-5300 or email greenthumbinfo@parks.nyc.gov and they will connect you with the volunteer group nearest you.

Membership rules, dues and waiting lists are set by each garden. Ask before you plant. The lead rules from section 1 apply in every garden: grow in raised beds of clean soil, do not let children play in bare dirt, wash your hands and your produce, and take your shoes off at your apartment door.

\n\n

Composting in a small space

\n

Compost turns vegetable scraps into potting mix, which matters when you cannot buy any. In an apartment the workable options are a worm bin (a lidded tub with air holes, shredded paper and red wiggler worms, fed with vegetable and fruit scraps, coffee grounds and eggshells) or simply carrying scraps to a garden or drop-off site. Whatever you do, keep the bin sealed and never put meat, dairy, oily food or cooked leftovers in it: in New York, an open food-scrap bin is a rat feeder.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The city has been rolling out curbside composting and food-scrap drop-off sites at Greenmarkets and community gardens, and the rules on which bins are required and whether fines apply have changed more than once. Confirm before you rely on this: check nyc.gov/curbsidecomposting, the GrowNYC drop-off list, or call 311 for what applies to your building this year.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

No sun: sprouts. Some sun: microgreens and herbs. Real sun and real soil: a GreenThumb garden. Raw sprouts only for healthy adults; everyone else gets them cooked.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Buy one packet of sprouting seed (lentil or mung bean is cheapest) and set up a jar with cloth and a rubber band; start a batch this week so you learn the rhythm before you need it.
  • Decide now who in your household or building may eat raw sprouts and who must have them cooked. Write it on the jar.
  • Sow one takeout-tray of microgreens on your best windowsill.
  • Open the GreenThumb map, find the two gardens nearest you and note their open hours. Visit one this month.
  • Put a lidded container in the freezer for vegetable scraps until you have a compost plan; no smell, no rats.
\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • Virginia Cooperative Extension (Virginia Tech), “Sprout Safety” FST-344 (warm humid sprouting favours E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria; outbreaks; contaminated seed as the main source): pubs.ext.vt.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • University of Connecticut Food Safety, “Seed and Bean Sprouts” (FDA advice that children, older adults, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems avoid raw sprouts; cook thoroughly; rinsing does not make them safe): foodsafety.uconn.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NYC Parks, “How to Join a Community Garden” and GreenThumb main page (more than 550 gardens; (212) 602-5300; greenthumbinfo@parks.nyc.gov): nycgovparks.org, nycgovparks.org/greenthumb, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • New York State Department of Health, NYC Community Garden Soil Study (raised beds and clean soil lower lead; wash produce; children and tracked-in soil): health.ny.gov, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • FDA, “Food and Water Safety During Power Outages” (when in doubt, throw it out): fda.gov, checked 26 Sep 2026

Write two dates on your calendar: the average last spring frost and the average first fall frost for New York City. Every planting decision counts forward from the first and backward from the second. A frost kills tomatoes, peppers and basil in one night; lettuce, spinach and kale shrug it off. Knowing which is which is most of what a season plan is.

\n\n

Your zone and your season

\n
📘 DEFINITION

A USDA hardiness zone (USDA is the U.S. Department of Agriculture) is a band of average annual minimum winter temperature. It tells you which perennial plants survive winter outdoors; it does not tell you when to plant vegetables. Frost dates do that.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
FactNew York CitySource
USDA hardiness zone (2023 map)7b in most neighbourhoods, all five boroughsNew York Botanical Garden library; Brooklyn Botanic Garden
Zone 7b average winter low5°F to 10°FUSDA map as reported by the same sources
Average last spring frostEarly April (about April 3)Cornell Cooperative Extension Harvest NY planting guide; Urban Farmer NY calendar
Average first fall frostAbout October 20Same
Outdoor growing seasonRoughly 6.5 months, early April to mid-OctoberSame
\n

These are averages. A late frost in mid-April happens; so does an early one in October. The city is warmer than the suburbs because of buildings and the ocean, and a south-facing sill behind glass is warmer still. Watch the NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) forecast for a frost warning and bring tender pots inside for the night.

\n\n

What to plant when

\n

Vegetables split into two groups. Cool-season crops can be sown outdoors in early spring and again in late summer, and light frost improves some of them. Warm-season crops are killed by frost and go out only after the last frost date, usually started indoors on the sill first.

📊 FIGURE — The New York growing year between the two frost dates
Read left to right across the year. The dashed lines are the two frost dates everything counts from; cool-season crops get two sowings, warm-season crops live only between the frosts.
\n\n\n\n
GroupCropsWhen (NYC)
Cool-seasonLettuce, spinach, arugula, radish, kale, chard, peas, scallions, cilantro, parsleySow outdoors from around the last frost (early April) into May; sow again in August and September for a fall crop
Warm-seasonCherry tomatoes, peppers, cucumbers, beans, basilStart indoors on the sill in March; move out after the early-April last frost only when nights stay warm; protect or bring in by mid-October
\n

The fall crop is the one most people miss and the one that matters for a winter emergency. Count back from October 20 using the days-to-harvest from section 1: a radish needs 25–35 days, so the last outdoor sowing is about mid-September; baby spinach at about 25 days, the same; mature lettuce at 45 days, early September. Anything sown later grows on the windowsill instead.

\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Cornell Cooperative Extension publishes a planting guide for the New York City area with dates keyed to the local frost dates (Harvest NY, linked below). Print it or save it on your phone: it is the calendar for this city, not for upstate. Cornell offices also answer gardening questions by phone and email, and GreenThumb gardens run free workshops through the season.

\n\n

Saving seeds that will actually grow

\n
📘 DEFINITION

An open-pollinated (or heirloom) variety breeds true: seed saved from it grows the same plant next year. An F1 hybrid is a cross made by the seed company; seed saved from it grows a random mix of its parents, often worse. The packet says which it is. For seed saving, buy open-pollinated.

\n
    \n
  • Easiest to save: beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes. They mostly pollinate themselves, so the seed stays true even in a small space.
    • \n
  • Harder: squash, cucumbers, corn, brassicas (kale, cabbage, broccoli) cross with their neighbours; skip them unless you have room and time.
    • \n
  • Method: let beans and peas dry on the plant until the pods rattle; let lettuce bolt and collect the fluff; scoop tomato seed with its gel, let it ferment in a jar of water a few days until the good seed sinks, rinse and dry on a plate. Dry everything fully, label with variety and year, and store in a sealed jar in a cool, dark, dry place.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

How long seed stays alive in storage varies by crop and I could not verify a chart today; the common rule of thumb is one year for onions and parsnips and several years for beans, tomatoes and lettuce. Confirm before you rely on this: check the packed-for date on the packet and do a germination test (ten seeds on a damp paper towel in a bag for a week) before you trust old seed. Cheapest insurance: buy fresh packets of your six core crops every spring and keep them in your emergency kit.

\n\n

Pests without poison

\n

Indoors the usual pests are aphids (clusters of tiny green or black insects on new growth), fungus gnats (small black flies rising from wet soil), spider mites (fine webbing, speckled leaves) and whiteflies. Start with the least-toxic fix and move up only if it fails.

\n
    \n
  1. Look under leaves every few days. Catching ten aphids is easy; a thousand is not.
    2. \n
  2. Squash or wipe insects off by hand, or rinse them off in the sink with a firm spray of water.
    3. \n
  3. For fungus gnats let the top of the soil dry out between waterings and use yellow sticky traps.
    4. \n
  4. If you use a product, use only one whose label says it is for use on edible plants, and follow the label exactly: the label is the law. Insecticidal soaps and horticultural oils sold for vegetables are the usual choice.
    5. \n
  5. Throw out a plant that is overrun before it infects the rest.
    6. \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Spraying roach spray, ant killer or any household insecticide on a plant you will eat. Those products are not labelled for food crops, the residue stays on the leaves, and you cannot wash it off. If a pest problem cannot be fixed with hands, water, sticky traps or a product labelled for edibles, you lose the plant, not your health.

\n
🦺 SAFETY

Rats. Any garden, compost bin or bag of scraps in this city draws them. Keep compost sealed, harvest ripe fruit promptly, do not leave bird seed or pet food out, and store seed and potting mix in lidded bins. Rat droppings on produce are a disease risk: wash and cook anything they may have touched, or discard it.

\n\n

Growing through winter indoors

\n

From November to February the sun is low and short and the window is cold. Light is the limit, not temperature. What works in winter, in order of reliability: sprouts in a jar (no light needed); microgreens and scallions in the brightest window; a pot of chives, parsley or a hardy lettuce that grows slowly and gives a leaf or two a week. Tomatoes and peppers do not ripen in a winter window without a grow light, and a grow light needs the power that a winter blackout takes away. Keep the plan simple: pantry calories, sprouts for fresh food, seed packets and a bag of potting mix ready for the first warm week of spring.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

If you do buy a grow light, most guides recommend an LED light a few inches above the plants for roughly 12–16 hours a day on a plug-in timer; I could not verify a specific figure today. Confirm before you rely on this: follow the light’s own instructions and the seed packet.

\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Last frost early April, first frost about October 20, zone 7b. Cool crops before and after; warm crops between. Count back from October 20 for the fall sowing. Save seed only from open-pollinated beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Put “last frost about April 3” and “first frost about October 20” in your phone calendar with reminders two weeks before each.
  • Write a one-page sowing plan: which six crops, which window, which month. Tape it inside a cupboard door.
  • Buy open-pollinated packets of lettuce, radish, spinach, a bush bean, a cherry tomato and basil; put them in a sealed jar in your emergency kit.
  • Do a ten-seed germination test on any packet more than a year old.
  • Buy one packet of yellow sticky traps and check under the leaves of every plant you own this week.
  • Save the Cornell Harvest NY planting guide PDF to your phone.
\n
✅ VERIFIED
  • New York Botanical Garden, Mertz Library Reference, “What zone is New York City?” (zone 7b): libanswers.nybg.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • Brooklyn Botanic Garden, “Everything You Need to Know About the New Plant Hardiness Zone Map” (2023 USDA map, NYC 7b, about 2.5°F warmer than the previous map): bbg.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • Garden.org USDA zone finder by ZIP code (zone 7b, 5°F to 10°F): garden.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • Cornell Cooperative Extension Harvest NY, “Planting Guide for the New York City Area: Dates of Importance”: harvestny.cce.cornell.edu; Urban Farmer, “New York Vegetable Planting Calendar” (last frost about April 3, first frost about October 20): ufseeds.com, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • University of Maryland Extension, “Growing Radishes in a Home Garden” (25–35 days): extension.umd.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NC State Extension Horticultural Science, fast-growing vegetables (spinach, lettuce, arugula days to harvest): cals.ncsu.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026

Buy one pair of safety glasses marked Z87 and put them where your tools live, before you buy any other tool. In an emergency you will be cutting plastic sheeting in the dark, prying a swollen door, hammering a board over a broken window, and every one of those jobs throws fragments at your face. Prevent Blindness reports that about 90 percent of eye injuries are preventable with the right safety eyewear, and the home is now the fastest-growing source of eye injuries because there are no safety rules there. You can replace a tool. You cannot replace an eye, and an eye injury at 3 a.m. with no power and no way to reach a hospital is a disaster inside a disaster.

📘 DEFINITION

ANSI Z87.1 is the American National Standards Institute standard for eye and face protection. Glasses, goggles and face shields that pass it are stamped \"Z87\" on the frame or lens. Ordinary sunglasses and reading glasses are not rated and can shatter into the eye. The American Academy of Ophthalmology urges every household to keep at least one pair of ANSI-approved protective eyewear.

1. The apartment toolkit, cheapest and most useful first

You do not need a workshop. You need a small box of tools that solve the emergency jobs in this course: shutting a valve, covering a hole, fastening a board, cutting cord and sheeting, and getting a stuck door open. Buy in this order as money allows.

ToolWhat it does in an emergencyNotes
Safety glasses (Z87)Protects your eyes from glass, wood, metal and dustBuy two pairs: one for you, one for whoever helps you
Work glovesBroken glass, splinters, hot pans, wet debrisLeather palm or cut-resistant; keep a pair in the go-bag
HeadlampBoth hands free to work in a blackoutSpare batteries in the same bag
Adjustable wrench and slip-joint pliersStiff water valves, nuts, hose fittingsReady.gov lists \"a wrench or pliers to turn off utilities\" in the basic kit
Multi-bit screwdriverHinges, strike plates, outlet covers, appliance panelsPhillips and flat bits in the handle
Claw hammerNails in, nails out, tapping a swollen doorAlso a pry tool for small jobs
Utility knife with spare bladesPlastic sheeting, cardboard, tape, cord, packagingA dull blade slips; change blades often
Tape measureCutting a board or sheet to fit an openingMeasure the opening twice before cutting once
Small pry bar (flat bar)Jammed doors, stuck windows, lifting boardsFar safer than using a screwdriver as a lever
Hand sawCutting a board, a shelf, a broom handle to lengthWorks with no power; a cordless drill is the next step up
Duct tape, plastic sheeting, zip ties, paracordSealing, covering, tying, bundlingReady.gov includes plastic sheeting and duct tape in the basic kit
Assorted screws, nails, wood shimsFastening a board, stopping a rattle, levellingA small organiser box; buy screws longer than you think you need

2. Measure, mark and cut without hurting yourself

Measure the opening or the board, write the number down, then measure again. Under stress people transpose digits. Mark the cut line with a pencil and a straight edge. When cutting with a utility knife, put the material on a surface you do not mind scarring, keep your free hand behind the blade, and always cut away from your body. Retract or cover the blade the moment you stop cutting. With a hand saw, hold or clamp the work so it cannot move, start the cut with slow short pulls to make a groove, then use long strokes and let the teeth do the work. Forcing a saw makes it jump.

3. Screws versus nails: which one holds

The two fasteners fail in different ways, and picking the wrong one is why emergency boards fall off.

📊 FIGURE — Screws or nails: choosing by the force on the joint
Start at the top and follow the branch that matches the force. Screws win against pull-apart and for anything you will remove; nails win only in shear. The rule at the bottom is the one for emergency boards.
Force on the jointBetter fastenerWhy
Pull-apart (withdrawal), such as wind trying to peel a board off a window frameScrewsThe threads grip the wood; screws have far greater pull-out resistance than nails of similar size
Sideways slide (shear), such as a brace pushed along its lengthNailsNails bend instead of snapping; screws can fail suddenly in shear
Something you will need to remove in a day or twoScrewsA driver backs them out cleanly; prying nails splits the board

Practical rule for this course: use screws for anything covering an opening, and drive them into solid wood (the frame or a stud), never into trim, plaster or drywall alone. Drill a small pilot hole first in hardwood or near the end of a board so it does not split. Screws into hollow drywall pull straight out; if you must fasten to a wall, find the stud by tapping for the solid sound or use a stud finder.

4. Drilling and fastening safely

A cordless drill-driver is the one power tool worth owning in an apartment. Keep the battery charged as part of your blackout routine. Before you change a bit, remove the battery. Keep hair, drawstrings and jewellery away from the spinning chuck. Start slow, let the bit bite, then speed up. If the drill catches and twists, let go of the trigger rather than fighting it. Everything you drill makes dust; wear the glasses and, for masonry or plaster, the dust mask from your kit.

🦺 SAFETY

Before every job: glasses on, gloves on if there is glass or splinters, headlamp on if the light is poor, bystanders behind you or out of the room, because flying fragments injure watchers as often as workers.

During: cut away from the body, keep the free hand behind the blade, clamp or hold the work, never lever with a screwdriver, never carry a tool by its cord or hose.

After: retract blades, remove drill batteries, sweep up screws and glass, and put the glasses back on top of the toolbox so they are the first thing you touch next time.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Running a tool in a room that smells of gas. Con Edison says that when you smell gas you must not turn lights, flashlights or appliances on or off, use a phone, or do anything else that could make a spark. A drill, a hammer striking a nail and a metal saw all make sparks. If you smell gas, stop, leave, take everyone with you, and call 911 or 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633) from outside.

The second deadly mistake is a deep cut with no plan. Any cut that will not stop with firm direct pressure needs 911. Press hard with a clean cloth and do not lift it to look.

5. The tool roll in the go-bag

If you have to leave, you will not carry the toolbox. Make a small roll or pouch that lives in the go-bag: a folding multi-tool with pliers and a blade, a spare utility-knife blade in its wrapper, a small roll of duct tape (wrap it around a pencil or a water bottle), 25 feet of paracord, six zip ties, a handful of screws, the second pair of safety glasses, thin work gloves, and a small headlamp. It weighs less than a water bottle and lets you fix a strap, close a bag, cover a window at a shelter or hang a tarp.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Never store tools, lumber, plywood or anything else on a fire escape or in front of a fire escape window. FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) tells residents to keep the fire escape and its window clear of furniture, plants and air conditioners, and storing items on a fire escape is illegal. It is your way out and your neighbours' way out.

In an apartment you rent, big repairs are the landlord's job. Your toolkit is for stopping damage tonight, not for rebuilding. Report anything structural to the super and, if nothing happens, to 311.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Buy Z87 safety glasses and work gloves and put them in the kitchen drawer where you will find them in the dark.
  • Buy a headlamp and put spare batteries next to it.
  • Buy an adjustable wrench, pliers, a multi-bit screwdriver and a utility knife, and try each one on something harmless tonight.
  • Buy a roll of duct tape, a roll of plastic sheeting and 50 feet of paracord.
  • Find a stud in one wall by tapping and mark it in pencil behind a picture.
  • Assemble the go-bag tool roll and weigh it: if it is heavier than a full water bottle, take things out.
✅ VERIFIED

Prevent Blindness, \"Preventing Eye Injuries\" (90 percent of eye injuries preventable with safety eyewear; home is the fastest-growing source; bystanders at risk), https://preventblindness.org/preventing-eye-injuries/, checked 26 Sep 2026.

American Academy of Ophthalmology, \"Eye Safety at Home: Preventing Eye Injuries\" (every household should own ANSI-approved eyewear; hammering, drilling and sawing throw fragments), https://www.aao.org/eye-health/tips-prevention/injuries-in-home, checked 26 Sep 2026.

OSHA, \"Eye and Face Protection - Standards\" (ANSI Z87.1 and the Z87 marking), https://www.osha.gov/eye-face-protection/standards, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Builder magazine, \"Dear Builder's Engineer: Nails or Screws?\" and Anawalt Lumber, \"Nail Withdrawal vs. Shear Strength\" (screws hold better in withdrawal, nails in shear), https://www.builderonline.com/building/dear-builders-engineer-nails-or-screws_o and https://blog.anawaltlumber.com/nail-withdrawal-vs-shear-strength/, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Con Edison, \"Gas Safety\" (no switches, phones or appliances near a gas smell; call 911 or 1-800-75-CONED from outside), https://www.coned.com/en/safety/energy-safety/gas-safety, checked 26 Sep 2026.

FDNY, \"Residential Apartment Building Fire Safety\" (keep fire escape and its window clear), https://fdnysmart.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/apartment_fire_safety-en.pdf, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Ready.gov, \"Build A Kit\" (wrench or pliers for utilities, plastic sheeting and duct tape, dust mask), https://www.ready.gov/kit, and Stop the Bleed (direct pressure first), https://www.stopthebleed.org/, from FACTS.md, verified 26 Sep 2026.

Tonight, before anything else, open the cabinet under your kitchen sink and find the two small valves on the pipes, then do the same behind the toilet. Turn each one clockwise until it stops, then back. Those are the shut-offs you control. A burst supply hose floods your floor and the apartment below within the hour; the difference between a mop-up and a ruined home is knowing which valve to turn. Utilities in an apartment are shared: you control some valves, the building controls the rest, and the city controls what is under the street. Learn where each line is drawn.

📘 DEFINITION

A shut-off valve stops the flow in one pipe. The small valves under a sink or behind a toilet are fixture stops. The main (or house valve) stops water to the whole apartment or building and is usually in the basement, controlled by the super. The curb valve under the sidewalk belongs to the city's system; you do not touch it. Gas has the same layers: an appliance valve, a meter valve and the street main, and in an apartment building the meter is normally not yours to operate.

1. Know what you control and who to call for the rest

📊 FIGURE — Which water, gas and electric shut-offs are yours to touch
Each row is one utility, from the valves in your apartment (left) to the street (right). Green is what you may operate; the red gas cell means there is nothing to touch, only leave.
UtilityWhat you can usually reachWhat the building controlsWho to call
WaterFixture stops under the sink, behind the toilet, at the washing machine hosesRiser and main valves, roof tank, pumpsSuper or management first; 311 for a street main break or if the landlord will not act
GasNothing while there is a smell: leaveMeter valves and building piping911 or Con Edison 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633) from outside
ElectricityYour apartment's breaker panel or fuse boxBuilding service, meters, the main disconnectSuper for building problems; Con Edison for outages; 911 for fire or sparking wires

2. Water: a leak, a burst hose, a street main break

Turn the fixture stop clockwise to close it. If the valve is stuck, do not force it with a big wrench; a corroded stop can snap off and turn a drip into a flood. Put a bucket under the leak, wrap the joint in a towel, and call the super to close the riser or main. Ready.gov says every household member should know how to shut off water at the main valve, because closing the main also stops contaminated water entering your pipes and stops your pipes draining if there is a break outside. In an apartment that valve may be behind a locked door, so know the super's number and where the valve is.

If water is bubbling out of the street or your pressure suddenly drops, call 311 and ask for DEP (the New York City Department of Environmental Protection). Tell them exactly where and what you see. NYC 311 also answers at 212-639-9675 and by TTY at 212-504-4115. Do not put a wrench on the sidewalk curb valve: it is not yours, and breaking it makes a city repair into a private one.

3. Gas: leave first, phone second, and never turn it back on yourself

Con Edison's rule is short. If you smell or hear gas, get out at once and take everyone with you. Do not use a phone, light a match, turn lights or flashlights or appliances on or off, or start a car. Once you are safely outside, call 911 or 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633). Do not go back in until the authorities say you can. Gas utilities across the country print the same second rule: if gas has been turned off at a meter, do not turn it back on yourself. Appliances and lines must be checked for damage first, and only the utility or a qualified professional restores service and relights pilot lights. In a building this is the landlord's and Con Edison's job; your job is to be outside.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Many guides say a gas meter valve is closed by turning it a quarter turn so the bar sits across the pipe, using a wrench kept near the meter. I could not confirm the layout of your building's meters, which are usually locked away and belong to the building. Confirm before you rely on this: ask the super to show you where the meters are and who is allowed to touch them, and ask Con Edison or 311 whether a tenant should ever operate one. In a smell-of-gas emergency the answer is always the same: leave and call from outside.

Some ranges have their own small shut-off valve on the pipe behind the stove. Confirm with the super whether yours does and how it turns.

4. Electricity: circuits before the main, and never in water

Ready.gov says to switch off the individual circuit breakers first, then the main breaker. That lets you turn things back on one circuit at a time to find the fault. Your panel is usually in the hallway, a closet or by the front door; label it now while the lights work. If there is water on the floor near the panel, or the panel itself is wet, do not touch it. NYC Emergency Management says not to turn on lights or appliances in a flooded basement until a qualified professional says it is safe. Report a sparking, smoking or buzzing panel as a 911 call, then leave.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Turning the gas back on yourself after it was shut off, or relighting appliances, is how leaks become explosions. Only the utility or a qualified professional restores gas.

Standing in water to reach a breaker, or wading into a flooded basement to save belongings. Water and electricity together can stop your heart before you feel a shock.

Staying in a basement apartment to hold back water. During Hurricane Ida on 1 September 2021, 10 of the 14 people who died in New York City drowned in basement apartments. When water comes in, go up, not down.

5. A broken window in a storm

FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) says permanent storm shutters are the best protection, boarding windows with 5/8-inch plywood cut to fit and ready to install is an option, and tape does not stop a window breaking. If a taped window shatters, the tape only makes bigger, heavier shards. In an apartment you usually cannot board the outside, so before the storm bring everything loose in off a balcony, close the blinds, move your bed away from the glass, and be ready to shut yourself in an interior room if the wind is dangerous.

If the glass breaks: glasses and gloves on first, then get everyone out of that room and close its door. Do not try to cover the hole while the wind is still tearing through; wait for the lull. Then, from the inside, cut plastic sheeting several inches larger than the opening and duct-tape it to the frame on all four sides, pressing the tape down hard. For a lasting patch screw a piece of plywood, a shelf or the back of a bookcase into the wooden window frame, not into the plaster, using screws because wind pulls outward. Sweep the glass into a box, photograph everything, and report it to the super the same day.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Your patch must never block a fire escape window. FDNY requires that window to stay clear, and window guards are not allowed on it because they cannot be removed in a fire. Cover the glass from inside in a way you can rip out with one pull.

A door that will not lock after a break-in is a reportable condition: broken locks can be reported to HPD (the NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development) through 311 if the landlord does not fix them. Call 911 first if someone may still be inside or you are in danger, then the landlord, then 311 if you get no repair.

Sign up for Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692) and, if you live in a basement, join its Basement Alert Group, which NYC Emergency Management runs for people who need extra warning of flooding.

6. Water at the door: sandbags and barriers

NYC Emergency Management tells New Yorkers to keep materials that block water from entering the building: water barriers, sandbags, plywood, plastic sheeting or lumber. A sandbag wall only works if it is built the way flood crews build it.

StepRuleWhy
FillHalf to two-thirds full, never packedA half-full bag weighs about 35–40 pounds and moulds to the ground; a packed bag weighs 65–70 pounds and leaves gaps
CloseFold the open end over and tuck it under the bagThe bag's own weight seals the flap; no tying needed
LayLike bricks, each row offset by half a bag, flap side down and facing the waterStaggered joints stop water finding a straight path
SealPlastic sheeting under and against the water sideSand slows water; plastic stops it
LiftTwo people, bend the knees, short carriesBack injuries are the commonest sandbagging injury

NYC Emergency Management says six inches of moving water can knock over an adult. Sandbags at a ground-floor door are for keeping a few inches out of a hallway, not for surviving a flash flood. If you live in a basement apartment in a flood-prone area and rising water or a Notify NYC or National Weather Service warning arrives, move to a place higher than the flood water, immediately, and let the belongings go.

7. A tarp over a damaged roof or wall

After hurricanes the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers' Operation Blue Roof covers damaged roofs with reinforced plastic sheeting held down by strips of wood nailed or screwed through the sheeting into the roof. That is the method to copy on any wall, shed or balcony rail you are allowed to touch: lay the tarp flat, put a wood strip along every edge and screw through the strip, so the load is spread along the whole edge. Screws or ties through the grommets alone tear out. Seal every edge so the wind cannot get underneath; a tarp with one loose edge becomes a sail and rips itself and whatever it is fastened to. Loose bricks or sandbags on top shift in wind and are not anchoring. In an apartment building the roof is the landlord's: report the damage and stay off it.

8. A door that will not close or lock

For tonight: wedge a rubber doorstop or a folded piece of wood under the door from the inside, and jam a straight-backed chair under the knob so the top of the chair back is tight against it. A length of 2x4 cut to fit between the knob and the floor does the same job better. If the strike plate has torn out of the frame, drive the longest screws you have through the plate into the solid framing behind the trim; short screws into trim are what failed in the first place. If the lock itself is broken, sleep at a friend's.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Tenant guides say New York's Multiple Dwelling Law lets a tenant add their own lock to the apartment door as long as it is small and the landlord gets a duplicate key on request, and that HPD gives landlords a set number of days to fix a hazardous condition such as a broken lock. Confirm before you rely on this: ask 311 or a tenant lawyer (the Legal Aid Society housing line) before you change a lock or refuse a key.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Find and turn the fixture stops under the sink and behind the toilet; if one is stuck, tell the super now, not during a leak.
  • Write the super's phone number and 1-800-752-6633 (Con Edison) on the inside of a kitchen cabinet door.
  • Label every breaker in your panel while the lights are on.
  • Ask the super where the building's water main and gas meters are and who may operate them.
  • Buy a roll of plastic sheeting and two rolls of duct tape and store them with the toolkit, not on the fire escape.
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and, if you live below street level, join the Basement Alert Group.
  • Put a rubber doorstop and a spare set of long screws by the front door.
✅ VERIFIED

Con Edison, \"Gas Safety\" (leave immediately, no switches or phones, call 911 or 1-800-75-CONED from outside, do not re-enter), https://www.coned.com/en/safety/energy-safety/gas-safety, checked 26 Sep 2026.

NW Natural and SoCalGas, emergency gas shut-off pages (gas turned off at the meter is not turned back on by the customer; the utility restores service and relights pilots), https://www.nwnatural.com/safety/emergency-preparedness and https://www.socalgas.com/safety/emergency-information/shut-off-natural-gas, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Learn the bowline first, tonight, with a shoelace, until you can tie it with your eyes shut. It makes a loop that will not slip or jam under load, which is the one thing you most often need from a rope: a fixed loop to hang a lantern, tie a tarp corner, lower a bucket, or make a handle on a bag. Then learn five more knots and you can build almost anything this course asks of you with cord, tape and what is already in the apartment. A knot that fails at the wrong moment drops a load on someone or lets a tarp go in the wind, so practise the six until they are boring.

📘 DEFINITION

A loop knot (bowline) makes a fixed eye in a rope. A hitch (clove hitch, two half hitches, taut-line hitch) ties a rope to a post, ring, rail or another rope. A bend (sheet bend) joins two ropes end to end. A binding knot (square knot) holds a bundle or a bandage closed. The standing part is the rope under load; the working end is the free end you tie with; a bight is a U-shaped fold in the rope.

1. Cordage: paracord and what else works

Type III parachute cord, called 550 cord, is the best all-round cordage for an apartment kit. The military specification requires a minimum breaking strength of 550 pounds and a core of seven inner nylon strands inside a woven sheath. The inner strands pull out and serve as sewing thread, fishing line, a bootlace or a bundle tie, so 50 feet of cord is really 50 feet of rope and hundreds of feet of thread. Buy cord that names the military specification (MIL-C-5040H) and not \"paracord-style\" decorative cord.

CordageGood forNot for
550 paracordTarp lines, clotheslines, lashings, handles, repairsHolding a person, lowering anyone from a window
Clothesline, sash cordTarps, bundles, light hangingAnything heavy or sharp-edged
Zip tiesFast, one-handed fixes: fencing, cables, gates, splints on a broken bag strapAnything that must be untied later
Duct tapeSealing, patching, wrapping a handle, closing a tarp seamWet surfaces; it lets go in the cold and the wet
Bed sheets torn in stripsBandage ties, slings, bundlingBearing weight over an edge
🦺 SAFETY

The 550-pound figure is a minimum breaking strength for new cord pulled straight. Wear, knots, sharp edges and shock loads reduce what a cord will hold in practice. Never use paracord, a sheet rope or any improvised line to lower a person or to climb down from a window or fire escape; use the stairs, the fire escape itself, or wait for FDNY at a window with the door closed and a wet towel at the gap. Wear glasses when cutting cord under tension: the ends snap back.

2. Six knots and what each one is for

📊 FIGURE — The six knots, what kind each is and what it is for
Each cell is one knot as a simple sketch: the coloured line is the rope, grey is the post or rail. Read the name, its type and the job it does; the three in the first row and the taut-line rig a tarp.
KnotTypeUse it forHow to check it
BowlineFixed loopA loop that will not slip or jam: tarp corners, hanging a lantern or bucket, a handle, the anchor end of a lineThe loop stays the same size when you pull hard on the standing part; leave a long tail
Two half hitchesHitchThe everyday hitch for tying a line to a post, ring, railing, pipe or tree; can be tied under loadBoth hitches wrap the same way; snug them against the object
Clove hitchHitchFast attachment to a pole or rail; the start of a lashing that binds two polesTwo crossing turns; it can roll on a smooth pole, so finish with a half hitch
Taut-line hitchAdjustable hitchTent and tarp guy lines: slide it to tighten or loosen, it holds where you leave itSlides under hand pressure, grips under load; re-tighten after wind or rain
Sheet bendBendJoining two ropes, especially of different thickness; tying a line to the corner of a tarp or sheet with no grommetBoth tails end on the same side of the knot; the thicker rope forms the bight
Square (reef) knotBindingTying a bandage, closing a bundle or a parcel, reefing a tarp edge\"Right over left, then left over right\"; it lies flat. It is not a knot for joining ropes that carry load

Practise in this order: bowline, two half hitches, taut-line hitch. Those three rig a tarp. Then sheet bend, clove hitch, square knot. Tie each knot ten times with cord, then ten times with a shoelace, then once with gloves on, then once in the dark. Keep a two-foot practice cord on your desk; the skill fades in weeks if you do not touch it.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Joining two ropes with a square knot and trusting it with weight. The square knot is a binding knot for bandages and parcels; under a changing load it can capsize and slide apart. Join ropes with a sheet bend, or tie a bowline in each rope through the other's loop. And never tie yourself, a child or a pet to anything with a knot that tightens under load.

3. A tarp that is not a sail, and a rain catcher

Wind is the enemy of every tarp. Pitch it low and taut, with the long edge into the wind, so air passes over it rather than under it. Tie a bowline in the tarp corner or, if it has no grommet, push a small stone into the corner, fold the fabric over it and tie a sheet bend around the neck. Run each line to an anchor with two half hitches, and put a taut-line hitch on at least two lines so you can re-tension without untying. The Operation Blue Roof rule applies here as well: every edge secured, because a single loose edge lets the wind get underneath and the whole tarp rips free.

A rain catcher is the same tarp pitched with one low corner sagging over a clean bucket or pot. Weight the corner with a stone tied on with a sheet bend so the water runs to one point. On a balcony, fire escape or roof this is the fastest way to collect water when the taps stop, but treat it like any found water: boil it for one minute at a rolling boil, or add 8 drops (about 1/8 teaspoon) of regular unscented 5–9 percent bleach per gallon of clear water, 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) if cloudy, and wait 30 minutes.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

A tarp cannot be tied to a fire escape and nothing can be stored on one. FDNY requires the fire escape and its window to be kept clear at all times, and storing anything on a fire escape is illegal. Rig a rain catcher on a balcony or, with the landlord's permission, on the roof, and never across the escape route.

If you live in a basement apartment, a raised sleeping platform is not a flood plan. Ten of the fourteen New Yorkers killed by Hurricane Ida on 1 September 2021 drowned in basement apartments. Sign up for the Notify NYC Basement Alert Group and leave for higher ground when a warning comes.

4. A raised sleeping platform

When a floor is wet, cold or crawling, sleeping on it steals body heat and invites illness. Build a platform in minutes: two rows of milk crates, sturdy storage bins or a stack of pallets, with a flat door, a bookcase laid on its back or a sheet of plywood on top, lashed at the corners with clove hitches so nothing walks apart when you move. Put a foam pad, blankets or flattened cardboard on top; insulation under you matters as much as blankets over you. Test it by kneeling on the middle before you trust it with a sleeping person.

5. Repairing a chair, a shelf and a door

  • Wobbly chair: turn it over, pull the loose leg or rung, scrape the old glue off, work wood glue into the joint, push it home and tie it tight with a loop of cord twisted with a stick (a Spanish windlass) until the glue dries. A screw driven at an angle through the joint holds it while the glue cures.
  • Sagging shelf: the fasteners have pulled out of the wall, not the shelf. Move the bracket to a stud and use screws long enough to go well into the wood. Screws in hollow drywall or plaster alone will pull out again the next time you load it.
  • Door that drags or will not latch: the top hinge has loosened. Tighten its screws; if they spin, replace them with longer screws that reach the framing behind the jamb, or pack the hole with glue-coated toothpicks or matchsticks, snap them flush and drive the screw again. If the latch misses the strike plate, mark where it hits and move or file the plate.
  • Broken drawer or bag strap: zip ties through two drilled holes, or a paracord loop with a sheet bend, will outlast the emergency.

6. Improvised tools

A hammer is any heavy thing with a flat face: a full can wrapped in a sock, a smooth stone. A wedge is a folded piece of cardboard or a shim cut from a paint stirrer. A lever is a broom handle over a fulcrum of a book. A clamp is a loop of cord with a stick twisted through it. A funnel is the top of a plastic bottle cut off. A sewing needle is a paperclip straightened and bent, threaded with paracord core. A splint is a rolled magazine and two strips of bed sheet tied with square knots. A door-brace is a 2x4 or a broom handle cut to fit from the knob to the floor. The habit to build is looking at every object and asking what force it can apply, hold or spread.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Bowline for a loop, two half hitches to tie on, taut-line to tension, sheet bend to join, clove hitch to start a lashing, square knot to bind. Practise until boring. Every edge of a tarp secured. Paracord for gear, never for people. Nothing on the fire escape.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Cut a two-foot length of cord, tie a bowline ten times, then two half hitches, then a taut-line hitch.
  • Buy 100 feet of 550 paracord that names MIL-C-5040H and a small tarp with grommets; keep them with the sheeting and tape.
  • Rig the tarp once on a balcony or in the living room between two chairs so you know how long the lines need to be.
  • Tighten the top hinge of every door in the apartment with a screwdriver.
  • Look at what you own and list three things that could make a sleeping platform.
  • Check that nothing of yours sits on the fire escape or in front of its window.
✅ VERIFIED

Scout Life, \"How to Tie the 7 Basic Scout Knots\" and ScoutSmarts, \"How To Tie The Required Scouting Knots (With Practical Uses)\" (bowline fixed loop that does not slip or jam; square knot for bandages and parcels; two half hitches as the general utility hitch; taut-line hitch for adjusting tension; sheet bend joins ropes of different thickness and ties to a tarp corner; clove hitch starts a lashing), https://scoutlife.org/outdoors/176401/how-to-tie-the-7-basic-scout-knots/ and https://scoutsmarts.com/scouting-knots-with-uses/, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Animated Knots by Grog, \"Scouting Knots\", https://www.animatedknots.com/scouting-knots, and Troop Leader Resources (Scouting America), \"Knot-Tying Skill Activities\", https://troopleader.scouting.org/activities/scout-skill-challenges/knot-tying-skill-activities/, checked 26 Sep 2026.

Wikipedia, \"Parachute cord\", citing military specification MIL-C-5040H (Type III minimum breaking strength 550 pounds, seven inner strands), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parachute_cord, checked 26 Sep 2026.

FEMA, \"FEMA Tarps and USACE Blue Roofs Aid in Protecting Homes From Further Damage\" (sheeting held by wood strips; every edge secured), https://www.fema.gov/print/pdf/node/319276, checked 26 Sep 2026.

FDNY, \"Residential Apartment Building Fire Safety\" (fire escape and window kept clear), https://fdnysmart.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/apartment_fire_safety-en.pdf, checked 26 Sep 2026.
