Do this first: get a paper map of the city and learn the four rules of the Manhattan grid. In a real emergency your phone is the first thing to fail — the battery dies, the cell towers are overloaded, or the network is down. In the blackout of 14 August 2003 the subways stopped mid-tunnel and most people walked home. If you cannot find your way without a screen, you are lost the moment the screen goes dark. This lesson gives you the rules, the landmarks, the bridges with walkways and a way to estimate how long a walk will take.

\n\n

The Manhattan grid in five rules

\n

Manhattan above about 14th Street is a grid laid out by the Commissioners' Plan of 1811. Learn these rules and you can find any address without a phone.

📊 FIGURE — The Manhattan grid: avenues, streets, Fifth Avenue and uptown
The island runs top (uptown) to bottom (downtown) with the rivers either side. Avenues run up and down, numbered streets across; Fifth Avenue splits East from West. The compass shows the 29-degree twist.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
RuleWhat it means for you
Streets run east–west and are numberedNumbered streets run from 1st Street to 228th Street. Numbers rise as you go north (“uptown”) and fall as you go south (“downtown”).
Avenues run north–southThe Hudson River is on the west side of the island, the East River on the east. Walk along an avenue and you are moving uptown or downtown.
Fifth Avenue is the East/West lineFifth Avenue divides the island into an east side and a west side. Building numbers on a street start again at Fifth Avenue: “East 34th Street” is east of Fifth, “West 34th Street” is west of it. Below 8th Street the dividing line is Broadway instead.
20 street blocks is about 1 mileAbout 20 north–south street blocks (each about 264 feet) make one mile. Avenue blocks are much longer: roughly 7 avenue blocks make a mile. “Ten blocks” is about half a mile if you walk uptown, but about 1.4 miles if you walk crosstown.
Grid north is not true northThe grid is rotated about 29 degrees east of true north. When you walk “uptown” you are walking north-north-east. The sun, a compass and the grid will disagree by that much.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

Uptown means north on the grid (street numbers rising). Downtown means south (street numbers falling). Crosstown means east or west along a street, from avenue to avenue.

The grid is the pattern of numbered streets and avenues in Manhattan. It was laid out in 1811 and is why an address like “East 42nd Street” tells you where to walk before you know anything else.

\n\n

Landmarks that never move

\n

When you come out of a subway or a strange building and do not know which way is which, use things that cannot be turned off.

\n
    \n
  • The rivers. In Manhattan, water on your left as you walk uptown is the Hudson; water on your right is the East River. If you reach a river, you have found the edge of the island and the grid.
    • \n
  • The sun. It rises in the east and sets in the west. At midday it is to the south. Remember the grid is turned about 29 degrees, so the sun will not sit exactly at the end of a street except on a few days a year.
    • \n
  • Tall buildings. The Empire State Building stands in Midtown; One World Trade Center stands at the southern tip of the island. If you can see both, the line between them runs downtown.
    • \n
  • Central Park. A long rectangle running north–south through the middle of upper Manhattan. Its long sides are avenues; its short sides are streets.
    • \n
  • Street signs. Read two of them at any corner and you know your exact spot on the grid. Walk one block and read the next sign: if the number went up, you are heading uptown.
    • \n
\n\n

The other boroughs are not a grid

\n

Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island grew from separate villages and their streets do not follow one plan. Do not assume Manhattan rules apply.

\n
    \n
  • Queens addresses are hyphenated. In “38-01 35th Avenue” the number before the hyphen (38) is the nearest cross street and the number after it (01) is the building on that block. So 38-01 35th Avenue is on 35th Avenue at 38th Street. Queens has numbered streets, avenues, roads, drives and places that can all carry the same number, so read the whole name.
    • \n
  • Brooklyn has several grids that meet at angles, plus numbered streets and lettered avenues in the south of the borough. Use the big avenues and the subway lines as your reference.
    • \n
  • Everywhere: the subway map printed on paper is also a rough map of the city. Elevated train lines are visible landmarks you can follow on foot.
    • \n
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

On 14 August 2003 about 50 million people lost power across the Northeast. In New York City the subways stopped, high-rises lost water pressure and most people walked home across the bridges. The people who got home fastest knew which bridge had a walkway and where its entrance was.

You can find out which hurricane evacuation zone you live in at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311. Zone 1 is evacuated first. Knowing your zone tells you which direction “away from the water” is before you ever need to walk it.

\n\n

A compass in a city of steel

\n

A cheap compass works in New York, but steel pulls the needle. Cars, fences, subway grates, scaffolding and steel-frame buildings can all swing it. So:

\n
    \n
  1. Step into the middle of an open space: a park, a plaza, the middle of a wide sidewalk away from parked cars.
    2. \n
  2. Hold the compass flat at waist height, away from your phone, keys and bag.
    3. \n
  3. Take three readings a few steps apart. If they agree, trust them. If they do not, move further from the steel and try again.
    4. \n
  4. Remember the 29-degree twist: compass north points a little to the left of “uptown” on the grid.
    5. \n
\n

Your phone's compass is affected in the same way, and it needs a battery. The grid, the rivers and the sun need nothing.

\n\n

Crossing the rivers on foot: bridges with walkways

\n

You cannot walk through a vehicle tunnel. To leave Manhattan on foot you must use a bridge that has a pedestrian path. These do:

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
BridgeConnectsWalking notes
Brooklyn BridgeCity Hall area, Manhattan ↔ Downtown BrooklynPedestrian walkway is above the traffic lanes; the bike path is on the lower level. Manhattan entrance is across the street from City Hall. About 1.1 miles; 20–30 minutes at a regular pace without stopping.
Manhattan BridgeChinatown, Manhattan ↔ Downtown BrooklynHas a pedestrian walkway and a separate bikeway. Less crowded than the Brooklyn Bridge.
Williamsburg BridgeLower East Side, Manhattan ↔ Williamsburg, BrooklynTotal length 7,308 feet (about 1.4 miles). Has pedestrian and bike paths.
Ed Koch Queensboro (59th Street) BridgeMidtown Manhattan ↔ Long Island City, QueensSince 18 May 2025 the south outer roadway is for pedestrians only and the north outer roadway is for cyclists only.
Willis Avenue BridgeManhattan ↔ the Bronx (Harlem River)Carries pedestrians and bicycles in both directions.
Third Avenue BridgeManhattan ↔ the Bronx (Harlem River)Has pedestrian and bicycle access.
Macombs Dam BridgeWest 155th Street, Manhattan ↔ South BronxPedestrian pathway at the edge of the span.
Broadway BridgeInwood, Manhattan ↔ the BronxCarries Broadway; open to pedestrians.
\n

NYC Ferry is a second way across the water while it runs. Its routes are East River, South Brooklyn, Astoria, Rockaway–Soundview, St. George and the Governors Island shuttle; the Rockaway–Soundview route links the Rockaways, Sunset Park, the Bronx and Lower Manhattan. Routes changed in December 2025, so check the live status at ferry.nyc/live-ferry-status before you count on a boat. Expect ferries to stop in high wind or a storm.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Setting out for a bridge in a storm. The MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority) may close its bridges to all traffic when sustained winds reach 60 mph or more, and NYC DOT (Department of Transportation) closes or slows its bridges as conditions demand. A pedestrian on an open bridge in that wind can be blown into the railing or the roadway.

Evacuate early, while the bridges, buses and subways are still open. Once the wind is up, shelter where you are and wait.

\n\n

How long will the walk take?

\n

Use the grid to turn distance into time. The Brooklyn Bridge is 1.1 miles and takes a regular walker 20–30 minutes. Use that as your yardstick.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
DistanceGrid equivalentTime at Brooklyn Bridge pace (arithmetic from the figures above)
1 mile20 street blocks, or about 7 avenue blocksAbout 20–30 minutes
3 miles60 street blocksAbout 1 to 1.5 hours
5 miles100 street blocksAbout 1.5 to 2.5 hours
10 miles200 street blocksAbout 3 to 5 hours, plus rests
\n

Add time for crowds, rain, a heavy bag and every bridge climb. Add a lot of time in heat. The honest way to know your own pace: this week, time yourself walking 20 street blocks in Manhattan with your usual bag. That number is your personal mile.

\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

The following are widely reported but I could not confirm them from an official page today — confirm before you rely on this by calling 311, checking NYC DOT bridges, or asking the Port Authority: the George Washington Bridge has a sidewalk for walking to New Jersey; the RFK (Triborough) Bridge has pedestrian paths via Randalls Island to Queens and the Bronx; the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge has no pedestrian path; the Pulaski Bridge links Greenpoint, Brooklyn and Long Island City, Queens with a walkway.

Walk any bridge you plan to use on a calm day first. Entrances are often a block away from where you expect.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Free: pick up a paper subway map at any station booth, fold it into your bag and never take it out.
  • Free: write your route home from work on an index card — the streets, the bridge, the entrance. Put it behind your ID.
  • Free: time yourself walking 20 street blocks with your usual bag. Write the minutes on the same card.
  • Free: on a calm weekend, walk the bridge nearest your home and photograph the entrance.
  • Under $10: a small button compass on your key ring. Practise reading it in a park.
  • Free: find your evacuation zone at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane and note which direction is away from the water.

When the city tells you to evacuate, leave early and leave on foot or by transit while it still runs. Before Hurricane Sandy in 2012 the MTA (Metropolitan Transportation Authority) stopped the subways at 7 p.m. and the buses at 9 p.m., and people were told to stay off the roads because traffic blocks emergency crews. Before Hurricane Irene in 2011 the subway was shut down for a natural disaster for the first time ever and more than a quarter of a million New Yorkers were ordered out. The people who waited for a car, a taxi or a ride-share were the ones who got stuck. This lesson is about moving yourself, and whoever depends on you, across the city on your own feet.

\n\n

Why driving out of the city fails

\n
    \n
  • Everyone has the same idea. A few bridges and tunnels serve millions of people. Cars queue for hours and then the crossings close: the MTA may close its bridges to all traffic when sustained winds reach 60 mph.
    • \n
  • Water stops cars first. The NWS (National Weather Service) says 6 inches of water reaches the bottom of most passenger cars and can cause loss of control or stalling; 12 inches will float many vehicles and carry away a small car; 2 feet of rushing water carries away most vehicles, including SUVs and pickups. More than half of all flood deaths are vehicle-related.
    • \n
  • A car is a trap. If it stalls in water you must get out into the water anyway, now in the dark, with a door that may not open.
    • \n
  • Fuel and power. Gas stations need electricity to pump. In a blackout the pumps stop.
    • \n
\n
📘 DEFINITION

An evacuation order is an instruction from the city to leave an area because staying is expected to be life-threatening. NYC has six hurricane evacuation zones; zone 1 is the highest risk and is evacuated first, zone 6 the lowest.

An evacuation center is a building the city opens when an order is issued. NYC evacuation centers are pet-friendly and accessible. Find the ones open at the time via the official finder or by calling 311 — centers change with each emergency, so confirm via 311 or the finder at the time.

\n\n

The ten-mile rule: carry only what you can walk ten miles with

\n

A bag that feels fine in the hallway is a punishment after two hours. Pack for walking, not for camping. Weigh it with your bathroom scale and then walk 20 blocks with it. If you would not carry it for ten miles, it stays.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
CarryLeave
Water in bottles you can drink from while moving; a little food that needs no cookingGallon jugs, cans without a can opener, anything that needs a stove
Medicines for at least several days, in their labelled containersThe whole medicine cabinet
Phone, charger and a charged backup battery; a paper map; a whistle; a small flashlightLaptop, iPad, chargers for things you are not carrying
ID, cash in small bills, a card with the phone numbers you would otherwise look up, copies of key documents (photos on the phone count)Original documents you can replace later, valuables you cannot protect
A rain layer, a warm layer, a spare pair of socks, sunscreen or a hat by seasonExtra outfits
Pet food, leash, carrier, vaccination record for the animal you are takingThe aquarium
\n

Put the things you will use while walking (water, map, whistle, flashlight) in outside pockets so you never have to stop and unpack.

\n\n

Footwear, pace and rest

\n

Blisters end evacuations. A person who cannot walk on the second day is a person who needs rescue.

\n
    \n
  • Shoes: closed, sturdy shoes you have already worn for long walks. Never new shoes, sandals or heels. If you must leave work in dress shoes, carry the walking shoes and change before you start.
    • \n
  • Socks: moisture-wicking socks (wool or synthetic), not cotton. Cotton holds sweat and rubs. Change socks when they are damp; carry a spare pair.
    • \n
  • Hot spots: the moment you feel a rubbing spot, stop and cover it with moleskin or tape before it becomes a blister. Ten seconds now saves an hour later.
    • \n
  • Pace: walk at the speed of the slowest person and keep it steady. Fast then stop then fast again tires everyone. Rest for a few minutes each hour, sitting, with the bag off and, if you can, the shoes loosened.
    • \n
  • Drink before you are thirsty, in small amounts, all day. Eat something small every couple of hours.
    • \n
\n\n

Heat, cold and rain on the road

\n\n\n\n\n\n
ConditionWarning signsWhat to do
Heat exhaustionHeavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool clammy skinMove to shade or a cool place, loosen clothing, sip water. Cooling centers: finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or 311.
Heat strokeConfusion, hot skin, temperature 103°F or above, may stop sweatingCall 911 and cool the person immediately. Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious.
HypothermiaShivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsinessGet to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm the core first (chest, neck, head, groin). Warm drinks only if fully alert. Call 911.
Cold night, nowhere to goTemperature including wind chill at or below 32°F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m.Code Blue is in effect: Department of Homeless Services drop-in centers and shelters accept walk-ins and more than 50 hospitals keep an open door. Call 311.
\n

Rain is a cold-weather hazard even in autumn: wet clothing pulls heat out of you. Put the rain layer on before you are wet, not after.

\n\n

Flooded streets and downed wires

\n

A flooded New York street is not a puddle. It hides everything that kills.

📊 FIGURE — Turn Around, Don’t Drown: water depth on the street and what to do
Left: how little water it takes to stop a person or a car. Right: the decision when you meet water on the road, ending with the rule for a downed wire.
\n
    \n
  • Open manholes. During floods, water pressure from below pushes manhole covers up and off. The FDNY (Fire Department of New York) has answered calls for covers pushed up by water and for manhole fires; DEP (Department of Environmental Protection) crews respond to missing covers. Brown water hides the hole completely.
    • \n
  • Live wires. Tree limbs, leaves or water can cover a downed wire from view. Con Edison says: stay 30 feet away from a downed wire, keep others away, call 911 first and then Con Edison at 1-800-752-6633 (1-800-75-CONED). Never touch a wire with your hands or with any object.
    • \n
  • Moving water. Six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult over and carry her away. You cannot judge depth or speed from the curb.
    • \n
  • Basements. During Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021, 14 people died in New York City and 10 of them drowned in basement apartments. Rain fell at 3.5 inches per hour, about double the 1.75 inches per hour the sewers were built for. Never go down into a flooding basement, and never shelter in one during a flood warning.
    • \n
\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Walking or driving into water on the street because it “looks shallow”. The NWS rule is Turn Around, Don’t Drown: 6 inches of moving water can take you off your feet; 12 inches can carry away a small car. Under the water may be an open manhole or a live wire you cannot see.

Go back the way you came and find a route on higher ground, even if it adds an hour. An hour is cheap.

\n\n

Children, the elderly and pets

\n
    \n
  • Children: put a card with the child's name, your name and two phone numbers in their pocket. Hold hands at every crossing. Set the pace by the child, and carry the small ones before they are exhausted, not after.
    • \n
  • Older or disabled people: ask before you assume. Carry their medicine list and their glasses. A folding stool or a walker with a seat turns any block into a rest stop. If someone truly cannot walk out, call 311 for evacuation help before the order takes effect; call 911 if they are in immediate danger.
    • \n
  • Pets: take them. Ready.gov warns that pets left behind end up lost, injured or worse, and NYC evacuation centers accept pets. Dogs on a short leash, cats in a carrier, food and water for the animal in your bag, vaccination record on your phone.
    • \n
  • Neighbours: knock on the doors of anyone you know lives alone. A minute of knocking may be the only warning they get.
    • \n
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Sign up for Notify NYC before you need it: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts, or use the app. It will tell you when an evacuation order is issued and when transit is about to stop.

911 is for life-threatening emergencies. 311 is for everything else, including your evacuation zone, open centers and help evacuating someone who cannot walk. Text-to-911 has worked in NYC since June 2020: call if you can, text if you can’t.

\n\n

Before you close the door

\n
    \n
  1. Leave a note telling others when you left and where you are going. Tape it inside the door where a rescuer or family member would see it, and text the same message to someone outside the city.
    2. \n
  2. Close and lock doors and windows.
    3. \n
  3. Unplug small electrical equipment such as radios and small appliances. Leave the refrigerator and freezer plugged in unless there is a risk of flooding.
    4. \n
  4. Take your pets and your bag. Put on the walking shoes. Fill your water bottles from the tap on the way out.
    5. \n
  5. Follow the routes the city recommends. Shortcuts may be flooded, closed or blocked by debris.
    6. \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Commonly quoted but not confirmed from an official page today — confirm before you rely on this: that an average adult walks about 3 miles per hour on flat ground, so 10 miles takes over 3 hours without rests (ask a doctor or physiotherapist what is realistic for you, or measure it yourself over 20 blocks); and that gasoline pumps at most stations stop in a blackout (ask the station or 311).

Plan with the slower figure, never the faster one.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Free: pack a “walk-out bag” from things you own and weigh it. Walk 20 blocks with it this weekend.
  • Free: write the note you would leave on the door now, with blanks for the time and the destination, and keep it with the tape.
  • Under $5: a roll of moleskin or athletic tape and one spare pair of wool or synthetic socks in the bag.
  • Free: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and find your zone at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane.
  • Free: agree with one person outside the city that they are your check-in contact.
  • Free: learn the names of two neighbours who live alone or with small children.
✅ VERIFIED
  • National Weather Service, “Turn Around Don’t Drown” and flood safety pages, weather.gov and weather.gov/tsa/hydro_tadd (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Con Edison, “Electric Safety” and “Contact Us” (downed wires, 30 feet, 1-800-75-CONED), coned.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services, “Flood Safety Tips” (hidden downed wires), dhses.ny.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • NYC Comptroller, “Is New York City Ready for Rain?” (manhole covers pushed up in floods), comptroller.nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Ready.gov, “Evacuation” (leave a note, lock up, unplug, take pets), ready.gov/evacuation (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Ready.gov, “Prepare Your Pets for Disasters”, ready.gov/pets (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Do this first: put a whistle on your key ring today. Three blasts on a whistle is the international distress signal. It carries farther than your voice, it works when you are hoarse, in the dark, or too weak to shout, and it costs about a dollar. Being found is a skill: you make yourself loud, bright and easy to describe, and you leave word behind so the people looking for you know where to start. This lesson covers the signals, how to tell rescuers exactly where you are, what to do if you are trapped in a building, and how to leave a trail.

\n\n

Three of anything means help

\n

Rescuers all over the world are trained to look for the number three. Three of any signal, evenly spaced, means “I need help”.

\n\n\n\n\n\n
SignalHow to make it
Three whistle blastsBlow three long blasts, pause, then repeat. Wait between sets so you can hear an answer.
Three flashes of lightFlashlight, phone torch or a mirror aimed at the searcher. Three, pause, repeat.
Three fires or three pilesOutdoors, three fires or three bright objects evenly spaced in a line or a triangle. In the city, three bright items on a rooftop or lawn.
SOSIn Morse code: three short, three long, three short (· · · – – – · · ·). Tap it, flash it or whistle it: short bursts of about one second, long bursts of about three seconds.
\n
📘 DEFINITION

SOS is the universal distress signal. As sound or light it is three short, three long, three short. Written large on the ground or in a window, the three letters S O S are understood by pilots and rescuers everywhere.

A ground-to-air signal is a large symbol laid out on the ground so that a helicopter or plane can read it: X means medical emergency, SOS means help, and an arrow shows the direction you travelled.

\n\n

Whistles, lights and mirrors

\n
    \n
  • Whistle. It is in the Ready.gov basic kit for a reason. A pea-less plastic whistle works wet and frozen. Blow from the diaphragm; three blasts; rest; listen.
    • \n
  • Flashlight. At night a small flashlight is visible for blocks. Point it at the searchers, not at the sky, and flash in threes. A phone screen turned up bright and waved slowly is the next best thing, but it eats the battery you need for calls.
    • \n
  • Mirror or anything shiny. In daylight a flash of reflected sun can be seen from very far away. A compact mirror, a phone screen or a foil blanket all work. Practise in a park: you will see the spot of light land on the ground near you and can walk it up onto the target.
    • \n
  • Bright colour. Hang a bright sheet, towel or jacket from a window or railing. Rescuers scanning a building look for what does not belong.
    • \n
  • Noise from a car. A car horn in threes works, and it is louder than you.
    • \n
\n\n

Ground and window signals in a city

\n

After a flood or a storm, helicopters fly over New York looking for people. Make yourself a shape they can read.

📊 FIGURE — The three ground signals a helicopter can read, and the rule of three
Top: the three shapes to lay out large on a roof or lawn and what each tells a pilot. Bottom: the sound and light patterns, three of anything and the SOS rhythm.
\n
    \n
  • Use the roof, a lawn or an empty lot. Make each letter as large as you can and with strong contrast: dark sheets on a light roof, bright clothing on dark ground.
    • \n
  • X = someone needs medical help. SOS = we need help. An arrow shows which way you went if you have to move.
    • \n
  • From a window: tape a large sheet of paper with SOS and your apartment number in the glass, or hang a bright cloth. At night, flash a light in threes toward the street.
    • \n
  • Do not stand on a wet roof edge or lean out of a high window to signal. Being seen is not worth a fall.
    • \n
\n\n

Telling rescuers where you are

\n

The single most useful thing you can do is give a location a stranger can find without you.

\n
    \n
  1. Call 911 if life is in danger. If you cannot speak or the call will not connect, text 911: Text-to-911 has worked in New York City since June 2020. Call if you can, text if you can’t.
    2. \n
  2. Say it in this order: borough, street address, cross streets, floor, apartment number, which side of the building (front, back, facing which street). Then the problem, then how many people.
    3. \n
  3. If you do not know the address, read two street signs at the corner, or describe the nearest landmark, subway entrance or store name.
    4. \n
  4. Keep the phone free after the call. Do not drain it with video. Turn on low-power mode.
    5. \n
  5. Use Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692) for the city’s instructions, and 311 for help that is not life-threatening.
    6. \n
\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

New York addresses confuse rescuers. “East 34th” and “West 34th” are a mile apart. A Queens address like 38-01 35th Avenue needs the hyphen. Say the borough first, always, because street names repeat across the five boroughs.

Sign up for Notify NYC in advance: text your ZIP code to 692-692 for alerts about your neighbourhood, or use a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov. 911 is for danger to life; 311 is for everything else.

\n\n

If you are trapped in a building

\n

After a collapse, an explosion or an earthquake, follow the FEMA (Federal Emergency Management Agency) and Ready.gov rules for being trapped under debris:

\n
    \n
  1. Send a text if you have any signal. Texts get through when calls do not.
    2. \n
  2. Bang on a pipe or a wall. Metal carries sound through a building far better than your voice. Use a shoe, a belt buckle, a key. Three taps, pause, three taps.
    3. \n
  3. Use a whistle instead of shouting. Shouting makes you breathe in dangerous amounts of dust. Shout only as a last resort.
    4. \n
  4. Cover your mouth with your shirt or a cloth to filter the dust.
    5. \n
  5. Do not move about or kick up dust. Stay still, stay calm, save your air and your strength.
    6. \n
\n

If you are stuck in an elevator: press the alarm button, use the intercom or call 911, and wait. Do not try to climb out. If the building is on fire, never use the elevator at all; use the stairs.

\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Shouting yourself hoarse in the first ten minutes. Under rubble, shouting fills your lungs with dust and burns the strength you need for the hours that rescue can take. Rescuers listen for tapping on pipes and for whistles; they may not hear a voice through concrete at all.

Tap, whistle, text. Shout only when you hear someone close.

\n\n

Leaving word behind

\n

Search teams and family members start from the last place they know you were. Give them a trail.

\n
    \n
  • The door note. Ready.gov: leave a note telling others when you left and where you are going. Write the date and time, your destination, who is with you (including pets), and a phone number for your out-of-town contact.
    • \n
  • The out-of-town contact. Local lines jam; long-distance texts often get through. Send the same message to one person outside the city and ask them to relay it to everyone else.
    • \n
  • On the move. If you must leave a place where you told people you would be, leave a second note there, and an arrow if outdoors. Update your contact at every stop.
    • \n
  • If someone is hurt and you go for help, leave them with the whistle, mark the spot with something bright, write the exact location on your hand or phone, and tell the first responder you meet.
    • \n
\n
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Not confirmed from an official page today — confirm before you rely on this by asking FDNY (Fire Department of New York) at a firehouse, or 311, or by reading your building’s fire safety plan: that if you are trapped in an apartment by a fire you should stuff wet towels along the bottom of the door, call 911 and give your floor and apartment number, and wave a cloth from the window; and that the letter V laid on the ground means “require assistance” in the ground-to-air code.

Your building must post a fire safety plan; read the one in your lobby this week.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Under $2: a plastic pea-less whistle on your key ring and another in the walk-out bag.
  • Free: practise three whistle blasts and the SOS rhythm (three short, three long, three short) until you can do it without thinking.
  • Free: write your full address the rescuer way — borough, street, cross streets, floor, apartment, side of building — on the card in your wallet.
  • Free: choose your out-of-town contact and save them as “ICE” (In Case of Emergency) in your phone.
  • Free: find the metal pipe or radiator in your apartment that runs through the building. That is what you tap on.
  • Under $10: a small flashlight kept by the bed, and a compact mirror in the bag.
  • Free: read the fire safety plan posted in your building lobby.
✅ VERIFIED
  • Ready.gov (FEMA), “Earthquakes” (if trapped: text, bang on a pipe or wall, whistle instead of shouting, cover your mouth, do not kick up dust), ready.gov/earthquakes (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • FEMA, “Earthquake Safety Checklist” FEMA B-526, fema.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Hunter-Ed National Hunter Safety Course, “Signaling for Help” (three of any signal; X, SOS, arrow ground signals), hunter-ed.com (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Be Ready Utah, “Signaling” (three whistle blasts), beready.utah.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Wikipedia, “SOS” (Morse pattern and visual use), en.wikipedia.org (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Ready.gov, “Build A Kit” (whistle, flashlight in the basic kit), ready.gov/kit (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • Ready.gov, “Evacuation” (leave a note telling others when you left and where you are going), ready.gov/evacuation (checked 26 Sep 2026)
  • NYC Emergency Management, Notify NYC and Text-to-911, a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov (checked 26 Sep 2026)

Do this first, tonight, before anything else in this chapter: walk through your apartment with your phone and film every room, every closet and every drawer, then take a photo of the front and back of your ID, your insurance cards and your lease and put those photos in a cloud folder. It takes twenty minutes and costs nothing. After a fire, a flood or a burglary the paper is gone, and every single form of help — the insurer, FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency), the bank, the pharmacy, the landlord, the housing court — starts with the same question: prove who you are and prove what you had.

1. Why the folder matters more than the flashlight

Water and batteries get you through the first three days. The document folder gets you through the next three months: the insurance claim, the FEMA application, a replacement passport, a prescription refill when the doctor’s office is closed, and getting back into your own bank account when your phone is at the bottom of a flooded basement.

📘 DEFINITION

EFFAK (Emergency Financial First Aid Kit) is the free checklist and set of forms that Ready.gov and FEMA publish to help you collect and secure your financial, medical and household information before a disaster. It has four sections: Household Identification, Financial and Legal Documentation, Medical Information and Household Contacts.

It is free at ready.gov/emergency-financial-first-aid-kit, or by phone from FEMA at (800) 480-2520. Download the PDF to your iPad now, while the internet works, and tick the items as you collect them.

2. What goes in the folder

Copy, do not move. The originals stay where they are (passport in the drawer, lease with your papers). The folder holds copies, because a copy is enough to start every claim and application, and a copy you can carry is worth more than an original you cannot reach.

📊 FIGURE — What goes in the document folder and where the three copies live
The folder holds copies in the four EFFAK groups plus one handwritten summary page. The green row shows the three places a copy should exist, because each survives something the others do not.
Group (EFFAK section)Copy theseWhy you will need it
Household identificationDriver licence or state ID, passport, birth certificate, Social Security card (or just the number written down), immigration papers, marriage or divorce papers, pet vaccination record and microchip numberEvery FEMA and insurance form asks for identity and Social Security number. Shelters ask for pet vaccination records.
Financial and legalLease and the landlord’s name, address and phone; renters insurance policy number and the claims phone line; bank and credit card account numbers with the customer-service numbers; last pay stub; tax return first page; car title and registration; will, power of attorney, health-care proxyTo prove where you live, what you are insured for, and to reach the bank when the app is dead.
MedicalHealth insurance card (front and back), list of every medication with dose and prescribing doctor, pharmacy name and phone, allergies, immunisation record, doctors’ names and numbers, medical equipment detailsSo a stranger at a shelter or a new pharmacy can keep you on your medicine.
Household contactsOut-of-town contact, family, employer and HR phone line, building super and management office, school, vet, utility account numbers (Con Edison, gas, internet)Phones lose their contact list when they die. Paper does not.

Add one more thing that no official checklist mentions: a one-page summary in your own handwriting — your full name, date of birth, address, Social Security number, insurance policy number and claims line, bank name, doctor, pharmacy, out-of-town contact. Frightened and exhausted, you will not want to search a folder; one page answers most of the questions you will be asked.

3. Three copies in three places

Ready.gov and FEMA describe the same pattern: paper copies at home in a fireproof and waterproof box or safe, or in a bank safe-deposit box, or with a trusted friend or relative; and electronic copies stored password-protected on a flash drive or external drive kept in that fireproof, waterproof box, or in a secure cloud service. Do all three if you can; each fails in a different way.

CopyWhereWhat it survivesWhat it does not survive
PaperZip-top freezer bag inside your go-bag, plus a second set with a friend or relative in another borough or stateDead phone, no internet, no power, being asked for a document in personFire or flood in the one place it is kept
Flash drivePassword-protected files, on your keys or in the go-bagNo internet, cloud account lockedLosing the keys; a drive left in a flooded basement
CloudA folder in the cloud service you already use, plus the photos of every roomFire, flood, theft of everything you ownLosing access to the account itself — which is why the next section on backup codes exists
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Keeping the only copy in a basement or ground-floor apartment. During Hurricane Ida on 1–2 September 2021, rain fell on New York City at about 3.5 inches per hour, roughly double the 1.75 inches per hour the sewers were built for; 14 people died in the city and 10 of them drowned in basement apartments. Water fills a basement in minutes. If your paper, your drive and your cash all live below street level, they are gone with the first storm. Store the paper set high up, and give the second set to someone in another building.

The same applies to a fire: the cheapest fireproof document bag costs less than a week of coffee. If you cannot afford a box, the friend-in-another-borough copy is free.

4. Photograph every room tonight

An insurance claim, and much of a FEMA application, is a list of what you owned and what it was worth. After a loss you will not remember. The Insurance Information Institute (III) says a visual record can be a video walk-through of your home or a series of photographs with written descriptions, and that your list should include the type of item, the original price (with the receipt if you have it), the year you bought it, and the serial number. Store a copy outside your home — with a friend or in a safe-deposit box — so you can hand it to the insurance representative even if the apartment is destroyed.

  1. Stand in each doorway and film a slow 360-degree sweep. Say out loud what you are looking at (“living room, sofa, the TV I bought in 2024”).
  2. Open every closet, drawer and cabinet on camera. Clothes, shoes, kitchen equipment and bedding add up to thousands of dollars that people forget to claim.
  3. Photograph the label or serial-number plate on the laptop, iPad, phone, TV, bike and any appliance you own.
  4. Photograph receipts for anything expensive; forward email receipts to a folder called inventory.
  5. Upload the video and photos to the cloud tonight. A video on a phone that then drowns is not a record.
  6. Repeat once a year and after any big purchase.

5. Cash in small bills

When the power goes, the card readers, the ATMs and the payment apps go with it. Ready.gov says to keep a small amount of cash at home in a safe place, in small bills, because ATMs and credit cards may not work in a disaster when you need to buy supplies, fuel or food, and businesses may not be able to give change. A bodega open by flashlight will take a five; it cannot break a hundred or run your card.

  • Mostly ones, fives and tens; a few twenties. Some quarters for a laundromat or a payphone-style emergency.
  • Split it: part in the go-bag, part in the document box, a small amount in your everyday wallet.
  • Add a few dollars every payday rather than finding it all at once.
  • Never tell anyone outside your household where it is.
❓ NOT VERIFIED

Ready.gov does not print a dollar amount. A common rule of thumb is enough to cover a few days of food, a taxi or bus fare out of the city, medicine and a night somewhere safe, but that figure is an opinion, not an official number. Work it out against your own budget and confirm before you rely on this: your bank’s branch staff or a housing counsellor can help you size it.

Also unconfirmed: how long a given bank keeps ATMs running on backup power. Assume none.

6. Passwords, two-factor backup codes and the lost phone

This is the failure almost nobody plans for. Your cloud copies, your bank, your email and your insurer’s app are all protected by two-factor authentication (2FA) — a code sent to your phone or generated by an app on it. If the phone is lost, drowned or stolen in the emergency, you are locked out of the very copies you made. Google describes the fix: backup codes, a set of ten single-use eight-digit codes you generate in advance, to use if you lose your phone, change your number or otherwise cannot get codes. Google’s own advice is to print them and keep them where you keep your passport or other important documents; do not share them, and remember each code works once.

  1. For each account that matters (email first, then bank, cloud storage, insurer, iCloud or Google account), open the security settings and generate backup codes.
  2. Print or hand-copy them on to the one-page summary in the document folder. Do not keep the only copy as a screenshot on the phone you are protecting against losing.
  3. Add a second 2FA method where the service allows it, such as a second trusted device or your iPad.
  4. Write down the recovery email and phone number attached to each account, and keep those accounts alive.
  5. If you use a password manager, know its master password by heart and store its own recovery kit on paper in the folder.
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Email is the master key: almost every other account resets through it. Protect the email account’s backup codes first.

7. The pocket you grab on the way out

Put the paper set, the flash drive, the cash and the one-page summary in one zip-top bag in the front pocket of the go-bag. If you leave with nothing else, leave with that bag and your phone charger.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Sign up now for the city’s official alerts so the warning reaches you before the water does: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692, or text your ZIP code to 692-692 for neighbourhood alerts; the web version is a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov and there is an app.

Two numbers go on the one-page summary: 911 for a life-threatening emergency, 311 for everything else in the city (no heat, flooding in the street, a landlord who will not fix things, finding an open center). Text-to-911 has worked in NYC since June 2020: call if you can, text if you cannot.

Find and write down your hurricane evacuation zone (zone 1 is evacuated first, zone 6 last) at maps.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311.

🛠 DO THIS NOW

Cheapest first — all of this can be done this week:

  • Tonight: film every room, closet and drawer; photograph ID, insurance cards, lease; upload to the cloud. Cost: nothing.
  • Generate and print backup codes for your email, bank and cloud accounts; put the paper in the folder. Cost: nothing.
  • Write the one-page summary by hand. Cost: nothing.
  • Download the EFFAK from Ready.gov to the iPad and tick what you already have.
  • Put the first small bills in an envelope; add to it every payday.
  • Photocopy the folder and hand the second set to a friend or relative in another building.
  • Buy a zip-top freezer bag now; a fireproof, waterproof document bag when the budget allows.
  • Text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources checked 26 Sep 2026:

  • Ready.gov, “Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK)” — ready.gov/emergency-financial-first-aid-kit.
  • Ready.gov / FEMA, “Safeguard Critical Documents and Valuables” — ready.gov/collection/safeguard-critical-documents-valuables.
  • Ready.gov, “Financial Preparedness” — ready.gov/financial-preparedness.
  • Insurance Information Institute, “Brochure: Home Inventory” — iii.org/article/brochure-home-inventory.
  • Google Account Help, “Sign in with backup codes” — support.google.com/accounts/answer/1187538.
  • NYC Emergency Management, Notify NYC, Know Your Zone, Text-to-911 and Hurricane Ida figures — from the course FACTS file, verified 26 Sep 2026: a858-nycnotify.nyc.gov, maps.nyc.gov/hurricane.

If there is water on the floor: get safe first, then photograph everything before you move, dry or throw away a single thing. Then call your insurer, then report to the city through 311 and reportdamage.nyc.gov, then apply to FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) if a disaster is declared. That order matters because money follows evidence: the insurer pays on photographs, FEMA pays only for what insurance does not, and the city’s damage reports feed the request for a federal declaration.

📊 FIGURE — After flood damage: get safe, photograph, insurer, city, then FEMA
Work down the numbered boxes in this order and no other; the notes beside each say what to do in that step. Step 2 comes before any cleaning because every payment depends on the photographs.

1. Renters insurance and the flood gap

Renters insurance covers your belongings after a fire, a theft or a burst pipe. It is cheap, and it has one hole: standard renters insurance does not cover flooding. It covers water from a burst pipe or a leaking appliance, not water that rises from outside — storm surge, a street that turns into a river, a sewer backing up into a basement. For that you need a separate flood policy.

📘 DEFINITION

NFIP (National Flood Insurance Program) is the federal flood-insurance programme run by FEMA. Renters can buy a contents-only policy that covers belongings — furniture, clothing, electronics, bedding, kitchen items — up to $100,000. It does not cover the building; that is the landlord’s problem. You buy it through an insurance agent; the starting point is floodsmart.gov.

The NFIP renters brochure says contents cover applies to units above the lowest elevated floor. In a basement or ground-floor unit, ask the agent exactly what is covered before you pay.

LossStandard renters policyNFIP contents policy
Fire, smoke, theft, burst pipe, appliance leakUsually coveredNot covered
Storm surge, street flooding, rising waterNot coveredCovered up to $100,000 of your belongings
The building, walls, boiler, wiringLandlord’s insuranceLandlord’s flood policy

2. The 30-day waiting period

A new NFIP policy usually takes effect 30 days after you buy it. The common exception (a policy required by a lender for a loan) does not apply to a renter. The wait exists to stop people buying cover when the hurricane is already on the news.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting for the forecast. A hurricane named on Monday can be in the harbour by Friday; a flood policy bought that Monday pays nothing for it. Buy by early summer. If you live in evacuation zone 1, 2 or 3, or below street level, decide this week, not in the week of the storm.

The second mistake is assuming the landlord’s insurance covers your things. It does not: it pays the owner for the building. Your sofa, laptop and clothes are yours to insure.

3. Document the damage before you clean up

New York City’s flood-claims guidance: once the home is safe, the most important immediate step is to take pictures and write specific notes on the damage to the home and to your belongings. Then register the claim with your insurer as soon as possible. Do not make permanent repairs before the insurer or adjuster has seen the damage. Keep every receipt and record; you need them for the claim and again if government help comes.

  1. Safety first: standing water near outlets, a basement still filling, or a gas smell means get out and call 911.
  2. Film a slow walk-through of every damaged room, then close-ups: the water line on the wall, each ruined item, each serial-number label.
  3. List as you go: item, when bought, what it cost. Your pre-disaster video is the “before” that makes the “after” believable.
  4. Call the insurer’s claims line; write down the claim number and the adjuster’s name.
  5. Stop further damage (move dry things up, mop), but keep ruined items until the adjuster has seen them or says in writing you may discard them.
  6. One envelope for every receipt: cleaning supplies, a hotel night, clothes, a taxi.
🦺 SAFETY

Floodwater is sewage. Gloves, closed shoes, wash hands after every session; throw out food, medicine and soft furnishings the water touched — after photographing them.

4. Report it to the city: 311 and the damage report

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC Emergency Management asks every New Yorker hit by flooding to take two separate steps: submit a damage report at reportdamage.nyc.gov and file a 311 service request (call 311, use the 311 website or the 311 app). The city uses these to measure the storm, and the total may support a request for federal disaster assistance.

The damage report does not replace an insurance claim and does not guarantee any financial help; it is for assessment and planning. Claim to the insurer, application to FEMA, report to the city. Do all three.

Use 311 also for what the landlord must fix (section 8), a flooded street, a blocked catch basin, and to find an open center. Video relay 212-639-9675; TTY 212-504-4115.

5. Applying to FEMA

FEMA Individual Assistance is federal help for people whose homes and belongings were hit by a declared disaster, for needs that insurance does not cover. Four ways to apply; online is fastest.

HowWhere
Online (fastest)DisasterAssistance.gov — create an account to save the application, check status, answer messages and upload documents
Phone1-800-621-3362 (FEMA Helpline, toll-free)
AppThe FEMA mobile app
In personA Disaster Recovery Center (section 6)

Have ready: your home address, mailing address and email; phone number; Social Security number; bank account details for direct deposit; and your insurance information. FEMA states that you, another adult in the household, or a minor child must have a Social Security number and be a U.S. citizen, non-citizen national or qualified alien.

Insurance first, FEMA second. By law FEMA cannot duplicate benefits: it cannot pay for anything your insurance covers, so file the insurance claim right away. FEMA may then help with uninsured or under-insured losses, and may help if the insurance settlement is delayed more than 30 days. When FEMA asks for insurance documents, it must receive your settlement or denial within 60 days of the date on its letter. If FEMA says no or incomplete, you can complete or appeal within 60 days of the decision letter — a “no” is often a request for one more document.

🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Never throw away a FEMA or insurance letter; each carries a date and a deadline. Photograph it the day it arrives.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

The following are widely repeated but I could not confirm them from a FEMA page today — confirm before you rely on this at DisasterAssistance.gov or on the FEMA Helpline 1-800-621-3362:

  • Individual Assistance exists only after a presidential major-disaster declaration that covers your county; no declaration means no FEMA money, only insurance and city help.
  • The usual window to register is about 60 days from the declaration. Apply the day it is announced and the deadline never matters.
  • Current FEMA Helpline hours and relay services.

6. The Disaster Recovery Center

A Disaster Recovery Center (DRC) is a temporary FEMA office opened near the affected neighbourhood after a declaration. Staff help one-on-one: applying, questions about an existing application, uploading documents. You need bring nothing but yourself, though insurance information and the address and ZIP code of the damaged home make it faster.

  • Find one: the locator at FEMA.gov/DRC, or text DRC and your ZIP code to 43362 (for example DRC 11221).
  • Confirm via 311 or the official finder at the time — centers change with each emergency. Never trust an address from a previous storm.
  • Bring the one-page summary, the folder and every FEMA letter. If denied, ask what document would change the answer.

7. When the insurer will not pay: the state hotline

The New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) regulates insurers. In a disaster it activates a Disaster Hotline at (800) 339-1759, in more than 200 languages, to answer insurance questions, advise on documenting losses and take complaints against a stalling insurer (dfs.ny.gov/consumers/disaster_flood). Undocumented New Yorkers can call the Office for New Americans hotline, (800) 566-7636, Monday to Friday 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

8. What your landlord must legally provide

Under New York’s warranty of habitability every tenant has the right to safe, functional housing, and the Housing Maintenance Code, enforced by HPD (NYC Department of Housing Preservation and Development), sets exact numbers for heat and hot water. They are the law; 311 is how you enforce it.

RuleWhat the law requires
Heat season1 October to 31 May
Daytime, 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.Inside at least 68°F whenever it is below 55°F outside
Night, 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.Inside at least 62°F, whatever the outside temperature
Hot waterAt least 120°F at the tap, 365 days a year
After a floodLandlords are responsible for building-related flood damage under the Housing Maintenance Code (HPD flooding guidance for renters)

To report: call 311 or use the 311 website or app, with address, apartment number and a phone number. HPD contacts the owner and may call you to ask whether service is back; if not, an inspector verifies and issues a violation. If the landlord ignores violations, HPD can make emergency repairs and bill the owner, and you can bring an HP Action in Housing Court to force repairs. Keep a log: date, time, the reading on a cheap thermometer, every call or text to the super. The log is the evidence.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Confirm before you rely on this — ask 311 or HPD, or a tenant lawyer through the City Bar Justice Center:

  • Non-government guides say HPD aims to inspect a heat complaint within 24 hours in heat season and that complaints can be anonymous.
  • The same guides list working plumbing, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, common-area lighting and pest-free conditions under the warranty. Ask HPD which code section applies.
  • A tenant whose apartment cannot be used normally after a flood may be able to seek a rent reduction. Get free legal advice before withholding any rent; withholding without advice risks eviction.
🛠 DO THIS NOW

This week, cheapest first:

  • Read your renters policy and find “flood” in the exclusions. Cost: nothing.
  • Below street level or in zones 1–3: get an NFIP contents quote at floodsmart.gov this week, because of the 30-day wait.
  • Save these to the one-page summary: insurer claims line; 1-800-621-3362; DFS (800) 339-1759; text DRC + ZIP to 43362; reportdamage.nyc.gov; 311.
  • Create your DisasterAssistance.gov account now, while you are calm.
  • Buy a cheap indoor thermometer and put it in the room where you sleep; start a heat log on 1 October if the apartment is cold.
  • Write the super’s and management office’s numbers in the folder.
✅ VERIFIED

Sources checked 26 Sep 2026:

  • FEMA, “Flood Insurance” — fema.gov/flood-insurance; NFIP, “Flood Insurance for Renters” — agents.floodsmart.gov; NFIP, “Buy a Flood Insurance Policy” — floodsmart.gov.
  • NYC, “Flood Insurance: Filing Claims” — nyc.gov (PDF); NYC Emergency Management press release 1 Aug 2025, “Report Flood Damage and Submit 311 Service Requests” — nyc.gov/site/em.
  • FEMA, “Apply for Disaster Assistance” — fema.gov; DisasterAssistance.gov, “What to Expect When You Apply Online” — disasterassistance.gov; FEMA fact sheet, “FEMA Assistance for Survivors with Insurance Coverage” — fema.gov.
  • FEMA, “What is a Disaster Recovery Center?” — fema.gov; “Text to Find a DRC” — fema.gov; DRC Locator — egateway.fema.gov.
  • NYS Department of Financial Services, “Disaster and Flood Recovery” — dfs.ny.gov.
  • NYC HPD, “Heat and Hot Water Information” — nyc.gov/site/hpd; HPD, “Flooding Resources for Renters” — nyc.gov (PDF); HPD, “Tenant Rights and Responsibilities” — home.nyc.gov/site/hpd; City Bar Justice Center, “Hurricane Ida, Now What?” — citybarjusticecenter.org.

Do this first: write one card that says who may collect your child, who holds a spare key to any older or disabled neighbour you look after, and what medicines each of them takes. Keep it in your go-bag and a photo of it on your phone. In every large emergency the people who are hurt worst are the ones who cannot leave on their own and whom nobody was clearly responsible for: a child waiting at a school gate, an 80-year-old on the ninth floor when the elevator stops.

1. Teach a child three things before anything else

Ready.gov (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security preparedness site) says to involve children in the family plan early: taking part lowers their fear and prepares them to act. Teach these in this order, and practise them like a game until they are automatic.

What the child must knowWhy it matters
How to dial 911 on your phone and on a locked phone, and when it is right to call (someone hurt, fire, cannot wake an adult)Ready.gov: teach children how to use the phone and when it is appropriate to call 911
Their home address, a phone number, and the first and last names of their parents or caregiversA crying child who can say “Natasha Henry, 4th floor” can be reunited in minutes instead of hours
The one out-of-town contact everyone in the family textsReady.gov: pick the same person for every family member, out of town, because they are easier to reach in a disaster; text, do not talk, unless in immediate danger
Where the family meets if you cannot get home (a spot outside the building, and a spot in the neighbourhood)A child who has a plan does what the plan says instead of freezing
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Text, do not call. Texts get through when calls fail, and they keep phone lines free for 911. Put the out-of-town contact in the child’s phone as a favourite and write it on paper in their school bag.

2. The school will not hand your child to you unless you are on the card

NYC Public Schools keep an Emergency Contact Card (the “blue card”) for every child. If the school closes early or your child is ill, the school calls the people on that card. Schools will not release a child to anyone not listed, and the person collecting must show identification. You can update the card online through your NYC Schools Account at schoolsaccount.nyc under “Emergency Contacts”, or on paper at the main office.

📊 FIGURE — What a NYC school does in an incident and who may collect a child
Top to bottom: the school calls 911, then runs one of the four General Response Protocol responses. The last box is the rule that decides whether your child comes home with you.

Every NYC public school drills the General Response Protocol. It has four responses, and it helps to know the words your child will hear:

  • Evacuation — leave the building, usually to a nearby site.
  • Shelter-In — stay inside because the danger is outside (weather, an incident on the street).
  • Hold — stay in the classroom while something is dealt with elsewhere in the building.
  • Lockdown — doors locked, out of sight, silent, because of a threat inside or near the building.

In every incident the school administration calls 911 first. Families are told to register with Notify NYC (text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692) and to call 311 for information about a school during an emergency. During a lockdown the school cannot release children until police clear it; standing at the gate does not shorten that.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Sending a friend, a new partner or a grandparent who is not on the card to collect your child. The school will refuse, the child stays, and you have spent your one trip across town for nothing.

Fix it this week: put at least three people on the card who live or work within walking distance of the school, and tell each of them they are on it.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

School closures and early dismissals are announced through Notify NYC and the school’s own messaging. Sign up for both. For questions about a specific school during an emergency, call 311 (Video Relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115).

If your child is in daycare or an after-school programme, ask them the same three questions: who may collect, where do you evacuate to, and how will you tell me? Write the answers on the card.

3. Comfort items and routines are equipment, not luxuries

A frightened child eats, sleeps and follows instructions better when something is familiar. Give the child a small bag of their own:

  • One small comfort object — a duplicate, not the favourite that must never be lost.
  • A card with their name, your name, your number and the out-of-town contact.
  • A snack they like, a small water bottle, a cheap flashlight.
  • Crayons and paper or a card game.

Keep meals and bedtime at the usual hour even in a shelter. Section 3 covers what to say to a child after the event.

4. Elders and disabled people: the seven-day rule

Ready.gov’s guidance for older adults and people with disabilities is built on one fact: pharmacies and doctors’ offices may be closed for days. Plan for at least seven days of medication and medical supplies. Then build a small support network. Use this table for yourself, a parent, or the neighbour you check on.

NeedArrange nowWho to call
Medicines7 days or more on hand; a written list of every medicine, dose instructions and allergies in the kitPharmacist for an early refill; doctor for a spare prescription
Support networkAt least one person has a spare key, knows where the supplies are, and knows how to use any lifesaving equipment or give medicineFamily, a neighbour, the building super
Dialysis or clinic treatmentAsk the clinic for its emergency plan and backup providersThe clinic (NYC Health publishes a guide for dialysis patients)
OxygenAsk the supplier about emergency replacementsThe oxygen supplier
Powered equipment (ventilator, cardiac device, powered wheelchair)Register with Con Edison’s Life Sustaining Equipment programme; the equipment must be certified by a medical professionalCon Edison 1-877-582-6633 or the online account; Con Edison Senior Direct for elderly, blind and disabled customers 800-404-9097, Mon–Fri 8:30 a.m.–5 p.m.
Getting out of the zoneKnow the evacuation zone (Section 2 of the chapter on flooding); decide now where they would go311 for transport when the Mayor orders an evacuation

Con Edison says registered customers get preparedness tips, alerts before possible outages, and wellness checks during an outage. Registration is free and includes people who do not receive a Con Edison bill in their own name.

📘 DEFINITION

Special Medical Needs Shelter (SMNS) — a City shelter, opened during an evacuation, for people who do not need a hospital or nursing home but need help such as oxygen administration, wound care or monitoring of vital signs. Clinical staff, including a physician and a nurse lead, are on site. An ordinary evacuation center is accessible and has accommodations for disabilities, but it does not have medical staff in the same way.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

When the Mayor issues an evacuation order for a coastal storm or hurricane, a person with a disability or access and functional need who has no other way to leave safely can request transport by calling 311. Depending on need they are taken either to an accessible evacuation center in an accessible vehicle, or by ambulance to a hospital outside the zone.

Do not wait for the order to make the first call. Call 311 before the storm to ask what to do for a specific person, and write the answer down.

5. When the elevator is out and she cannot do the stairs

A blackout or a flooded basement takes out the elevator, and an older neighbour on a high floor is trapped by nine flights of stairs. What to do, in order:

  1. Go to her door within the first hour. Knock, say who you are, ask three things: any medicine that needs a fridge or power, any equipment that needs power, and how much water she has.
  2. Bring supplies up, not her down. Water, food that needs no cooking, a flashlight, her medicines from the fridge in a bag with ice. Carrying a frail adult down a dark stairwell injures you both.
  3. If she is in medical trouble — confused, hot to the touch, shivering and slurring, short of breath, or on equipment that has lost power — call 911. Say the floor, that the elevator is out, and what the problem is. Then call the out-of-town contact for her family.
  4. Check twice a day and agree a signal (a towel on the door handle, a text at 9 and 6). Write her name and floor on your card.
  5. In a heat emergency, an apartment on a high floor with no fan can become deadly. If she cannot get to a cooling center (finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or 311), bring cool wet cloths, water, and stay with her; confusion means 911. In a Code Blue (32°F or below including wind chill, 4 p.m. to 8 a.m.), blankets, dry clothes and warm drinks only if she is fully alert.
❓ NOT VERIFIED

How fast a landlord must restore an elevator, and who performs a stuck-elevator rescue, could not be confirmed today. If someone is inside a stuck elevator and unwell, call 911; for an elevator that is simply out of service, call 311 and, in a NYCHA building, the NYCHA Customer Contact Center.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask 311 or your building management what the rule is for your building.

6. The neighbour check: what you are looking for

A check is not a chat. You are looking for the signs that turn a bad day into a death:

SignMeansDo
Confusion, hot skin, temperature 103°F or above, may have stopped sweatingHeat strokeCall 911, cool the person immediately, no fluids if confused or unconscious
Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, cool clammy skinHeat exhaustionCool place, loosen clothing, sip water; 911 if it does not improve
Shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsinessHypothermiaWarmth, remove wet clothes, warm the chest, neck, head and groin first, warm drinks only if fully alert; 911
🦺 SAFETY

Knock, announce yourself, and do not enter an apartment that smells of gas or where you hear a carbon-monoxide alarm. Step back, call 911, and let the building know.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Tonight: write the one card — who may collect your child, who holds keys for whom, medicines and doses. Photograph it.
  • Free: log in to schoolsaccount.nyc (or the daycare office) and put three nearby adults on the emergency contact card.
  • Free: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 and your ZIP code to 692-692.
  • Free: ask one older or disabled neighbour if they would like to be on your check list. Swap numbers.
  • Free: if anyone in your circle uses powered medical equipment, call Con Edison 1-877-582-6633 to register it.
  • Under $10: a child’s comfort bag — duplicate toy, snack, card with names and numbers, small flashlight.
  • This month: ask the pharmacist about an early refill so each older person you look after holds seven days of every medicine.
✅ VERIFIED

Do this first: put the pet carrier by the front door tonight, open, with a towel inside, and leave it there. Why: when an evacuation order comes, the animal that has never seen the carrier hides under the bed, and you spend the minutes you needed for the stairs crawling after it. People delay leaving, or go back into a flooded building, for a pet they could not catch. Ready.gov’s rule is short: if officials tell you to evacuate, your pet evacuates too. Pets left behind end up lost, injured or worse.

1. Two kits: one heavy, one you can carry down the stairs

Ready.gov recommends two pet kits: a larger one for sheltering in place at home and a lightweight one for evacuation. The ASPCA (American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) says to plan three to seven days of food and water per pet.

ItemHow muchNote
Food3–7 days per petSealed; rotate every few months; a manual can opener if canned
Water3–7 days per pet, on top of your own gallon per person per dayCollapsible bowl in the light kit
Medicines and medical recordsA week of any medicine; vaccination recordPhoto of the records on your phone as well
Carrier or crate, leash, collar with tagOne per animalCats and small animals go in a carrier, always; a loose cat in a stairwell is gone
Litter and a small tray, waste bags, paper towelsEnough for a weekA shelter gives you a cot, not a litter box
Photos of you and the pet togetherPrinted and on your phoneReady.gov: proves ownership and helps others identify the pet if you are separated
Familiar itemsA toy, treats, a piece of beddingReady.gov: familiar items reduce the animal’s stress
Pet first-aid suppliesSmallASPCA lists these in a pet disaster kit

2. ID: the microchip, the tag and the sticker

The ASPCA recommends three layers: a microchip, an up-to-date ID tag on the collar, and a pre-arranged evacuation plan for the pet. Make sure the phone number on the chip registration is current — a chip with an old number finds nobody. Add the out-of-town contact’s number to the tag if there is room.

Put an ASPCA pet rescue alert sticker on your front door or a window where responders will see it. It lists the type and number of pets inside and your vet’s phone number. The ASPCA sends a free Pet Safety Pack with these stickers if you sign its disaster preparedness pledge online. If you evacuate with the pets, write “EVACUATED” across the sticker so nobody risks a search for an empty apartment.

3. Where a pet can go in New York City

📘 DEFINITION

Evacuation center — a City-run site (usually a school) opened when the Mayor orders an evacuation. NYC Emergency Management says evacuation centers are accessible and pet-friendly. Pets and service animals are allowed at City shelters. You must bring the supplies to care for the animal: food, leash, a carrier and any medication. Centers change with each emergency: confirm via 311 or the official finder at the time.

🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Find the open centers at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311 (Video Relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115). Ready.gov warns that many public shelters and hotels elsewhere do not allow pets, so if you plan to leave the city, decide now where the animal sleeps: a friend, a relative, a pet-friendly hotel you have already phoned.

During a heat emergency, cooling centers are listed at finder.nyc.gov/coolingcenters or through 311. Ask 311 or the center whether animals are admitted before you carry a cat across the neighbourhood in 95°F heat.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

Whether every NYC cooling center admits pets, what Animal Care Centers of NYC does for lost or surrendered animals during a disaster, and the number for the ASPCA Animal Poison Control Center could not be confirmed today.

Confirm before you rely on this: call 311 for cooling centers and lost-pet services, and check aspca.org for the current poison control number and its fee. Keep your own vet’s number and the nearest 24-hour animal hospital on the rescue sticker.

4. The child who will not leave the cat

A child will not walk out of the apartment while the cat is under the bed, and neither will you. Solve it before the day:

📊 FIGURE — Leaving with a pet: open carrier, pet officer, two-minute limit
Follow the arrows from the preparation at the top to the decision diamond. Whichever branch you take, both end at the same rule in red: nobody goes back into the building.
  1. Practise the carrier. Feed the cat in the open carrier for a week. Then close the door for a minute. Then carry it to the hallway and back. Do it monthly.
  2. Give the child the job. The child is the “pet officer”: they carry the light pet kit and hold the leash, and they know the plan is that the pet comes. A child with a job moves; a child with no job clings.
  3. Set a time limit out loud. “We look for two minutes, then we go.” If the animal cannot be found when water is coming in or a fire alarm is sounding, you leave with the child. Tell the child the truth: the pet hides where it feels safe, and rescuers and neighbours will be told.
  4. Never send anyone back. Not the child, not yourself, not for the cat, not for the dog.
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Going back into a building for a pet after you have got out — into a flooded basement, a smoke-filled hallway, a building the fire department has cleared. In Hurricane Ida, 10 of the 14 people who died in New York City drowned in basement apartments as water rose faster than anyone expected.

The way to make sure you never face that choice is the open carrier by the door and the monthly practice.

5. Animals in a heat wave

The ASPCA’s hot-weather advice: give pets a shady place out of the sun, plenty of fresh water, do not over-exercise them, and keep them indoors when it is extremely hot. Never leave an animal alone in a parked vehicle. Flat-faced animals (pugs, Persian cats) cannot pant well and overheat faster; elderly, overweight animals and those with heart or lung disease should be in an air-conditioned room as much as possible. Trim long coats but never shave to the skin — the coat protects from overheating and sunburn.

Signs of overheating (ASPCA)Do
Excessive panting or difficulty breathing, fast heart and breathing rate, drooling, mild weaknessShade or an air-conditioned room, cool water to drink, wet the fur with cool (not ice) water, call the vet
Stupor, collapse, seizures, bloody diarrhoea or vomit, body temperature over 104°FThis is an emergency: cool the animal and get to a vet or 24-hour animal hospital now

NYC Health issued a 2026 advisory to veterinarians on heat-related illness in pets. Walk dogs early morning or after dark on the hottest days, and on grass where you can — hot pavement burns paw pads (Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine). If your own apartment has no power and no air-conditioning, the animal is in the same danger as you: find a cooler room, a cool wet towel to lie on, and a friend with power.

6. Animals in the cold

The American Red Cross and the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) both say: when temperatures drop, bring pets inside. In a Code Blue, a dog left on a fire escape or balcony is in the same danger as a person outdoors.

  • Frostbite (ears, tail, paws): bring the animal in at once, warm the area gently with warm — never hot — water, do not rub or massage it, and see a vet promptly.
  • Ice-melt and rock salt on the sidewalk can irritate, sicken or kill an animal that licks its paws: wipe paws after every walk.
  • Antifreeze tastes sweet and is deadly. Keep it sealed and clean spills at once; a pet that may have licked some needs a vet immediately.

7. If you truly cannot take the pet

Ready.gov’s position is that the pet comes with you, and that leaving it means it may end up lost, injured or worse. Sometimes a person is carried out by ambulance, or a rescue boat has no room. The most useful thing you can do is what you did before: the rescue sticker with the number and type of animals, your phone number and your vet’s, and a neighbour with a key who knows the pet exists.

❓ NOT VERIFIED

The detailed advice sometimes printed for a pet that must be left behind — do not tie it up, leave it in a room with many bowls of water, leave a note on the door — could not be confirmed from an official page today.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask your vet, or check the ASPCA and Ready.gov pet pages, and tell 311 or the rescuers that an animal is inside and where.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Free: put the carrier by the door, open, with a towel in it. Start feeding the cat in it tonight.
  • Free: check the microchip registration and the tag: your current number and the out-of-town contact.
  • Free: photograph the pet, and you with the pet, and the vaccination record. Save to the phone and the cloud.
  • Free: sign the ASPCA disaster preparedness pledge online for the free rescue stickers; until they arrive, write “1 cat inside” and your number on a card taped to the door.
  • Under $15: a collapsible bowl, a week of food in a sealed bag, a small litter tray and litter in the light kit.
  • Free: phone one friend or relative outside the city and ask, “If we had to leave, could the pet come?” Write the answer on your plan card.
  • Free: give the child the pet-officer job and rehearse “two minutes then we go” once.
✅ VERIFIED
  • Ready.gov, “Prepare Your Pets for Disasters”, ready.gov/pets, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NYC Emergency Management, “Pets & Service Animals” and “Hurricane Evacuation”, nyc.gov/site/em/ready/pets.page, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • ASPCA, “Disaster Preparedness” and “Disaster Prep Kits: What You Need to Keep Your Pets Safe”, aspca.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • ASPCA, “Hot Weather Safety Tips”, aspca.org/pet-care/general-pet-care/hot-weather-safety-tips, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NYC Health, 2026 veterinary advisory “Extreme Heat Risk for Heat-Related Illness in Pets”, nyc.gov (PDF); Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine, “Summer heat safety tips for dogs”, vet.cornell.edu, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • American Red Cross, “10 Ways to Help Keep Pets Safe When It’s Cold” (2026), redcross.org; AVMA, “Cold weather animal safety”, avma.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
