Do this first: decide now, while you are calm, that in any emergency lasting more than a day you will sleep on a schedule, and that you will make no big decision alone after a night without sleep. Why: the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH, part of the CDC) reports that being awake for 24 hours impairs you about as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.10%, which is over the legal driving limit. At hour 48 of a blackout you will feel that you are thinking clearly. You will not be.

1. What 48 hours of stress does to your decisions

Hours awakeImpairment is about the same asSource
17 hoursBlood alcohol 0.05%; reaction time about 50% slower than restedNIOSH / CDC
24 hoursBlood alcohol 0.10%, above the legal driving limitNIOSH / CDC

You would not let someone that drunk decide whether to wade through flood water, drive out of the city, or leave a pet. So build the safeguards in while you are sober:

  • Two-person rule. Any decision that cannot be undone — leaving the apartment, going back in, giving a medicine, crossing water — is said out loud to one other person (in person, or the out-of-town contact by text) before you do it.
  • Write it down. A notebook with the time, what you decided and why. Reading it back catches errors that a tired brain cannot feel.
  • Eat and drink on the clock, not by appetite. Stress kills appetite; low blood sugar and dehydration make the thinking worse.
  • No alcohol to “take the edge off”. It adds to the impairment in the table and ruins the sleep you are trying to protect.
  • Slow down the one thing that cannot be slowed. If you are about to do something irreversible, count to ten and say the reason aloud. If the reason is “I can’t stand this any more”, that is stress talking, not the situation.
📘 DEFINITION

Acute stress reaction — the body’s normal response in the hours and days after a frightening event: racing heart, shaking, tunnel vision, poor sleep, irritability, trouble concentrating, replaying the event. It is not a weakness and it is not an illness; it is expected. What matters is that it narrows judgement, which is why the rules above exist.

2. Sleep and routine as survival tools

In a shelter or a dark apartment, routine is the cheapest protection you have. The National Child Traumatic Stress Network (NCTSN) says children feel safer with structure and routine even in the middle of chaos, and adults are not different.

  • Sleep in shifts if there are two adults. One awake for the radio and the door, one asleep with earplugs and an eye mask. Swap every four hours. Alone: sleep when it is dark, and set an alarm for the hourly radio check rather than lying awake for it.
  • Fixed times: a meal at 8, 1 and 6; a radio or Notify NYC check on the hour; the neighbour check at 9 and 6; lights out at 10. Write it on the wall.
  • Limit the feed. Check official sources (Notify NYC, NOAA weather radio, 311) at set times and put the phone down between. Doom-scrolling burns the battery and the mind.
  • Do one useful physical task an hour — refill bottles, sort the kit, check on a neighbour. Doing beats waiting.
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

Earplugs and a fabric eye mask cost a few dollars and weigh nothing. They are the difference between four hours of real sleep in a gym full of strangers and none.

3. Psychological first aid for other people

Psychological first aid (PFA) is the method the NCTSN and the National Center for PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) built for the hours and days after a disaster. It does not require training or a licence. Its eight core actions, translated into a stairwell:

📊 FIGURE — The eight steps of psychological first aid, top to bottom
Work down the numbered rows in order: the left column is the NCTSN core action, the right is what you actually do in a stairwell. The red lines are the things never to do.
Core action (NCTSN)What you actually do
Contact and engagementApproach calmly, say your name, ask if you can help. Do not force conversation.
Safety and comfortGet them out of the immediate danger, sitting, warm or cool, with water. Protect them from more frightening sights and sounds.
StabilizationFor someone overwhelmed: speak slowly, use their name, ask them to breathe with you and name three things they can see. Keep them oriented: where they are, what time it is, what happens next.
Information gatheringAsk what they need most right now: medicine, a person, a phone, their pet. Listen for the one thing.
Practical assistanceHelp with that one thing: a charged phone, a text to their family, water, a blanket.
Connection with social supportsHelp them reach the person who matters most, or sit them with someone they know.
Information on copingTell them what they are feeling is a normal reaction and what usually helps: rest, food, routine, talking when ready.
Linkage with servicesGive them 988 or the Disaster Distress Helpline number; if there is a medical problem, 911.

What not to do: do not tell them what they “should” feel, do not make them describe the event, do not promise things you cannot deliver, and do not leave a person who talks about not wanting to live alone — stay, and call 988 with them or 911 if they are in immediate danger.

4. Children after the event

The NCTSN parent guidelines after hurricanes and other disasters come down to five actions:

  1. Reassure them they are safe — and expect to repeat it many times. Say also that many people and organisations are working to help, so they know adults are protecting their home, pets and neighbourhood.
  2. Limit media exposure. Repeated disaster images on TV, phones and the internet increase fear and anxiety, most of all in younger children. Turn it off; you can check the news on your own phone at set times.
  3. Keep routines, especially meals and bedtime. Structure feels like safety.
  4. Keep the family rules. The usual rules about behaviour and respect stay, because they are part of normal.
  5. Spend extra time and stay connected. Let them help with small jobs; being useful calms a child as much as an adult.

Expect sleep trouble, clinginess, tantrums, stomach aches or going back to younger behaviour for a while. If these are still severe weeks later, or the child talks about hurting themselves, use the numbers in the next section — they are for children and parents too.

5. When to call 988, and what it is

988 is the national Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: free, confidential, 24 hours a day, by call, text or chat. It is not only for suicide. It is for emotional distress of any kind, and it is where you go when you cannot settle, cannot sleep for the third night, cannot stop shaking, or start thinking that the people around you would be better off without you.

SituationCall
Someone is in immediate danger: has taken something, has a weapon, is about to act911 (or text 911 in NYC if you cannot call)
You or someone else is overwhelmed, hopeless, thinking about self-harm, drinking or using to cope, or just cannot cope988 — call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org; 24/7, free, confidential
Distress after a disaster specifically (a storm, flood, blackout, attack), for anyone in the U.S.Disaster Distress Helpline 1-800-985-5990 (SAMHSA, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) — call or text, 24/7; no identifying information needed; Spanish press 2; interpreters in more than 100 languages; ASL users through their relay provider
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

NYC 988 (formerly NYC Well, renamed September 2023) is the City’s own arm of the lifeline. Reach a counsellor 24/7/365 by calling 988 or 1-888-NYC-WELL (1-888-692-9355), by texting WELL to 65173, or by chat at nyc988.cityofnewyork.us. Counselling is in English, Spanish and Mandarin or Cantonese, with translation in more than 200 languages, and specialised lines for veterans, Spanish speakers and LGBTQI+ people aged 25 and under.

NYC 988 does more than talk: crisis counselling, referral to care, help scheduling an appointment, mobile crisis teams that come to you, short-term counselling, peer support and follow-up calls, regardless of insurance or immigration status.

⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting until it is “bad enough”. A person who says they cannot go on, or who starts giving things away, or who goes very calm after days of anguish, is telling you something. Do not leave them alone. Call 988 together; if they have already acted or are about to, call 911.

For yourself: if the thought “I would rather not wake up” appears, that is the moment to text 988. Not tomorrow.

6. When to get professional help after the emergency is over

Most people recover with sleep, routine, people and time. The lifeline services above are also the route to longer help: NYC 988 refers to ongoing care and offers short-term counselling. Use them if, after the danger has passed, you notice any of the following in yourself or a family member:

  • Sleep that does not come back once you are safe, or nightmares that keep you from wanting to sleep.
  • Replaying the event, jumping at every siren, avoiding the subway or the street where it happened, in a way that stops you working or studying.
  • Drinking or using more to get through the day or the night.
  • Feeling numb, cut off from people, or hopeless.
  • Any thought of harming yourself. That one is a today call, not a “wait and see”.
❓ NOT VERIFIED

How many weeks of symptoms count as “too long” before a diagnosis such as PTSD is considered is a clinical question this course could not confirm from an official page today.

Confirm before you rely on this: ask a doctor or a 988 counsellor. You do not need a threshold to call 988; distress is enough.

🛠 DO THIS NOW
  • Free: save three contacts in your phone tonight — “988”, “Disaster Distress 1-800-985-5990” and “NYC 988 1-888-692-9355 / text WELL to 65173”. Add them to the paper plan card.
  • Free: write the two-person rule and the sleep schedule on the plan card so you do not have to invent them at 3 a.m.
  • Under $5: foam earplugs and a fabric eye mask in the go-bag.
  • Free: pick the person you will text before any irreversible decision, and tell them that is their job.
  • Free: read the NCTSN parent tips once, so the words “you are safe, and people are helping” are ready.
  • Free: decide your media rule for a crisis — official sources at set times, phone down between.
✅ VERIFIED
  • CDC / NIOSH, “Impairments due to sleep deprivation are similar to impairments due to alcohol intoxication”, cdc.gov/niosh, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • National Child Traumatic Stress Network, “Psychological First Aid” fact sheet and Field Operations Guide, nctsn.org/interventions/psychological-first-aid, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NCTSN, “Parent Guidelines for Helping Children after a Hurricane” and “Parent Tips for Helping School-Age Children after Disasters”, nctsn.org, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, 988lifeline.org; New York State Office of Mental Health, “988 FAQ”, omh.ny.gov (PDF), checked 26 Sep 2026
  • NYC 988 (formerly NYC Well), “Get Help Now” and “NYC Well Texting Service”, nyc988.cityofnewyork.us; ACCESS NYC, “NYC 988”, access.nyc.gov/programs/nyc-988, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • SAMHSA, “Disaster Distress Helpline”, samhsa.gov/find-help/helplines/disaster-distress-helpline, checked 26 Sep 2026
  • Text-to-911 in NYC, as listed in FACTS.md for this course, checked 26 Sep 2026

Do this first: print the lists below, tape them inside a kitchen cupboard door, and tick the \"done\" column as you go. A kit that exists only in your head does not exist at 3 a.m. This lesson puts every item from every chapter in one place. Start with water and a way to hear alerts: they cost the least and save the most lives.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

72-hour kit: the core supplies Ready.gov (FEMA, the Federal Emergency Management Agency) says every household needs to survive alone for at least three days.

Stay kit: the same core scaled to 14 days at home with no shops, water or power. This is the Red Cross and CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) target.

Go-bag: one bag per person you can carry out the door in under two minutes. NYC Emergency Management calls it a \"Go Bag\".

Car kit: supplies kept in a vehicle's trunk in case you are stranded.

\n\n

1. How to use these lists

\n
    \n
  • Work top to bottom. Rows are ordered cheapest life-saving item first.
    • \n
  • \"Quantity\" is for one adult. Multiply by people; add extra water for pets, illness or pregnancy (CDC).
    • \n
  • Ready.gov: keep supplies in airtight plastic bags inside one or two easy-to-carry containers; prepare supplies for home, work and car. A clear bin under the bed works in a small apartment.
    • \n
  • Write the date on anything with a shelf life; the maintenance table in the twelve-month lesson uses those dates.
    • \n
\n\n

2. The 72-hour core kit (Ready.gov basic list)

\n

Every row is on the Ready.gov \"Build A Kit\" list.

📊 FIGURE — The ten items of the 72-hour kit laid out in one bin
The bin holds every row of the Ready.gov list with the quantity for one adult, in the lesson’s order from the cheapest life-saver (water, highlighted) onward.
\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ItemQuantity (one adult)WhyDone
Water1 gallon per person per day, 3 days minimum (3 gallons)Drinking, food and sanitation. Thirst kills long before hunger.☐
Non-perishable foodAt least 3 days, no cooking neededShops close; fridges fail.☐
Battery or hand-crank radio, ideally with NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) Weather Radio1Broadcasts official warnings 24/7, even in a power outage.☐
Flashlight1 per person, plus a headlamp if you canStairs go black; candles start fires.☐
First-aid kit1Ambulances are delayed in every big emergency (medical chapter).☐
Extra batteriesEnough for radio and flashlight, datedA dead radio is a paperweight.☐
Whistle and dust masks1 whistle per person; several masksSignal for help; filter dust and smoke.☐
Plastic sheeting and duct tape; moist towelettes, garbage bags and ties1 roll each; 1 packSeal a room in a chemical release; sanitation when the toilet will not flush.☐

Phone charger and backup battery (power bank)1 each, power bank kept chargedA dead phone gets no alerts.☐
\n\n

3. The two-week stay kit (home, sheltering in place)

\n

The core kit scaled to 14 days, plus these rows. Two weeks is the Red Cross and CDC home target.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ItemQuantity (one adult)WhyDone
Water14 gallons (1 gallon per day for 14 days)CDC goal. Bottled is safest: follow its expiry date. Self-filled water: replace every 6 months.☐

Food, ready to eat (and pet food)14 daysFirst in, first out (food chapter).☐
Medications; multi-purpose toolRed Cross: a 1-month supply if possible (see the medical chapter on how to get it); 1 toolPharmacies close.☐

Warm layers, blankets; cash in small bills1 set per person; what you can affordBoilers, card readers and ATMs all die with the power.☐
Fire extinguisher; smoke and carbon monoxide (CO) alarms, plus a battery CO alarm1; alarms where people sleepCO has no smell. FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) urges 10-year sealed alarms.☐
\n\n

4. The go-bag (NYC Emergency Management \"Go Bag\")

\n

One per person, kept by the door. Never in a basement storage cage you would have to go down to in a flood.

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
ItemQuantityWhyDone
Copies of documents in a waterproof containerInsurance cards, birth certificate, lease, photo IDProves who you are and where you live.☐
Extra keys; copies of credit and ATM cards; cash1 set; small billsYou may leave in a rush; card readers die with the power.☐
Bottled water and non-perishable food (energy or granola bars)What you can carryA center may take hours to reach.☐
Flashlight, battery AM/FM radio, extra batteries, whistle, dust mask, phone charger and power bank1 eachLight, information and signalling on the move.☐
List of medications and dosages; a 7-day supply if you can1 cardA shelter nurse needs this.☐

Child care and pet care itemsAs neededNYC evacuation centers accept pets; you bring supplies.☐

\n\n

5. The car kit and the work kit

\n

Ready.gov: keep a kit in the car with blankets, food and water, first aid and other items you may need if you are stranded, because a stranded car in a snowstorm becomes a freezer. Add a car phone charger and paper maps. No car? Give this list to the friend whose car is in your plan. Ready.gov also says to be ready to shelter at work for at least 24 hours: food, water, medicines and comfortable walking shoes in a grab-and-go case under your desk.

\n\n\n\n\n

Blankets, warm clothes1 set per seatEngine heat runs out; a running engine in snow risks CO.☐
Water, food, first-aid kit, flashlight1 day per personReady.gov car list.☐
Work kit: water, snacks, medicines, walking shoes, phone charger24 hours, in one grab-and-go bagReady.gov: be ready to shelter at work for at least 24 hours; in 2003 most people walked home.☐
\n\n

6. The medical list and the document list

\n
    \n
  • Medical card: name, date of birth, conditions, allergies, every medication and dose, doctor's phone, emergency contact. One in the go-bag, one in your wallet.
    • \n
  • Medical items (Red Cross): medications (a 1-month supply if possible), glasses or contacts, hearing-aid batteries, syringes if used, baby supplies. Powered equipment: register with Con Edison (callout below).
    • \n
  • Document set (Red Cross and Ready.gov EFFAK, the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit): medication list, proof of address, lease, passport or ID, birth certificate, insurance policies, bank and account information. Waterproof copies in the go-bag plus encrypted cloud copies.
    • \n
\n\n

7. Seasonal checks

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n

Do this first: pick one evening this week and run the two-minute evacuation drill described below, alone, with the lights off. It costs nothing. Under stress the brain does not invent new plans; it repeats what it has already done. Every drill in this lesson is a rehearsal of a real night: a fire alarm at 3 a.m., a blackout, a boil-water notice, a hurricane evacuation order, a network outage. Run each one once, write down what failed, fix it, and run it again. A plan you have never rehearsed is a plan you have never tested.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Drill: a timed, realistic rehearsal of one part of your emergency plan, run in calm conditions so that the moves become automatic. FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) says to make home drills realistic: start in the sleeping area, darken the home as if it were full of smoke, begin with the sound of the smoke alarm, crawl low, and follow the plan all the way to the meeting place outside.

Debrief: the five minutes after a drill when you write down what went wrong. The debrief is where the drill pays off.

\n\n

1. The two-minute evacuation drill (fire and gas)

\n

Why two minutes: Ready.gov says a fire can become life-threatening in just two minutes, so practise getting out in under two minutes, know two ways out of every room, pick a meeting place a safe distance from home, and hold a home fire drill at least twice a year. Tie the two drills to the clock changes, when FDNY (Fire Department of the City of New York) tells you to change alarm batteries, so you never forget either.

📊 FIGURE — The six moves of the two-minute evacuation drill
Follow the numbers in a snake from the bed at top left to the meeting place at bottom left; the timer runs the whole way. The last line is the one change for a gas smell.
\n
    \n
  1. Lie on the bed, lights off. Start a timer and press the test button on the smoke alarm so you hear the real sound.
    2. \n
  2. Roll out of bed low. Touch the bedroom door with the back of your hand before opening it. Hot? Use the second way out.
    3. \n
  3. Grab only the go-bag (it is by the door) and your keys and phone. Nothing else.
    4. \n
  4. Crawl or stay low to the apartment door. Close every door behind you: a closed door slows fire and smoke.
    5. \n
  5. Take the stairs, never the elevator. Count the floors.
    6. \n
  6. Stop the timer at your outside meeting place. Write the time down.
    7. \n
\n

What it teaches: where the go-bag really is, whether you can find keys in the dark, how long the stairs take, whether the second way out is actually usable (a window that will not open, a fire escape blocked by a planter). If you smelled gas instead of smoke, the same drill applies with one change: touch no light switch and make the phone call from outside.

\n\n

2. The no-power evening

\n

Pick a Friday from 6 p.m. to bedtime. Turn off the main breaker if your building lets you, or simply leave every light, outlet and the Wi-Fi off. Use only what is in your kit.

\n
    \n
  • Light: can you reach the headlamp without a phone torch? Where do you put it once the lights are on?
    • \n
  • Information: tune the hand-crank radio to a NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) weather broadcast and to a local AM station. Write the frequencies on tape stuck to the radio.
    • \n
  • Food: eat one meal from the stay kit, cold, opened with the manual can opener. Note what you disliked; swap it next shopping trip.
    • \n
  • Fridge: keep it shut the whole evening. Remember the FDA rule: a closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full freezer about 24 hours.
    • \n
  • Phone: turn on low-power mode and see how many hours the power bank buys you.
    • \n
  • Heat or cool: in winter, notice how fast one room cools and practise the one-warm-room setup; in summer, practise the wet-cloth-and-fan routine from the shelter chapter.
    • \n
\n

What it teaches: the gap between owning a kit and being able to use it. Most people discover on this evening that the batteries are dead or the radio has no NOAA band.

\n\n

3. The water-off day

\n

Choose a Saturday. Turn off the shut-off valve under the sink or simply promise yourself not to open a tap from waking until bedtime. Use only stored water.

\n
    \n
  • Measure what one person really uses in a day for drinking, cooking, washing and a bucket flush. Compare it with the 1 gallon per person per day planning figure.
    • \n
  • Practise the bleach dose on one gallon of tap water: 8 drops (about 1/8 teaspoon) of unscented 5–9% bleach for clear water, 16 drops (1/4 teaspoon) if cloudy, stir, wait 30 minutes.
    • \n
  • Set up the handwashing station and the twin-bucket toilet from the sanitation chapter, even if you do not use it.
    • \n
  • Find the water heater and the toilet tank (not the bowl) as backup sources, as the water chapter describes.
    • \n
\n

What it teaches: whether 14 gallons is really two weeks for you, and where the gallon jugs should live so they are reachable.

\n\n

4. The walk to your evacuation center

\n

Look up your hurricane zone at nyc.gov/knowyourzone or by calling 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115). Then, on a dry weekend day, walk with your go-bag on your back to the nearest evacuation center you would use. The official finder shows which centers are open only once an order is issued, so on a normal day pick the nearest one that has been used before and confirm via 311 or the official finder at the time; centers change with each emergency.

\n
    \n
  • Time the walk and note the weight of the bag. If it hurts by the halfway point, the bag is too heavy: water is 8 pounds a gallon.
    • \n
  • Note the low points on the route: underpasses, streets that flood, blocks near the shoreline.
    • \n
  • Walk a second route that avoids those low points.
    • \n
  • Note where you could rest, refill water or use a toilet along the way.
    • \n
\n

What it teaches: real distance, real weight, real hazards. Hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November; do this walk in May.

\n\n

5. The family communication test

\n

Ready.gov's plan rests on one out-of-town contact whom everyone calls or texts, because a text message needs far less bandwidth than a call and often gets through when calls do not. Test it.

\n
    \n
  1. Send the test text to your out-of-area contact and to everyone in your plan at the same time, without warning: \"Drill. Where would you go right now?\"
    2. \n
  2. Everyone replies with the name of the neighbourhood meeting place, the out-of-neighbourhood meeting place and the out-of-town meeting place.
    3. \n
  3. Anyone who cannot answer from memory gets a fresh paper copy of the plan for their wallet.
    4. \n
  4. Confirm your Notify NYC subscription is still live: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692 again; it does no harm.
    5. \n
\n

What it teaches: who has forgotten the plan, whose phone number changed, and whether the paper copies still exist.

\n\n

6. The drill calendar

\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n
DrillWhat it provesHow oftenDone
Two-minute evacuationTwo ways out, go-bag reachable, stairs timedAt least twice a year (Ready.gov); do it at the clock changes☐
No-power eveningKit usable in the dark; batteries and radio workTwice a year: before summer and before winter☐
Water-off dayStorage is enough and reachable; bleach dose knownOnce a year☐
Walk to the evacuation centerRoute, weight, flood-prone streetsOnce a year, in May before hurricane season☐
Family communication testContact numbers and meeting places rememberedTwice a year, plus whenever someone moves or changes number☐
Alarm testSmoke and CO alarms soundRegularly: press the test button (FDNY); this course says monthly. Batteries twice a year at the clock changes.☐
\n\n

7. The debrief: five questions, on paper

\n
    \n
  1. What did I reach for that was not there?
    2. \n
  2. What took longest, and why?
    3. \n
  3. What did I not know how to do?
    4. \n
  4. What would have been different with a child, a pet, an injured person or a neighbour who cannot walk?
    5. \n
  5. What is the one cheapest fix, and when will I buy or do it?
    6. \n
\n

Write the answers on the back of the printed checklist from section 1 and date them. The next drill starts by reading the last debrief.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Practising the fire drill with the elevator, or in daylight with the lights on. Elevators stop when power fails and fill with smoke; drills done in comfort teach the wrong path. FDNY's rule is to darken the home and start from bed, because that is how it will happen.

The second mistake is skipping the debrief. People who run a drill and change nothing have only rehearsed their failures.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

Your building may already hold fire drills or have a posted fire safety plan; read it, because in some fireproof high-rises the right move in a fire elsewhere in the building is to stay in your apartment with the door shut (fire chapter). Your drill must match your building's plan.

For the walk drill: evacuation centers are opened by the city only when an order is issued, and they are pet-friendly and accessible. The finder at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane and 311 show the ones open at the time.

For the communication test: 911 is for life-threatening emergencies, 311 for everything else, and Text-to-911 is \"call if you can, text if you can't\". Never place a test call to 911.

\n\n
🦺 SAFETY

Do not turn off gas for a drill; only a utility worker should turn gas back on. Do not run any stove, grill or generator indoors as part of the no-power evening. If your no-power drill uses the main breaker, tell anyone who relies on powered medical equipment first, and skip the breaker if they cannot manage without it.

\n\n
🛠 DO THIS NOW
    \n
  • Tonight: press the test button on every smoke and CO alarm. No sound? New battery today; no alarm? Landlord in writing, then 311.
    • \n
  • This week: run the two-minute evacuation drill, lights off, timer on. Write the time on the checklist.
    • \n
  • This week: send the surprise \"Where would you go?\" text to everyone in your plan.
    • \n
  • This month: look up your zone at nyc.gov/knowyourzone and pick your walk route on a paper map.
    • \n
  • This month: a no-power Friday evening using only the kit.
    • \n
  • Next month: the water-off Saturday.
    • \n
\n\n
✅ VERIFIED
    \n
  • FDNY Smart, \"Keys to escape planning\", https://www.fdnysmart.org/safetytips/escape-plan-practice/, checked 26 Sep 2026: realistic drills start in the sleeping area, darken the home as if smoke-filled, begin with the alarm sound, crawl low, follow the plan to the meeting place.
    • \n
  • FDNY, \"Change Batteries in Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms\", https://www.nyc.gov/site/fdny/news/ma2821/fdny-urges-new-yorkers-change-batteries-smoke-carbon-monoxide-alarms, checked 26 Sep 2026: test alarms regularly with the test button, change removable batteries twice a year at the clock changes, prefer 10-year sealed alarms where people sleep.
    • \n
  • Ready.gov, \"Make A Plan\", https://www.ready.gov/plan, checked 26 Sep 2026: out-of-town contact, texts use less bandwidth than calls, three meeting places, carry a copy in the wallet.
    • \n
  • Ready.gov, \"Practice Your Home Fire Escape Plan\", https://www.ready.gov/home-fire-escape-plan, and \"Home Fires\", https://www.ready.gov/home-fires, checked 26 Sep 2026: two ways out of every room, meeting place, out in under 2 minutes, drill at least twice a year.
    • \n
  • CDC, \"Making Water Safe in an Emergency\", https://www.cdc.gov/water-emergency/about/making-water-safe-in-an-emergency.html, checked 26 Sep 2026: bleach doses and 30-minute wait.
    • \n

    • \n

Do this first: do the free steps in month 1 this week, then buy water. Nothing else on this page matters until those two are done. A kit built in the right order protects you from month 1; a kit built in the wrong order protects you only when it is finished. The Red Cross puts it plainly: start with what you already own, make a plan, and add a few useful items as your budget allows, perhaps one item every time you shop. This lesson turns that advice into twelve months, cheapest life-saving items first, with rough costs so you can plan a data analyst's budget, and it ends with the maintenance that keeps the kit alive after month 12.

\n\n
📘 DEFINITION

Build-up plan: a fixed order of purchases and skills, one small block per month, so the most likely killers (no water, no warning, no light, untreated bleeding, no proof of who you are) are covered before the rare ones.

Rotation (first in, first out): using the oldest stored food, water and batteries in everyday life and replacing them at the back, so nothing in the kit is ever past its date.

Maintenance: the calendar of checks that starts when the buying stops: dated water, battery changes at the clock changes, seasonal reviews in June and November, and Ready.gov's yearly re-think of what your household needs.

\n\n

1. The five rules of the build

\n
    \n
  1. Free before cheap, cheap before dear. Signing up for alerts, writing the plan, photographing documents and testing alarms cost nothing and cover more risk than any purchase.
    2. \n
  2. Water first. One gallon per person per day; three days this week, fourteen days by month 4 (CDC).
    3. \n
  3. One item per shopping trip (Red Cross). Add a gallon of water, a can, a pack of batteries. It never feels like a bill.
    4. \n
  4. Use what you own (Ready.gov \"Low and No Cost Preparedness\"): the old backpack, the drawer flashlight, spare blankets, a saucepan. Thrift stores and sales for the rest.
    5. \n
  5. Every month has a drill. The drills lesson gives you five; spread them over the year so each new piece of kit is tested the month it arrives.
    6. \n
\n\n

2. The twelve months

\n

Month 1 is whatever month you start. Two dates override the order: if hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) is less than two months away, pull month 6 (the go-bag) forward; if heat season (1 October) is near and your building's heat is unreliable, pull month 10 forward.

\n\n
🔑 REMEMBER THIS

The order is the lesson: water, a way to hear alerts, light, first aid, documents. If money stops after month 3 you still have the five things that decide most emergencies. Everything after that makes the wait more bearable; the first three months make it survivable.

\n\n
⚠ DEADLY MISTAKE

Waiting to start until you can afford \"a proper kit\". The free steps in month 1 (alerts, plan, medical card, document photos, alarm test) do most of the life-saving and cost nothing; every month they wait is a month with no warning and no plan. The second version of the same mistake is buying a sealed pre-packed \"bug-out bag\" and never opening it: you will not know at 3 a.m. what is inside or whether the batteries are dead.

Third: spending the budget on a generator. A generator must run outdoors at least 20 feet from any window, door or vent (CDC), which almost no apartment can do. Buy water, a radio, a light and a battery CO alarm instead.

\n\n
🗽 IN NEW YORK CITY

The city's free workbook, \"Ready New York: My Emergency Plan\", is at nyc.gov/readyny in 13 languages and audio; use it as the paper copy of your plan. NYC Emergency Management says to keep enough at home for up to seven days; this course builds to fourteen because a high-rise can lose water pumps and elevators with the power.

Two city dates shape the calendar: hurricane season, 1 June to 30 November (re-check your zone at nyc.gov/knowyourzone or by calling 311), and heat season, 1 October to 31 May (no heat: 311).

Alerts are free: text NOTIFYNYC to 692-692. Life-support equipment at home: register with Con Edison at 1-877-582-6633. Never store gasoline or propane in an apartment; the power chapter explains why.

What is the most useful thing she can do tonight?", "options": ["Plan to fill containers after the power goes out, since the tap will still run for a while", "Fill every pot and glass in the apartment now and leave them uncovered on the counter", "Go to the store now and buy at least three gallons of bottled water, then fill a bathtub liner or clean containers from the tap on Thursday", "Wait for the evacuation decision on Friday morning and buy water only if she is told to stay"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Bottled water sells out within hours of a storm announcement, and once power fails the pumps that lift water to the 12th floor stop; three gallons is the three-day floor and the tub liner adds bulk water while the taps still run.", "distractors": {"3": "By Friday morning shelves are empty and delivery is suspended; water must be in the apartment before the day it is needed.", "1": "Open pots collect dust and spill, hold very little, and do nothing about the store running out; sealed containers and a tub liner hold far more.", "0": "On a high floor the taps can die within seconds of a blackout because the electric pumps stop; fill before, not after."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "water-s1-q2", "text": "Natasha wants a full two-week supply for herself and her cat. How should she adjust the daily water budget for the two of them?", "options": ["Cut back to half a gallon each so the supply lasts longer", "Give the roommate no water until the diarrhoea stops so it does not get worse", "Keep to one gallon a day each; the rule does not change", "Plan on roughly two gallons a day each and make the sick roommate drink on a schedule, not only when thirsty"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Ready.gov says needs can double in very hot conditions and that sick people need more; heat and fluid loss from illness together push the budget toward two gallons a day each.", "distractors": {"2": "The base gallon assumes normal conditions; both heat and illness raise the need.", "0": "Rationing water in extreme heat leads to heat illness; use the supply and start finding more water instead.", "1": "Withholding fluids from someone with diarrhoea causes dangerous dehydration; keep them drinking and call a doctor or 911 if they become confused."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "water-s1-q6", "text": "Natasha finds a case of bottled water under the bed that passed its printed date four months ago, and the water main has just broken on her block. What should she do with it?", "options": ["Use it only for flushing the toilet", "Boil every bottle before drinking to remove the plastic taste", "Drink it; a sealed bottle past its date is a quality mark, not a poison, and replace the case when stores reopen", "Pour it out, because water past its date can cause illness"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Ready.gov says to observe the expiration date in normal times; in an emergency a sealed, undamaged bottle that was stored cool and dark is still the safest water in the building.", "distractors": {"3": "Sealed commercial water does not become unsafe on its printed date; pouring it out wastes the supply she needs most.", "1": "Boiling does nothing useful for sealed clean water and uses fuel she may not have; taste is not a safety issue.", "0": "Flushing can use bathtub or toilet-tank water; the sealed bottles are drinking water."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "water-s1-q7", "text": "Her building is a 20-story tower. Which question to the super matters most for her water plan?", "options": ["Does the building depend on an electric pump and rooftop tank, and is there a generator to run the pump in a blackout?", "When was the rooftop tank last painted?", "How many gallons does the building use per day?", "Is the tap water filtered before it reaches the apartments?"], "correct": 0, "explain": "In the 2003 blackout high-rise residents lost water because the electric pumps stopped; knowing whether the building has a generator tells her whether the taps will die and how fast she must fill containers.", "distractors": {"2": "Total building use does not tell her whether her tap will run in a blackout.", "3": "Filtration is not the issue in a blackout; pressure and pumping are.", "1": "Paint is a maintenance detail; the pump and generator decide whether she has water."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}], "SURVIVE/water/s2": [{"id": "water-s2-q1", "text": "The lights go out on Natasha's 15th-floor apartment at 9 p.m. and the tap is still running. What should she change about her morning routine?", "options": ["Nothing until the water looks or smells bad", "Stop showering entirely and wash only with bottled water", "Boil water for one minute and then add bleach to be sure", "Boil water one minute and cool it for drinking and brushing teeth, throw out ice made this morning, and keep water out of her mouth in the shower"], "correct": 3, "explain": "NYS Department of Health: rolling boil one minute then cool, boiled or bottled water for drinking, teeth and food, discard ice made during the notice, showering allowed for healthy adults with water kept out of the mouth.", "distractors": {"0": "Germs that cause a notice are invisible and tasteless; the notice, not the look of the water, decides.", "1": "Healthy adults may shower; the rule is to keep the water out of the mouth and open cuts.", "2": "Boiling alone is enough; adding bleach after boiling wastes bleach she may need if the gas fails."}, "topic": "Finding water when the taps stop"}, {"id": "water-s2-q7", "text": "Natasha wants to catch rain during a long outage. What should she say?", "options": ["Fine, as long as the pot has a lid to trap the fumes", "Fine, as long as the stove is on for under fifteen minutes", "Fine, as long as they open the kitchen tap so the steam escapes", "Not indoors: carbon monoxide from a flame in a closed apartment kills; use it at a wide-open window or balcony with a battery CO alarm on, or use bleach instead"], "correct": 3, "explain": "CDC and FDNY warn that flame appliances indoors produce carbon monoxide; the bleach method needs no flame, and any stove use belongs outside or at an open window with a CO alarm running.", "distractors": {"2": "A running tap does nothing about carbon monoxide, which is in the air from the flame.", "1": "Carbon monoxide builds in minutes in a closed room; time limits are not a safeguard.", "0": "A lid traps steam in the pot; the carbon monoxide comes from the burner flame, not the pot."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "water-s3-q8", "text": "She is dosing a gallon of clear water. What is the correct home care for the first two days?", "options": ["Rest, a wrapped cold pack for 20 minutes at a time, a snug elastic bandage, and the foot raised above her heart", "Walk on it as normally as possible to keep it from stiffening", "Ice directly on the skin for as long as she can stand it", "A hot bath and a heating pad to increase blood flow"], "correct": 0, "explain": "RICE: rest, ice (wrapped, 20 minutes on), compression and elevation for the first days; get it checked if she cannot bear weight after a day.", "distractors": {"1": "Rest comes first; loading a fresh sprain worsens the tear.", "3": "Heat in the first days increases swelling; cold reduces it.", "2": "Ice on bare skin causes cold burns; always wrap it and limit to about 20 minutes."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}, {"id": "medical-s2-q7", "text": "Cleaning up after a flood, she steps on a rusty nail that goes through her shoe. The bleeding stops quickly. Her last tetanus shot was 12 years ago. What should she do?", "options": ["Soak it in hot salt water and wait a week to see if it heals", "Pour bleach into the puncture to kill the bacteria", "Cover it with a bandage; the small size means it is not serious", "Rinse it under clean water and go to a clinic today for the wound and a tetanus booster"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A puncture from a dirty object needs cleaning and a clinic today; adults need a tetanus booster every 10 years, and hers is overdue.", "distractors": {"1": "Bleach damages tissue and does not replace a booster; rinse with clean water only.", "2": "Punctures look small but drive dirt deep; they are high-risk for infection and tetanus.", "0": "Waiting a week lets an infection establish; tetanus prevention has to happen now."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}], "SURVIVE/medical/s3": [{"id": "medical-s3-q1", "text": "On a 98°F afternoon in a blackout, her upstairs neighbour, 78, is found hot to the touch, red-faced, not sweating and answering questions with nonsense. What is the right sequence?", "options": ["Help her lie down in the dark and check on her in an hour", "Call 911, then cool her with water on the skin, a fan and ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin", "Give her a large glass of cold water, then call the doctor", "Give her a fever-reducing tablet and a cool shower"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Hot skin plus confusion is heat stroke: 911 first, then aggressive cooling. No fluids by mouth to a confused person.", "distractors": {"2": "A confused person can choke on fluids; and a doctor is too slow, this is 911.", "0": "Heat stroke worsens by the minute; an hour alone can be fatal.", "3": "Fever tablets do not treat heat stroke and a confused person cannot safely be showered or given pills."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q2", "text": "Her roommate has had vomiting and diarrhoea all night, has no ORS packets and cannot keep plain water down well. Natasha mixes a home solution. Which recipe is correct?", "options": ["1 litre of water, 1 tablespoon of salt, 1 tablespoon of sugar", "1 litre of water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar, half a level teaspoon of salt", "1 cup of water, 6 teaspoons of sugar, 1 teaspoon of salt", "A sports drink diluted with an equal amount of milk"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The CDC home ORS recipe is 1 litre clean water, 6 level teaspoons sugar and half a level teaspoon salt, sipped often; too much salt is dangerous and too much sugar worsens diarrhoea.", "distractors": {"0": "A tablespoon of salt per litre is far too much and can be harmful.", "2": "The same sugar and salt in one cup instead of a litre is a dangerously strong mix.", "3": "Milk can worsen diarrhoea and this is not a recognised rehydration mix."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q3", "text": "In a January blackout her neighbour, who was shivering hard an hour ago, is now still, confused and slurring. What has happened and what should she do?", "options": ["Give him a shot of whisky to warm him from inside", "He is getting worse; call 911, get him warm and dry, and warm his chest, neck and head first, gently", "He is warming up; let him sleep under a blanket", "Put him in a hot bath and rub his arms and legs briskly"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Shivering that stops as confusion sets in means severe hypothermia; call 911, remove wet clothes and warm the core first. Handle gently.", "distractors": {"2": "Stopping shivering in the cold is a danger sign, not recovery.", "3": "Hot baths and rubbing limbs push cold blood to the heart and can stop it.", "0": "Alcohol speeds heat loss and confused people should not drink; warm drinks only if fully alert."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q4", "text": "After an hour outside in a snowstorm, her fingertips are white, waxy and numb. What should she do once indoors?", "options": ["Rub them hard with her other hand or with snow to get the blood moving", "Put them in warm, not hot, water that feels comfortable to her other hand", "Hold them against the radiator until she can feel them", "Ignore it; the colour will come back on its own by morning"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Frostbite is rewarmed in warm (not hot) water; never rub, and never use a radiator, stove or heating pad on numb skin, which burns without her feeling it.", "distractors": {"0": "Rubbing frostbitten tissue destroys it; do not massage or use snow.", "2": "Numb skin cannot feel the radiator and will burn.", "3": "White, hard, numb frostbite needs medical care today; waiting risks losing the fingers."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q5", "text": "After a small kitchen fire, her friend has soot around his nostrils and a hoarse voice, but says he feels fine and wants to go back in to grab his laptop. What does she do?", "options": ["Keep him out, sit him up in fresh air, and call 911 despite him feeling fine", "Have him lie flat and breathe into a paper bag", "Let him fetch the laptop, then rest with a window open", "Give him a glass of milk to soothe his throat"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Soot in the nose and a hoarse voice mean the airway was burned; it can swell shut hours later, so 911 even if he feels fine, and nobody goes back into smoke.", "distractors": {"2": "Re-entering smoke adds injury; the laptop is not worth an airway.", "3": "Milk does nothing for an airway burn and can complicate treatment.", "1": "A paper bag is for hyperventilation, not smoke injury, and lying flat makes breathing harder."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q6", "text": "During a blackout, everyone in the apartment, including the cat, has a headache and feels sick, but nobody has a fever. The gas oven has been on for warmth. What is the very first thing to do?", "options": ["Get everyone out into fresh air immediately, then call 911 from outside", "Take a fever reducer and go to bed early", "Open all the windows and switch off the oven", "Call 311 to report the heating problem"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Flu-like symptoms in everyone at once, without fever, after a fuel-burning appliance was used, is carbon monoxide until proven otherwise: out first, then 911. Do not stop to ventilate.", "distractors": {"2": "Every second inside adds CO to your blood; leave first, let the Fire Department deal with the source.", "1": "People who go to sleep with CO poisoning may never wake up.", "3": "311 is not for emergencies; CO poisoning is a 911 call."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "medical-s3-q7", "text": "Her building’s CO alarm is missing from her apartment. What does NYC law say, and what should she do?", "options": ["The owner must provide one within 15 feet of each sleeping-room entrance; tell the landlord in writing and call 311, and buy a battery one meanwhile", "CO alarms are optional in apartments; she can buy one if she wants", "Only buildings with gas heat need CO alarms", "The tenant is responsible for installing the first alarm at her own cost"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Local Law 7 of 2004 requires the owner to install at least one working CO alarm in every apartment within 15 feet of each sleeping-room entrance; HPD enforces it via 311, and a $20-$30 battery alarm covers the gap.", "distractors": {"1": "They are required by law in New York City apartments, not optional.", "2": "The law applies to all multiple dwellings and one- and two-family homes, whatever the fuel.", "3": "The owner must provide and install the first alarm; the occupant replaces it only if it is later removed or broken."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}], "SURVIVE/medical/s4": [{"id": "medical-s4-q1", "text": "A hurricane is forecast in four days. Natasha takes a daily seizure medication and has six days left. What is the best move?", "options": ["Borrow a similar medication from a neighbour to bridge the gap", "Call the pharmacy now and ask for an early refill or a 90-day supply, explaining she is preparing for the storm", "Wait until the storm passes, since pharmacies reopen fast", "Skip every other dose so the bottle lasts twice as long"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Seizure drugs cannot be stopped suddenly; asking now for an early refill or a 90-day supply builds the reserve before the pharmacy closes.", "distractors": {"3": "Halving a seizure medication risks breakthrough seizures; doses are never stretched.", "2": "Pharmacies flood, lose power and close for days; that is exactly when she runs out.", "0": "Sharing prescription drugs is unsafe and can be dangerous; the pharmacist or a virtual visit is the route."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q2", "text": "It is July, the power has been out for six hours, and her diabetic neighbour is about to throw away all her insulin because the fridge is warm. What does Natasha tell her?", "options": ["Put it in the freezer compartment, which stays cold longest", "She is right; insulin is useless the moment it leaves the fridge", "Insulin kept between 59 and 86°F stays usable for up to 28 days, so keep it as cool as possible, away from ice contact, and do not use any that has frozen", "Insulin is fine at any temperature as long as the bottle looks clear"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The FDA says insulin in vials or cartridges can be unrefrigerated at 59-86°F for up to 28 days; keep it cool, never frozen, and replace it once heat-exposed insulin can be swapped.", "distractors": {"1": "Throwing out good insulin in a disaster can leave her with none; it keeps for weeks at room temperature.", "0": "Frozen insulin is ruined and must not be used; even in a working freezer this is wrong.", "3": "Above 86°F insulin loses strength over time; heat matters even if it looks clear."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q3", "text": "Her neighbour on the 14th floor uses an oxygen concentrator. The power fails and the elevators stop. Which preparation should already have been in place to keep him safe tonight?", "options": ["A note asking the super to restore power to his apartment first", "Backup oxygen cylinders from his supplier, with the hours they last written down, plus Con Edison registration and a place to go", "A spare extension cord to reach the hallway outlet", "A bottle of water and a box of candles"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A concentrator dies with the grid; only cylinders that need no electricity, a known number of hours, and a plan to leave (or 911 before they run out) keep him breathing.", "distractors": {"2": "Hallway outlets are on the same dead grid.", "3": "Candles and oxygen together are a fire; and neither helps him breathe.", "0": "The super cannot restore power; registering with Con Edison gives notice and outreach, not priority restoration."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q4", "text": "She wants to register her father’s home ventilator with Con Edison. What does the process require?", "options": ["Only an email to customer service with the device serial number", "A visit from a Con Edison technician who inspects the device", "Nothing; hospitals register patients automatically", "A form or a call to 1-877-582-6633, a certification by a doctor, nurse practitioner, physician assistant or health official, renewed every year"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Con Edison’s Life-Sustaining Equipment program takes registration online, by mail or at 1-877-582-6633, needs medical certification (Con Edison says within 30 days of receipt) and annual renewal.", "distractors": {"0": "A serial number is not enough; medical certification is required.", "1": "There is no inspection; the certification is from a clinician, not a technician.", "2": "No one registers you automatically; the family has to do it and renew it yearly."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q5", "text": "After basement flooding, her blood-pressure pills were in a bottle that sat in the water. The pills inside look damp. What should she do?", "options": ["Rinse them under the tap to clean off the flood water", "Discard them and get a replacement today, using the emergency refill routes or Rx Open to find an open pharmacy", "Use them but double the dose to make up for lost strength", "Dry them on a windowsill and keep using them"], "correct": 1, "explain": "FDA guidance: pills that got wet with flood water are contaminated and should be discarded and replaced; only pills that stayed completely dry inside a wet container may be used until replaced.", "distractors": {"3": "Flood water carries sewage and chemicals; drying does not make them safe.", "2": "Doubling a blood-pressure dose is dangerous and does not fix contamination.", "0": "Rinsing dissolves and further contaminates the pills."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q6", "text": "Natasha is making a medical card for her wallet. Which item is the most important to include for the medics who might treat her unconscious?", "options": ["Her gym membership number", "Her medications, allergies, conditions, whether she takes blood thinners, and two emergency contacts", "A list of her past addresses", "Her employer’s name and job title"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The card exists so a stranger can keep her alive: drugs, doses, allergies, conditions, blood thinners (which change bleeding treatment), and who to call.", "distractors": {"3": "Job details do not change treatment.", "0": "Membership numbers are irrelevant to emergency care.", "2": "Past addresses help nobody in an emergency."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "medical-s4-q7", "text": "Her aunt in Queens has run out of her thyroid medication during a storm and her doctor’s office is closed. Natasha remembers a possible New York emergency refill rule. What is the right approach?", "options": ["Tell her aunt the pharmacist must give her 30 days, no questions asked", "Ask the pharmacist directly whether they can give an emergency refill for this drug under New York law, and use Virtual ExpressCare or Rx Open if not", "Wait until the doctor’s office reopens, since a few days off thyroid medicine are harmless", "Have her aunt buy a similar supplement online instead"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The emergency-refill provision is one Natasha could not fully verify and applies only in limited cases, so the pharmacist’s answer for that drug is what counts; a 24/7 virtual visit or another open pharmacy is the fallback.", "distractors": {"0": "The rule has conditions (non-controlled, chronic, prescriber unreachable, one time) and is not guaranteed; demanding it helps nobody.", "3": "Supplements are not a substitute for a prescribed hormone dose.", "2": "Whether a gap is safe depends on the drug; the point of the reserve and the fallbacks is to avoid guessing."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}], "SURVIVE/medical/s5": [{"id": "medical-s5-q1", "text": "The water is off in her building during a stomach-bug outbreak on her floor. What is the best handwashing plan?", "options": ["Pour water from a jug over soaped hands for 20 seconds, saving the 60% alcohol sanitizer for when the jug is empty", "Skip handwashing but avoid touching her face", "Wipe hands on a clean towel between tasks", "Rely on hand sanitizer for everything until the water returns"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Soap and water for 20 seconds beats sanitizer for stomach bugs like norovirus; a jug and a bowl make a washing station, and 60%+ sanitizer is the backup.", "distractors": {"3": "Sanitizer is less effective against norovirus and does not work on dirty hands.", "2": "A towel spreads germs; it does not remove them.", "1": "Handwashing is the single most effective barrier during a diarrhoeal outbreak."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "medical-s5-q2", "text": "Her cousin’s 6-week-old baby feels warm; the thermometer reads 100.6°F. The baby is feeding a little and seems sleepy. It is 11 p.m. What should happen?", "options": ["Bathe the baby in cool water and keep the room dark", "Book a virtual urgent care visit for the next day", "Call the paediatrician immediately, and if unreachable go to an emergency department tonight", "Give infant fever medicine and check again in the morning"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Any temperature of 100.4°F or higher in a baby under 3 months is an emergency: immediate evaluation, not fever medicine and waiting.", "distractors": {"3": "Medicine can hide a serious infection in a newborn; the baby needs to be examined now.", "0": "Cool baths do not treat the cause and delay care.", "1": "A newborn fever is beyond virtual care and cannot wait until morning."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "medical-s5-q3", "text": "Her 80-year-old neighbour has no fever but since yesterday is suddenly confused, not eating and breathing quickly. What is the most likely explanation and the right response?", "options": ["A possible serious infection despite the lack of fever; get her seen today, and call 911 if she is hard to wake", "Normal ageing; keep an eye on her over the week", "A bad night’s sleep; let her rest", "Dehydration only; give her tea and see tomorrow"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Older adults can have serious infections with little or no fever; sudden confusion, not eating and fast breathing need same-day care, and 911 if she is drowsy or hard to rouse.", "distractors": {"1": "Sudden confusion is never normal ageing; it is a symptom.", "3": "Dehydration may be part of it but does not explain fast breathing; she needs assessment.", "2": "Confusion plus fast breathing can be sepsis, which kills within hours."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "medical-s5-q4", "text": "Three days after cutting his hand, her roommate’s wound is redder than yesterday, with thick yellow discharge, and a red line is creeping up his forearm. Where should he go?", "options": ["A virtual urgent care visit to get antibiotics sent to a pharmacy", "Continue home dressing changes; the redness shows healing", "The pharmacy for a stronger antiseptic cream", "An emergency department today; red streaks and fever mean the infection is spreading"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Red streaks running toward the heart plus fever or chills mean a spreading infection that needs emergency care today; confusion or fast breathing would make it 911.", "distractors": {"1": "Redness that spreads after day two is infection, not healing.", "2": "Creams cannot treat a spreading infection with streaks and fever.", "0": "This has gone beyond what a phone visit can safely handle; he needs to be examined."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "medical-s5-q5", "text": "Her friend has had diarrhoea for 24 hours. What is the most sensible option?", "options": ["Drink cranberry juice and wait for the power to return", "Call 911 so an ambulance can take her past the queue", "Take leftover antibiotics from a previous illness", "Use Virtual ExpressCare or a walk-in urgent care; go to the emergency department only if fever with back pain, vomiting or confusion develops"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A non-life-threatening infection belongs in the clinic or virtual urgent care layer; the emergency department and 911 are for the danger signs.", "distractors": {"1": "Ambulances are for life-threatening emergencies; a urinary infection is not one and she would still wait in triage.", "0": "Untreated infections can spread to the kidneys; she needs a clinician, and 24/7 virtual care exists for this.", "2": "Leftover antibiotics may be the wrong drug or dose and delay proper treatment."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "medical-s5-q7", "text": "An undocumented neighbour is having severe chest pain but refuses to go to hospital because she has no insurance and fears questions about her status. What can Natasha tell her, truthfully?", "options": ["Only private hospitals will see her if she pays cash upfront", "She should wait until Monday and apply for insurance first", "By law every emergency department must examine and stabilise her; NYC public hospitals treat everyone regardless of pay or status; call 911 now", "Hospitals can refuse patients without insurance, so a clinic is her only option"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Under EMTALA every emergency department must screen and stabilise an emergency, and NYC Health + Hospitals treats everyone regardless of ability to pay or immigration status without recording status; chest pain is a 911 call.", "distractors": {"3": "Federal law forbids turning away an emergency patient for lack of insurance.", "1": "Chest pain cannot wait for paperwork; the financial office is dealt with afterwards.", "0": "Public hospitals treat without upfront payment; cash is not a condition of emergency care."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}], "SURVIVE/sanitation/s1": [{"id": "sanitation-s1-q1", "text": "The water has been off for six hours. Natasha still has bucket water. What is the right move?", "options": ["Flush with extra water to push the blockage through", "Pour drain cleaner down her toilet to clear it", "Stop flushing, switch to the bucket toilet, and call 311 about the sewer", "Keep flushing only at night when fewer people are using the sewer"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Water rising in a lower apartment's tub means the sewer line is blocked or full. Every flush from above comes up in the lowest unit. Stop, use the bucket system, report it.", "distractors": {"0": "More water only sends more sewage into the lowest apartment; the block is in the building line or the street main, not in her bowl.", "3": "Timing does not help a blocked line; the sewage still has nowhere to go but the lowest drain.", "1": "Drain cleaner cannot clear a building sewer main, and chemicals in a backed-up line end up in someone else's bathroom."}, "topic": "Toilets without running water"}, {"id": "sanitation-s1-q3", "text": "Natasha is lining the SOLIDS bucket for the first time. Which action matches the city's own rat rules?", "options": ["Put rat poison around the bins herself", "Take the trash to a park bin so it is away from the building", "Bag the trash tightly and stack the bags neatly in the hallway", "Keep all garbage in hard lidded containers, put it out late, and file a 311 rodent complaint"], "correct": 3, "explain": "NYC Health says garbage belongs in hard plastic rat-resistant containers with tight lids, set out close to pick-up (after 8 p.m.), and rodent complaints go through 311 to the Health Department.", "distractors": {"2": "Rats chew through bags in hours; a hallway of bags is a rat buffet and blocks an exit.", "0": "Poison in a shared building endangers children and pets and does not remove the food source that draws rats.", "1": "Dumping household trash in park bins is not a plan; the rats simply move, and it leaves the bins overflowing."}, "topic": "Toilets without running water"}, {"id": "sanitation-s1-q7", "text": "Natasha lives on the 14th floor. What should she do in the first minutes?", "options": ["Fill the bathtub and every container now, because the building's water pumps have stopped", "Run the taps to check they work, then wait", "Nothing about water; only the electricity failed", "Go down to the lobby to ask if the water is off"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Tall buildings pump water to upper floors. During a citywide emergency, how should she use that contact?", "options": ["Text the aunt her location and plan at every stop and ask her to relay it to everyone else", "Skip the aunt and call each family member in the city individually", "Only call the aunt once she is safe, to avoid worrying her", "Post updates online and assume the aunt will see them"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Local networks jam in an emergency; one long-distance text that a contact relays reaches everyone with the least battery and airtime.", "distractors": {"2": "The point of the contact is to know where she is while things are still uncertain.", "1": "Many local calls drain the battery and often fail when local lines are jammed.", "3": "Online posts may not send and the aunt may not see them; a direct text is the plan."}, "topic": "Signalling and being found"}], "SURVIVE/docs/s1": [{"id": "docs-s1-q1", "text": "It is 9 p.m., Natasha has one free hour and no money to spend this week. What should Natasha tell her to change first?", "options": ["Give a second full set to someone in another building and move the box off the floor, because a flash flood can fill a low apartment in minutes", "Nothing; under the bed is out of sight, which is the main risk", "Photograph the box so she can prove she had it", "Move everything to the freezer, which is waterproof"], "correct": 0, "explain": "During Ida in 2021, rain fell at roughly twice the rate the sewers were built for and most of the city's deaths were in basement apartments. What would have prevented this?", "options": ["Turning off two-factor authentication on every account", "Keeping a screenshot of her backup codes on the same phone", "Backup codes for each account, printed and kept with her passport in the document folder", "Memorising the code the app showed her last week"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Google's guidance: generate a set of single-use backup codes in advance and keep them printed where you keep your passport, for exactly the case where the phone is lost. Paper in the folder works when the phone does not.", "distractors": {"1": "A screenshot on the lost phone is lost with it; the point is a copy that survives losing the device.", "0": "Removing two-factor protection makes the accounts far easier to steal, especially when a device is missing.", "3": "Authenticator codes change every few seconds and cannot be memorised in advance; backup codes are the fixed, single-use alternative."}, "topic": "The document folder, the photo record and emergency cash"}, {"id": "docs-s1-q5", "text": "Natasha's renters insurance adjuster asks for a list of everything lost in a fire, with what each item cost and when she bought it. the record has to exist before the loss.", "3": "The landlord does not know or vouch for her belongings; the insurer wants her own evidence.", "0": "Packaging burns with everything else and does not prove price or purchase date."}, "topic": "The document folder, the photo record and emergency cash"}, {"id": "docs-s1-q6", "text": "Which of these should Natasha copy into the document folder, according to the EFFAK's four sections?", "options": ["Her medication list with doses, the pharmacy's phone number and her health insurance card", "The Wi-Fi password and the TV remote codes", "The serial numbers of her neighbours' bicycles", "Every text message from her landlord for the last year"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The EFFAK's Medical Information section covers exactly this: health insurance details, medications, doctors and pharmacy, so a stranger at a shelter or a new pharmacy can keep her on her medicine.", "distractors": {"1": "Convenience settings are not needed to prove identity, get medicine or claim money.", "3": "A few key messages may be evidence in a dispute, but they are not part of the household, financial, medical or contacts sections.", "2": "Her neighbours' property is their inventory to record, not hers."}, "topic": "The document folder, the photo record and emergency cash"}, {"id": "docs-s1-q7", "text": "A hurricane warning is issued and Natasha has five minutes to leave. One bag, one place, so that leaving with nothing else still means leaving with identity, money and the summary page.", "distractors": {"3": "Scattered storage protects against theft but fails the five-minute test; she would leave without half of it.", "2": "Originals can live at the bank, but the copies she needs during evacuation must be in her hand.", "0": "A car she does not control may be gone, flooded or unreachable when she has to leave."}, "topic": "The document folder, the photo record and emergency cash"}], "SURVIVE/docs/s2": [{"id": "docs-s2-q1", "text": "A tropical storm is forecast to reach New York in four days.
