What must she bring, according to NYC Emergency Management?", "options": ["The dog's food, leash, a carrier or crate, and any medication", "Only the dog; pets are kept in a separate animal shelter", "A signed letter from her vet certifying the dog is friendly", "Nothing; the center supplies pet food, crates and vet care"], "correct": 0, "explain": "NYC Emergency Management says pets and service animals are allowed at City shelters and that owners must bring supplies: food, leashes, a carrier and medication.", "distractors": {"3": "Centers give people a cot; they do not stock pet food or crates.", "2": "No vet letter is required, but a vaccination record in the kit is wise.", "1": "Pets stay at the evacuation center with their owners, in carriers."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "people-s2-q3", "text": "It is 97 degrees, the power is out, and her pug is panting hard, drooling and wobbly. What is the best action?", "options": ["Shave the dog to the skin to cool it faster", "Move it to the coolest room, wet its fur with cool water, offer water, and call the vet; if it collapses or seizes, go to an animal hospital now", "Walk it to the park so it can rest on the grass in the shade", "Leave it in the parked car with the windows cracked while she finds ice"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The ASPCA lists panting, drooling and weakness as overheating; flat-faced breeds are at extra risk. Cool the animal, offer water and call the vet; collapse, seizures or a temperature over 104 F is an emergency.", "distractors": {"0": "The ASPCA says never shave to the skin; the coat protects against overheating and sunburn.", "3": "Never leave an animal alone in a parked vehicle, cracked window or not.", "2": "A walk on hot pavement in 97 degree heat makes an overheating dog worse."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "people-s2-q4", "text": "Which set of ID gives a lost pet the best chance of coming home after a disaster?", "options": ["A microchip with a current phone number, a collar tag, and a photo of her with the pet", "A collar tag with the name of the pet only", "A post on a neighbourhood forum after the pet is lost", "A note in her wallet describing the pet"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The ASPCA recommends a microchip and up-to-date ID tags; Ready.gov says a photo of you with your pet proves ownership and helps others identify it.", "distractors": {"1": "A name without a phone number reaches nobody.", "3": "A note in her wallet is not on the animal and helps no finder.", "2": "Posting afterwards is fine, but it cannot replace ID on the animal."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "people-s2-q5", "text": "During a Code Blue night her neighbour's dog is left on the fire escape. She brings it in and finds the tips of its ears pale and hard. What is right?", "options": ["Leave the dog to warm up by itself under a blanket", "Warm the ears gently with warm, never hot, water, do not rub, and get to a vet", "Rub the ears briskly to restore circulation", "Put the dog in a hot bath immediately"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The American Red Cross says to bring a frostbitten pet in at once, warm the area gently with warm water, not rub or massage it, and seek veterinary care promptly.", "distractors": {"2": "Rubbing frostbitten tissue damages it further.", "3": "Hot water burns numb tissue; warming must be gentle.", "0": "Frostbite needs a vet; a blanket alone does not treat it."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "people-s2-q6", "text": "She is putting together the light evacuation pet kit for the stairs. Which is the best version?", "options": ["A week of food, the full bag of litter and the big crate", "Three to seven days of food and water, a week of medicine, a collapsible bowl, leash, small litter tray, and the vaccination record", "Just the leash; she can buy food after evacuating", "The dog's bed, three toys and its favourite blanket"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Ready.gov advises a lightweight evacuation kit separate from the larger shelter-in-place kit; the ASPCA says to plan three to seven days of food and water per pet, with medicines and records.", "distractors": {"0": "That is the heavy home kit; it cannot be carried down nine flights with a child.", "2": "Stores may be closed for days; the pet's food and medicine must come with you.", "3": "One familiar item helps; a bag of comfort items with no food does not."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "people-s2-q7", "text": "After a walk on a salted sidewalk in January, what should she do before the dog settles in the apartment?", "options": ["Let the dog lick its paws clean to warm them", "Give the dog a little antifreeze-free water and a treat", "Nothing; snow melt is harmless once dry", "Wipe the paws, because ice-melt and rock salt can sicken or kill an animal that licks them"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The American Red Cross and AVMA advise wiping paws after each trip outside because ice-melting chemicals and rock salt can irritate, sicken or be fatal.", "distractors": {"2": "Dried salt residue is exactly what the animal licks off later.", "0": "Licking is how the poison gets in.", "1": "Water is fine but does not remove the salt from the paws."}, "topic": "Pets"}], "SURVIVE/people/s3": [{"id": "people-s3-q1", "text": "It is hour 40 of a blackout. Natasha has slept about two hours. She is sure the fastest way to her sister's is to drive through a flooded underpass. What is the right safeguard?", "options": ["Say the plan out loud to another person or text her out-of-town contact before acting, and treat her own judgement as impaired", "Drink coffee, then go", "Trust her instinct; she knows the road", "Go faster to get it over with"], "correct": 0, "explain": "NIOSH says 24 hours awake impairs a person about as much as a 0.10 blood alcohol level. The two-person rule exists because she cannot feel that impairment; driving into flood water is a common cause of death.", "distractors": {"2": "Instinct after 40 hours awake is the impaired judgement the table warns about.", "1": "Coffee does not restore judgement; it hides how tired she is.", "3": "Speed is the opposite of the count-to-ten rule for irreversible decisions."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q2", "text": "A neighbour in the stairwell is shaking, breathing fast, and cannot answer where her children are. Using psychological first aid, what should she do first?", "options": ["Leave her to recover on her own; people need space", "Say her own name, get the woman sitting somewhere safe, and help her breathe slowly and name what she sees around her", "Tell her firmly to calm down because she is upsetting others", "Ask her to describe exactly what happened so she can process it"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The NCTSN core actions start with calm contact, safety and comfort, then stabilization: orienting an overwhelmed person to where they are and helping them settle before gathering information.", "distractors": {"3": "Forcing someone to retell the event is what PFA tells you not to do.", "2": "Orders to calm down add pressure and do not stabilise anyone.", "0": "An overwhelmed person left alone may wander into danger."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q3", "text": "Two days after the flood, her 8-year-old will not sleep and keeps asking if the water will come back. What do the NCTSN guidelines recommend?", "options": ["Say she is safe and people are helping, repeat it as often as needed, keep bedtime and meals at the usual times, and turn the news off", "Skip the usual rules for a few weeks so she can relax", "Avoid the subject until she stops asking", "Let the child watch the news so she understands the flood is over"], "correct": 0, "explain": "NCTSN: reassure repeatedly that the child is safe and that adults are helping, keep routines and family rules, and limit exposure to disaster images.", "distractors": {"3": "Repeated disaster images raise fear and anxiety, especially in younger children.", "1": "NCTSN says to keep the family rules because they are part of normal life.", "2": "Children need the reassurance said out loud, many times."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q4", "text": "Her friend, exhausted after a week without power, texts: 'Everyone would be better off without me.' Which is the right response?", "options": ["Reply that she should get some sleep and it will look better tomorrow", "Wait to see if she still feels that way in the morning", "Stay in contact, do not leave her alone, and call 988 with her; call 911 if she has taken something or is about to act", "Send her the address of a cooling center"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A statement like this is a crisis signal. 988 is free and 24/7 by call, text or chat; if someone is in immediate danger or has already acted, call 911.", "distractors": {"0": "Sleep helps, but this message needs a response tonight, not a postponement.", "1": "Waiting until it is 'bad enough' is the deadly mistake.", "3": "A cooling center does not address what she has just said."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q5", "text": "Which is a correct way to reach the SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline?", "options": ["Dial 311 and ask for the mental health line", "Email a description of the disaster and wait for a counsellor to reply", "Call or text 1-800-985-5990, any hour, without giving identifying information", "Text WELL to 65173"], "correct": 2, "explain": "SAMHSA's Disaster Distress Helpline is 1-800-985-5990 by call or text, 24/7, and no identifying information is needed.", "distractors": {"0": "311 is city services; it can give referrals but is not the helpline.", "3": "That text keyword reaches NYC 988, a different service.", "1": "The helpline is call or text; there is no email intake."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q6", "text": "She and her sister are sheltering in place for a multi-day outage. What is the best way to organise sleep?", "options": ["Sleep in shifts of about four hours: one awake for the radio and the door, one asleep with earplugs and eye mask", "Sleep whenever tired, no schedule", "Both stay awake so nobody misses an alert", "Take turns napping only in daylight when it is safer"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Routine and real sleep protect judgement. With two adults, alternating shifts keeps one person alert while the other gets uninterrupted sleep.", "distractors": {"2": "Two exhausted adults have the judgement of two drunk ones by the second night.", "1": "No schedule means neither sleeps well and both hover on the phone.", "3": "Night is when sleep is deepest and alerts are fewest; daytime-only napping wastes it."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "people-s3-q7", "text": "Three weeks after the emergency she still jumps at sirens, avoids the subway, and is drinking every night to sleep. What is the right next step?", "options": ["Contact NYC 988 by call, text or chat for a referral and short-term counselling, regardless of insurance", "Go to the emergency room and ask for a sedative", "Nothing; everyone feels this way after a disaster and it always fades", "Stop taking the subway permanently to avoid the trigger"], "correct": 0, "explain": "NYC 988 provides referrals to care and short-term counselling, regardless of insurance or immigration status. Lasting avoidance, sleep problems and drinking to cope are reasons to reach out.", "distractors": {"2": "Most people recover, but ongoing avoidance and drinking to cope are signs to get help.", "1": "The ER is for immediate danger; ongoing distress goes to 988 and a referral.", "3": "Avoidance that grows is the problem, not the cure."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}], "SURVIVE/drills/s1": [{"id": "drills-s1-q1", "text": "Natasha has $15 this week and nothing stored. Reading the master checklist, which single purchase should she make first?", "options": ["A small generator to keep the fridge running", "A large pre-packed 72-hour kit on a payment plan", "A week of freeze-dried camping meals", "Three gallons of water per person, stored inside the apartment"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The lists are ordered cheapest life-saving item first, and water tops every one of them: one gallon per person per day, three days this week, because thirst kills long before hunger.", "distractors": {"1": "A sealed pre-packed kit costs more, is not opened and checked, and delays the one item that matters most.", "0": "A generator must run outdoors 20 feet from windows and doors, which an apartment cannot do, and it costs far more than water.", "2": "Food comes after water; ordinary canned food is cheaper and needs no special meals."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q2", "text": "Natasha's building has a storage cage in the basement and she is short of closet space. Where should the stay kit and go-bag live?", "options": ["At a friend's apartment in another borough", "Inside the apartment, in a clear bin under the bed and by the door", "In the hallway outside her door so it is easy to grab", "In the basement cage, since it is locked and dry"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Anything you must go downstairs to reach is not part of your kit: 10 of the 14 New Yorkers who died in Hurricane Ida drowned in basements. Ready.gov says one or two easy-to-carry containers in a known place at home.", "distractors": {"3": "A basement floods first and fastest; Ida's rain fell at about twice the rate the sewers were built for.", "2": "Hallways are fire exits and building rules usually forbid storage there; the bag can also be taken.", "0": "A kit in another borough is unreachable when the subway stops; keep supplies where you are."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q3", "text": "It is 1 June. Natasha has a working stay kit. What does the seasonal-check row for that date ask her to do?", "options": ["Nothing until a hurricane watch is issued for the city", "Re-check her evacuation zone, refresh the go-bag, confirm 14 days of water and top up cash", "Change the batteries in every smoke alarm and buy new blankets", "Start a heat log and call 311 if the apartment is below 68 degrees"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Hurricane season runs 1 June to 30 November and zones can change, so the June check is zone, go-bag, water and cash, before any storm is on the map.", "distractors": {"2": "Battery changes go with the clock changes in March and November; blankets are the November winter check.", "3": "The heat-season rule starts 1 October; heat is not the June hazard.", "0": "Waiting for a watch leaves no time to walk the route or refresh the bag; the check is done in advance."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q4", "text": "Natasha is packing a go-bag for a possible evacuation order. Which item on her list should she remove because it belongs to the stay kit instead?", "options": ["Copies of her ID and lease in a waterproof bag", "Fourteen gallons of water", "A Mylar blanket and rain poncho", "A written list of medications and doses"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The go-bag is one bag you can carry out the door in under two minutes; water weighs about 8 pounds a gallon. The 14-gallon supply is the two-week stay kit at home; the go-bag holds bottled water you can carry.", "distractors": {"0": "Documents in a waterproof container are on the NYC Emergency Management Go Bag list.", "2": "Wet and cold is how people die on a long walk; both are light and belong in the bag.", "3": "A shelter nurse needs the medication list; it is on the Go Bag list."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q5", "text": "It is 15 October and Natasha's apartment is 60 degrees at 2 p.m. while it is 50 degrees outside. What is the checklist's instruction?", "options": ["Report it: heat season started 1 October and the landlord must keep 68 degrees by day when it is below 55 outside, so call 311 if the landlord does nothing", "Move to a cooling center until the heat comes back", "Wait until November when the winter check begins", "Run the oven with the door open to warm the kitchen"], "correct": 0, "explain": "HPD's heat season runs 1 October to 31 May: 68 degrees by day when it is below 55 outside, 62 at night. The checklist says act on day one: tell the landlord, then 311.", "distractors": {"2": "The rule is already in force in October; waiting means weeks in the cold.", "3": "Ovens and stoves used for heat produce carbon monoxide and start fires; the shelter chapter forbids it.", "1": "Cooling centers are for heat emergencies; the fix here is the landlord's legal duty and 311."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q6", "text": "Natasha's neighbour uses an oxygen concentrator that runs on mains power. Which item on the medical list applies to him?", "options": ["Tell him to call 911 on the first of every month to be put on a list", "Register the equipment with Con Edison at 1-877-582-6633, with a medical professional's certification", "Add a spare oxygen cylinder to Natasha's own go-bag", "Put his name on the building's fire safety notice"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The checklist says powered life-support equipment should be registered with Con Edison online or at 1-877-582-6633; the equipment must be certified by a medical professional.", "distractors": {"2": "Oxygen supplies are prescribed and handled by his provider; the registration is the step that gets him warned and prioritised.", "0": "911 is for life-threatening emergencies, never for routine registration.", "3": "The fire safety notice is the landlord's building document; it does not create a utility record."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "drills-s1-q7", "text": "Natasha works in Midtown and lives in Brooklyn. What does the checklist ask her to keep at work?", "options": ["A full two-week stay kit in her desk drawer", "A tent and sleeping bag in case the office closes", "Nothing; the home kit is enough because she can always get home", "A grab-and-go case with water, snacks, medicines and comfortable walking shoes for 24 hours"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Ready.gov says be ready to shelter at work for at least 24 hours with food, water, medicines and walking shoes in a grab-and-go case; in 2003 most people walked home.", "distractors": {"2": "Subways stopped mid-tunnel in the 2003 blackout; you cannot count on getting home.", "0": "Two weeks is the home target; the work kit is one day, light enough to carry.", "1": "A tent in a park is a last resort in the shelter chapter; walking shoes get her home."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}], "SURVIVE/drills/s2": [{"id": "drills-s2-q1", "text": "Natasha plans her first fire drill for Saturday afternoon: lights on, walk calmly to the lobby, take the elevator back up. What should she change?", "options": ["Skip the drill and read the building's fire plan instead", "Nothing; a calm walk-through teaches the route just as well", "Do it with the lights on but time it, since darkness is unsafe to practise in", "Start in bed with the lights off, begin with the alarm sound, stay low, take the stairs and time it to the outside meeting place"], "correct": 3, "explain": "FDNY says make drills realistic: most fires happen overnight, so start in the sleeping area, darken the home as if smoke-filled, begin with the alarm, crawl low and go all the way to the meeting place. Elevators are never used.", "distractors": {"1": "A comfortable daylight drill teaches the wrong path; the real event is dark and smoky.", "0": "Reading the plan matters, but a plan you have never rehearsed is a plan you have never tested.", "2": "Darkness is the point; a headlamp by the bed makes it safe, and the elevator is never part of the route."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q2", "text": "During her no-power Friday evening, Natasha finds the hand-crank radio has no NOAA band and her flashlight batteries are dead. What is the right conclusion?", "options": ["She should keep the fridge open to check the food while the lights are off", "The drill worked: it found two gaps to fix before the real blackout, so write them in the debrief and buy a NOAA radio and dated batteries", "The drill failed and should be abandoned", "The kit is fine because her phone torch still works"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The no-power evening exists to expose the gap between owning a kit and being able to use it; most people discover dead batteries or a radio without NOAA on this evening. The debrief turns it into a purchase.", "distractors": {"2": "A drill that finds a problem has succeeded; only a drill that changes nothing has failed.", "0": "A closed fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours; opening it wastes that time.", "3": "A phone dies in hours and gets no alerts without a network; the radio and light must work on their own."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q3", "text": "On her water-off day, Natasha uses three gallons before dinner for drinking, cooking, washing and one bucket flush. What does this tell her?", "options": ["The 1-gallon-per-day planning figure is wrong and she should ignore it", "She needs a generator to pump water from the street", "She should use the toilet bowl water for drinking to save the stored supply", "Her 14 gallons is closer to a five-day supply at that rate, so she must either store more or cut washing and flushing to stretch it"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The water-off day measures what one person really uses against the planning figure of 1 gallon per person per day. If real use is higher, either storage goes up or non-drinking use goes down; that is the lesson.", "distractors": {"0": "The gallon a day is a drinking-and-basic-sanitation minimum; the drill shows where the extra goes.", "2": "The toilet tank is a backup source; the bowl never is.", "1": "Generators cannot run in an apartment and do not make water; storage and rationing do."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q4", "text": "It is late May. Natasha wants to rehearse the walk to her evacuation center but the official finder shows no centers open. What should she do?", "options": ["Skip the walk; the city will provide buses on the day", "Wait until an evacuation order opens the centers, then walk", "Walk to the nearest center that has been used before, confirm via 311 or the finder at the time, and note the low-lying streets on the way", "Drive the route instead so it is faster"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Centers open only when an order is issued, so the practice walk uses a center that has been used before, marked confirm-at-the-time. The point is real distance, real bag weight and the flooded underpasses to avoid.", "distractors": {"1": "Rehearsing during the real order is not a rehearsal; the walk is done in May, before hurricane season.", "0": "Buses may run, but the drill is about the route on foot when they do not.", "3": "Driving hides the weight of the bag and the streets that flood, and driving out often fails in an evacuation."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q5", "text": "Natasha sends the surprise 'Drill. What is the next step?", "options": ["Call 911 to have them record her mother's address", "Remove her mother from the plan since she cannot remember it", "Mark the drill passed because most people answered correctly", "Give her mother a fresh paper copy of the plan for her wallet and repeat the test in a few months"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The communication test finds who has forgotten the plan. Ready.gov's advice is a written copy in every wallet; anyone who cannot answer from memory gets a fresh copy, and the test is repeated.", "distractors": {"2": "One person without the plan is the person who will be lost; the drill is passed only when everyone answers.", "0": "911 is for life-threatening emergencies and never for test or record calls.", "1": "The fix is a paper copy, not exclusion; the plan exists for exactly the people who forget."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q6", "text": "Natasha's friend suggests they test the plan by phoning each other during a real storm to see if calls connect. Why does the course prefer a text?", "options": ["Texts are free while calls cost money during emergencies", "Texts need less bandwidth, so they get through when networks are jammed and leave lines open for emergency workers", "Calls are illegal during a declared emergency in New York", "Texts cannot be traced, which protects privacy"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Ready.gov: text, don't talk. Text messages need less bandwidth and are transmitted more reliably when many people are using their phones, and they leave phone lines open for emergency workers.", "distractors": {"0": "Cost is not the reason; congestion is.", "2": "Calls are legal; they simply fail more often when the network is overloaded.", "3": "Privacy is not the point, and texts are not untraceable."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "drills-s2-q7", "text": "Natasha lives in a building whose posted fire plan says it is fireproof. Her drill has her running down 15 floors every time. What should she check?", "options": ["Whether the building plan says to stay in the apartment with the door shut when the fire is elsewhere, so her drill matches it", "Whether the elevator can be used as the second way out", "Whether the roof is a better meeting place than the street", "Whether she can practise on the fire escape with a planter still on it"], "correct": 0, "explain": "In some fireproof high-rises the right move when the fire is elsewhere is to stay in the apartment with the door shut; the drill must match the building's posted plan, and leaving only when the apartment itself is dangerous.", "distractors": {"1": "Elevators stop when power fails and fill with smoke; they are never a way out in a fire.", "3": "A blocked fire escape is a finding to fix; it is one of the things the drill checks.", "2": "Roof doors are often locked and smoke rises; the meeting place is outside at a safe distance."}, "topic": "Drills"}], "SURVIVE/drills/s3": [{"id": "drills-s3-q1", "text": "Natasha starts the plan in month 1 with $10. What adjustment does the plan tell her to make?", "options": ["Move the tools month forward to board up the windows", "Pull the go-bag month forward so the bag and the walk to the center are done before 1 June", "Follow the months in order; the season does not change the plan", "Skip water storage because floods bring plenty of water"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Two dates override the order: if hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) is less than two months away, month 6 (the go-bag and the walk) comes forward; if heat season is near and the heat is unreliable, month 10 does.", "distractors": {"2": "The order is a default; the two seasonal overrides exist for exactly this case.", "3": "Flood water is never drinkable, and a storm can cut the mains; water stays first.", "0": "Tools are month 11; an apartment evacuation depends on the bag and the route, not boards."}, "topic": "The twelve-month build-up on a real budget"}, {"id": "drills-s3-q3", "text": "Natasha's cousin offers her a used generator for free in month 3. What maintenance date does that create?", "options": ["Add bleach to each container every week", "Replace the self-filled containers every 6 months, and drink and rebuy bottled water by its printed date", "None; sealed water lasts forever", "Boil the stored water every month to keep it safe"], "correct": 1, "explain": "CDC: if you fill containers yourself, replace the water every 6 months; the plan pins that to 1 June and 1 December. Those are months 1 to 3, so if money stops there she still has the five things that decide most emergencies.", "distractors": {"0": "Sanitation and fire items are months 7 and 8.", "3": "The go-bag is month 6 and tools are month 11.", "1": "The two-week pantry is month 5."}, "topic": "The twelve-month build-up on a real budget"}, {"id": "drills-s3-q6", "text": "It is March, a year after Natasha finished her kit. What does the plan's maintenance rule say about the kit?", "options": ["The kit was finished at month 12 and needs no change", "Re-think needs every year and after any change: add the medication to the card and kit, and pet food, a carrier and water to the lists", "Only the go-bag changes; the stay kit stays as it was", "Start the twelve months again from month 1"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Ready.gov: replace expired items as needed and re-think your needs every year as the household changes. A new medication and a pet change the medical card, the stay kit and the go-bag.", "distractors": {"0": "A kit is never finished while the household changes; that is why the yearly re-think exists.", "3": "The order of the build does not restart; only the items affected by the change are added.", "2": "The cat needs food and water in the stay kit too, and the medication card lives in both."}, "topic": "The twelve-month build-up on a real budget"}], "SURVIVE/pa_sim/sim": [{"id": "pa-q1", "text": "A friend on the 18th floor lives alone and asks how much drinking water to keep to reach the two-week goal, and whether the shelf above her steam radiator is a fine place for it. Heat and sunlight age the plastic, and water absorbs fumes, so it goes in a cool, dark, low place away from radiators and chemicals.", "distractors": {"2": "Three days is the bare minimum, not the goal; main breaks and long blackouts run longer, and a high-rise pump can fail for days.", "1": "Steam radiators cook plastic containers every winter; heat is exactly what shortens the life of stored water.", "0": "The gallon a day already includes cooking and hygiene; cutting the figure in half leaves her short on the hot or sick days when needs double."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "pa-q2", "text": "In October she finds two jugs she filled from the kitchen tap and dated 1 March. They look clear. What does the Ready.gov rotation rule say to do with them?", "options": ["Add a capful of bleach to each jug and keep them another year", "Keep them; sealed tap water never goes bad", "Throw the jugs out with the trash because water that old is poisonous", "They have passed the six-month mark for self-filled water: pour them into plants or the tub, wash and sanitize the jugs, refill and re-date them"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Ready.gov says water you bottled yourself should be replaced every six months; only store-bought sealed bottled water is good until its printed date. The old water still flushes a toilet or waters plants, and the jugs are re-used after cleaning and sanitizing.", "distractors": {"1": "Self-filled water is not treated or sealed like commercial bottled water, which is why the six-month replacement rule exists.", "2": "The water is not poisonous and the jugs are reusable; it is simply past the point where you should trust it for drinking without treatment.", "0": "A capful is a guessed dose, far above the 8 drops per gallon rule, and rotation, not extra bleach, is the answer for stored water."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "pa-q3", "text": "It is day three of a water-main break and her stored bottles are finished. In the apartment she can see ice trays in the freezer, the toilet bowl, the hot radiator in the bedroom, and a friend offers a bucket from the gym's swimming pool. Which is the right source?", "options": ["The pool water, after adding 16 drops of bleach per gallon", "The toilet bowl, after boiling it hard for one minute", "The ice trays, melted in a clean pot", "The radiator water, because it has already been heated"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The EPA lists melted ice cubes among the safe alternative sources, right after bottled water; ice made from tap water before the emergency needs no treatment. Toilet bowls, radiators and swimming pools are on the EPA's do-not-use list because of chemicals that boiling and bleach cannot remove.", "distractors": {"1": "The bowl is never a source; only the tank behind the seat is even discussed, and then only as a last resort after treatment.", "3": "Radiators and boilers hold rust and anti-corrosion chemicals that no boiling removes; the EPA lists them as sources not to use.", "0": "Pool chemicals and body waste are not fixed by bleach; bleach only kills germs, and the EPA says pools and spas are not drinking sources."}, "topic": "Finding water when the taps stop"}, {"id": "pa-q4", "text": "A boil-water notice for her ZIP code arrived at noon. At 3 p.m. she filled the ice trays from the tap and brushed her teeth with tap water. What should she do now?", "options": ["Discard the ice, use boiled or bottled water for teeth, food and drinks, and treat the notice as in force until the same channel lifts it", "Keep the ice but boil the tap water for three minutes from now on", "Throw away the ice, wait for the water to look clear, then go back to normal", "Nothing; the notice only covers water you drink by the glass"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The New York State Department of Health rules are to throw away ice made during the notice and to use boiled (one minute rolling boil) or bottled water for drinking, brushing teeth, washing food and preparing formula. A notice usually lasts 24 to 48 hours and is lifted by the channel that issued it, not by how the water looks.", "distractors": {"3": "Brushing teeth, making ice and preparing food all put tap water in the mouth; the notice covers all of them.", "2": "Clear-looking water can still carry germs; the notice ends when the DEP or Health Department lifts it, not when the tap looks fine.", "1": "New York is at sea level, so the boil is one minute, not three, and ice made during the notice must go."}, "topic": "Finding water when the taps stop"}, {"id": "pa-q5", "text": "She has a quart jar of clear rainwater already poured through a coffee filter, no working stove, and a dropper of plain unscented 6% bleach. What dose makes it drinkable?", "options": ["2 drops, stir, wait 30 minutes", "8 drops, stir, wait 30 minutes", "1/8 teaspoon, stir, wait 10 minutes", "16 drops, stir, wait 30 minutes"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The CDC gallon dose is 8 drops of 5 to 9 percent unscented bleach for clear water, and a quart is a quarter of a gallon, so the print sheet gives 2 drops per quart of clear water (4 if cloudy), followed by a 30-minute wait.", "distractors": {"1": "Eight drops is the dose for a full gallon of clear water; four times too much for a quart.", "3": "Sixteen drops is the cloudy-water dose for a whole gallon, not for one clear quart.", "2": "One-eighth teaspoon is roughly the gallon dose, and the wait after any bleach dose is 30 minutes, not 10."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "pa-q6", "text": "A camping-store clerk says the straw filter she bought makes any water safe. Its label says it removes parasites and bacteria. She wants to use it on water drained from the building's basement tank. What does the CDC guidance mean for her?", "options": ["Run the water through the filter twice and it will be virus-free", "Viruses are too small for most portable filters, so filter first to clear the water and then boil it or add the bleach dose", "The label is enough; anything that removes bacteria removes everything smaller too", "A filter is useless in an emergency; only boiling ever works"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The CDC says most portable filters remove parasites but not viruses, and advises adding a chemical disinfectant or boiling after filtering. The safe order is filter first to make the water clear, then disinfect.", "distractors": {"2": "Viruses are smaller than bacteria and pass through a 0.1 to 1 micron filter; the label lists what it catches, not what it misses.", "3": "A filter is a real part of the kit: it clears grit and parasites so that bleach or boiling can finish the job.", "0": "A second pass does not shrink the pore size; viruses still go through, and only disinfection kills them."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "pa-q7", "text": "At the store she is choosing between a 12-pack of canned broth (label: 15 calories per serving) and a large jar of peanut butter (label: 190 calories per serving, 14 servings) for the emergency shelf. Which is the better buy for a two-week no-cook pantry?", "options": ["The peanut butter: about 2,660 calories in one jar, eaten cold with a spoon, is more than a full day's food", "Neither: only rice and dry beans belong in an emergency pantry", "The broth: twelve cans last longer on a shelf than one jar", "The broth: liquid food counts toward the water supply"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A pantry is measured in calories, not cans. Multiplying calories per serving by servings shows the jar holds about 2,660 calories, while the broth is water, salt and almost nothing else. The first two weeks should be dense food that needs no cooking.", "distractors": {"2": "Shelf life is not the problem; broth simply does not contain the calories that keep a person on her feet.", "3": "Broth is not a drinking-water substitute, and the water plan is one gallon per person per day from stored water.", "1": "Rice and dry beans are stage-2 food because they need fuel and water to cook; the first two weeks should be eatable straight from the package."}, "topic": "Building a two-week pantry, then a three-month one"}, {"id": "pa-q8", "text": "Power returned after being out for 20 hours. The refrigerator door stayed shut the whole time and the kitchen never rose above 75 F. Inside are milk, cooked chicken and an unopened jar of pickles. What does the FDA rule say?", "options": ["Everything is fine because the door never opened", "Only the chicken must go; milk lasts a full day unrefrigerated", "Smell the milk and chicken and keep whatever seems fine", "The milk and chicken are discarded: a closed fridge keeps food safe only about 4 hours, and 20 hours is far past that"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The FDA says a refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours with the door shut; perishables that have been above 40 F for more than 2 hours are discarded. Twenty hours means the milk, meat and leftovers go out. When in doubt, throw it out.", "distractors": {"0": "A closed door buys about 4 hours, not 20; after that the inside is at room temperature.", "1": "Milk is a perishable like meat; both follow the same 4-hour fridge window and 2-hour rule.", "2": "Bacteria that cause food poisoning cannot be smelled or tasted; the FDA says never taste food to check it."}, "topic": "Cooking without power and keeping food safe when the fridge dies"}, {"id": "pa-q9", "text": "During a winter blackout her roommate wants to light the charcoal grill on the fire escape outside the kitchen window, arguing that a fire escape is outdoors. What is the correct answer?", "options": ["Yes, but only with propane instead of charcoal", "Yes, as long as the window is open so the fumes can escape", "Only if the grill is moved to the roof, which the fire code allows for charcoal", "No: a fire escape is neither legal for a grill nor 20 feet from a window, and the smoke and carbon monoxide come straight in"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The CDC rule is no fuel-burning device indoors or outdoors within 20 feet of a window, door or vent, and the FDNY fire code bans grilling on balconies, roofs and fire escapes. Charcoal is legal only on a terrace or in a backyard, 10 feet from the building, with an extinguisher or hose at hand.", "distractors": {"1": "An open window does not make carbon monoxide safe; the CDC says opening windows does not protect you.", "0": "A standard propane grill may not even be stored at an apartment building, and the fire escape rule applies to every grill.", "2": "Grilling on a roof is illegal too; only a terrace or backyard qualifies, and only 10 feet from the building."}, "topic": "Cooking without power and keeping food safe when the fridge dies"}, {"id": "pa-q10", "text": "On day ten of an outage a neighbour comes back from the park with a bag of white mushrooms he identified from a library book. He tasted one at breakfast and says he feels fine six hours later. What is the right response?", "options": ["Boil the mushrooms for ten minutes to destroy any toxin before eating", "They are safe if the book shows a matching photo and the gills are white", "Since six hours have passed with no symptoms, the mushrooms are safe to share", "No wild mushrooms, ever: death cap symptoms are delayed, so feeling fine means nothing, and he should call Poison Control now"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The death cap causes about 90 percent of fatal mushroom poisonings, has poisoned people in New York State, and its symptoms are delayed before the liver fails. The course rule is no wild mushrooms in an emergency, and anyone who has eaten one calls Poison Control (212-764-7667 or 1-800-222-1222).", "distractors": {"2": "Delayed onset is exactly what makes the death cap deadly; a symptom-free morning is not evidence of safety.", "0": "Boiling does not destroy the death cap's toxin; the ten-minute boil rule is for raw kidney beans, not mushrooms.", "1": "White gills are a feature of the deadliest Amanita group, and the Health Department's advice is never to eat wild mushrooms at all."}, "topic": "Alternatives"}, {"id": "pa-q11", "text": "For her three-month layer she buys 20 pounds of rice and asks which kind stores longest and where to keep it. What does the Utah State University guidance in the course say?", "options": ["Either kind lasts about a year in the original bag", "Brown rice, because its oils keep it fresh; store it near the warm stove so it stays dry", "White rice in a lidded bin away from the radiator: up to 10 years at a steady 70 F with oxygen absorbers, longer sealed oxygen-free in cool storage", "Rice cannot be stored beyond six months in an apartment"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The extension guidance is to store white rice, not brown, for the long term: up to 10 years at 70 F with oxygen absorbers and up to 30 years sealed oxygen-free in cool storage, kept in a lidded bin away from heat.", "distractors": {"1": "Brown rice's oils go rancid, which is why the guidance says buy white for storage, and heat shortens the life of every stored food.", "0": "White rice properly stored lasts many years, far beyond a year; the bag is the weak point, not the rice.", "3": "Rice, dry beans, salt and sugar are the long-term staples precisely because they store for years or decades."}, "topic": "Alternatives"}, {"id": "pa-q12", "text": "A hurricane will bring both high wind and coastal flooding. Her zone has not been ordered to leave. She is on the third floor and the building has a basement laundry room. Where should she ride out the storm?", "options": ["In the lobby beside the glass front doors so she can see the street", "In an interior room on her own floor, away from windows, never below ground", "In the basement laundry room, the lowest floor available", "On the roof landing, above any possible water"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Wind says go low and water says go high; when both are possible, water wins, because a broken window on the third floor is survivable and a flooded basement is not. The interior room away from glass handles the wind.", "distractors": {"2": "Ten of the fourteen New Yorkers killed by Ida drowned in basements; nothing below ground is a shelter when flooding is possible.", "3": "Wind is strongest high up and the roof offers no walls; the goal is as many walls as possible between her and the outside.", "0": "Glass is what injures people in high wind; the lobby's front doors are the worst place to stand."}, "topic": "Sheltering in place"}, {"id": "pa-q13", "text": "She is walking home, six blocks from her apartment, when a Wireless Emergency Alert says a chemical release nearby and orders everyone to shelter in place. What should she do?", "options": ["Go into the nearest building, close windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning, and get to an interior room", "Hurry the six blocks home so she can seal her own bathroom with the sheeting in her kit", "Stay outside but cover her mouth with a scarf until the cloud passes", "Head for the subway, because underground air is protected from a plume"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Ready.gov's chemical guidance is to get inside the nearest building, not home, then close and lock windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning, and go to an interior room with few windows.", "distractors": {"1": "Six blocks in a chemical plume is six blocks of breathing it; the sealed room is any interior room, not only her own.", "2": "A scarf does not stop a chemical cloud; the safest air is the air already inside a closed building.", "3": "Subway entrances draw in street air and can trap her below ground; the rule is a closed building, not a tunnel."}, "topic": "Sheltering in place"}, {"id": "pa-q14", "text": "Her roommate came in soaked from sleet during a heating outage and is now confused and slurring. What is right?", "options": ["Call 911, strip the wet clothes, warm her chest, neck, head and groin with blankets and body heat, and give nothing by mouth while she is confused", "Skip the bath but give the whiskey, because alcohol warms the core", "The plan is fine as long as the bath is not too hot", "Walk her briskly around the block to generate heat"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Red Cross hypothermia care is to call 911, move to warmth, remove wet clothing, and warm the core first; do not rub limbs or use a hot bath, and give warm drinks only if the person is fully alert. Confusion means nothing by mouth.", "distractors": {"2": "A hot bath and rubbing the limbs push cold blood to the heart and can stop it; both are on the do-not list.", "1": "Alcohol makes a person feel warm while cooling them faster, and a confused person can choke on any drink.", "3": "A very cold person must be handled gently; exertion and rough movement can trigger cardiac arrest."}, "topic": "Staying warm with no heat"}, {"id": "pa-q15", "text": "The power is back but the building's boiler is broken. She plugs an electric space heater into the power strip beside her bed and leaves it running under the duvet's edge while she sleeps. Which rule from the course does this break?", "options": ["None; a space heater is the recommended safe way to add heat when the power is on", "Only the noise rule; heaters should be in the living room", "Space heaters must never be used in an apartment at all", "Plug it straight into the wall, keep it well away from bedding and turn it off when you sleep or leave the room"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The course's space heater rules are: plug it directly into the wall (never an extension cord or power strip), keep it well away from bedding, curtains and furniture, place it on a hard level floor, and switch it off when you sleep or leave the room.", "distractors": {"0": "A space heater is allowed, but only with the placement and plug rules that stop it starting a fire while she sleeps.", "1": "The problem is not noise: it is the power strip, the bedding and running it unattended overnight.", "2": "An electric space heater is one of the few safe ways to add heat because it burns no fuel; the rules govern how, not whether."}, "topic": "Staying warm with no heat"}, {"id": "pa-q16", "text": "She has just called 911 for an elderly neighbour with heat stroke and the dispatcher says the ambulance is twelve minutes away. What should she do while she waits?", "options": ["Leave him where he is so the paramedics can assess him untouched", "Move him to the coolest room, remove outer clothing, wet his skin and fan it, and put cold wet cloths on his neck, armpits and groin", "Wrap him in a blanket to stop shivering", "Give him a large glass of cold water and let him lie down in his bedroom"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Heat stroke is treated by cooling the body immediately while help comes: coolest room, clothing off, cool water on the skin with air moving across it, and ice or wet cloths at the neck, armpits and groin. A confused person gets nothing by mouth.", "distractors": {"3": "A confused person cannot protect his airway; the water can go into the lungs. Cool the outside and let the medics handle fluids.", "0": "Every minute at 103 F or above damages the brain; cooling starts now, not when the ambulance arrives.", "2": "A blanket traps heat in a body that has stopped cooling itself; shivering is not the problem in heat stroke."}, "topic": "Staying cool with no air conditioning"}, {"id": "pa-q17", "text": "An evacuation order covers her zone. Her cousin lives in the building across the street, also in zone 1; her aunt lives in a walk-up the finder shows is in no zone; there is a parking garage under her building. Where should she plan to sleep?", "options": ["In her car in the underground garage, with the engine running for heat", "In the park across the street with a tarp, to stay near her belongings", "At her aunt's apartment outside every zone, texting her the moment the order is announced", "At her cousin's, because it is the closest and easiest to reach"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The best evacuation shelter is a couch with family or friends outside the danger zone, arranged in advance and confirmed by text as soon as the order comes. A friend in the same zone is not a safe place to go.", "distractors": {"3": "The cousin's building is under the same order; both of them have to leave.", "0": "A car never sleeps below ground in a flood, and an engine running while you sleep is a carbon monoxide death.", "1": "A tent or tarp is the last resort for one night after every other option has failed; parks are closed overnight and it is never the plan."}, "topic": "If you must leave"}, {"id": "pa-q18", "text": "Her neighbour across the street looked up his address and is in zone 2. He tells her she must be in zone 2 as well because they share a block. What is the correct move?", "options": ["Use the old letter system, in which everything near the water was Zone A", "Assume she is in zone 6 until the city tells her otherwise", "Accept his number; zones follow the block", "Look up her own exact address on the finder or through 311, because two buildings on one block can be in different zones"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Your zone is the number the finder gives for your exact address, not your neighbourhood or your block; NYCEM says two buildings on the same block can be in different zones. Check at finder.nyc.gov/hurricane or by calling 311.", "distractors": {"2": "Zone lines run between buildings, not around blocks; the only reliable answer is her own address in the finder.", "0": "The letters A, B and C have not been used since 2013; the six numbered zones replaced them.", "1": "Guessing a low zone could leave her ignoring an order that applies to her; the lookup takes one minute."}, "topic": "Know your zone"}, {"id": "pa-q19", "text": "An evacuation order is issued at 9 p.m. Her building's group chat posts a 2012 news article listing centers, and a neighbour sets off in the rain for one three blocks away. What should she do before following him?", "options": ["Go instead to the nearest police precinct, which always serves as a shelter", "Wait at home until the rain stops before going anywhere", "Follow him; a school on any past list will be open tonight", "Check finder.nyc.gov/hurricane or call 311 to confirm that center is open right now, and leave early enough to reach a second if it is full"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The city opens centers for each emergency, and only the finder and 311 show which are open. People have walked to a locked school from an old list and had nowhere to go as the water rose; confirm first, and go early enough to have a backup.", "distractors": {"2": "Old lists are exactly the trap the lesson warns about; centers change with each emergency.", "1": "Waiting is the mistake that kills: transit stops and streets flood before the storm peaks. Confirm and go.", "0": "A police station is not an evacuation center; it has no cots, food or registration."}, "topic": "Evacuation centers and emergency shelters"}, {"id": "pa-q20", "text": "At 7 p.m. in January the thermometer reads 34 F, but the wind chill makes it 29 F. Her building's heat has failed and she is worried about sleeping there. Is Code Blue in effect, and what does it give her?", "options": ["No; Code Blue needs an air temperature at or below 32 F, wind chill does not count", "Yes, but it only sends outreach teams to people sleeping on the street", "Yes; the threshold includes wind chill between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m., so DHS drop-in centers take walk-ins and she can call 311 for the nearest one", "No; Code Blue only applies between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m."], "correct": 2, "explain": "Code Blue is in effect when the temperature including wind chill is at or below 32 F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m. Drop-in centers and shelters accept walk-ins and more than 50 hospitals keep an open door; 311 finds the nearest.", "distractors": {"0": "The threshold is explicitly the temperature including wind chill, so 29 F qualifies.", "3": "The hours are the overnight ones, 4 p.m. to 8 a.m., which is when cold kills people indoors and out.", "1": "Outreach is one part; the drop-in centers take anyone who walks in, including someone whose apartment has become unsafe."}, "topic": "Cooling centers, warming places and Code Blue"}, {"id": "pa-q21", "text": "It is 91 F with no heat advisory issued. Her top-floor apartment is stifling, she calls 311 and is told no cooling centers are open today. Where can she spend the afternoon for free?", "options": ["A public library branch: free, air-conditioned, with bathrooms, outlets and staff every day it is open", "Nowhere; cooling relief exists only during declared heat emergencies", "The nearest evacuation center, which is always open in summer", "A hospital emergency room, which is obliged to let anyone sit in the waiting area to cool off"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Cooling centers activate only with a National Weather Service heat advisory or warning or a city-declared heat emergency, but a library is the everyday version: free, air-conditioned, with bathrooms, outlets and Wi-Fi. Malls and large stores work too.", "distractors": {"1": "Libraries, malls, movie theatres and large supermarkets are air-conditioned on every hot day, not only during emergencies.", "2": "Evacuation centers open only when an evacuation order is issued; they are not summer refuges.", "3": "Emergency departments are for medical emergencies; the open-door policy is a Code Blue measure, and a waiting room is not a cooling plan."}, "topic": "Cooling centers, warming places and Code Blue"}, {"id": "pa-q22", "text": "Someone is in her apartment and she is hiding in the closet, unable to speak. Which first message to 911 follows the city's Text-to-911 rules?", "options": ["'intrdr in apt pls hurry' sent to the building group chat and 911 together", "Intruder in my apartment. 250 West 88th Street between Broadway and Amsterdam, Manhattan, apartment 4F. I am hiding in a closet.", "A photo of the closet with the caption 'help'", "Her location pin only, with no words, so the dispatcher can trace it"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Text-to-911 in NYC: enter 911 as the recipient, say what the emergency is, give the full address with cross streets and the borough, use complete words with no abbreviations, and send no photos, videos or group texts. Location from a text is less exact than a call, so the address is typed out.", "distractors": {"2": "Photos, videos, GIFs and emoji are not accepted; the first message must be words describing the emergency and the address.", "0": "Abbreviations and slang are against the rules, and 911 must never be texted in a group chat.", "3": "A text's location is less exact than a voice call's, which is exactly why the address, cross streets and borough must be typed."}, "topic": "Alerts and who to call"}, {"id": "pa-q23", "text": "She is walking home over a bridge as a storm builds and reaches a police barrier across the pedestrian walkway. Her apartment is on the other side. What should she do?", "options": ["Step around the barrier and cross quickly before the wind gets worse", "Try the vehicle tunnel instead, since it is out of the wind", "Turn back, find shelter on this side, and wait; bridges close to walkers in high wind and the barrier is the closure", "Wait beside the barrier on the bridge until it is removed"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Bridges close to pedestrians in high wind, and MTA bridges may close to all traffic at sustained winds of 60 mph or more. A barrier across the walkway means do not go around it; shelter where you are and wait for conditions to pass.", "distractors": {"0": "A pedestrian on an open bridge in that wind can be blown into the railing or the roadway; the barrier is there for that reason.", "3": "Standing on the exposed bridge approach is the danger itself; go back to a building on the near side.", "1": "The Lincoln, Holland, Queens-Midtown and Hugh L. Carey tunnels are never open to pedestrians and are the first to flood."}, "topic": "Getting around when the subway stops"}, {"id": "pa-q24", "text": "A bystander is giving chest compressions to a collapsed man while she waits with 911 on speaker. She counts about 60 pushes a minute, barely an inch deep. What should she tell him?", "options": ["Stop compressions and give rescue breaths only until the ambulance arrives", "Slow down further so the heart has time to fill between pushes", "Push hard and fast: 100 to 120 a minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, letting the chest come all the way back up, and swap with her when he tires", "Press on the stomach instead, where there are no ribs to break"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The American Red Cross and American Heart Association figures are 100 to 120 compressions a minute at 2 to 2.4 inches for an adult, with full chest recoil; compressions are tiring, so rescuers swap with minimal pause.", "distractors": {"1": "Sixty a minute is half the required rate; slow, shallow pushes do not move blood to the brain.", "0": "Hands-only CPR is compressions without breaths; stopping compressions is what kills. Breaths are added only by trained rescuers at 30 to 2.", "3": "Compressions go on the centre of the chest, the lower half of the breastbone; fear of breaking a rib has killed more people than bad CPR."}, "topic": "The kit, check-call-care, CPR, choking and when it is 911"}, {"id": "pa-q25", "text": "Her neighbour fell from a ladder in the hallway. He is unresponsive but breathing steadily. A passer-by starts to roll him into the recovery position. What should she say?", "options": ["Stop: a fall from height means a possible neck or back injury, so keep his head still and wait for 911", "Good idea; every unresponsive breathing person goes on their side", "Sit him upright against the wall to help his breathing", "Roll him on to his stomach instead so he cannot swallow his tongue"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The recovery position protects the airway of an unresponsive breathing person, but the course says not to use it when a neck or back injury is suspected, such as a fall from height; keep the head still and wait for 911, checking breathing.", "distractors": {"1": "The exception matters: rolling someone with a spinal injury can paralyse them.", "3": "Face-down blocks the airway and moves the spine; there is no such technique.", "2": "Sitting up moves the neck and back; a suspected spinal injury is kept still until medics arrive."}, "topic": "The kit, check-call-care, CPR, choking and when it is 911"}, {"id": "pa-q26", "text": "An hour after she put a tourniquet on a neighbour's leg, the wound starts bleeding again. Her friend says to loosen it for a minute to let some blood through to the foot. What is right?", "options": ["Loosen it briefly every 20 minutes to save the leg", "Remove it and go back to direct pressure, which is gentler", "Move it below the knee so it is closer to the wound", "Tighten it further, or add a second tourniquet above the first; never loosen it, and keep the time written down for the hospital"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Stop the Bleed: if bleeding restarts, tighten the tourniquet or add a second one above the first. A tourniquet is never loosened or removed outside a hospital; note the time and leave it. Loosening to 'let blood through' is the deadly mistake.", "distractors": {"0": "Loosening restarts life-threatening bleeding; the leg is far more likely to survive than a person who bleeds out.", "1": "Direct pressure already failed, which is why the tourniquet went on; only a hospital removes it.", "2": "Tourniquets go 2 to 3 inches above the wound and never on a joint; moving one over the knee makes it useless."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}, {"id": "pa-q27", "text": "Cleaning a flooded bathroom, her roommate spills dry drain-cleaner crystals on her forearm and the skin begins to burn. What is the first-aid sequence?", "options": ["Brush the dry powder off first, then flush the arm under running water and keep flushing while someone calls Poison Control or 911", "Cover the arm with butter to stop the burning", "Wrap the arm tightly in a dry bandage and drive to a clinic", "Rub the arm with a wet cloth to dissolve the crystals"], "correct": 0, "explain": "For a chemical burn the course says: brush off dry powder first, then flush with running water and keep flushing while someone calls 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, until they say to stop. Strong chemical burns are a 911 case.", "distractors": {"3": "Wetting dry crystals in place activates more of the chemical on the skin; they are brushed off before water goes on.", "1": "Grease of any kind seals in heat and chemicals; nothing greasy ever goes on a burn.", "2": "A tight dry wrap traps the chemical against the skin; flushing with water is the treatment, and a strong chemical burn needs 911, not a drive."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}, {"id": "pa-q28", "text": "Her neighbour had heat exhaustion after a hot walk: sweaty, weak, nauseous. She has had him in the coolest room sipping water for an hour, but he is still weak and has started vomiting. What now?", "options": ["Send him home to sleep it off with the fan on", "Get medical help now; heat exhaustion that is not better within an hour, or with vomiting, needs a clinician, and 911 if he becomes confused", "Put him in a bath of ice water", "Give him a salt tablet and another hour of rest"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The course's heat exhaustion rule is cool place, loosen clothing, sip water, and if not better in an hour or vomiting, get medical help. Confusion at any point moves it to heat stroke and a 911 call.", "distractors": {"3": "Salt tablets are not in the guidance and vomiting means he cannot keep fluids down; that is the signal to escalate.", "2": "Aggressive ice-water cooling is for heat stroke; here the alarm sign is failure to improve, which needs medical assessment.", "0": "'Let him sleep it off' is the deadly mistake for heat illness; a person who worsens alone in a hot room can slide into heat stroke."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "pa-q29", "text": "During a July blackout she helps a diabetic neighbour move insulin vials out of the warming fridge. The neighbour drops the vials directly on to a bag of ice in a cooler. What should she change?", "options": ["Nothing; colder is always better for insulin", "Take the insulin out of the cooler and leave it on the sunny windowsill instead", "Wrap the cold pack or ice in a towel so it does not touch the vials; insulin must never freeze, and it keeps 59 to 86 F for up to 28 days", "Throw the insulin away, because once out of the fridge it is useless"], "correct": 2, "explain": "FDA emergency guidance: insulin in vials or cartridges can be kept unrefrigerated between 59 and 86 F for up to 28 days, but it must never be frozen and never used after freezing, so ice is kept out of direct contact with the vials.", "distractors": {"0": "Frozen insulin is ruined; direct contact with ice risks exactly that.", "1": "Above 86 F insulin loses strength, and a sunny window is the hottest spot in the apartment.", "3": "Throwing away good insulin is the other way people get this wrong; it works for weeks at room temperature."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "pa-q30", "text": "Her 80-year-old neighbour has a leg wound that has been oozing for days. Tonight he is suddenly confused and breathing fast. His son says the emergency room is packed and they will wait until morning. What should she say?", "options": ["Give him a double dose of fever medicine and check again in four hours", "Call 911 now: confusion and fast breathing with an infection is how sepsis looks, and he will be triaged first, not made to wait", "Wait until morning as the son suggests; queues are shorter then", "Take him to an urgent-care clinic when it opens at 8 a.m."], "correct": 1, "explain": "The course says confusion, fast breathing or a very fast pulse with any infection is a 911 call because that is how sepsis presents and hours matter. In an overloaded system the queue is for people who can wait; a suddenly confused older person is not in that queue.", "distractors": {"2": "Waiting because the hospital is busy is how a treatable infection becomes sepsis overnight.", "0": "Fever medicine is used only as the label directs and does not treat sepsis; it can hide the fever while the infection advances.", "3": "A clinic is for things that can wait 24 hours; sudden confusion with infection cannot."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "pa-q31", "text": "The smoke alarm wakes her at night. She crawls to the apartment door and the doorknob is hot to the touch. What does she do?", "options": ["Keep the door shut, call 911 with her floor and apartment number, and get to a window where firefighters can see her", "Wrap her hand in a towel and go out through the door quickly", "Take the elevator, since the stairwell is probably where the fire is", "Open the door a crack to see how thick the smoke is"], "correct": 0, "explain": "If the door or knob is hot, do not open it: keep the door shut, call 911 and say exactly where you are, and make yourself visible at a window. Opening a hot door lets superheated smoke into the only safe space she has.", "distractors": {"3": "A hot knob means fire on the other side; opening it even a crack can flood the room with smoke and heat.", "1": "Speed does not help in a hallway full of smoke; smoke, not flame, is what kills in apartment fires.", "2": "Elevators can stop between floors or open on to the fire floor; in a fire it is always the stairs, and here the door stays shut."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "pa-q32", "text": "The smoke alarm sounds every time she fries food, so her roommate has taken the battery out and keeps it in a drawer. What is the correct fix?", "options": ["Move the alarm inside a kitchen cabinet where the steam cannot reach it", "Put the battery back tonight and never remove it for cooking; a chirp means a dying battery, and alarms are replaced every 10 years", "Leave it out while cooking and replace it before bed each night", "Keep it out; the building's hallway alarm will cover the apartment"], "correct": 1, "explain": "NFPA and USFA rules: test monthly, replace batteries at least yearly, replace the whole alarm every 10 years, and never pull the battery because cooking sets it off. An alarm turns a fire you sleep through into one you walk away from.", "distractors": {"2": "A routine that depends on remembering to replace the battery fails on the night it matters.", "0": "An alarm inside a cabinet cannot sense smoke in the room; alarms belong inside bedrooms, outside sleeping areas and on every level.", "3": "City law requires a working smoke detector inside the apartment within 15 feet of each sleeping room; a hallway alarm is not a substitute."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "pa-q33", "text": "A grease fire in the pan has already spread to the curtains above the stove. She has a multipurpose extinguisher in her hand. What should she do?", "options": ["Open the window to let the smoke out before using the extinguisher", "Get everyone out, close the door behind her and call 911 from a safe place; a fire that has grown beyond the pan is a leave-now job", "Fight it with P.A.S.S. until it is out, then call 911", "Throw a pot of water on the curtains and then the pan"], "correct": 1, "explain": "USFA says extinguishers are useful for small contained fires, and the course rule is that a fire that has grown beyond the pan or bin it started in means leave now, close doors behind you and call 911. Fight only if the fire is small, everyone is out, 911 is called and the exit is at your back.", "distractors": {"2": "Fighting a spreading fire with a small extinguisher costs the seconds she needs to get out; two minutes is all NFPA gives from the first beep.", "3": "Water on burning oil throws flaming grease across the kitchen; a lid on the pan is the tool for a pan fire, and this fire is past that.", "0": "Opening a window feeds the fire with air; the door is closed on the way out, and 911 is called from outside."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "pa-q34", "text": "She smelled gas, left the apartment and is standing on the sidewalk. Her neighbour wants to go back in to open the windows and find which burner is leaking. What should she tell him?", "options": ["Do not go back in; call 911 or the gas company from outside and let the crew with a meter decide when it is safe", "Go ahead, but use the phone flashlight instead of the light switch", "Only go back if the smell is faint", "Go back in, but turn off the main breaker first to prevent sparks"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Con Edison's rule is leave first, call second: do not go back in to open windows or find the source, and call 911 or the gas company once you are away from the gas. Only the crew with a meter decides when re-entry is safe.", "distractors": {"1": "The phone is an electronic device that can spark; nothing electrical is touched near a gas smell, and re-entering is the mistake anyway.", "2": "Leave even if the odour is faint; the smell does not have to be strong to be dangerous.", "3": "Flipping any switch, including a breaker, can make the spark that ignites gas; the only job is to be outside."}, "topic": "Gas leaks, carbon monoxide and wildfire smoke"}, {"id": "pa-q35", "text": "Wildfire smoke has settled over the city and AirNow shows an AQI of 120. She has asthma and her roommate says anything under 150 is fine for everyone. What does the AirNow scale actually say?", "options": ["An AQI of 120 is satisfactory for almost everyone, so she should go for her run", "Anything under 150 is good air quality", "Only readings over 300 matter for people with asthma", "Above 100 the air is unhealthy and the higher the number the greater the concern, so she stays in, closes up, and keeps one clean room"], "correct": 3, "explain": "AirNow states that 50 or below is good, 100 or below is satisfactory for almost everyone, and above 100 air quality is unhealthy, with concern rising as the number rises; over 300 is hazardous. The action is to stay inside, close windows and doors, and keep one clean room.", "distractors": {"1": "Good air is 50 or below; 120 is already in the unhealthy range.", "2": "Over 300 is hazardous for everyone; the unhealthy range starts above 100, and people with lung disease feel it first.", "0": "The 'satisfactory for almost everyone' band ends at 100; a 5-mile run in unhealthy air is the wrong day."}, "topic": "Gas leaks, carbon monoxide and wildfire smoke"}, {"id": "pa-q36", "text": "The block has gone dark. She wants to leave the television and laptop plugged in so they are ready the moment service returns, and turn every light off to save power. What does the city's and Ready.gov's outage advice say?", "options": ["Plug everything into one power strip so it can be switched at once", "Unplug the electronics because power can return with a surge, and leave one lamp switched on so she knows when service is back", "Leave everything plugged in; the grid returning does no harm to electronics", "Turn off the main breaker and leave it off until morning"], "correct": 1, "explain": "NYC Emergency Management and Ready.gov both warn that power can come back with surges or spikes that damage equipment, so electronics are unplugged; the city's own tip is to leave a single lamp or radio on so you know the moment service returns.", "distractors": {"2": "Surges on restoration are a known cause of destroyed laptops, TVs and routers.", "3": "Killing the main breaker leaves her no lamp to signal restoration and no way to know when the fridge is running again.", "0": "A power strip does not protect against a surge, and a single strip carrying everything is its own hazard."}, "topic": "Light, batteries, phone power and generators"}, {"id": "pa-q37", "text": "While charging after a two-day outage, her power bank grows hot, gives off a strange smell and its case looks swollen. What should she do?", "options": ["Keep charging; batteries always warm up after a long outage", "Stop using it and move away from it; if it smokes or catches fire, get out and call 911", "Wrap it in a wet towel and keep it by the bed to watch it overnight", "Put it in the refrigerator to cool it down"], "correct": 1, "explain": "FDNY lithium-ion guidance: if a battery gets hot, smells strange or swells, stop using it; if there is smoke or fire, get out and call 911. A failing lithium battery erupts rather than smoulders, and in 2023 such fires killed 18 people in the city.", "distractors": {"0": "Heat, smell and swelling are the warning signs of a battery about to fail, not normal behaviour.", "3": "A swelling cell can erupt anywhere; the fridge is inside the apartment and does not stop the reaction.", "2": "Keeping a failing battery beside the bed overnight is the exact scenario that blocks the exit and kills people in their sleep."}, "topic": "Light, batteries, phone power and generators"}, {"id": "pa-q38", "text": "Her cousin on Long Island runs a portable generator inside the attached garage with the garage door wide open, saying the open door lets the exhaust out. What should Natasha tell her?", "options": ["Run it only at night when everyone is asleep and windows are shut", "It is fine as long as the door stays open and a fan blows outward", "Never in a garage, even with the door open: it goes outdoors, more than 20 feet from any window, door or vent, with a battery CO alarm inside the house", "Move it to the porch, about 8 feet from the kitchen window"], "correct": 2, "explain": "CDC and CPSC: a generator runs outdoors only, more than 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away, and never inside a home, garage, basement or shed even with doors open or fans running. A battery CO alarm belongs indoors.", "distractors": {"1": "Open doors and fans do not clear carbon monoxide; the CDC lists 'even with doors and windows open' as still deadly.", "3": "Eight feet is inside the danger zone; nearly half of non-fatal hurricane CO poisonings involved generators within 7 feet of the home.", "0": "People asleep cannot notice symptoms; CO from a generator near a closed house kills in the night."}, "topic": "Light, batteries, phone power and generators"}, {"id": "pa-q39", "text": "While the network is calm she is deciding what to prepare. Which combination still works on day three of a blackout when her phone is dead and the towers are down?", "options": ["Her contacts list backed up to the cloud and an offline map on the phone", "A second phone app for alerts and a saved Notify NYC web page", "A pair of FRS radios to reach her sister in another borough", "A paper contact card in her wallet, a printed subway and borough map, and a battery or hand-crank NOAA weather radio"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Paper and broadcast radio need no network and no battery she cannot replace: the card carries the numbers her phone would have had, the paper map gets her home as it did for most New Yorkers in 2003, and NOAA radio broadcasts even when cell service and the internet are gone.", "distractors": {"1": "Apps and web pages die with the phone and the towers; Notify NYC by text stops working the moment the phone is dead.", "0": "Cloud backups need the internet and the offline map needs a charged phone; both fail in the scenario described.", "2": "FRS radios reach about half a mile to a mile among buildings; they connect a neighbour, not a sister across the borough."}, "topic": "Communication when networks are down or jammed"}, {"id": "pa-q40", "text": "Power was just restored after a six-hour outage. The elevator's lights are on and the doors open when she presses the button. She is on the 14th floor with groceries. Should she ride?", "options": ["No: elevators are sensitive to fluctuations and often need a reset after an outage, so she takes the stairs until the building confirms they are reset", "No; elevators are never safe to use again for 48 hours after any outage", "Yes; lit buttons prove the elevator is safe", "Yes, but only if she rides alone so a rescue would be quick"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The rule is flicker, brownout or power 'just restored' means stairs. In the July 2019 Manhattan blackout more than 400 elevators got stuck, and in December 2023 people were trapped even though power returned in moments, because elevators need a reset after fluctuations.", "distractors": {"2": "Lit buttons and open doors were true for the cars that trapped people in 2023; the controller may still fault mid-ride.", "3": "Riding alone changes nothing about a car that stops between floors and needs an FDNY crew to open.", "1": "There is no 48-hour rule; the elevator is safe once the building confirms it has been reset."}, "topic": "Elevators, refrigeration and medical devices in a blackout; reporting an outage"}, {"id": "pa-q41", "text": "She has $25 this week and nothing prepared. She is torn between a 10-pound bag of rice and a battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm. Using the rule of threes, which comes first?", "options": ["The rice: three weeks without food is the longest survival window, so start there", "Neither: the first purchase should always be a generator", "The rice, because the CO alarm is the landlord's responsibility so she never needs her own", "The CO alarm: air comes first in the rule of threes, and smoke, carbon monoxide and gas are the killers of the first three minutes"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The rule of threes orders the work: 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. In an apartment the 3-minute line is smoke, carbon monoxide and gas, so a working smoke alarm and a battery CO detector are the first money spent.", "distractors": {"0": "Food is important but last; a pantry does nothing for someone who cannot breathe.", "1": "A generator must run 20 feet from any opening, which almost no apartment can do; the course says spend the money on water, light and a CO alarm instead.", "2": "The landlord must install one, but a plug-in unit without battery backup is dead in a blackout, which is when she needs it most."}, "topic": "How this course works, the rule of threes, and the survival mindset"}, {"id": "pa-q42", "text": "She has just moved into a garden-level apartment in Queens.
