Beyond the citywide Notify NYC signup, which alert should she add specifically because of where she lives?", "options": ["The Notify NYC basement alert group, which sends targeted warnings of life-threatening rain", "The AirNow smoke advisory emails", "Con Edison's outage text alerts", "The MTA service alerts for her subway line"], "correct": 0, "explain": "NYC Emergency Management tells basement and ground-floor residents to sign up for the Notify NYC basement alert group, which sends targeted warnings for life-threatening rain, and to move to a higher floor before water arrives. Ten of the fourteen people killed by Ida drowned in basement units.", "distractors": {"2": "Useful for blackouts, but it says nothing about the flash flooding that kills basement residents.", "3": "Transit alerts do not warn of rain that will fill her apartment in minutes.", "1": "Smoke advisories matter, but the specific hazard of a below-ground apartment is water."}, "topic": "The NYC hazard map — what actually kills people here"}, {"id": "pa-q43", "text": "She has chosen her out-of-area contact in Ohio and wants to agree the first text in advance so it is fast under stress. What should that message contain?", "options": ["Just the word 'safe', because anything longer will not get through", "A full description of what happened, with photos, so the contact can judge the danger", "A request for the contact to phone everyone in the family immediately", "Her name, OK or HURT, where she is and where she is going, in about fifteen words"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The course says to agree the first text in advance: name, OK or HURT, where you are, where you are going; about fifteen words. The contact's job is to collect these check-ins and relay them so nobody has to reach everybody.", "distractors": {"1": "Long messages and photos burn battery and bandwidth; the point is a short text that queues and sends when the jammed network frees up.", "0": "'Safe' gives the contact nothing to relay; where she is and where she is going are what the family needs.", "2": "Calls are what jam local networks; the contact relays by text, and the first message is about her status, not instructions."}, "topic": "Your household emergency plan"}, {"id": "pa-q44", "text": "The water is off. Her roommate pours bathtub water slowly into the toilet tank, waits for it to fill, and then flushes after each visit to urinate, topping the tank up from their drinking bottles when the tub runs low. Which correction matters most?", "options": ["Pour faster, but keep using the tank", "Pour one to two gallons of non-drinking water straight into the bowl, fast, and only for solids; never spend drinking water on a flush", "Use the drinking bottles for every flush so the bowl stays clean", "Flush urine every time but skip the solids"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A toilet flushes when water is poured into the bowl fast enough to start the siphon; the tank is not needed. Flush only for solids to save water, and never with drinking water: one flush is one to two days of drinking water for a person.", "distractors": {"0": "Filling the tank wastes water on a slow refill; the rush of water into the bowl is what makes the flush.", "2": "Drinking water is the one supply she cannot replace; a flush uses a day or two of it.", "3": "It is the reverse: save flush water for solids and do not flush for urine alone."}, "topic": "Toilets without running water"}, {"id": "pa-q45", "text": "On day five without water a neighbour suggests emptying everyone's bucket toilets into the storm drain on the corner to get rid of the smell. What is the correct plan?", "options": ["Dump them down the building's trash chute so the super deals with it", "Empty them into the toilet instead, even though it will not flush", "Keep every bag tied, double-bagged and stored in a hard lidded container, and hand it over only when 311 or Notify NYC says bagged waste may go out with the trash", "Pour them into the park at night where nobody will see"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The apartment plan is bag, seal, store, hand over: double-bagged waste in a hard lidded container, away from food and off the fire escape, until the city announces that bagged human waste may go out with regular trash. Ask 311 or watch Notify NYC for that instruction.", "distractors": {"1": "A toilet that will not flush, or a blocked sewer, sends waste straight back into the lowest apartment in the building.", "3": "Loose waste feeds rats within hours and spreads disease across the block.", "0": "A split bag in a chute contaminates the whole building's trash room; nothing loose or single-bagged goes in a shared bin."}, "topic": "Toilets without running water"}, {"id": "pa-q46", "text": "After a sewer backup she mixed a bucket of bleach solution for the bathroom floor three days ago and it is still half full. She wants to use it on the visibly muddy bucket-toilet seat. What should she do?", "options": ["Use the old bucket; bleach solution keeps its strength for a month", "Mix a fresh batch (5 tablespoons per gallon), wash the seat with soap and water first, then apply bleach and keep it wet for at least a minute", "Add ammonia-based glass cleaner to the old bucket to boost it", "Pour undiluted bleach on the seat to be safe"], "correct": 1, "explain": "CDC: the surface dose is 5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) of unscented bleach per gallon, made fresh each day because the diluted solution loses strength after 24 hours; clean the dirt off with soap first, then disinfect with at least one minute of contact time.", "distractors": {"0": "Diluted bleach is effective for about 24 hours; a three-day-old bucket is mostly water.", "3": "Straight bleach burns skin and lungs and does not work on a dirty surface; the dose is 1/3 cup per gallon after cleaning.", "2": "Bleach plus ammonia makes a gas that can kill in a small bathroom; never mix bleach with any other cleaner."}, "topic": "Keeping disease out"}, {"id": "pa-q47", "text": "At a New Year's Eve crowd the pressure surges, she loses her footing and cannot get back up. What does the course say to do in that moment?", "options": ["Curl on her side, knees to chest, arms over her head and neck, to protect her airway and skull until the pressure moves on", "Lie flat on her back and shout for help", "Grab the nearest legs and pull herself up whatever it takes", "Crawl against the flow of the crowd toward where she came from"], "correct": 0, "explain": "If you fall in a crowd crush and cannot get up, curl on your side with knees to chest and arms covering head and neck; it protects the airway and skull until the wave passes. People die in crushes from chest compression, not trampling.", "distractors": {"1": "Flat on the back leaves the chest and head exposed to the full weight of the crowd; shouting uses air she needs.", "2": "Pulling others down adds bodies to the pile; nobody behind can see or stop.", "3": "Moving against the flow uses the oxygen she needs; on her feet the rule is to move with the wave, then diagonally to an edge."}, "topic": "Situational awareness, de-escalation and crowd safety"}, {"id": "pa-q48", "text": "Firefighters arrive at 2 a.m. during a fire on her floor. The neighbours have already done their paired sweep of the hallway. What is the most useful thing to hand the first firefighter?", "options": ["The building contact sheet marked with who is out, who is not accounted for, and which apartments to check", "The spare keys to every apartment on the floor", "A description of where the fire started", "A list of everyone's phone numbers so the crew can call them"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The first-hour plan ends with reporting the count: hand firefighters or police the contact sheet showing who is out, who is not, and which apartments to check, especially the 'needs help' doors. That is what searchers need to know how many people should be coming out.", "distractors": {"3": "Phone numbers do not tell a search team which apartments still have people inside.", "1": "Keys may help later, but the crew's first need is who is missing and where; they can force a door.", "2": "Useful, but secondary; the sheet with the unaccounted-for names is what directs the search."}, "topic": "Neighbours, mutual aid and NYC CERT"}, {"id": "pa-q49", "text": "A man in a work vest knocks after a storm saying he is from Con Edison and needs to inspect her kitchen. She is alone. What should she do?", "options": ["Refuse and call 911 immediately, because all such visits are scams", "Keep the chain on, ask him to wait, and call Con Edison or 311 on a number she looks up herself; a real worker will wait", "Let him in; utilities send crews without appointments after storms", "Ask him to slide his ID under the door and then let him in"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The door check: chain on, ask for ID, and call the company or 311 on a number you find yourself rather than one he gives you. A real worker will wait; anyone who pushes is the one you close the door on and call 911.", "distractors": {"2": "'Con Ed', 'building inspector' and 'FEMA' are the standard covers for post-disaster impostors.", "0": "Real crews do exist; the point is to verify, not to assume. 911 is for someone who pushes or threatens.", "3": "An ID can be faked; the verification is the phone call to a number she looked up herself."}, "topic": "Scams, rumours and where the truth comes from"}, {"id": "pa-q50", "text": "She gets a plot in a community garden and plans to grow lettuce and spinach directly in the old in-ground bed beside a painted fence. What does the state soil study suggest she change?", "options": ["Add more of the existing soil to the bed to dilute the lead", "Nothing; garden soil in the city is tested and safe", "Grow root crops like carrots instead, because they are protected underground", "Grow in a raised bed of clean bought soil, favour fruiting crops like tomatoes and beans, wash everything, and take her shoes off at home"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The state's study of NYC community gardens found 70 percent had at least one sample above lead guidance; raised beds of clean soil carried less lead, fruiting crops carry far less than leafy and root crops, and most exposure comes from swallowed soil and dust tracked home on shoes.", "distractors": {"1": "The study is exactly the evidence that city soil is often contaminated; old paint near a fence makes it worse.", "2": "Root crops sit in the soil and carry more lead than fruiting crops; leafy and root crops are the ones to be careful with.", "0": "More of the same soil does not dilute anything; clean bought soil in a raised bed is the fix."}, "topic": "Container and window gardening"}, {"id": "pa-q51", "text": "She reads that New York City is in USDA hardiness zone 7b and concludes that tells her when to put tomato seedlings outside. Is she right?", "options": ["No: hardiness zones apply only to upstate farms, not city windows", "No: the zone gives the average winter low for perennials, while the frost dates (last frost about early April, first about 20 October) decide vegetable timing", "Yes; the zone number is the number of the month to plant", "Yes; zone 7b means tomatoes can go out on 1 March"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A hardiness zone is a band of average annual minimum winter temperature and tells you which perennials survive outdoors; it does not tell you when to plant vegetables. NYC's average last spring frost is early April and first fall frost about 20 October; warm-season crops go out only after the last frost.", "distractors": {"3": "March nights in the city still freeze; tomatoes are started indoors in March and moved out after early April when nights stay warm.", "2": "The zone number has nothing to do with calendar months.", "0": "Zone 7b covers all five boroughs; the zone is real, it just answers a different question."}, "topic": "Seasons, seeds and pests in New York"}, {"id": "pa-q52", "text": "Short of closet space, she keeps her toolbox and a sheet of plywood for storm repairs on the fire-escape landing outside the kitchen window. What is wrong with this?", "options": ["Only the plywood is a problem because it could blow away; the toolbox is fine", "The fire escape is her and her neighbours' way out; storing anything on it is illegal and blocks the escape, so the tools go inside", "Nothing, as long as the items are tied down against the wind", "It is fine in summer but must come in before winter"], "correct": 1, "explain": "FDNY requires the fire escape and its window to stay clear, and storing items on a fire escape is illegal; a toolbox and a board on the landing trip a person escaping in smoke at night and can fall on a firefighter below.", "distractors": {"2": "Tied down or not, anything on the landing obstructs the escape route, which is the violation.", "0": "Every object on the escape is a hazard and a fire-code violation, including the toolbox.", "3": "The rule has no season; the escape route must be clear at all times."}, "topic": "The basic toolkit and how to use it safely"}, {"id": "pa-q53", "text": "Before a hurricane her friend tapes a big X across each window pane, saying it will keep the glass from breaking. What does FEMA say?", "options": ["Tape works if it is duct tape rather than masking tape", "Tape stops the glass breaking only on the windward side", "Tape does not stop a window breaking and can make bigger, heavier shards; instead bring loose items in, move the bed away from the glass and use an interior room", "Tape is the recommended protection for apartment windows"], "correct": 2, "explain": "FEMA: permanent shutters are best, fitted 5/8-inch plywood is an option, and tape does not prevent a window from breaking. A taped window that shatters produces larger, heavier pieces. In an apartment the real protection is distance from the glass.", "distractors": {"0": "The type of tape makes no difference to whether the glass fails under wind pressure.", "1": "Tape does not change the strength of the glass on any side of the building.", "3": "FEMA lists shutters and cut-to-fit plywood, not tape, and warns specifically that tape does not stop breakage."}, "topic": "Shutting off utilities and stopping water, wind and rain"}, {"id": "pa-q54", "text": "To hang a full 5-gallon water container from a beam she joins two lengths of cord with a square knot. What is the problem?", "options": ["The knot is fine but the cord should be doubled", "A square knot is a binding knot for bandages and parcels; under a changing load it can capsize and slide apart, so ropes are joined with a sheet bend or two bowlines", "She should have used a clove hitch to join the two ropes", "Nothing; the square knot is the strongest knot for joining ropes"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The course's deadly mistake for knots is joining two ropes with a square knot and trusting it with weight; it is a binding knot and can capsize under load. Join ropes with a sheet bend, or tie a bowline in each rope through the other's loop.", "distractors": {"3": "The square knot lies flat and holds a bandage; it is not designed to carry a load between two ropes.", "0": "Doubling the cord does not fix a knot that can slide apart; the knot choice is the failure.", "2": "A clove hitch attaches a rope to a pole or rail and starts a lashing; it does not join two ropes."}, "topic": "Knots, cordage and things you can build from almost nothing"}, {"id": "pa-q55", "text": "With a dead phone she must walk along 34th Street from First Avenue to Eighth Avenue. Using the grid rules, about how far is that?", "options": ["About a third of a mile; avenue blocks are short", "About a mile, because roughly seven avenue blocks make a mile", "About 20 blocks, so roughly a mile", "About four miles; crosstown blocks are the same length as uptown blocks"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Twenty north-south street blocks make about a mile, but avenue blocks are much longer: roughly seven avenue blocks equal a mile. First to Eighth Avenue is seven avenue blocks, so about one mile, or 20 to 30 minutes at the Brooklyn Bridge pace.", "distractors": {"0": "Avenue blocks are the long ones; seven of them are a mile, not a third of a mile.", "2": "Twenty is the number of street blocks in a mile when walking uptown; she is walking crosstown.", "3": "Crosstown blocks are about three times longer than uptown blocks, but seven of them are still only a mile."}, "topic": "Finding your way in the city without a phone"}, {"id": "pa-q56", "text": "For a long evacuation walk she packs new hiking boots she has never worn and three pairs of cotton socks. What should she change before leaving?", "options": ["Take the boots but skip socks altogether to avoid rubbing", "Switch to sandals so her feet stay cool", "Wear closed shoes she has already walked long distances in, with wool or synthetic socks, a spare pair and moleskin or tape for hot spots", "Nothing; new boots have the best support"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Blisters end evacuations. The course rule: sturdy shoes already worn for long walks, never new shoes, sandals or heels; moisture-wicking wool or synthetic socks, not cotton; a spare pair; and cover a rubbing spot the moment it is felt.", "distractors": {"3": "New boots rub in new places; a person who cannot walk on day two needs rescue.", "1": "Sandals offer no protection in flooded, debris-strewn streets and blister fast on long distances.", "0": "Bare feet in boots blister worst of all; the right socks are the protection."}, "topic": "Evacuating on foot"}, {"id": "pa-q57", "text": "After a flood her neighbour has a broken ankle and cannot move from a stairwell landing. Natasha decides to go and find help. What should she do before leaving her?", "options": ["Take the whistle with her so she can signal on the way", "Carry the neighbour on her back rather than leave her", "Tell her to keep shouting continuously so rescuers can hear", "Leave the whistle with her, mark the spot with something bright, write the exact location down, and tell the first responder she meets"], "correct": 3, "explain": "If someone is hurt and you go for help, leave them with the whistle, mark the spot with something bright, write the exact location on your hand or phone, and tell the first responder you meet. Three blasts on a whistle carry farther than a voice.", "distractors": {"2": "Shouting goes hoarse in minutes and, in dust, fills the lungs; a whistle in threes is the signal.", "0": "The injured person is the one who needs to be found; the whistle stays with her.", "1": "Carrying an adult with a fracture down wet stairs injures both of them; the injury is kept still and help is brought to her."}, "topic": "Signalling and being found"}, {"id": "pa-q58", "text": "She has time tonight to generate backup two-factor codes for only one account before bed. Which one should it be?", "options": ["Her email account, because almost every other account resets through it", "Her transit app, so she can pay fares in a blackout", "Her insurer's app, because claims matter most after a disaster", "Her streaming service, because she uses it most"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The course's rule: email is the master key, since almost every other account (bank, cloud, insurer) resets its password through it, so protect the email account's backup codes first and print them into the document folder.", "distractors": {"3": "A streaming login is not what keeps her from her bank, cloud copies and insurer after losing her phone.", "2": "Important, but the insurer's account itself is recovered through the email account; email comes first.", "1": "Fare apps do not run in a blackout anyway; cash in small bills covers that."}, "topic": "The document folder, the photo record and emergency cash"}, {"id": "pa-q59", "text": "A major disaster has been declared for her borough and she wants one-on-one help with her FEMA application. How does she find a Disaster Recovery Center?", "options": ["Go to the address of the center that opened after Sandy in 2012", "Wait for FEMA to mail her an appointment", "Ask at any post office, which doubles as a recovery center", "Use the FEMA.gov/DRC locator or text DRC and her ZIP code to 43362, then confirm it is open via 311 because centers change with each emergency"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Disaster Recovery Centers are temporary FEMA offices opened after a declaration; find one through the FEMA.gov/DRC locator or by texting DRC plus your ZIP code to 43362 (for example DRC 11221), and confirm at the time. Never trust an address from a previous storm.", "distractors": {"0": "Centers are opened per disaster; an address from 2012 is meaningless today.", "2": "Post offices are not part of the FEMA recovery system.", "1": "You need bring nothing but yourself and there is no appointment; the locator and text service show where to walk in."}, "topic": "Insurance, FEMA and your rights as a tenant"}, {"id": "pa-q60", "text": "In a blackout the elevator is out and an 88-year-old neighbour on the 11th floor has insulin in a warming fridge and one bottle of water. A neighbour offers to carry her down the dark stairwell to the lobby. What is the better plan?", "options": ["Bring supplies up to her (water, no-cook food, a flashlight, her insulin in a bag with wrapped ice), check twice a day, and call 911 only if she shows medical trouble", "Leave her alone until the power returns; she is safest in her own apartment", "Carry her down now while the neighbour is willing", "Call 911 immediately to have her evacuated regardless of how she feels"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The course's order for a high-floor elder when the elevator fails: go to her door within the first hour, ask about medicines, powered equipment and water, then bring supplies up rather than her down, because carrying a frail adult down a dark stairwell injures both. 911 is for confusion, heat, shivering, breathlessness or equipment that has lost power.", "distractors": {"2": "A frail adult carried down eleven dark flights is a fall waiting to happen for both people.", "1": "Silence is not safety; the check within the first hour and twice a day is what catches a slide into heat illness or low blood sugar.", "3": "911 is for a medical emergency; an ambulance tied up on a well person is one not available for a cardiac arrest."}, "topic": "Children and elders in an emergency"}, {"id": "pa-q61", "text": "She leaves under an evacuation order with her cat in its carrier. The ASPCA sticker on her door still says '1 cat inside' with her phone number. What should she do about the sticker?", "options": ["Leave it as it is; it helps rescuers know she is a pet owner", "Write EVACUATED across it so no responder risks a search of an empty apartment", "Peel it off so nobody can see she has left", "Add her cousin's address so responders can deliver the cat there"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The ASPCA rescue sticker tells responders how many animals are inside; if you evacuate with the pets, write EVACUATED across it so nobody risks entering a flooded or burning building to search for an animal that is not there.", "distractors": {"2": "Removing it leaves neighbours and responders unsure whether an animal is trapped; the marked sticker answers the question.", "0": "An unmarked sticker sends a firefighter into an empty apartment on a dangerous errand.", "3": "The sticker's purpose is to tell responders whether to search; a forwarding address is for the vet and the microchip record."}, "topic": "Pets"}, {"id": "pa-q62", "text": "Two weeks after a flood a neighbour cannot sleep, cannot stop replaying it, and wants counselling, but she has no insurance and is undocumented. Which service fits?", "options": ["The hospital emergency department, the only free option", "911, which dispatches a counsellor to the apartment", "NYC 988 at 988 or 1-888-692-9355, or text WELL to 65173: crisis counselling and referrals regardless of insurance or immigration status", "The FEMA Helpline, which pays for private therapy"], "correct": 2, "explain": "NYC 988 (formerly NYC Well) offers counselling, referral to care, mobile crisis teams and short-term counselling 24/7 in many languages, regardless of insurance or immigration status; reach it at 988, 1-888-NYC-WELL, text WELL to 65173, or its chat.", "distractors": {"1": "911 is for immediate danger to life; ongoing distress goes to 988, and the Disaster Distress Helpline at 1-800-985-5990 is the other option.", "3": "The FEMA Helpline handles disaster assistance applications, not therapy.", "0": "An emergency department is for life-threatening emergencies; 988 and the Disaster Distress Helpline are free and built for exactly this."}, "topic": "Stress, sleep and psychological first aid"}, {"id": "pa-q63", "text": "She and a friend are stranded in his car in a snowstorm on the way out of the city. He wants to keep the engine running all night for heat. What does the car-kit guidance say?", "options": ["Leave the car and walk for help in the dark", "Use the blankets and warm clothes from the car kit; engine heat runs out, and a running engine in snow risks carbon monoxide", "Open all the windows and keep the engine running for fresh air", "Run the engine all night; a car is a safe shelter"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Ready.gov's car kit exists because a stranded car in a snowstorm becomes a freezer: blankets, warm clothes, water, food, first aid and a flashlight. The checklist notes that engine heat runs out and a running engine in snow risks carbon monoxide.", "distractors": {"3": "A car with a snow-blocked exhaust fills with carbon monoxide; the kit, not the engine, is the plan.", "0": "Walking into a snowstorm at night is how people die of hypothermia; the car is shelter from wind and the kit keeps them warm.", "2": "Open windows do not make an idling engine's exhaust safe, and they let the cold in."}, "topic": "The master checklists"}, {"id": "pa-q64", "text": "Running the family communication drill, her friend suggests that they each dial 911 once to check that the number connects from their phones. What is the right answer?", "options": ["Text 911 the word 'test' instead, which the system ignores", "Fine on a quiet weekday afternoon when call volume is low", "Good idea, as long as they hang up before a dispatcher answers", "Never place a test call to 911; the drill is the surprise text to the out-of-town contact and everyone in the plan"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The course is explicit: never place a test call to 911. The communication test is a surprise text to the out-of-area contact and everyone in the plan asking where they would go, which checks memory, numbers and paper copies without tying up an emergency line.", "distractors": {"2": "A hang-up still reaches dispatch and may trigger a callback or a response; it ties up an emergency resource.", "1": "There is no acceptable time to test-call 911.", "0": "Text-to-911 is a real emergency channel, and a test text has the same problem as a test call."}, "topic": "Drills"}, {"id": "pa-q65", "text": "Starting the twelve-month build-up, she wants to skip ahead by ordering a sealed pre-packed bug-out bag online and never opening it. What does the plan say?", "options": ["Fine as long as it is stored in the basement cage", "It is a listed mistake: at 3 a.m. she will not know what is inside or whether the batteries are dead; do the free month-1 steps, buy water, then build from what she owns", "Acceptable in month 6 only, when the go-bag is due", "Good; a professionally packed bag beats anything she could assemble"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The build-up's deadly mistakes include buying a sealed pre-packed bag and never opening it, because you will not know its contents or the state of its batteries when it matters. The order is free steps first (alerts, plan, medical card, document photos, alarm test), then water, then one item per shopping trip.", "distractors": {"3": "A kit you have never opened and never drilled with is a kit you cannot use in the dark.", "0": "The basement is where the kit must never live; anything you must go downstairs to reach in a flood is not part of your kit.", "2": "Month 6 builds the go-bag from a backpack she owns, with contents she has chosen, weighed and carried once to the evacuation center."}, "topic": "The twelve-month build-up on a real budget"}], "SURVIVE/oa_sim/sim": [{"id": "oa-q1", "text": "A coworker in a fourth-floor walk-up shows Natasha her water stash during a water-main break: three gallon jugs she filled from the tap 14 months ago, kept under the kitchen sink beside drain cleaner, and a sealed store-bought case two months past its printed date on the closet floor. Which is drinkable tonight?", "options": ["The jugs: tap water never goes off, while the bottled case is past its date and must be poured out", "Both, as long as the water looks clear and has no smell", "The sealed case: the printed date is a quality mark, not a safety limit; the jugs are past six months and sat beside chemicals, so they are flush water only", "Neither: both need a rolling boil for three minutes before anyone drinks them"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Ready.gov says sealed bottled water past its date is not poisonous; in an emergency drink it. Self-filled containers should be replaced every six months, and plastic beside drain cleaner can absorb fumes that no boiling removes, so those jugs are for flushing and washing only.", "distractors": {"0": "Self-filled water is replaced every six months and water stored next to chemicals can pick up fumes; the bottled case is the safe one.", "3": "Boiling cannot remove chemical fumes absorbed from drain cleaner, and NYC is at sea level so one minute, not three, is the boil time anyway.", "1": "Looks and smell do not detect chemical contamination; the jugs beside drain cleaner should not be drunk."}, "topic": "How much water to store and how to store it"}, {"id": "oa-q2", "text": "Natasha is at dinner in a friend's 18th-floor apartment when the whole block goes dark. The friend heads for the candle drawer and says they will deal with everything else after dessert. What should happen in the very first minute?", "options": ["Open the refrigerator and move everything into a cooler with ice before it warms", "Find a flashlight, then check the news for how long the outage will last", "Take the elevator down while it still works and buy bottled water on the corner", "Plug the bathtub and open the cold tap, then fill every pot and bottle, because the roof tank empties from the top floor down once the pump stops"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Above roughly the sixth floor, water reaches apartments from a rooftop tank filled by an electric pump. When power fails the pump stops and the tank empties floor by floor, so the highest apartments run dry first, in minutes. Filling the tub and pots comes before the flashlight or the news.", "distractors": {"1": "Light matters, but the water in the pipes is the thing that disappears first and cannot be recovered; fill first.", "0": "Opening the fridge throws away cold; it stays safe about 4 hours shut. Water pressure is the urgent loss.", "2": "Never take an elevator when power is unstable; it can trap her between floors, and the corner store's water sells out anyway."}, "topic": "Finding water when the taps stop"}, {"id": "oa-q3", "text": "Day three of a main break. Natasha's stored water is gone and a neighbour says the water in his toilet tank is drinkable once bleached; she notices a blue cleaning tablet dissolving in it. The freezer still holds two bags of ice and the pipes have not been drained. What is the right call?", "options": ["Boil the tank water for three minutes; heat destroys the cleaner", "Skip the tank: one that has held a cleaner is never drinking water. Use melted ice, then pipe water, then the building tank and rain; ask 311 for distribution points", "Drink from the toilet bowl instead, since the tablet is only in the tank", "Dose the tank water with 16 drops of bleach per gallon, wait 30 minutes and drink it"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The EPA lists safe alternative sources in order: bottled water, melted ice, the hot-water tank, drained pipes. Toilet-tank water is a last option and never if any cleaner has been in the tank; bleach and boiling do not remove cleaning chemicals. The city sets up distribution points during outages; 311 knows where.", "distractors": {"3": "Bleach kills germs but adds nothing against chemicals, and the cleaning tablet is a chemical.", "0": "Boiling concentrates chemicals rather than removing them, and the sea-level boil time is one minute anyway.", "2": "The bowl is never a source; it is dirtier than the tank and the EPA lists both as not for drinking."}, "topic": "Finding water when the taps stop"}, {"id": "oa-q4", "text": "A boil-water notice covers Natasha's office ZIP code. The office has no stove, and a coworker fills the activated-carbon pitcher filter twice and announces the water is now safe for everyone's coffee. What should Natasha say?", "options": ["A pitcher filter is a taste filter and does not disinfect: use bottled water, or add 8 drops of plain unscented 5-9% bleach per gallon of clear water and wait 30 minutes", "Two passes through the pitcher is plenty; carbon removes bacteria and viruses", "Pour it through a coffee filter first, then the pitcher, and it will be safe", "Microwave each cup for 30 seconds instead; that is the same as boiling"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Carbon pitcher filters remove chlorine taste and some chemicals but are not disinfection devices: bacteria, viruses and parasites pass through. When boiling is impossible, the CDC dose is 8 drops of unscented 5-9% household bleach per gallon of clear water, stirred, with a 30-minute wait.", "distractors": {"1": "Running water through a carbon filter twice still removes no germs; it was never designed to.", "3": "A short microwave burst does not bring water to a rolling boil held for one minute; it is not disinfection.", "2": "A coffee filter only catches grit; neither it nor the pitcher kills the germs a boil notice is about."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "oa-q5", "text": "Natasha's neighbour treats a gallon of cloudy bathtub water by adding 8 drops of a scented 'splashless' bleach, stirring, and pouring a glass after ten minutes. How many things are wrong with what he did?", "options": ["One: scented bleach is the only problem; the dose and the wait were right for cloudy water", "One: he only needed to wait longer than ten minutes", "Three: cloudy water must be settled and poured through a cloth and then gets 16 drops, the bleach must be plain unscented 5-9%, and the wait is 30 minutes", "Nothing: cloudy water gets 8 drops and a ten-minute wait is standard"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The CDC method: let cloudy water settle, pour the clear top through a clean cloth or coffee filter, then use 16 drops (about 1/4 teaspoon) per gallon of regular unscented 5-9% bleach and wait 30 minutes. Scented, colour-safe and splashless bleaches carry additives not meant to be swallowed.", "distractors": {"1": "The wait is wrong, but so are the dose for cloudy water and the type of bleach.", "0": "The bleach type is wrong, but cloudy water also needs pre-filtering, double the dose and a 30-minute wait.", "3": "Eight drops is the clear-water dose; cloudy water needs 16 drops, and the wait is 30 minutes, not ten."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "oa-q6", "text": "Day five of a summer blackout: no bleach left and the gas is off. Natasha lays two clear 2-litre bottles of slightly cloudy tank water on their sides on the windowsill behind the closed glass at noon and plans to drink them at 3 p.m. What is wrong with her solar disinfection plan?", "options": ["She should have added bleach first; sunlight alone never disinfects", "Nothing: three hours of midday sun is enough for a clear bottle", "Only the bottle size: SODIS needs 5-litre bottles", "Three: filter the water clear through cloth first, give the bottles at least 6 hours of direct sun (two days if cloudy), and open the window, since glass blocks UV"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The CDC Yellow Book method: clear water in clean, clear plastic bottles no bigger than two litres, laid on their side in direct sunlight for at least 6 hours, shaken now and then; two consecutive days if cloudy. Particles shield germs, and window glass blocks part of the UV, so the bottles go where the sun hits them directly.", "distractors": {"1": "Six hours is the minimum, the water must be clear, and closed window glass cuts the ultraviolet that does the work.", "2": "Bottles must be no bigger than two litres; larger bottles let less light through the water.", "0": "Sunlight and heat do kill bacteria, viruses and parasites when the method is followed; bleach is not required, and she has none anyway."}, "topic": "Making water safe"}, {"id": "oa-q7", "text": "On the second morning of a blackout a friend with a car offers Natasha a 50-pound block of dry ice for her 18-cubic-foot freezer. Her roommate wants to unwrap it and lay it straight on top of the frozen chicken with bare hands. What is right?", "options": ["Refuse it: dry ice makes frozen food unsafe to eat", "Accept it: 50 pounds should hold a freezer that size for about two days, but handle it with gloves and keep it from touching the food directly", "Put it in the refrigerator instead; freezers do not need it", "Lay it directly on the food so the cold transfers fastest"], "correct": 1, "explain": "USDA: 50 pounds of dry ice should keep an 18-cubic-foot full freezer for 2 days. Never touch it with bare hands and do not place it in direct contact with food. In a blackout it sells out within hours, so know the seller in advance.", "distractors": {"0": "Dry ice is a standard USDA-recommended way to hold a freezer; the food stays safe.", "2": "The USDA figure is for a freezer; the fridge is emptied into a cooler with ordinary ice at hour three or four.", "3": "Dry ice burns skin and should not sit on food; wrap it and keep it separated from what you will eat."}, "topic": "Cooking without power and keeping food safe when the fridge dies"}, {"id": "oa-q8", "text": "The floor is pooling dinner supplies during a winter outage. A neighbour sets a charcoal grill on the fire escape outside Natasha's kitchen window with the window open so people can pass plates through. He says the fire escape is outdoors, so the carbon-monoxide rule does not apply. What is true?", "options": ["Illegal and dangerous: FDNY bans grills on balconies, roofs and fire escapes, and a fire escape is not 20 feet from the window, so the carbon monoxide drifts in", "It is fine as long as the window is closed between plates", "It is allowed after dark when the building is quiet", "It is legal if he switches to a propane grill"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The CDC rule is no fuel-burning device indoors or outdoors within 20 feet of a window, door or vent. NYC fire code allows charcoal grilling only on a terrace or in a backyard, 10 feet from the building, with an extinguisher or hose at hand; grilling or storing a grill on a fire escape is illegal. A fire escape is a window with a railing, not 'outdoors'.", "distractors": {"1": "Closing the window between plates does not make the distance 20 feet, and the grill still blocks the fire escape everyone above depends on.", "3": "A standard propane grill may not even be stored at an apartment building, let alone used on a fire escape.", "2": "Time of day changes nothing about carbon monoxide or the fire code."}, "topic": "Cooking without power and keeping food safe when the fridge dies"}, {"id": "oa-q9", "text": "During a long outage Natasha finds her diabetic neighbour slumped in the hallway, sweating and mumbling, unable to answer where she lives. Her meter reads 48 mg/dL. Natasha has juice boxes and honey in her kit. What does she do?", "options": ["Nothing by mouth: below 55 is severe, and a confused person can choke; use her injectable glucagon if she has it and call 911", "Put a tablespoon of honey under her tongue and let it absorb", "Give half a cup of juice, wait 15 minutes and check again", "Give a peanut-butter sandwich to raise her sugar slowly"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The CDC rule of 15 (15 grams of fast carbohydrate, wait 15 minutes) is for someone awake who can swallow safely. Below 55 mg/dL is severe: it needs injectable glucagon if available and a 911 call, and food or drink must never go into the mouth of someone confused or unable to swallow.", "distractors": {"2": "Juice is the right treatment only for an alert person above the severe line; this neighbour is confused and can choke.", "1": "Anything in the mouth of a confused person can go into the airway; honey is not an exception.", "3": "Even if she could swallow, peanut butter is slow carbohydrate; the emergency treatment is glucagon and 911."}, "topic": "Building a two-week pantry, then a three-month one"}, {"id": "oa-q10", "text": "With $30 for her first emergency shop, Natasha's roommate comes home with ten pounds of rice, five pounds of dry beans and a bag of pasta, and no can opener. Why does the course say this is the wrong first purchase, even though it is the cheapest per calorie?", "options": ["Because canned vegetables hold more calories per dollar", "Because she should have bought a slow cooker to go with them", "Because the first two weeks must be eatable cold from the package: dry staples need carried water and fuel she may not have, and a manual can opener comes first", "Because rice and beans spoil within a year"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The budget order is a manual can opener, then water, then dense no-cook food like peanut butter, crackers, canned beans and fish. Rice, pasta and dry beans are stage-2 food, added only once two no-cook weeks are on the shelf, because they need a gallon of water and a safe way to boil it.", "distractors": {"3": "White rice and dry beans keep for years; the problem is what they need to become a meal.", "0": "Canned vegetables are mostly water, fibre and salt; a can of green beans holds about 70 calories.", "1": "A slow cooker needs power the outage takes away, and it cannot even destroy the toxin in kidney beans."}, "topic": "Building a two-week pantry, then a three-month one"}, {"id": "oa-q11", "text": "A friend fishing off a Harlem River pier during a long emergency lands an eel and says it will feed the whole floor once it is fried hard. Natasha checks the state advice. What does it say?", "options": ["Fine for men, but women under 50 should skip it", "Fine as long as he holds a freshwater fishing licence", "Fine for everyone if cooked thoroughly", "No eels may be possessed for food from the East River, Harlem River or tidal Hudson; release it"], "correct": 3, "explain": "New York State's health advisory for the city's waters bans possessing eels for food from the East River, Harlem River and tidal Hudson because of PCBs and other chemicals that build up in them. Cooking does not remove those chemicals. Other species have their own limits at health.ny.gov/fish.", "distractors": {"2": "PCBs and dioxin are stored in the fish's fat and are not destroyed by frying.", "0": "The eel rule is a ban for everyone, not just the sensitive population.", "1": "Marine waters like the Harlem River need the free marine registry, not a freshwater licence, and no licence makes the eel legal to keep for food."}, "topic": "Alternatives"}, {"id": "oa-q12", "text": "On day nine of an outage a neighbour served the floor a pan of mushrooms picked in a Brooklyn park. Six hours later nobody feels sick, and he says that proves they were safe. What should Natasha do?", "options": ["Wait 24 hours and only call if someone vomits", "Call NYC Poison Control at 212-764-7667 (or 1-800-222-1222) now and keep a piece of the mushrooms: death-cap symptoms are delayed and the liver fails later", "Agree: six symptom-free hours means the mushrooms were edible", "Boil the leftover mushrooms for ten minutes to make them safe for tomorrow"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The death cap causes about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings and has poisoned people in New York State; its symptoms are delayed, so feeling fine six hours later means nothing. Anyone who has eaten a wild mushroom needs Poison Control now, with a sample kept for identification; unconsciousness, trouble breathing or seizures mean 911.", "distractors": {"2": "Delayed onset is exactly what makes the death cap deadly; absence of symptoms early is no evidence.", "3": "No cooking destroys death-cap toxins, and the course rule is no wild mushroom, ever.", "0": "By the time vomiting starts, liver damage may be under way; the call is made before symptoms."}, "topic": "Alternatives"}, {"id": "oa-q13", "text": "A hurricane is hours away and Natasha is riding it out at a friend's second-floor apartment. The friend, worried about the wind, wants everyone to wait it out in the building's basement laundry room. Where should they actually be?", "options": ["On the roof landing, above any surge", "In an interior room on a low floor but never below ground: a hurricane brings wind and water, and water wins because a flooded basement is not survivable", "In the basement: lowest floor is always safest in wind", "Beside the living-room window, watching for rising water"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Wind says go low; water says go high. When both are possible, water wins: you can survive a broken window on the third floor but not a flooded basement. Ten of the fourteen New Yorkers killed by Ida drowned in basements. The right spot is an interior room, away from glass, above any flood level.", "distractors": {"2": "A basement is the deadliest place in a storm that brings rain or surge; the doors jam under water pressure.", "0": "The roof is exposed to the full wind and flying debris; walls, not height, are the protection from wind.", "3": "Glass is what injures people in high wind; stay away from windows entirely."}, "topic": "Sheltering in place"}, {"id": "oa-q14", "text": "Natasha is walking home, ten blocks away, when a Wireless Emergency Alert says a chemical release is drifting through the neighbourhood and everyone should shelter in place. What is the right first move?", "options": ["Walk fast the ten blocks home so she can seal her own apartment", "Head for the subway and ride out of the area", "Go into the nearest building, close and lock its windows and doors, turn off fans and air conditioning and get to an interior room", "Lie flat on the pavement; chemical clouds rise"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Ready.gov's chemical-release steps begin with 'get inside': the nearest building, not home. Then close and lock windows and doors, turn off anything that pulls in outside air, go to an interior room and seal gaps with plastic and tape. The safest air is the air already in a closed room.", "distractors": {"0": "Ten blocks in a chemical cloud is ten blocks of breathing it; the nearest door is the shelter.", "3": "Lying outdoors keeps her in the release; the instruction is to get indoors and close up.", "1": "A subway entrance is a hole in the ground open to the air, and trains may be stopped; the rule is get inside a building."}, "topic": "Sheltering in place"}, {"id": "oa-q15", "text": "Six hours after a nuclear detonation across the city, Natasha and her roommate are in the middle of their brick building. The roommate says the radio reported radiation falling fast, so it is safe to walk to a relative's now. What does Ready.gov say?", "options": ["Leave only by the elevator so no dust is disturbed in the stairs", "Leave now: the first hours are the dangerous ones and they have passed", "Stay inside for at least 24 hours unless officials say otherwise, and keep listening to Notify NYC or the radio", "Go up to the roof for cleaner air away from the dust below"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Fallout radiation does drop fastest in the first hours, but Ready.gov says to remain inside for at least 24 hours unless officials tell you otherwise. The middle of a large brick or concrete building, away from outer walls and roof, is the best place to wait.", "distractors": {"1": "Radiation falling fast does not mean it is gone; 24 hours is the minimum before officials advise moving.", "3": "The roof is where fallout lands; the safest spot is the middle floors or basement, away from the roof and outer walls.", "0": "Neither leaving nor the elevator is right; the instruction is to stay put for at least a day."}, "topic": "Sheltering in place"}, {"id": "oa-q16", "text": "At a friend's unheated house in January, the friend's grandmother is shivering hard, then goes quiet and confused. The friend runs a hot bath, rubs the old woman's arms and legs and holds a mug of hot tea to her lips. Which of these is wrong?", "options": ["Only the bath: rubbing and hot drinks are fine", "Only the tea: everything else is correct treatment", "All three: a hot bath and rubbing the limbs push cold blood to the heart, and a confused person can choke on a drink; call 911 and warm the core with blankets", "Nothing: this is textbook hypothermia care"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Red Cross hypothermia care: call 911, move to warmth, remove wet clothing, warm the core first with blankets, skin contact and warm (not hot) compresses. Do not rub arms and legs, do not use a hot bath, and give warm sweet drinks only if the person is fully alert. Shivering that stops while she is still cold is a worse sign, not a better one.", "distractors": {"1": "The drink is wrong for a confused person, but the hot bath and the limb rubbing are also dangerous.", "0": "The bath is wrong, and so are rubbing the limbs and giving a drink to someone who is confused.", "3": "Each of the three actions is on the Red Cross 'do not' list for hypothermia."}, "topic": "Staying warm with no heat"}, {"id": "oa-q17", "text": "Power is back but the boiler is not. Natasha's roommate plugs a space heater into a power strip under the desk, aims it at the bed, and leaves it running while she falls asleep. Which parts break the safety rules?", "options": ["None: electric heaters make no carbon monoxide, so they are safe anywhere", "Space heaters are banned in New York apartments altogether", "Only the power strip; sleeping with it on is fine", "Three: never an extension cord or power strip, keep it well away from bedding and curtains, and turn it off when you sleep or leave the room"], "correct": 3, "explain": "An electric heater is the safe way to add heat when power is on, but only by the rules: plug it straight into the wall, never an extension cord or power strip; place it on a hard, level floor well away from bedding, curtains and furniture; and switch it off when you sleep or leave the room.", "distractors": {"0": "No carbon monoxide, but heaters start fires through cords that overheat and bedding that ignites.", "2": "Sleeping next to a running heater is one of the classic ways a blackout ends in a fire.", "1": "They are allowed; the space heater is named as a safe heat source when used by the rules."}, "topic": "Staying warm with no heat"}, {"id": "oa-q18", "text": "Natasha has called 911 for a neighbour with heat stroke: hot dry skin, confused, 104 degrees F. The ambulance is eight minutes away. Which is the correct use of those minutes?", "options": ["Leave him alone in a dark room to rest quietly until the medics arrive", "Give him cold water to drink in small sips", "Wrap him in a blanket so he does not start shivering", "Move him to the coolest room, take off outer clothing, wet the skin and fan it, and put cold wet cloths or ice packs on his neck, armpits and groin; nothing by mouth"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Heat stroke is cooled aggressively while waiting: coolest room, outer clothes off, cool water on the skin with air moving over it, ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin, and a cool shower or bath if he can be held safely. A confused or unconscious person gets no fluids because he cannot protect his airway.", "distractors": {"1": "A confused person can inhale the water; fluids are for the paramedics to manage.", "2": "A blanket traps the heat that is killing him; the goal is to lose heat as fast as possible.", "0": "Every minute of cooling counts; he must be actively cooled and watched, not left alone."}, "topic": "Staying cool with no air conditioning"}, {"id": "oa-q19", "text": "A hurricane order covers Natasha's zone. She lists where she could sleep: a cousin's apartment in zone 1, a hotel, an evacuation center from the finder, a tent in a park. Which is the best first choice, and which is out?", "options": ["The cousin in zone 1 first, because family beats strangers", "The hotel first; centers are only for people without money", "The tent in the park first, because it is free and closest", "A friend outside every zone or the evacuation center first; the cousin is in zone 1 and being evacuated too, and a park tent is a last resort for one night"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The order is family or friends outside the danger zone, a hotel booked early, a city evacuation center, and only then a car or a tent. A friend or relative who is also in zone 1 is not a safe place to go. Parks close overnight and camping is not permitted; the tent is never the plan.", "distractors": {"2": "Parks are closed overnight and a tent leaves her alone in the dark with her belongings; it is the last resort.", "0": "Zone 1 is evacuated first; the cousin needs somewhere to go herself.", "1": "Centers are free, staffed and open to anyone with nowhere better; a hotel is fine if booked early but not a requirement."}, "topic": "If you must leave"}, {"id": "oa-q20", "text": "At noon on a clear Sunday the city orders zones 1 and 2 to evacuate ahead of a Monday-night storm. Natasha is at her office in the Financial District, which the finder puts in zone 1; her apartment is in zone 5 and her cousin's place two blocks from the office is also zone 1. What should she do?", "options": ["Leave the zone-1 office now and go home to zone 5 by subway before the MTA shutdown begins; the cousin's apartment is being evacuated too", "Stay at the office; a tall building is above any surge", "Walk to her cousin's, since it is two blocks away", "Wait until the rain starts so she does not lose a working day"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Evacuation is ordered by zone number and zone 5 is not named, so home is the right destination. Leave as soon as the order is issued: the MTA suspends service before sustained 39 mph winds and a full shutdown takes about eight hours. A friend or relative who is also in an ordered zone is not a safe place to go.", "distractors": {"1": "Height does not exempt a zone-1 building: surge takes out power, water pumps, elevators and the way out.", "2": "The cousin's block is also zone 1 and under the same order.", "3": "Waiting to see how bad it gets is the mistake that kills; by the time rain falls the subway may be closed."}, "topic": "Know your zone"}, {"id": "oa-q21", "text": "Natasha's aunt lives in zone 1, uses oxygen and a walker, and has no car. When the evacuation order comes at 10 a.m. she says she will call a cab later in the day. What is the better plan?", "options": ["Call 311 as soon as the order is issued to arrange accessible transport, and tell staff at the center's registration desk about the oxygen so they can accommodate her", "A cab later is fine as long as she leaves before dark", "Call 911 now for an ambulance to take her out", "Wait for the police loudspeaker before deciding"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The city arranges accessible transportation to evacuation centers outside the zone when you call 311 as soon as the order is issued (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115). Centers are accessible, but people using oxygen, dialysis or refrigerated medicine must tell staff at registration.", "distractors": {"2": "911 is for life-threatening emergencies; accessible evacuation transport is a 311 request.", "3": "The loudspeaker means the order is already urgent; the call for transport should be made hours earlier.", "1": "Cabs disappear and streets flood in the zone hours before the storm; 'later' is how people get stranded."}, "topic": "Evacuation centers and emergency shelters"}, {"id": "oa-q22", "text": "Natasha's building has lost heat. At 3 p.m. the thermometer says 30 degrees F with wind chill; by 9 p.m. the air temperature is 34 degrees F but the wind chill makes it 28. At which time is Code Blue in effect, letting her walk into a DHS drop-in center?", "options": ["Both, since either reading is at or below 32", "Neither, because the air temperature at 9 p.m. is above 32", "At 3 p.m. only, because that is when the temperature was lowest", "At 9 p.m.: wind chill counts and it falls inside the 4 p.m. to 8 a.m. window"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Code Blue is in effect when the temperature, including wind chill, is at or below 32 degrees F between 4 p.m. and 8 a.m. The 3 p.m. reading is outside the hours; the 9 p.m. reading is inside them and the wind chill of 28 counts. During Code Blue drop-in centers and shelters take walk-ins and more than 50 hospitals keep an open door; 311 finds the nearest.", "distractors": {"2": "3 p.m. is outside the 4 p.m. to 8 a.m. window that defines Code Blue.", "1": "The definition explicitly includes wind chill, so 28 with wind chill qualifies.", "0": "The afternoon reading does not count because Code Blue hours start at 4 p.m."}, "topic": "Cooling centers, warming places and Code Blue"}, {"id": "oa-q23", "text": "Hiding from an intruder, Natasha's friend texts 911: 'help pls!!' with a photo of the hallway and a scared-face emoji, and nothing else. What did she get wrong?", "options": ["She should have texted 311 instead, because 911 is voice only", "She should have typed 9-1-1 with hyphens so the message routes correctly", "Nothing; the dispatcher will locate her from the text", "Photos and emoji are not accepted and the location is missing: the first text must give the emergency, full address, cross streets and borough in complete words"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Text-to-911 has worked in all five boroughs since June 2020, for exactly this case. Enter 911 with no spaces or hyphens; the first message gives the emergency, the full address with cross streets and the borough, because location from a text is less exact than from a call; use complete words; no photos, videos, GIFs or emoji; keep the phone on and answer.", "distractors": {"2": "Location from a text is less exact than from a call, so the address must be typed.", "0": "311 is for city services; 911 accepts text in NYC and is the right number when she cannot speak.", "1": "The recipient is entered as 911 with no spaces or hyphens."}, "topic": "Alerts and who to call"}, {"id": "oa-q24", "text": "During a storm Natasha has four things to report. Which one is the 911 call?", "options": ["Her radiators have been cold for two days", "Her downstairs neighbour's basement apartment is filling with water and the neighbour is still inside", "She wants to know which evacuation zone her new address is in", "The intersection at the corner is flooded with no cars or people in it"], "correct": 1, "explain": "911 is for life-threatening emergencies: a person in a flooding basement is one. No heat, a flooded street with nobody in danger, and a zone lookup are all 311 matters. If unsure whether it is a 911 call, it is; dispatchers would rather redirect you.", "distractors": {"0": "No heat is a 311 complaint; landlords must supply heat in the heating season and 311 sends inspectors.", "3": "A flooded street with no one in danger goes to 311 so DEP can respond.", "2": "Zone lookups are the finder or 311 (video relay 212-639-9675, TTY 212-504-4115)."}, "topic": "Alerts and who to call"}, {"id": "oa-q25", "text": "The cell network is down and the power is out. Natasha has a battery radio with a weather band. Which setting reaches the National Weather Service's New York City transmitter?", "options": ["162.550 MHz, NOAA Weather Radio station KWO35 from the Empire State Building", "911 MHz, the emergency services band", "Channel 1 on an FRS walkie-talkie", "Any FM station between 88 and 108 MHz, which all rebroadcast the NOAA alarm tone"], "correct": 0, "explain": "KWO35 broadcasts on 162.550 MHz from the top of the Empire State Building, programmed by the NWS office in Upton. All NOAA stations use one of seven frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz; an ordinary AM/FM radio cannot pick them up, which is why the kit needs a weather-band receiver.", "distractors": {"3": "Ordinary FM stations cannot receive or relay NOAA broadcasts; the weather band is separate.", "1": "There is no public 911 radio band; 911 is a phone number.", "2": "FRS radios talk to other handhelds a few blocks away; they do not receive broadcasts."}, "topic": "Getting around when the subway stops"}, {"id": "oa-q26", "text": "A blackout hits at 4 p.m. Natasha's calls to her roommate in another borough will not connect and the subway has stopped. Under the plan in this course, what should each of them do?", "options": ["Follow the agreed time rule: text the out-of-state contact, and if they cannot reach each other both walk to the far meeting place outside every evacuation zone by dark", "Each waits where they are for the other to call", "Keep redialling until a call goes through", "Both go to the near meeting place across the street from their building"], "correct": 0, "explain": "The plan has a near meeting place (fire, gas leak), a far one outside every zone, an out-of-city contact whom everyone texts, and a time rule: if the subway is shut and we cannot reach each other, we both go to the far place by dark. Long-distance texts often get through when local calls do not.", "distractors": {"2": "Redialling jams the network and drains the battery; texts and the pre-agreed plan replace it.", "3": "The near meeting place is for leaving the building in a fire or gas leak, not for a citywide outage when one of them is across town.", "1": "Waiting for a call that cannot connect is how families lose a whole night; the plan works without a phone."}, "topic": "Getting around when the subway stops"}, {"id": "oa-q27", "text": "At an office lunch a colleague suddenly goes red-faced and starts coughing loudly and forcefully after a bite of sandwich. Another coworker jumps up to give abdominal thrusts. What should Natasha say?", "options": ["Start abdominal thrusts now; a cough means the airway is closing", "Give five back blows immediately, before she loses consciousness", "Encourage her to keep coughing and do nothing else; only if she cannot breathe, cough or speak do you begin five back blows and five abdominal thrusts", "Give her a glass of water to wash it down"], "correct": 2, "explain": "A person who can cough or speak still has an open airway; the Red Cross says encourage coughing and do nothing else. The five back blows and five abdominal thrusts are for someone who cannot breathe, cough or speak, or whose lips are turning blue, repeated until the object comes out or the person goes limp.", "distractors": {"1": "Back blows are for a blocked airway; a forceful cough is the body clearing it.", "0": "A loud cough means air is moving; thrusts on someone who can cough can injure her.", "3": "Water can turn a partial blockage into a full one; nothing goes in the mouth."}, "topic": "The kit, check-call-care, CPR, choking and when it is 911"}, {"id": "oa-q28", "text": "At the gym a man collapses, unresponsive and not breathing. Natasha shouts for someone to call 911 and fetch the AED and starts compressions: about 60 a minute, an inch deep, stopping every ten pushes to feel for a pulse. What needs to change?", "options": ["Switch to rescue breaths only; compressions are for trained rescuers", "Push faster and harder with no pauses: 100 to 120 a minute, 2 to 2.4 inches, and stop only when he breathes or moves, the AED is ready to analyse, or medics take over", "Nothing; that is standard hands-only CPR", "Only the rate; depth and pauses are fine"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Adult CPR is 100 to 120 compressions a minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, letting the chest come all the way back up, with as little interruption as possible; if giving breaths the ratio is 30 to 2. Untrained bystanders do hands-only CPR. Pausing to check pulses starves the brain; swap rescuers when tired.", "distractors": {"2": "Sixty per minute is half the required rate and an inch is half the depth; the pauses are the worst part.", "3": "The depth is too shallow and every pause stops blood reaching the brain.", "0": "Hands-only CPR is what the American Heart Association recommends for untrained bystanders; breaths are optional, compressions are not."}, "topic": "The kit, check-call-care, CPR, choking and when it is 911"}, {"id": "oa-q29", "text": "Over coffee at a friend's apartment, the friend's face suddenly droops on one side and her words come out slurred. She says she is just tired and wants to lie down for an hour. What is the right action?", "options": ["Let her nap and check on her in an hour", "Drive her to an urgent-care clinic in the morning if she is no better", "Give her an aspirin and wait to see if it clears", "Call 911 now: face drooping and speech trouble are stroke signs, and time to treatment decides the outcome"], "correct": 3, "explain": "B.E. F.A.S.T.: sudden loss of Balance, Eye changes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech trouble, and T is Time to call 911. Stroke is on the list of things to call 911 for and not drive yourself, because the crew starts treatment on the way and the hospital is warned.", "distractors": {"0": "An hour of sleep is an hour of brain lost; stroke treatment is measured in minutes.", "2": "Some strokes are bleeds where aspirin makes things worse; do not medicate, call.", "1": "Stroke is a 911 emergency, not a clinic problem for tomorrow."}, "topic": "The kit, check-call-care, CPR, choking and when it is 911"}, {"id": "oa-q30", "text": "A cyclist on Natasha's street has a spurting wound just below the knee. A bystander has strapped a commercial tourniquet directly across the kneecap and says he will loosen it every ten minutes so the leg gets some blood. What should be corrected?", "options": ["Move it 2 to 3 inches above the wound but off the knee joint, higher on the thigh; tighten until the bleeding stops, write the time on it, and never loosen it", "Nothing; the placement and the loosening schedule are both textbook", "Move the tourniquet below the wound, toward the ankle", "Take it off and rely on direct pressure alone until the ambulance comes"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Stop the Bleed: a tourniquet goes 2 to 3 inches above the wound, never on a joint (knee or elbow), tightened until bleeding stops, with the time noted. It is not loosened or removed except by a hospital. If bleeding restarts, tighten further or add a second above the first.", "distractors": {"1": "A joint cannot compress the artery properly, and loosening 'to let blood through' restarts the bleed.", "2": "A tourniquet below the wound does nothing; it must be between the wound and the heart.", "3": "Pressure is tried first, but once a limb wound is spurting a correctly placed tourniquet is what saves the life."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}, {"id": "oa-q31", "text": "A coworker has scalded her forearm with kettle water at the office. Someone is pressing ice cubes on it and someone else is spreading butter over the red, blistering skin. What is the right care?", "options": ["Pop the blisters so the burn can drain, then bandage tightly", "Both are fine: ice numbs it and butter keeps air off it", "Remove both: cool under cool running water for about 10 minutes, then cover loosely with a clean dry dressing; ice damages skin and grease seals in heat", "Only the butter is wrong; keep the ice on until the pain stops"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Red Cross burn care: stop the burning, cool under cool (not cold) running water for about 10 minutes, cover loosely with a clean dry dressing or plastic wrap. No ice, butter, oil, toothpaste or any greasy thing, no tight wrapping, and do not break blisters. A burn on the hands, face or larger than about 3 inches is a 911 call.", "distractors": {"1": "Grease traps heat in the tissue and ice deepens the injury; both make the burn worse.", "3": "Ice is as harmful as butter on a burn; cool water is the tool.", "0": "Breaking blisters invites infection and a tight wrap cuts circulation; cover loosely."}, "topic": "Bleeding, wounds, burns, breaks and sprains"}, {"id": "oa-q32", "text": "After an hour outside in a snowstorm, Natasha's friend has white, waxy, numb toes. He is also shivering and answering questions oddly. Back inside, what is the right order and method?", "options": ["Treat the hypothermia first (911, dry clothes, warm the core), then warm the toes in warm, not hot, water; never rub them and never use a radiator or stove", "Walk him around the block to get the blood moving", "Put his feet on the radiator, the fastest heat in the apartment", "Rub the toes briskly with snow to restore circulation"], "correct": 0, "explain": "When frostbite and hypothermia are both present, hypothermia is treated first. Frostbitten skin goes into warm water comfortable to an unaffected hand; it is never rubbed, never rubbed with snow, and never placed on a heating pad, radiator or fire, because numb skin burns. Do not thaw it if it may refreeze before care.", "distractors": {"3": "Rubbing, and rubbing with snow, tears frozen tissue; it is on the CDC 'do not' list.", "2": "Numb skin cannot feel a radiator burning it; dry heat is forbidden.", "1": "Walking on frostbitten feet damages them further, and a confused, shivering person needs 911, not a walk."}, "topic": "Heat, cold, smoke and carbon monoxide"}, {"id": "oa-q33", "text": "In a July blackout a neighbour packed her insulin vials into a cooler pressed directly against frozen ice packs. The next morning one vial has ice crystals in it. She plans to let it thaw and inject as usual. What should Natasha tell her?", "options": ["Warm it gently in a pan of hot water and it will work", "It is fine once it thaws; freezing preserves it", "Never use insulin that has been frozen; keep the rest between 59 and 86 degrees F, out of direct contact with ice, where it stays usable for up to 28 days", "Take a double dose to make up for lost strength"], "correct": 2, "explain": "FDA emergency guidance: insulin can be kept unrefrigerated between 59 and 86 degrees F for up to 28 days, but it must never be frozen and frozen insulin must not be used. In a cooler, wrap the cold pack in a towel so it does not touch the vial. Above 86 degrees it loses strength gradually.", "distractors": {"1": "Freezing destroys insulin; a thawed vial is not safe to inject.", "0": "Heat also degrades insulin; the aim is cool, not hot, and a frozen vial is already ruined.", "3": "Doubling doses of an unknown-strength drug is how hypoglycaemia happens; use a good vial from the reserve."}, "topic": "Medications, chronic conditions and medical devices"}, {"id": "oa-q34", "text": "Three days after a neighbour cut his hand cleaning up flood debris, Natasha finds him breathing fast, confused, with a very fast pulse, and the wound red and oozing. He says he will go to urgent care when it opens tomorrow. What is the correct door?", "options": ["A virtual ExpressCare video visit for a prescription", "911 now: confusion, fast breathing and a racing pulse with an infection are how sepsis looks, and hours matter", "Urgent care tomorrow, as he plans", "More antibiotic ointment and a fresh dressing tonight"], "correct": 1, "explain": "A wound that is worse after day two with pus or red streaks needs a clinic or emergency department today; confusion, fast breathing or a very fast pulse with any infection is 911, because that is sepsis and the crew treats on the way. Waiting for the queue to shorten is how a treatable infection becomes fatal overnight.", "distractors": {"2": "Sepsis kills in hours; tomorrow's clinic is too late for these signs.", "3": "Ointment treats a surface; a systemic infection needs intravenous treatment now.", "0": "Virtual care is for the not-life-threatening layer; a confused, fast-breathing patient needs an ambulance."}, "topic": "Illness, infection and hygiene when the system is overloaded"}, {"id": "oa-q35", "text": "Natasha lives in a 20-storey building whose door notice says 'fireproof'. A pan of oil catches fire in her own kitchen and flames reach the cabinets. She remembers that fireproof means stay put. What should she do?", "options": ["Stay inside with the door shut, as the notice advises", "Open the windows so the smoke can escape, then leave", "Get everyone out, stay low, close every door behind her and call 911 from a safe place: 'stay in place' applies only when the fire is elsewhere in the building", "Fight it with the extinguisher until it is out, then call 911"], "correct": 2, "explain": "FDNY's four steps apply to any building when the fire is in your own apartment: get everyone out, stay low, use the safest exit, close all doors as you leave, then call 911. The fireproof rule ('usually safer to stay in your apartment') is for a fire elsewhere in the building. A fire that has spread beyond the pan is a leave-now job.", "distractors": {"0": "The fireproof advice is for fires in other apartments; your own burning kitchen means get out.", "3": "An extinguisher is for a small contained fire with the exit at your back; flames on the cabinets have grown past that.", "1": "Open windows feed the fire and let smoke into the hallway; close doors and leave."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "oa-q36", "text": "The alarm sounds at 2 a.m. in a non-fireproof walk-up. Natasha feels the apartment door with the back of her hand and it is hot. The fire escape is reached through the hallway. What does she do?", "options": ["Take the elevator, since the stairs are behind the hot door", "Open the door fast and run for the stairs while she can", "Keep the door shut, wet towels along the bottom, call 911 with her floor and apartment number, and signal from a window with a light or bright cloth", "Wait silently in the bathroom for the alarm to stop"], "correct": 2, "explain": "In any building, a hot door or a smoke-filled hallway means keep the door shut, call 911 and say exactly where you are, and get to a window and signal. Opening a hot door lets fire and smoke into the apartment. Elevators are never used in a fire.", "distractors": {"1": "A hot door means fire on the other side; opening it brings the fire in.", "0": "Elevators stop between floors or open onto the fire floor; never in a fire.", "3": "Hiding without calling means firefighters do not know she is there; 911 with the apartment number is the lifeline."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "oa-q37", "text": "While charging on the sofa, Natasha's off-brand power bank starts to hiss, smells sweet and chemical, and its casing bulges. What should she do?", "options": ["Keep it charging but move it onto the floor", "Stop using it and move away; if it smokes or catches fire, get out, close the door behind her and call 911, never trying to fight a battery fire herself", "Put it in the refrigerator to cool it down", "Carry it to the sink and run water over it"], "correct": 1, "explain": "FDNY lithium-ion guidance: if a battery hisses, smells strange, gets hot, swells or smokes, stop using it and move away from it; a burning battery erupts rather than smoulders and is not something to fight yourself. Buy UL-marked devices, use the maker's cord, never charge overnight or near an exit.", "distractors": {"2": "A failing battery keeps heating from inside; a fridge full of food is the wrong place for a fire.", "3": "Handling a swelling battery risks it erupting in her hands; distance is the protection.", "0": "Continuing to charge a swelling battery is what turns it into a fire."}, "topic": "Home fire"}, {"id": "oa-q38", "text": "Natasha comes home to a dark apartment and a faint rotten-egg smell. She reaches for her phone to use its flashlight and find the stove knob. What is the correct move?", "options": ["Open all the windows first so the gas can clear, then look for the source", "Ring the neighbour's doorbell on the way out to warn them", "Walk out in the dark without touching switches, the phone or any appliance, take others with her, and call 911 or the gas company only from outside", "Use the phone flashlight; it is not a light switch"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Con Edison's rule: leave immediately, even if the odour is faint; do not light a match, flip a switch, ring a doorbell or touch appliances or electronics, including your phone, until you are away from the gas; then call 911 or the gas company. Opening windows and finding the source is the crew's job, not yours.", "distractors": {"3": "The phone is an electronic device and can spark; it stays in the pocket until she is outside.", "0": "Staying to air the place out is a named deadly mistake; leave first.", "1": "A doorbell is a switch; knock with a hand if you must, and warn from outside."}, "topic": "Gas leaks, carbon monoxide and wildfire smoke"}, {"id": "oa-q39", "text": "On a wildfire-smoke day AirNow shows an AQI of 160. Natasha's coworker, who has asthma, plans a lunchtime run wearing a loose surgical mask. What does the course say?", "options": ["Above 100 is unhealthy: skip the run and stay in; a surgical mask does not filter smoke, only a fitted N95-type respirator helps, and asthma means ask a doctor first", "An AQI of 160 counts as 'good', so the run is fine", "The AQI only matters above 300", "Two surgical masks layered will filter the smoke"], "correct": 0, "explain": "AirNow: 50 or below is good, 100 or below satisfactory, above 100 unhealthy with concern rising as the number climbs, over 300 hazardous. Asthma puts him in a sensitive group. The action that helps most is staying in and making one clean room; a fitted N95, KN95 or P100 is the mask that filters smoke, and people with heart or lung disease should check with a doctor before wearing one for long.", "distractors": {"1": "'Good' is 50 or below; 160 is well into the unhealthy range.", "3": "Layering loose masks does not create a seal or a fine-particle filter.", "2": "Health concern begins above 100; 300 is the hazardous line, not the first warning."}, "topic": "Gas leaks, carbon monoxide and wildfire smoke"}, {"id": "oa-q40", "text": "At 3 a.m. Natasha's carbon-monoxide alarm makes a single chirp about once a minute. Her roommate wants everyone out on the street. What is the right reading?", "options": ["Unplug or remove the alarm so everyone can sleep", "Ignore it until morning; chirps are harmless", "Everyone out and 911; any sound from a CO alarm is treated as a real alarm", "A regular single chirp is a low battery: replace it now; a continuous alarm means everyone out into fresh air and 911 from outside"], "correct": 3, "explain": "A chirp every minute means the battery is dying: change it that day, and if the unit is over about 5 years old replace it. A continuous alarm is treated like a fire alarm: everyone out, call 911, do not go back until the fire department says so.
