Never pull the battery to silence it; a plug-in unit without battery backup is dead in a blackout.", "distractors": {"2": "Treating a low-battery chirp as poisoning is not dangerous but it misses the real fix: the battery.", "1": "Ignoring the chirp leaves the alarm dead on the night it is needed; replace the battery at once.", "0": "Removing the alarm removes the only warning of a gas you cannot smell."}, "topic": "Gas leaks, carbon monoxide and wildfire smoke"}, {"id": "oa-q41", "text": "Natasha's cousin on Long Island runs a portable generator inside the attached garage with the door rolled up, exhaust pointed at the opening, and says the CDC rule is satisfied because the fumes go outside. What is true?", "options": ["Never in a garage, even with the door open: outdoors more than 20 feet from any window, door or vent, exhaust pointed away, with a battery CO alarm inside", "Fine if a box fan blows the fumes out", "Fine for up to an hour at a time", "Fine, because the open door makes it outdoors"], "correct": 0, "explain": "CDC and CPSC: a generator never runs inside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, even with fans on or doors and windows open. About 100 Americans a year die of generator CO, and nearly half of hurricane poisonings involved generators within 7 feet of the home.", "distractors": {"3": "An open garage door does not stop CO pooling; the rule names garages specifically.", "2": "There is no safe duration; CO builds in minutes and lingers for hours.", "1": "Fans do not change the rule; the CDC says 'even with fans on'."}, "topic": "Light, batteries, phone power and generators"}, {"id": "oa-q42", "text": "When the block goes dark Natasha turns off the stove and the iron, unplugs the laptop and TV, and then switches off every lamp so nothing draws power when service returns. Which step should she change?", "options": ["Turn every lamp on so the room lights up when service returns", "Leave the laptop plugged in so it charges the instant power is back", "Leave one lamp or radio switched on so she knows the moment power returns; the heat appliances off and the electronics unplugged are correct", "None; everything off is the safest state"], "correct": 2, "explain": "The city's own blackout tips: switch off heat-producing appliances so they do not come back on unattended, unplug electronics because power can return with surges, and leave a single lamp or radio on as the signal that service is back. Then flashlight, not candle, and the tub filled while pressure lasts.", "distractors": {"3": "With everything off she has no way to know when the outage ends, especially at night.", "1": "A surge on restoration can damage the laptop; it stays unplugged until power is steady.", "0": "Many lamps left on add load and heat; one is the signal."}, "topic": "Light, batteries, phone power and generators"}, {"id": "oa-q43", "text": "The hallway emergency lights are glowing during a blackout, so Natasha leaves the headlamp behind and starts down 14 floors. Twenty minutes later the stairwell goes black. What did she get wrong before she started?", "options": ["Nothing; stairwell emergency lights last all night", "She should have waited in the apartment for the power to return", "She should have used the elevator, since some power was clearly on", "Carry the headlamp every time: many stairwell emergency lights run only briefly on battery, so also know both stairwells and count the floors as you go"], "correct": 3, "explain": "Stairwell emergency lights in many buildings last only a short time on battery; after that the stairs are pitch black. The rule is to carry the headlamp, know both stairwells, and count floors, because numbers are hard to read in the dark. Neighbours who cannot manage stairs need a plan made in advance.", "distractors": {"0": "Emergency lighting is battery-backed and short-lived; it is not designed to light a long outage.", "2": "Flickering or partial power is exactly when elevators trap people; stairs are the rule.", "1": "Staying put may be reasonable, but the error asked about is leaving without a light."}, "topic": "Elevators, refrigeration and medical devices in a blackout; reporting an outage"}, {"id": "oa-q44", "text": "Natasha's whole street is dark. Her roommate calls 911 to report the outage and says Con Edison will hear about it from the police. What is the right way to report it?", "options": ["911 is correct; outages are emergencies", "Report it to Con Edison: text OUT to 688243 if registered, call 1-800-75-CONED (1-800-752-6633), or use coned.com or the app; 911 is only for danger like a sparking wire", "Text 311 to reach Con Edison's outage line", "Nobody needs to report it; a whole street going dark is obvious to Con Edison"], "correct": 1, "explain": "Con Edison learns about many outages from customers and does not assume the neighbours reported it. Report every time by text (REG to 688243 in advance, then OUT), phone, website or app; check outagemap.coned.com for status. 311 answers questions; 911 is for life-threatening situations like a downed wire.", "distractors": {"0": "An outage with nobody in danger is not a 911 call; it ties up a line someone else needs.", "3": "Con Edison relies on customer reports; assuming someone else called is how blocks stay dark longer.", "2": "311 handles city services; the outage report goes to Con Edison's own channels."}, "topic": "Elevators, refrigeration and medical devices in a blackout; reporting an outage"}, {"id": "oa-q45", "text": "A friend proudly shows Natasha her new emergency shelf: thirty cans of food, a camping stove, one gallon of water, and a smoke alarm she pulled the battery from because it kept going off when she cooks. Using the rule of threes, what should be fixed first, and next?", "options": ["Water first, then the stove, then the alarm", "Buy more food first; three weeks is the goal", "Practise with the camping stove indoors so she can cook the cans", "Put the smoke-alarm battery back and add a battery CO alarm first (three minutes: air), then bring water up to three gallons (three days), and treat the food as last"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The rule of threes: about 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. That order sets the spending: a working smoke alarm and a battery CO detector are the first money, then a gallon per person per day, and food last. A camping stove indoors is a CO hazard, not a plan.", "distractors": {"1": "Food is the three-week problem; she already has more food than water or warning.", "0": "Air comes before water; a dead smoke alarm is the failure that kills in the first hour.", "2": "Camp stoves are outdoor-only; the stove is the least useful item on the shelf and dangerous indoors."}, "topic": "How this course works, the rule of threes, and the survival mindset"}, {"id": "oa-q46", "text": "On a bitter January evening Natasha passes a man asleep on a bench who looks homeless and unwell. Back inside, her elderly neighbour opens the door confused, with skin hot to the touch, and the radiator is blasting. Which numbers?", "options": ["311 to send an outreach team to the man outside; 911 for the confused, hot neighbour", "Neither; help the man yourself and let the neighbour sleep it off", "911 for both; anyone who looks unwell is an emergency", "311 for both; neither is a fire or a crime"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Someone outside in the cold who looks homeless and in need: call 311 and an outreach team is sent. Someone confused and hot to the touch: 911, because confusion is the sign of heat stroke and is never waited out. Sudden confusion in an older person is also a sign of serious infection.", "distractors": {"2": "The man on the bench needs outreach, which is a 311 service, unless he is unresponsive or in immediate danger.", "3": "A confused, overheated person is dying; that is 911, not a service request.", "1": "'Let her sleep it off' is the phrase that precedes a death in the next room."}, "topic": "Your household emergency plan"}, {"id": "oa-q47", "text": "Four days into a water outage Natasha's neighbour drops his single-bagged toilet waste down the building's trash chute and pours his urine bucket into the street storm drain each morning. What should he be doing instead?", "options": ["Only the drain is a problem; single bags in the chute are fine", "Double-bag and tie every bag, store it in a hard lidded container until the city announces disposal, and never tip anything into a street drain", "Only the chute is a problem; the drain is fine for liquids", "Exactly that; it keeps the apartment clean"], "correct": 1, "explain": "The apartment plan is bag, seal, store, hand over. Every bag is tied, double-bagged and tied again; a split single bag in a chute contaminates the whole trash room. Bagged human waste goes out only when the city announces it (311, Notify NYC). Tipping a bucket into a drain, park, sink or dead toilet sends it back into the lowest unit and feeds rats within hours.", "distractors": {"3": "Both habits spread disease through the building and the block.", "2": "Street drains lead to a sewer that may be blocked; the contents return to a basement apartment.", "0": "A single bag splits in a chute; double-bagging is the rule for anything that leaves the apartment."}, "topic": "Toilets without running water"}, {"id": "oa-q48", "text": "After a sewage backup Natasha disinfects the bathroom with a bleach solution she mixed three days ago at 1/3 cup per gallon, spraying it on the unwashed floor and wiping it dry at once. What is wrong?", "options": ["Only the wiping is wrong", "The dose is too weak; surfaces need a full cup per gallon", "Nothing; 1/3 cup per gallon is the correct surface dose", "Three things: mix the bleach fresh daily because it weakens after 24 hours, clean the floor with soap first, and keep the surface wet at least a minute before it dries"], "correct": 3, "explain": "CDC surface disinfection: 5 tablespoons (1/3 cup) of unscented 5-9% bleach per gallon of room-temperature water, or 4 teaspoons per quart; clean with soap first because bleach works poorly on dirt; keep the surface visibly wet at least 1 minute, then air dry; make a fresh batch every day because the solution weakens after 24 hours. Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner.", "distractors": {"2": "The dose is right, but a three-day-old batch, no pre-cleaning and instant wiping mean it did almost nothing.", "1": "One cup per gallon is the upper limit for mold on hard surfaces, not the everyday surface dose.", "0": "The wiping wastes the contact time, but the stale batch and the dirty floor are also mistakes."}, "topic": "Keeping disease out"}, {"id": "oa-q49", "text": "Walking home after dark, Natasha realises the same man has turned every corner she has for six blocks. Her building is two blocks ahead. What does the course say to do?", "options": ["Walk faster, get inside her building and lock the door", "Cut through the park to lose him", "Go into a staffed, lit place such as a bodega, pharmacy or hotel lobby, tell them someone is following her, and call 911 from there", "Turn around and ask him what he wants"], "correct": 2, "explain": "If someone follows you, do not go home: that shows him where you live. How often, and how, should she check on him?", "options": ["Every hour through the night", "Only if he calls her first, so as not to intrude", "Once a day, by phone, is enough", "Twice a day, late morning and early evening, in person: see him, ask whether he is drinking water and whether the room is cool, and walk him somewhere cooler if not"], "correct": 3, "explain": "NYC Health's advice is to contact heat-sensitive people at least twice a day in a heat wave. Confusion is an early symptom, so the sick person is the last to call for help; you go to them. Which parts are red flags?", "options": ["Both: FEMA does not license or endorse contractors, and payment should be by credit card or check with the final payment only when the work is done", "Only the FEMA card; paying by app is normal", "Only the payment app; the FEMA card is a good sign", "None; FEMA approval means he is vetted"], "correct": 0, "explain": "FEMA never charges for assistance and does not license, endorse or certify contractors; 'FEMA-approved contractor' is a lie. The FTC's tells: cash or full payment up front, insistence on wire, gift card, payment app or crypto, sign-today discounts, and final payment before the work is done. Verify licences with the issuing agency (311 can direct you) and report fraud to 1-866-720-5721.", "distractors": {"3": "There is no such thing as a FEMA-approved contractor; the card itself is the fraud.", "2": "The FEMA card is a lie, not a credential.", "1": "Full payment up front through an app is unrecoverable; it is a red flag on its own."}, "topic": "Scams, rumours and where the truth comes from"}, {"id": "oa-q52", "text": "A friend fills a 5-gallon bucket with soil dug from the tree pit outside Natasha's building and plants a full-size tomato in it for the fire escape landing. How many problems are there?", "options": ["Four: city soil carries lead, so use bagged potting mix; garden soil packs and drowns roots; a 5-gallon bucket is too small for a tomato; nothing goes on a fire escape", "One: the bucket needs drainage holes and nothing else", "None; free soil, a free bucket and the sunniest spot", "Two: the bucket is too small and the tomato should be a pepper"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Lead from old paint and leaded fuel is in much of the city's soil; never dig yard, tree-pit or park soil for a pot. Containers use light bagged potting mix because garden soil packs and drains badly. Tomatoes, peppers and eggplant need at least 8 to 10 gallons and 12 to 16 inches of depth. Fire escapes must stay clear at all times under the fire code.", "distractors": {"2": "The soil, the pot size and the fire escape are all wrong, and the plant will likely fail anyway.", "1": "Drainage matters, but the lead, the soil type, the pot size and the fire escape are the real problems.", "3": "Peppers need the same 8 to 10 gallons; the species is not the issue."}, "topic": "Container and window gardening"}, {"id": "oa-q53", "text": "On 5 October Natasha sows radishes outdoors on her balcony expecting a harvest, and sets aside seed from her F1 hybrid cherry tomatoes for next year's emergency garden. Which plans will disappoint her?", "options": ["Neither; both are good autumn habits", "Only the radishes; hybrid seed saves well", "Both: with frost around 20 October and radishes needing 25 to 35 days, the last sowing was mid-September; and F1 hybrid seed does not breed true", "Only the tomato seed; radishes sown in October are fine"], "correct": 2, "explain": "NYC's average first fall frost is about 20 October; count back the days-to-harvest from the packet, so radish sowing ends around mid-September and anything later grows on the windowsill. Seed saved from an F1 hybrid grows a random mix of its parents; buy open-pollinated beans, peas, lettuce and tomatoes for seed saving.", "distractors": {"0": "October radishes meet frost before they mature, and hybrid seed reverts.", "1": "Hybrid seed is the second problem; it will not grow the same tomato.", "3": "Radishes need 25 to 35 days and frost arrives around 20 October; the sowing is too late."}, "topic": "Seasons, seeds and pests in New York"}, {"id": "oa-q54", "text": "Before a hurricane Natasha's roommate tapes a big X across every window, says the glass now cannot shatter, and leaves the balcony chairs out. What does FEMA say?", "options": ["Tape does not stop a window breaking and makes bigger, heavier shards; bring in loose balcony items, close the blinds, move the bed from the glass, pick an interior room", "The tape stops the glass breaking; the chairs are the only issue", "Tape works if applied in a grid rather than an X", "Board the outside of the windows from the fire escape instead"], "correct": 0, "explain": "FEMA: permanent shutters are best, 5/8-inch plywood cut to fit is an option, and tape does not prevent breaking; if a taped window shatters, the tape holds the glass into larger, heavier pieces. In an apartment the realistic steps are loose objects in, blinds shut, bed away from glass, interior room ready.", "distractors": {"1": "The chairs are one problem, but the tape gives false confidence and heavier shards.", "2": "Grid or X, tape has no effect on whether the window breaks.", "3": "The fire escape must stay clear and is no place to work in wind; boarding is usually not possible from an apartment."}, "topic": "Shutting off utilities and stopping water, wind and rain"}, {"id": "oa-q55", "text": "After a break-in Natasha's door frame is split where the strike plate tore out. Her roommate screws the plate back in with the original short screws into the trim so it 'looks the same'. What is the right repair for tonight and tomorrow?", "options": ["Glue the plate in place with wood glue", "Nail the plate on instead; nails hold better in wood", "Tonight, wedge the door and brace a chair or a cut 2x4 under the knob; tomorrow drive the longest screws through the plate into the framing behind the trim, and report it", "The original screws are fine; the frame will hold"], "correct": 2, "explain": "Short screws into trim are what failed the first time; long screws must reach the framing behind the jamb. For the night, a rubber doorstop wedged from inside and a straight-backed chair or a length of 2x4 between the knob and the floor holds the door. Broken locks are reportable to HPD through 311; call 911 first if anyone may still be inside.", "distractors": {"3": "The trim already tore once; the same screws in the same wood fail again.", "1": "Screws resist pull-out far better than nails; a door being kicked is a pull-apart load.", "0": "Glue alone cannot hold a strike plate against a kick; it needs long screws into framing."}, "topic": "Shutting off utilities and stopping water, wind and rain"}, {"id": "oa-q56", "text": "With phones dead after a blackout, a friend says the walk from First Avenue to Tenth Avenue along 42nd Street is 'only ten blocks, half a mile'. How far is it really?", "options": ["About 1.4 miles: avenue blocks are far longer than street blocks, roughly 7 to a mile, while 20 street blocks make a mile", "About 10 miles", "About 2.5 miles", "About half a mile, as she says"], "correct": 0, "explain": "Twenty north-south street blocks make about one mile, but only about seven crosstown avenue blocks do. 'Ten blocks' uptown is about half a mile; ten blocks crosstown is about 1.4 miles. Use the Brooklyn Bridge yardstick of 1.1 miles in 20 to 30 minutes to turn distance into time.", "distractors": {"3": "Half a mile would be ten street blocks; avenue blocks are nearly three times longer.", "2": "Nine avenue blocks at roughly seven per mile is under a mile and a half.", "1": "Ten miles is about 200 street blocks, the length of Manhattan itself."}, "topic": "Finding your way in the city without a phone"}, {"id": "oa-q57", "text": "Natasha's ride-share driver pushes through a flooded underpass and the car stalls with water rising past the door sills. The driver says to sit tight and wait for a tow. What should she do?", "options": ["Stay in the car with the windows up; it is the safest shell", "Call a tow company and wait on the roof", "Rev the engine to push through", "Get out now and go to higher ground on foot: six inches of water reaches a car's underside, twelve inches floats a small car, and a stalled car's doors may not open"], "correct": 3, "explain": "The NWS: 6 inches of water reaches the bottom of most cars and can stall them, 12 inches floats many vehicles, 2 feet carries away most, and more than half of flood deaths are vehicle-related. If a car stalls in water you must get out into the water anyway, so do it now, while the door still opens, and go up.", "distractors": {"0": "The car becomes a sealed box that floats and then fills; waiting is how people drown.", "2": "A stalled engine in water is done; revving wastes the seconds the door still opens.", "1": "Rising water does not wait for a tow; the roof of a floating car is not higher ground."}, "topic": "Evacuating on foot"}, {"id": "oa-q58", "text": "After a building collapse Natasha's neighbour has a broken leg and cannot move. Natasha decides to go for help. What should she do before she leaves the spot?", "options": ["Leave the whistle with the neighbour, mark the spot with something bright, write the exact location on her hand or phone, and tell the first responder she meets", "Carry the neighbour on her back so they stay together", "Take the whistle with her so rescuers can hear her coming", "Shout continuously as she walks so nobody loses track of her"], "correct": 0, "explain": "If someone is hurt and you go for help, the injured person keeps the whistle (three blasts means help), the spot is marked with something bright, the exact location is written down, and the first responder you meet gets it. She remembers a Disaster Recovery Center address from a storm three years ago. How should she find one?", "options": ["Text DRC and her ZIP code to 43362, or use the locator at FEMA.gov/DRC, then confirm via 311 or the finder at the time because centers change with each emergency", "Text DRC to 692-692", "Go to the address from three years ago; centers reopen in the same schools", "Call 911 and ask for directions to the nearest center"], "correct": 0, "explain": "A Disaster Recovery Center is a temporary FEMA office opened near the affected neighbourhood after a declaration. Bring the one-page summary, the folder and every FEMA letter.", "distractors": {"1": "692-692 is Notify NYC's number, not FEMA's DRC locator.", "2": "DRCs are temporary and move with each disaster; an old address may be a locked door.", "3": "911 is for life-threatening emergencies; a FEMA office is found by text, web or 311."}, "topic": "Insurance, FEMA and your rights as a tenant"}, {"id": "oa-q61", "text": "Natasha's aunt in zone 1 needs help with oxygen administration and wound care but does not need a hospital.
